items.prompt:
(1) Which general property pair makes a metal useful for electrical wiring?
A. Transparency and volatility.
B. Brittleness and poor conduction.
C. Insolubility and sweetness.
D. Conductivity and ductility. [1]

(2) Which diagram description best represents an alloy model?
A. Identical isolated molecules.
B. One gas atom in an empty box.
C. Metallic array with different atom types.
D. Alternating fixed positive and negative ions of one compound. [1]

(3) How do most metals occur in ores?
A. As gases of isolated atoms.
B. Chemically combined in compounds.
C. As empty spaces.
D. As pure metal sheets. [1]

(4) Which pair can occur native?
A. Gold and platinum.
B. Sodium and potassium.
C. Aluminium and zinc.
D. Calcium and magnesium. [1]

(5) Which ore is associated with iron?
A. Galena.
B. Haematite.
C. Chalcopyrite.
D. Bauxite. [1]

(6) Which metal is obtained from galena?
A. Aluminium.
B. Tin.
C. Zinc.
D. Lead. [1]

(7) Why is an electric arc furnace suited to a supply of sorted steel scrap?
A. It needs no energy.
B. It extracts aluminium from bauxite.
C. It electrically melts scrap for controlled steel production.
D. It turns every scrap alloy into pure iron without adjustment. [1]

(8) Why is molten cryolite used with aluminium oxide in aluminium extraction?
A. It supplies a copper anode.
B. It dissolves oxide at lower temperature.
C. It makes an aqueous aluminium solution.
D. It removes the need for current. [1]

(9) Why does recycling metals conserve ores?
A. Recycling reduces demand for ore extraction.
B. It removes the need for all energy.
C. It creates new geological deposits immediately.
D. It makes every waste material a metal. [1]

(10) Why are additions to steel controlled?
A. Composition changes properties and must suit the use.
B. More carbon improves every property without limits.
C. All alloying elements have identical effects.
D. Steel has one fixed molecular formula. [1]

(11) Which pair names uses of zinc?
A. Electrical wiring and aircraft skins.
B. Tin-plating and bronze.
C. Glassmaking and paper bleaching.
D. Galvanising and brass. [1]

(12) Which is a syllabus use of uranium?
A. A Universal Indicator dye.
B. A kitchen salt substitute.
C. Fuel in nuclear power stations.
D. A wire-cleaning reagent. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) D. Conductivity and ductility. A wire must carry current and be drawn into shape.

(2) C. Metallic array with different atom types. An alloy mixes elements in a metallic material.

(3) B. Chemically combined in compounds. Most occur combined with other elements.

(4) A. Gold and platinum. Low reactivity allows native occurrence.

(5) B. Haematite. Haematite contains iron oxide.

(6) D. Lead. Galena is PbS.

(7) C. It electrically melts scrap for controlled steel production. Electrical heating melts the scrap feed.

(8) B. It dissolves oxide at lower temperature. The molten mixture permits electrolysis at lower temperature than pure alumina.

(9) A. Recycling reduces demand for ore extraction. Reusing material reduces fresh extraction.

(10) A. Composition changes properties and must suit the use. Useful properties depend on controlled composition.

(11) D. Galvanising and brass. Zinc coats steel and combines with copper in brass.

(12) C. Fuel in nuclear power stations. Uranium provides nuclear fuel.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: A wire must carry current and be drawn into shape. Distractor explanations: B: unsuitable mechanical/electrical properties. A: unrelated. C: taste is not a material-selection test.
Part 2: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: An alloy mixes elements in a metallic material. Distractor explanations: A: not the model. D: ionic compound rather than alloy. B: no solid structure.

Part 3: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Most occur combined with other elements. Distractor explanations: D: native metals are exceptions, not the general form. C: no material. A: not ordinary ores.
Part 4: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Low reactivity allows native occurrence. Distractor explanations: B, D and C: these reactive metals normally occur combined.
Part 5: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Haematite contains iron oxide. Distractor explanations: D: aluminium. A: lead. C: copper-bearing sulfide.
Part 6: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Galena is PbS. Distractor explanations: A, B and C: not the metal in PbS.

Part 7: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Electrical heating melts the scrap feed. Distractor explanations: D: composition still requires control. A: electricity is energy input. B: different metal and process.

Part 8: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The molten mixture permits electrolysis at lower temperature than pure alumina. Distractor explanations: D: current is required. A: not the anode function. C: the medium is molten, not aqueous.
Part 9: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Reusing material reduces fresh extraction. Distractor explanations: C: no rapid deposit creation. B: recycling still uses energy. D: no such conversion.

items.prompt:
(a) State which is more reactive, magnesium or copper. [1]

(b) Describe the two visible changes in this original supplied record: magnesium is placed in blue CuSO4 solution; a reddish-brown coating appears on the strip and the solution becomes paler. Relate them to the displacement products. [2]

(c) Explain why an intact paint coating prevents iron rusting under ordinary moist-air conditions. [2]

(d) Explain why a scratch through a zinc coating need not cause immediate rusting of the exposed iron when surrounding zinc remains electrically connected in a moist environment. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Magnesium.

(b) Copper metal forms the reddish-brown coating, while removal of Cu²⁺ makes the blue solution fade.

(c) Paint blocks water and oxygen from reaching iron, preventing the simultaneous contact needed for rusting.

(d) Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it oxidises preferentially and provides sacrificial protection to the exposed iron.

Part a: Magnesium (1).
Part b: Copper coating forms (1).
Part b: Blue solution fades as Cu²⁺ is removed (1).
Part c: Excludes water/oxygen (1).
Part c: Prevents required rusting conditions (1).
Part d: Zinc more reactive (1).
Part d: Preferential oxidation of zinc (1).
Part d: Sacrificial protection of exposed iron (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Plan a teacher-supervised comparison of magnesium and zinc reacting with excess dilute hydrochloric acid to investigate relative reactivity. Include controls, gas measurements and the comparison used for a conclusion. No flames are permitted near the hydrogen-generating apparatus. [6]

(b) Calculate the average magnesium gas-production rate over 0–30 s. Original synthetic gas data: time / s 0, 10, 20, 30; Mg gas / cm³ 0, 12, 22, 30; Zn gas / cm³ 0, 5, 9, 12. Exposed areas, acid concentration and volume, and starting temperature are matched; acid is in excess. [2]

(c) State the two measured quantities needed to compare gas-production rates in these trials. Original synthetic gas data: time / s 0, 10, 20, 30; Mg gas / cm³ 0, 12, 22, 30; Zn gas / cm³ 0, 5, 9, 12. Exposed areas, acid concentration and volume, and starting temperature are matched; acid is in excess. [2]

(d) Explain how oxide coatings could distort the rate comparison, and give a practical improvement to surface preparation. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Use the same dilute HCl concentration, volume and temperature in separate comparable flasks. Match exposed strip areas and clean surfaces consistently. Collect hydrogen through a leak-free delivery tube into a freely moving gas syringe, starting timing at mixing. Record gas volume at equal time intervals and repeat each metal. Compare early gradients or average volume change per equal interval; a larger rate supports greater reactivity under these controlled conditions. Keep acid in excess and hydrogen away from flames; do not test sodium or potassium with acid.

(b) Average rate=(30−0)/(30−0)=1.00 cm³/s.

(c) Elapsed time and gas volume.

(d) An oxide layer can limit acid contact and make the apparent reaction slower. Clean the metal surfaces consistently before testing so unequal coatings are less likely to control the comparison.
marking_guidance: Apparatus and method, recorded data, then conclusion and improvement are assessed by the points below.
Part a: Same acid concentration (1).
Part a: Same acid volume and temperature (1).
Part a: Matched exposed metal area (1).
Part a: Safe workable gas collection (1).
Part a: Gas volume measured against time (1).
Part a: Compare rates to support relative-reactivity conclusion (1). Accept equivalent controlled safe collection; maximum six marks.
Part b: Volume change divided by elapsed time (1).
Part b: 1.00 cm³/s (1); accept 0.98–1.02 from allowed readings.
Part c: Time (1).
Part c: Gas volume (1).
Part d: Coating limits contact and alters apparent rate (1).
Part d: Consistent surface cleaning (1).

items.prompt:
(1) Why must pressure be considered when comparing a water sample’s boiling point with 100 °C?
A. Pure water cannot boil
B. Impurities remove atmospheric pressure
C. Pressure changes the boiling temperature
D. Pressure changes hydrogen into oxygen [1]

(2) What is soap scum?
A. Insoluble calcium or magnesium soap
B. A foam of pure oxygen
C. Water vapour
D. A soluble sodium salt formed by boiling [1]

(3) Why can washing soda soften calcium sulfate water?
A. It evaporates all water
B. Carbonate ions precipitate calcium ions
C. It filters out individual water molecules
D. It changes calcium into sodium atoms [1]

(4) Why may fertiliser improve growth in nutrient-deficient soil?
A. It converts soil directly into sugar
B. It removes every microorganism
C. It supplies deficient mineral nutrients
D. It replaces sunlight with heat [1]

(5) Why does shortage of irrigation water threaten crop production?
A. Every crop produces more when water is absent
B. Plants obtain all their carbon from irrigation salts
C. Dry soil converts nitrogen into lead
D. Water is needed for plant processes and growth [1]

(6) Which pairing correctly explains carbon dioxide formation?
A. Boiling pure water — water becomes carbon
B. Acid + carbonate → salt + CO2 + water
C. Melting ice — CO2 is the liquid product
D. Filtering sand — carbon atoms appear [1]

(7) Why is oxygen used in steelmaking?
A. It coats steel with unreactive air
B. It prevents every chemical reaction
C. It oxidises impurities in molten material
D. It acts as a carbon fuel [1]

(8) Why is carbon monoxide especially dangerous in a confined space?
A. It is detected reliably by smell
B. It supplies extra oxygen to blood
C. It is a harmless visible dust
D. It accumulates and impairs oxygen transport [1]

(9) Which process can produce methane?
A. Oxygen-poor decomposition of vegetation
B. Ordinary freezing of pure water
C. Complete combustion of methane
D. Filtration of dry sand [1]

(10) Which conversion is promoted by a suitable vehicle catalytic converter?
A. CO2 to lead
B. Nitrogen to sulfur
C. Water to unburned petrol
D. CO to CO2 [1]

(11) What happens when limestone is strongly heated to form lime?
A. CaCO3 combines with CO2 to form CaO
B. CaCO3 decomposes to CaO and CO2
C. CaO changes to sodium chloride
D. The solid gains the mass of the escaping gas [1]

(12) Why is an iron catalyst used in the Haber process?
A. It speeds the approach to equilibrium
B. It increases the equilibrium fraction of ammonia at fixed temperature
C. It supplies nitrogen atoms consumed each cycle
D. It replaces the hydrogen feed [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) C. Pressure changes the boiling temperature Boiling occurs when vapour pressure matches the external pressure.

(2) A. Insoluble calcium or magnesium soap Hardness ions form insoluble soap compounds.

(3) B. Carbonate ions precipitate calcium ions Precipitation removes calcium from solution even though boiling is ineffective.

(4) C. It supplies deficient mineral nutrients Fertiliser can correct a limiting mineral-nutrient supply.

(5) D. Water is needed for plant processes and growth Water availability can limit growth and crop yield.

(6) B. Acid + carbonate → salt + CO2 + water Acid–carbonate reaction releases CO2 from carbonate.

(7) C. It oxidises impurities in molten material Controlled oxidation helps remove impurities.

(8) D. It accumulates and impairs oxygen transport CO can accumulate without obvious sensory warning and bind haemoglobin.

(9) A. Oxygen-poor decomposition of vegetation Anaerobic decomposition can generate methane.

(10) D. CO to CO2 Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide.

(11) B. CaCO3 decomposes to CaO and CO2 Thermal decomposition releases CO2 and leaves CaO.

(12) A. It speeds the approach to equilibrium A catalyst increases reaction rates without changing equilibrium position.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Boiling occurs when vapour pressure matches the external pressure. Distractor explanations: D changes elements incorrectly; A denies boiling; B confuses composition with pressure.

Part 2: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Hardness ions form insoluble soap compounds. Distractor explanations: C is gas; D misses insolubility and relevant ions; B confuses foam with the solid deposit.

Part 3: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Precipitation removes calcium from solution even though boiling is ineffective. Distractor explanations: A would concentrate salts; D is an impossible element conversion; C is not the treatment mechanism.

Part 4: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Fertiliser can correct a limiting mineral-nutrient supply. Distractor explanations: D confuses nutrition with light energy; B is neither required nor desirable; A invents direct soil-to-sugar conversion.

Part 5: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Water availability can limit growth and crop yield. Distractor explanations: B ignores atmospheric CO2; C invents element conversion; A reverses the dependence.

Part 6: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Acid–carbonate reaction releases CO2 from carbonate. Distractor explanations: A and D violate element conservation; C confuses a physical change with reaction.

Part 7: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Controlled oxidation helps remove impurities. Distractor explanations: A does not describe the process; D confuses oxidant and fuel; B contradicts its intended reactivity.

Part 8: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: CO can accumulate without obvious sensory warning and bind haemoglobin. Distractor explanations: C denies toxicity and gas state; B reverses its effect; A CO is odourless.
Part 9: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Anaerobic decomposition can generate methane. Distractor explanations: C consumes methane; B and D are physical processes that do not generate it.
Part 10: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide. Distractor explanations: A and B change elements; C is not an exhaust-cleanup reaction.
Part 11: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Thermal decomposition releases CO2 and leaves CaO. Distractor explanations: A reverses atom accounting; C changes elements; D reverses the mass change.

Part 12: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: A catalyst increases reaction rates without changing equilibrium position. Distractor explanations: B confuses rate with yield; C incorrectly consumes catalyst; D removes a required reactant.

items.prompt:
(a) Plan a comparison of hardness for two water samples using soap solution. Include quantities, controlled procedure, a persistent-lather endpoint and how to interpret the data. [6]

(b) Draw labelled apparatus for measuring a 50.0 cm³ water portion and then adding soap solution in measured increments to a comparison tube. [2]

(c) State the initial and final burette readings for sample B from the learner scale panels in ![Learner stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-11-04-learner.svg). [2]

(d) Explain the conclusion about hardness from these original results: equal 50.0 cm³ water portions require 2.0 cm³ soap for A and 6.0 cm³ for B, using the same soap and endpoint. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Measure equal 50.0 cm³ water portions into matching tubes. Add the same concentration of soap solution from a burette in measured increments, recording initial and final readings. Stopper and shake each for the same time and intensity after each addition, then observe whether lather remains for 30 s. Repeat trials and compare the soap volumes required. A larger volume indicates greater hardness because more soap reacts with dissolved calcium/magnesium before lasting lather forms. Keep water temperature, tube geometry and the lather criterion constant.

(b) A graduated 50 cm³ measuring cylinder supplies the water portion to a stoppered comparison tube. A burette containing soap solution is held vertically by a stand and clamp, with its tap and tip positioned for controlled addition into the tube. The stopper is removed during addition and fitted for shaking.

(c) Initial B reading 0.40 cm³; final B reading 6.40 cm³. The soap volume delivered is the difference, 6.00 cm³.

(d) B is harder because it needs more of the same soap solution for the same water volume and endpoint. Its calcium/magnesium ions remove more soap as insoluble scum before a lasting lather forms.

![Answer reference](visuals/VIS-6117-11-04-answer.svg)
marking_guidance: Apparatus and method, recorded data, then conclusion and improvement are assessed by the points below.
Part a: Equal measured water volumes (1).
Part a: Same soap concentration (1).
Part a: Measured soap increments with volume record (1).
Part a: Standardised shaking (1).
Part a: Consistent persistent-lather endpoint, e.g. 30 s (1).
Part a: Compare soap volumes to infer hardness (1). Accept repetitions and sensible controls as supporting detail, not extra marks.
Part b: Labelled graduated vessel suitable for the water volume (1).
Part b: Labelled burette or other suitably graduated addition device arranged to add into comparison tube (1). Accept a calibrated syringe with a controlled dispensing method.
Part c: Initial 0.40 cm³, tolerance ±0.05 (1).
Part c: Final 6.40 cm³, tolerance ±0.05 (1). No separate mark for subtraction in this part.
Part d: B harder from larger matched-condition soap requirement (1).
Part d: Ca2+/Mg2+ react with/remove soap before lather (1).

items.prompt:
(1) What is an acid in the aqueous proton-transfer model?
A. An electron pair of any kind.
B. A proton donor.
C. A proton acceptor.
D. A neutron donor. [1]

(2) Why is insoluble copper(II) oxide a base but not an alkali?
A. Its formula contains no copper.
B. It is a gas at room temperature.
C. It cannot react with acids.
D. It neutralises acid but is water-insoluble. [1]

(3) Which claim about limewater is chemically sound?
A. Limited solubility and weak dissociation are different properties.
B. Its pH is fixed at 7 for every preparation.
C. It is neutral because it is clear.
D. Its limited solubility proves the dissolved portion is a weak base. [1]

(4) What is the usual product pattern when an acid reacts with a metal hydroxide?
A. Salt and hydrogen.
B. Metal and oxygen.
C. Salt and water.
D. Carbon dioxide and hydrogen. [1]

(5) What distinguishes a weak acid from a strong acid in water?
A. Absence of any ions.
B. Partial rather than complete ionisation.
C. A fixed higher concentration.
D. A smaller container. [1]

(6) Why is magnesium oxide classified as basic?
A. It gives carbon dioxide with every liquid.
B. It must dissolve completely in water.
C. It consists of hydroxide ions.
D. It neutralises acids. [1]

(7) Why can a neutralisation mixture remain acidic?
A. All acids have pH 7 after mixing.
B. Water is a strong acid.
C. Some acid may remain in excess.
D. No reaction can have occurred. [1]

(8) A learner must prepare CuSO4 from warm dilute H2SO4. CuO is insoluble; NaOH is soluble. Which route is appropriate?
A. React excess CuO, filter, then crystallise.
B. Mix NaCl and water.
C. Add NaOH and label the product CuSO4.
D. Add copper metal and assume rapid hydrogen formation. [1]

(9) Which equation correctly represents magnesium oxide with hydrochloric acid?
A. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O
B. MgO + HCl → MgCl2 + H2
C. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + CO2
D. MgO + HCl → MgCl + OH [1]

(10) Why is a precipitated insoluble salt washed after filtration?
A. To increase the amount by adding water.
B. To convert it into an element.
C. To remove adhering soluble impurities.
D. To recover it from the filtrate. [1]

(11) Which lead(II) salt is soluble in water?
A. Lead(II) carbonate.
B. Lead(II) chloride in cold water.
C. Lead(II) sulfate.
D. Lead(II) nitrate. [1]

(12) Which chloride is an insoluble exception in ordinary cold-water tests?
A. Sodium chloride.
B. Silver chloride.
C. Ammonium chloride.
D. Potassium chloride. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) B. A proton donor. Acids donate protons.

(2) D. It neutralises acid but is water-insoluble. The alkali category requires water solubility.

(3) A. Limited solubility and weak dissociation are different properties. A low dissolved amount does not establish partial dissociation of that amount.

(4) C. Salt and water. This is the familiar neutralisation pattern.

(5) B. Partial rather than complete ionisation. Strength concerns extent of ionisation.

(6) D. It neutralises acids. Acid neutralisation establishes basic behaviour.

(7) C. Some acid may remain in excess. Neutralisation can consume only part of the initial acid.

(credit-group-1) Add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid with stirring; filter away the unreacted solid to obtain CuSO4 solution.

(credit-group-2) Excess oxide consumes the acid, and its insolubility allows the remaining oxide to be removed by filtration.

items.prompt:
(a) Describe the sequence for preparing copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide and warm dilute sulfuric acid, including removal of excess solid and crystallisation. [3]

(b) State the observation indicating excess CuO after adequate stirring and warming, and the observation when concentrated CuSO4 filtrate cools. The supplied synthetic record says black solid remains in the reaction mixture and blue crystals appear on cooling. [2]

(c) Explain why a small volume of cold water is used rather than a large volume of hot water to rinse soluble salt crystals. [1]

(d) Plan a teacher-supervised preparation of a clean, dry sample of insoluble silver chloride from suitable soluble starting salts. Include measured mixing, separation, washing, drying and a practical check that precipitation is complete. Collect silver-containing waste separately. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Add CuO in small portions to warm dilute sulfuric acid until excess solid remains after stirring. Filter it off, gently concentrate the blue filtrate without boiling dry, and cool it to form crystals.

(b) Black undissolved CuO remains; blue crystals form when the concentrated filtrate cools.

(c) A small cold rinse removes adhering solution while dissolving less of the soluble product than a large hot rinse.

(d) Use silver nitrate solution and sodium chloride solution in measured suitable amounts. Mix with stirring to precipitate AgCl; a slight excess of chloride can be used. After settling, test a separate small clear portion with an additional drop of chloride solution: no further cloudiness supports completion of silver precipitation. Filter the main mixture and keep the white AgCl residue. Wash with small portions of distilled water to remove dissolved salts, then dry between clean filter papers or by a suitable low-temperature method while protecting from strong light. The visual completion check does not prove full purity; careful washing and uncontaminated apparatus support it.

items.prompt:
(1) Which observation best distinguishes chemical change from a change of state?
A. The shape changes.
B. Bubbles appear.
C. A new substance forms.
D. The sample becomes warmer. [1]

(2) Which description explains an endothermic reaction?
A. It absorbs energy from surroundings.
B. It releases energy to surroundings.
C. It has no energy change.
D. It requires no starting energy. [1]

(3) What heat is gained by 50 g water warming by 4 °C, with c=4.2 J/(g °C) and q=mcΔT?
A. 840 J.
B. 52.5 J.
C. 0.84 J.
D. 210 J. [1]

(4) Why can a burning fuel warm a pan?
A. Breaking fuel bonds alone releases heat.
B. Energy disappears from the surroundings.
C. Combustion transfers energy to the pan.
D. The pan supplies all the fuel atoms. [1]

(5) Which comparison of wind generation with fuel combustion is sound?
A. No operating combustion; weather-dependent output.
B. Wind output is constant in every location.
C. Wind generation has no material or land requirements.
D. Wind turbines produce energy without an energy input. [1]

(6) What does a steeper gradient on a gas-volume against time curve mean?
A. A larger final product amount.
B. The gas is denser.
C. Time has stopped.
D. A higher gas-production rate. [1]

(7) Why can higher solution concentration increase rate at constant temperature?
A. Particles become larger.
B. Each particle must move faster.
C. Activation energy must become zero.
D. Successful collisions occur more frequently. [1]

(8) How does a suitable catalyst increase reaction rate?
A. By increasing ΔH.
B. By being consumed as the main reactant.
C. By offering a lower-activation-energy pathway.
D. By changing every product formula. [1]

(9) What are protein catalysts called?
A. Electrolytes.
B. Enzymes.
C. Indicators.
D. Isotopes. [1]

(10) Why can adding water restore blue colour to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate?
A. The copper atoms become a different element.
B. Water removes all copper ions.
C. The solid burns.
D. The hydrated salt reforms. [1]

(11) A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq) is at equilibrium. What response follows removal of some C at fixed temperature?
A. No response because equilibrium is permanent.
B. Shift towards C.
C. Both reactions stop.
D. Shift towards A and B. [1]

(12) Which is the electron-transfer definition of oxidation?
A. Proton gain.
B. Electron loss.
C. Electron gain.
D. Neutron loss. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) C. A new substance forms. New substance formation defines chemical change.

(2) A. It absorbs energy from surroundings. Energy enters the reacting system.

(3) A. 840 J. 50×4.2×4=840 J.

(4) C. Combustion transfers energy to the pan. Net reaction energy is transferred to the surroundings.

(5) A. No operating combustion; weather-dependent output. Moving air supplies energy without on-site fuel burning.

(6) D. A higher gas-production rate. Gradient is change in volume per unit time.

(7) D. Successful collisions occur more frequently. Concentration changes particle number per unit volume.

(8) C. By offering a lower-activation-energy pathway. More collisions can succeed along the lower-barrier pathway.

(9) B. Enzymes. Enzymes are biological protein catalysts.

(10) D. The hydrated salt reforms. Hydration reverses the intended dehydration change.

(11) B. Shift towards C. The response tends to replace removed product.

(12) B. Electron loss. Oxidation is electron loss.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: New substance formation defines chemical change. Distractor explanations: D: physical heating can warm a sample. B: boiling can produce bubbles. A: shape change can be physical.

Part 2: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Energy enters the reacting system. Distractor explanations: B: exothermic. C: contradicts endothermic transfer. D: activation energy is a separate issue.
Part 3: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: 50×4.2×4=840 J. Distractor explanations: B: divides by temperature change. D: omits temperature change. C: confuses kJ and J.

Part 4: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Net reaction energy is transferred to the surroundings. Distractor explanations: D: material transfer is not the explanation. A: bond breaking absorbs energy. B: energy is transferred, not destroyed.

Part 5: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Moving air supplies energy without on-site fuel burning. Distractor explanations: C: infrastructure has impacts. D: wind is the input. B: wind conditions vary.

Part 6: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Gradient is change in volume per unit time. Distractor explanations: A: endpoint need not differ. B: density is not shown. C: neither axis indicates stopped time.

Part 7: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Concentration changes particle number per unit volume. Distractor explanations: A: particle size is unchanged. C: concentration does not remove the barrier. B: average speed is set principally by temperature for the same species.

Part 8: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: More collisions can succeed along the lower-barrier pathway. Distractor explanations: A: ΔH is unchanged. B: catalyst is regenerated. D: the overall reaction is not defined by such a change.

Part 9: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Enzymes are biological protein catalysts. Distractor explanations: A: ionic conduction. D: atomic variants. C: substances used to show a condition such as pH.

Part 10: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Hydration reverses the intended dehydration change. Distractor explanations: A: no element change. B: ions are not all removed. C: this is not combustion.

Part 11: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The response tends to replace removed product. Distractor explanations: D: further removes B. C: dynamic reactions continue. A: changed composition disturbs the balance.
Part 12: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Oxidation is electron loss. Distractor explanations: C: reduction. A: not this definition. D: nuclear change, not chemical oxidation.

items.prompt:
(a) Plot chip CO2 volume against time on the blank grid visuals/VIS-6117-6-blank.svg or suitable graph paper, with labelled axes and a smooth curve. Original synthetic observations: time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120. Chip CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 18, 30, 38, 43, 46, 48. Powder CO2 volume / cm³: 0, 28, 41, 47, 48, 48, 48. (b) Calculate the average chip gas-production rate from 20 s to 60 s. The collected CO2 volume is 18 cm³ at 20 s and 38 cm³ at 60 s. [2]

(c) State a suitable apparatus for measuring the volume of gas produced by carbonate reacting with excess acid. [1]

(d) Plan a teacher-supervised investigation of how dilute hydrochloric acid concentration affects the initial rate of CO2 production from carbonate chips. Include the changed variable, controls, measurements and a comparison supporting a conclusion. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Plot (0,0), (20,18), (40,30), (60,38), (80,43), (100,46), (120,48), with time / s horizontal and CO2 volume / cm³ vertical. Draw a smooth rising curve with decreasing gradient, without overshooting 48 cm³. The answer panel is visuals/VIS-6117-6-chip-answer.svg.

(b) Average rate=(38−18)/(60−20)=20/40=0.50 cm³/s.

(c) A gas syringe with a freely moving plunger.

(d) Connect a carbonate reaction flask by a bung and unobstructed delivery tube to a freely moving gas syringe. Vary dilute hydrochloric acid concentration over several stated values, keeping acid volume fixed and acid in excess in every trial. Keep carbonate mass and particle-size range fixed and maintain the same starting temperature. Start the clock consistently on mixing and record gas volume at the same short time intervals. Repeat each concentration and compare mean initial gradients or mean gas volume per equal early interval, with units, to conclude how concentration affects rate. Check for leaks and timing delay; wear eye protection under teacher supervision.

Part a: Suitable axes and units (1).
Part a: All points within ±1 cm³ at correct times (1).
Part a: Smooth sensible curve with decreasing gradient, no overshoot (1).
Part b: Volume change divided by time change (1).
Part b: 0.50 cm³/s (1); accept 0.48–0.52 from allowed graphical readings and correct follow-through.
Part c: Gas syringe (1); accept a suitable graduated water-displacement arrangement.
Part d: Workable gas-collection method (1).
Part d: Vary acid concentration explicitly (1).
Part d: Control carbonate mass and size (1).
Part d: Control temperature (1).
Part d: Gas volumes at fixed timed intervals (1).
Part d: Compare initial rates to form conclusion (1). Accept an equivalent safe mass-loss method with timed measurements and appropriate controls; maximum six marks.

items.prompt:
(1) A syringe reading rises from 6 cm³ to 27 cm³. What volume has been collected?
A. 33 cm³
B. 27 cm³
C. 21 cm³
D. 4.5 cm³ [1]

(2) Which value equals 5 × 10⁻³ g?
A. 5000 g
B. −5000 g
C. 0.005 g
D. 0.05 g [1]

(3) A learner reads water in an upright cylinder while looking down from above. Which change best improves the reading?
A. View the lower meniscus at eye level
B. Read the top of the water curve
C. Look upward from below
D. Tilt the cylinder [1]

(4) An empty balance reads +0.20 g each time. Which statement is correct?
A. Correcting the offset removes systematic bias
B. The error is random because measurements are repeated
C. The balance measures time inaccurately
D. Repeating without adjustment removes the error [1]

(5) Which is a suitable heading for a table column containing gas volumes measured in cubic centimetres?
A. Gas / s
B. Gas volume / cm³
C. cm³ / time
D. Volume / cm [1]

(6) Which is the SI base unit of mass?
A. gram
B. newton
C. kilogram
D. mole [1]

(7) Using K = °C + 273.15, which value corresponds to 15.00 °C?
A. 4097.25 K
B. 258.15 K
C. 273.15 K
D. 288.15 K [1]

(8) With other conditions controlled, collecting 20 cm³ takes 50 s at 20 °C and 30 s at 30 °C. Which conclusion follows?
A. All reactions must become faster at any temperature
B. Both reaction rates are equal
C. The warmer trial makes more total gas
D. The warmer trial produces gas faster [1]

(9) Which apparatus delivers one accurate 25.0 cm³ portion of solution?
A. A large beaker
B. A volumetric pipette
C. A filter funnel
D. A thermometer [1]

(10) Why does a clear appearance not prove that a water sample is chemically pure?
A. Colourless solutes can remain dissolved
B. Filtration removes every dissolved solute
C. Dissolved substances are all visible solids
D. Pure water must be coloured [1]

(11) Why is a pencil baseline used for paper chromatography?
A. The baseline must dissolve before the sample separates
B. Ink could produce additional spots
C. Pencil identifies every component
D. Pencil makes the solvent rise faster [1]

(12) Salt dissolves in water but sand does not. After stirring both with water, which step separates the sand?
A. Evaporate the whole mixture
B. Distil the dry solids
C. Add more sand
D. Filter the mixture [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) C. 21 cm³ Subtract the initial reading: 27 − 6 = 21 cm³.

(2) C. 0.005 g A negative power of ten represents a fraction: 5/1000 = 0.005 g.

(3) A. View the lower meniscus at eye level Eye-level viewing of the lower meniscus reduces parallax for water.

(4) A. Correcting the offset removes systematic bias A repeated positive zero offset is systematic.

(5) B. Gas volume / cm³ The heading names the measured quantity and its volume unit.

(6) C. kilogram The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram.

(7) D. 288.15 K 15.00 + 273.15 = 288.15 K.

(8) D. The warmer trial produces gas faster The same volume in less time means a larger average rate over that interval.

(9) B. A volumetric pipette A volumetric pipette is designed to deliver its specified volume.

(10) A. Colourless solutes can remain dissolved Colourless dissolved material can remain visually undetected.

(11) B. Ink could produce additional spots An ink line may introduce additional soluble dyes.

(12) D. Filter the mixture Filtration retains insoluble sand while the salt solution passes through.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Subtract the initial reading: 27 − 6 = 21 cm³. Distractor explanations: B ignores the initial reading; A adds the readings; D divides rather than finding the change.

Part 2: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: A negative power of ten represents a fraction: 5/1000 = 0.005 g. Distractor explanations: A reverses the exponent sign; D uses 10⁻²; B confuses a negative index with a negative mass.

Part 3: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Eye-level viewing of the lower meniscus reduces parallax for water. Distractor explanations: C retains parallax; D changes the liquid surface geometry; B uses the wrong part of the concave meniscus.

Part 4: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: A repeated positive zero offset is systematic. Distractor explanations: D confuses repetition with calibration; B confuses repeat measurements with random error; C names the wrong quantity.

Part 5: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The heading names the measured quantity and its volume unit. Distractor explanations: A gives a time unit; C implies a rate without naming it; D is a length unit.

Part 6: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram. Distractor explanations: A is a common laboratory mass unit but not the SI base unit; D measures amount of substance; B measures force.
Part 7: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: 15.00 + 273.15 = 288.15 K. Distractor explanations: B subtracts the Celsius value; C ignores it; A multiplies instead of adding the offset.

Part 8: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: The same volume in less time means a larger average rate over that interval. Distractor explanations: B ignores the different times; C confuses rate with final amount; A extends the evidence beyond this experiment.

Part 9: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: A volumetric pipette is designed to deliver its specified volume. Distractor explanations: A has coarse markings; D measures temperature; C supports filtration rather than calibrated delivery.

Part 10: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Colourless dissolved material can remain visually undetected. Distractor explanations: D is false; C confuses a solution with visible suspended solid; B misunderstands filtration.

Part 11: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: An ink line may introduce additional soluble dyes. Distractor explanations: D invents a solvent-rate effect; C confuses marking with identification; A would lose the starting reference.

Part 12: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Filtration retains insoluble sand while the salt solution passes through. Distractor explanations: A would leave mixed solids; C does not separate them; B does not fit the present liquid mixture or the wanted sand fraction.

items.prompt:
(a) State the SI unit of volume. [1]

(b) A solid reference melts at 80 °C. Describe two features of a melting observation that would support a sample being relatively pure and consistent with this reference. [2]

(c) A mixture contains sand and a salt solution. Explain why filtration can separate the sand but cannot recover the dissolved salt as a solid. [2]

(d) Water is needed from a salt solution, and the salt is non-volatile. Explain how simple distillation recovers the water. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The cubic metre, m³.

(b) The sample melts over a narrow range, with its melting temperature close to 80 °C under the same conditions.

(c) Insoluble sand is retained by the filter paper, while the dissolved salt passes through with the water in the filtrate.

(d) Heating vaporises water; the vapour is cooled and condenses in the condenser; non-volatile salt remains in the original flask while the water distillate is collected.
marking_guidance: Award marks for each distinct chemical point or reason listed below; accept equivalent accurate wording.
Part a: Correct unit m³ (1 mark).
Part b: Narrow/sharp melting range (1 mark).
Part b: Temperature close to 80 °C (1 mark).
Part c: Insoluble sand retained (1 mark).
Part c: Dissolved salt passes with solvent into filtrate (1 mark).
Part d: Water vaporises (1 mark).
Part d: Vapour cools and condenses (1 mark).
Part d: Salt remains because it is non-volatile, giving separated water (1 mark).
items.provenance: Original Chemistry 6117 authoring; no official question or report wording reproduced.

items.prompt:
(a) State the cylinder volume and thermometer temperature shown in the unkeyed instrument figure.

![Instrument scales](visuals/VIS-6117-1-01.svg) [2]

(b) Draw a labelled filtration setup to separate sand from salt solution. Label the filter paper, residue and collected filtrate. [2]

(c) Plot cylinder reading against reference volume using these pairs (both in cm³): (0,0), (10,10.2), (20,20.4), (30,30.6), (40,40.8), (50,51.0). Label both axes and draw a suitable best-fit line.

![Blank graph grid](visuals/VIS-6117-1-03-blank.svg) [3]

(d) Calculate the mean of three volume readings: 24.8, 25.0 and 25.2 cm³. [2]

(e) A learner views the cylinder meniscus from above on every trial. Explain a possible reading error and how to improve the procedure. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Cylinder volume = 36 cm³; thermometer temperature = 24 °C.

(b) The funnel holds filter paper; sand is retained as residue on the paper; salt solution passes into a beaker as filtrate.

![Filtration and distillation reference](visuals/VIS-6117-1-02.svg)

(c) Reference volume is on the horizontal axis and cylinder reading on the vertical axis, both in cm³. Plot the six pairs and draw a straight best-fit line through the pattern.

![Completed calibration graph](visuals/VIS-6117-1-03.svg)

(d) Mean volume = (24.8 + 25.0 + 25.2)/3 = 25.0 cm³.

(e) Viewing from above creates parallax: the apparent meniscus position is displaced relative to the scale, biasing the reading. Read the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it.
marking_guidance: Apparatus/method, data and observations, then a supported conclusion or improvement are marked by the explicit points below.
Part a: 36 cm³, accepting ±0.5 cm³ for this drawing (1 mark).
Part a: 24 °C, accepting ±0.5 °C (1 mark).
Part b: Funnel containing correctly placed filter paper (1 mark).
Part b: Residue on paper and a vessel collecting the labelled filtrate (1 mark).
Part c: Correct axis quantities/units and sensible linear scales (1 mark).
Part c: All six plotted points within ±0.25 cm³ vertically and half a small horizontal division (1 mark).
Part c: Straight best-fit line matching the points, not a staircase or arbitrary curve (1 mark).
Part d: Correct sum divided by three (1 mark).
Part d: 25.0 cm³, with unit (1 mark).
Part e: Identify parallax (1 mark).
Part e: Explain that the apparent scale position differs from the true level, causing bias (1 mark).
Part e: Eye-level lower-meniscus reading as the improvement (1 mark).

(7) Which pair forms during complete combustion of ethanol?
A. Carbon monoxide and carbon
B. Ethene and hydrogen
C. Carbon dioxide and water
D. Ethanoic acid and hydrogen [1]

(8) Which account describes formation of ethyl ethanoate?
A. Alcohol + acid → ester + water
B. Ethanoic acid loses its entire carbon group
C. Ethanol becomes an ester by filtration
D. Ethene and bromine form an ester [1]

(9) Which monomer matches [–CH2–CHCl–]n?
A. CH3CH2Cl
B. CH2ClCH2Cl
C. CH2=CHCl
D. CHCl=CHCl [1]

(10) Why is an electrically insulating plastic useful as a wire covering?
A. It supplies extra electrons to the circuit
B. It restricts unwanted current paths from the metal
C. It replaces the conducting core with air
D. It turns the metal into a gas [1]

(11) Which change describes protein hydrolysis?
A. Sugars join into starch
B. Protein chains become longer without reacting
C. Amide links form while water leaves
D. Water breaks amide links, releasing amino acids [1]

(12) Why should hydrolysate and reference spots be developed in the same chromatography run?
A. Matching conditions permit meaningful comparison
B. All substances must travel equal distances
C. The paper dissolves each component into the same substance
D. The reference converts the sample into glucose [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) A. Butanoic acid The carboxyl carbon belongs to the four-carbon chain.

(2) B. They have different boiling ranges Different volatility allows condensation at different column heights.

(3) B. Kerosene Kerosene is the relevant aircraft fuel fraction.

(4) D. They share the hydroxyl functional group The common functional group governs similar chemistry.

(5) D. Less oxygen allows incomplete combustion Incomplete oxidation occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient.

(6) C. Cracking breaks larger molecules into smaller ones Cracking is a chemical conversion, whereas distillation is physical separation.

(7) C. Carbon dioxide and water Complete oxidation gives CO2 and H2O.

(8) A. Alcohol + acid → ester + water An alcohol and carboxylic acid form an ester plus water.

(9) C. CH2=CHCl Restoring C=C between backbone carbons retains one chlorine substituent.

(10) B. It restricts unwanted current paths from the metal The coating separates people and other conductors from the conducting metal.

(11) D. Water breaks amide links, releasing amino acids Hydrolysis breaks the links and gives smaller amino-acid products.

(12) A. Matching conditions permit meaningful comparison Same solvent and stationary conditions support a valid positional comparison.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: The carboxyl carbon belongs to the four-carbon chain. Distractor explanations: B omits the carboxyl carbon; C mistakes COOH for alcohol OH; D describes an ester.

Part 2: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Different volatility allows condensation at different column heights. Distractor explanations: D is nuclear change; A describes neither separation nor correct cracking; C invents a chemical reaction.

Part 3: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Kerosene is the relevant aircraft fuel fraction. Distractor explanations: A is heavy road/roof residue; C is a chemical feedstock; D is used for cooking/heating.

Part 4: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: The common functional group governs similar chemistry. Distractor explanations: B confuses general with molecular formula; C ignores physical trends; A ignores increasing chain length.

Part 5: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Incomplete oxidation occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient. Distractor explanations: C violates element conservation; B methane is already saturated; A nitrogen contains no carbon.

Part 6: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Cracking is a chemical conversion, whereas distillation is physical separation. Distractor explanations: B and A describe aspects of distillation; D confuses a chemical reaction with changing elements.

Part 7: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Complete oxidation gives CO2 and H2O. Distractor explanations: B is not combustion; D is not the complete-combustion products; A lists incomplete-combustion carbon products.

Part 8: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: An alcohol and carboxylic acid form an ester plus water. Distractor explanations: D gives a brominated addition product; B does not conserve the required ester skeleton; C physical filtration cannot cause esterification.

Part 9: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Restoring C=C between backbone carbons retains one chlorine substituent. Distractor explanations: A is saturated; D has two chlorines per unit; B is saturated and has two chlorines.

Part 10: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The coating separates people and other conductors from the conducting metal. Distractor explanations: A invents an electron source; D is irrelevant chemical change; C would break the intended conducting path.

Part 11: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Hydrolysis breaks the links and gives smaller amino-acid products. Distractor explanations: A is carbohydrate condensation; C reverses hydrolysis; B does not describe bond breaking.

Part 12: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Same solvent and stationary conditions support a valid positional comparison. Distractor explanations: B denies separation; D invents a reaction; C confuses separation with conversion.

items.prompt:
(a) Plan chromatography to compare the components of a teacher-prepared carbohydrate hydrolysate with glucose and reference sugar B. Include preparation, apparatus, development, observation and a defensible conclusion. No specific locating-agent identity is required. [6]

(b) State the distances travelled by the lower sample spot and the solvent front from the pencil baseline in the learner panel of ![Learner stimulus](visuals/VIS-6117-10-04-learner.svg). Read the ruler, whose marks are heights above the paper bottom. [2]

(c) Calculate Rf for the lower sample spot. For this part, the measured baseline-to-spot distance is 2.4 cm and baseline-to-front distance is 8.0 cm. [2]

(d) Explain why a wide, wet starting spot can make the chromatogram hard to interpret, and how the spotting procedure should be improved. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Filter a suitable diluted portion of the teacher-prepared hydrolysate if suspended solids remain. Draw a pencil baseline above a shallow solvent reservoir in a covered chamber. Apply small hydrolysate, glucose and B spots in separate lanes, drying between applications. Develop all lanes on the same paper in the same solvent, with the paper upright and solvent initially below the baseline. Remove the paper before the front reaches the top, mark the solvent front immediately, and visualise the spots by a suitable supervised method. Compare positions or Rf values with references: in the original DATA-10 example the two detected sample spots match glucose and B, supporting their possible presence rather than proving unique identities.

(b) Lower sample spot: 2.4 cm from baseline. Solvent front: 8.0 cm from baseline. Subtract the baseline height, 1.0 cm, from the ruler heights 3.4 and 9.0 cm.

(c) Rf = distance travelled by spot / distance travelled by solvent front = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30. It has no unit.

(d) A large wet spot spreads and can make neighbouring component spots overlap. Apply smaller spots with a capillary and dry each application before adding more, so starting spots remain compact.

![Answer reference](visuals/VIS-6117-10-04-answer.svg)
marking_guidance: Apparatus and method, recorded data, then conclusion and improvement are assessed by the points below.
Part a: Prepare an appropriate sample, including filtration if needed (1).
Part a: Pencil baseline above solvent with suitable chamber/paper arrangement (1).
Part a: Small dried sample and reference spots in separate lanes (1).
Part a: Develop together in covered chamber under the same solvent conditions (1).
Part a: Mark front promptly and visualise spots suitably (1).
Part a: Compare reference positions/Rf for a qualified conclusion (1). Accept equivalent sound sequencing; no named locating chemical required.
Part b: 2.4 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1).
Part b: 8.0 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1). Reject uncorrected heights from paper bottom.
Part c: Correct spot/front ratio (1).
Part c: 0.30 without units (1). Accept 0.28–0.32 from permitted visual readings, with correct follow-through.
Part d: Broad/wet spots spread or overlap, obscuring components (1).
Part d: Smaller applications dried between additions (1).

items.prompt:
(1) Which flame colour is associated with lithium in the syllabus test?
A. Lilac.
B. Green.
C. Red.
D. Bright yellow. [1]

(2) Why should the wire be checked in a blank flame before a lithium sample is added?
A. It makes every flame red.
B. It detects contamination on the wire.
C. It measures the salt mass.
D. It converts lithium to sodium. [1]

(3) Why can sodium contamination obscure another flame-test colour?
A. It makes the sample insoluble.
B. It removes all metal ions.
C. Bright sodium emission masks other colours.
D. It turns the wire into glass. [1]

(4) Which flame colour supports potassium identification?
A. Bright yellow.
B. Brick-red.
C. Green.
D. Lilac. [1]

(5) Which flame colour supports calcium identification?
A. Lilac.
B. Bright yellow.
C. Brick-red.
D. Deep blue solution. [1]

(6) Which flame colour supports barium identification?
A. Green.
B. Bright yellow.
C. Red.
D. Lilac. [1]

(7) Why is red litmus dampened for an ammonia gas test?
A. Water turns every paper blue.
B. Dissolved ammonia creates alkaline conditions.
C. The paper must dissolve completely.
D. Dry paper burns too quickly in ammonia. [1]

(8) What happens to damp red litmus in ammonia gas?
A. It relights.
B. It turns green.
C. It becomes a precipitate.
D. It turns blue. [1]

(9) Why does carbon dioxide make limewater milky?
A. Insoluble calcium carbonate precipitates.
B. All calcium ions become metal.
C. The water freezes.
D. Carbon dioxide gas changes into white smoke. [1]

(10) Which observation identifies chlorine in the specified damp-litmus test?
A. Red paper turns blue.
B. A squeaky pop occurs.
C. A glowing splint relights.
D. The damp paper is bleached. [1]

(11) Which test/result pair is correct for hydrogen?
A. Glowing splint relights.
B. Lighted splint: squeaky pop.
C. Damp red litmus turns blue.
D. Limewater becomes milky. [1]

(12) Which test/result pair is correct for oxygen?
A. Glowing splint relights.
B. Limewater becomes milky.
C. Lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
D. Damp litmus bleaches. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) C. Red. Lithium gives a red flame.

(2) B. It detects contamination on the wire. A blank distinguishes carry-over from sample evidence.

(3) C. Bright sodium emission masks other colours. A strong yellow observation can mask weaker colours.

(4) D. Lilac. Potassium gives lilac.

(5) C. Brick-red. Calcium gives brick-red.

(6) A. Green. Barium gives green.

(7) B. Dissolved ammonia creates alkaline conditions. The damp indicator responds to the aqueous alkaline condition.

(8) D. It turns blue. Ammonia gives an alkaline response.

(9) A. Insoluble calcium carbonate precipitates. A precipitate scatters light in the liquid.

(10) D. The damp paper is bleached. Chlorine removes the litmus colour.

(11) B. Lighted splint: squeaky pop. Hydrogen uses a lighted splint and pop.

(12) A. Glowing splint relights. Oxygen supports renewed burning of the glowing splint.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Lithium gives a red flame. Distractor explanations: A: potassium. B: barium. D: sodium.

Part 2: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: A blank distinguishes carry-over from sample evidence. Distractor explanations: D: elements are not converted. C: no mass measurement. A: colour still depends on sample and contamination.
Part 3: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: A strong yellow observation can mask weaker colours. Distractor explanations: B: no ion removal. A: not the explanation. D: impossible material claim.
Part 4: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Potassium gives lilac. Distractor explanations: B: calcium. C: barium. A: sodium.
Part 5: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Calcium gives brick-red. Distractor explanations: A: potassium. D: solution colour is not a flame observation. B: sodium.
Part 6: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Barium gives green. Distractor explanations: C: lithium in this comparison. D: potassium. B: sodium.

Part 7: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The damp indicator responds to the aqueous alkaline condition. Distractor explanations: A: neutral water does not establish that change. D: this is not an ignition test. C: paper dissolution is unnecessary.
Part 8: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Ammonia gives an alkaline response. Distractor explanations: B: not the litmus result. C: paper is not a precipitate. A: splint observation, not litmus.
Part 9: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: A precipitate scatters light in the liquid. Distractor explanations: D: the gas is colourless. C: not freezing. B: no metal deposition.
Part 10: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Chlorine removes the litmus colour. Distractor explanations: A: ammonia. C: oxygen. B: hydrogen.
Part 11: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Hydrogen uses a lighted splint and pop. Distractor explanations: A: oxygen. C: ammonia. D: carbon dioxide.
Part 12: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Oxygen supports renewed burning of the glowing splint. Distractor explanations: C: hydrogen. D: chlorine. B: carbon dioxide.

items.prompt:
(a) State the effect of ammonia on damp red litmus. [1]

(b) Describe how limewater is used to test for carbon dioxide and give the positive observation. [2]

(c) Explain why a glowing splint relights in oxygen. [2]

(d) Suggest a method and reason for checking a suspected potassium flame result that appears mainly yellow with a faint lilac component. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) It turns blue.

(b) Bubble a small gas sample through clear limewater; it becomes milky if carbon dioxide is present.

(c) Oxygen supports combustion, so the glowing splint starts burning with a flame again.

(d) Clean the wire, check its blank flame and repeat the test. This removes possible sodium carry-over so a persistent lilac potassium colour can be distinguished from yellow contamination.
marking_guidance: Award marks for the distinct chemical point and reason below; accept equivalent accurate reasoning.
Part a: Blue (1).
Part b: Gas through limewater (1).
Part b: Milky/cloudy observation (1).
Part c: Glowing splint relights (1).
Part c: Oxygen supports combustion (1).
Part d: Clean/check blank/repeat (1).
Part d: Distinguish sodium yellow contamination from lilac potassium (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Describe the NaOH procedure and the initial and excess-reagent observations for X. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate. [3]

(b) Deduce the cation in X from these observations. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate. [1]

(c) Describe the halide-test procedure on a fresh portion of X and its observation. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate. [3]

(d) Explain why separate portions and nitric-acid pretreatment are used, and identify the anion by comparing the white precipitate with the chloride, bromide and iodide alternatives. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate. [3]

(e) State two apparatus choices that help keep unknown-solution tests organised and control reagent addition. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Add aqueous NaOH dropwise to a small portion, then add excess. A light-blue precipitate forms initially and remains insoluble in excess.

(b) Copper(II), Cu²⁺.

(c) Acidify a fresh portion with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. A white precipitate forms.

(d) Separate portions prevent earlier reagents carrying over into a different test. Nitric-acid pretreatment removes carbonate interference without adding halide. White silver precipitate supports chloride rather than the cream bromide or yellow iodide alternatives.

(e) Clean labelled test tubes and separate droppers for controlled addition.
marking_guidance: Apparatus and method, recorded data, then conclusion and improvement are assessed by the points below.
Part a: NaOH gradually then excess (1).
Part a: Light-blue precipitate (1).
Part a: Remains insoluble in excess (1).
Part b: Cu²⁺/copper(II) (1).
Part c: Fresh portion with dilute nitric acid (1).
Part c: Aqueous silver nitrate added (1).
Part c: White precipitate (1).
Part d: Prevents reagent carry-over (1).
Part d: Acidification removes carbonate interference (1).
Part d: Cl⁻ identified by white versus cream/yellow alternatives (1).
Part e: Clean labelled test tubes (1).
Part e: Dropper(s) for controlled addition (1).

items.prompt:
(1) Which reference is used in defining relative atomic mass?
A. One hydrogen molecule.
B. One gram of carbon.
C. The number of neutrons only.
D. One twelfth of a carbon-12 atom’s mass. [1]

(2) What does relative formula mass represent?
A. Only the heaviest atom in a formula.
B. The number of molecules in a gram.
C. The summed relative atomic masses.
D. The total electron charge. [1]

(3) Which quantity is one mole of water molecules?
A. Exactly 1 g of any water sample.
B. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ hydrogen atoms only.
C. One H2O molecule.
D. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ H2O molecules. [1]

(4) If Mr(CO2)=44, what is the mass of one mole of CO2?
A. 44 g.
B. 6.022 × 10²³ g.
C. 44 mol.
D. 1 g. [1]

(5) Which description defines an empirical formula?
A. The complete three-dimensional shape.
B. The simplest whole-number atom ratio.
C. The number of electrons in a sample.
D. The exact number of atoms in every molecule. [1]

(6) What is empirical formula mass?
A. The relative mass sum for the simplest formula unit.
B. The mass of the whole laboratory sample.
C. The volume of one mole of gas.
D. The sum of all coefficients in an equation. [1]

(7) 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. What MgO mass forms from 2.4 g Mg with excess oxygen and complete conversion? Ar: Mg 24, O 16.
A. 2.4 g.
B. 1.6 g.
C. 40 g.
D. 4.0 g. [1]

(8) What amount of solute is present in 50.0 cm³ of a 0.200 mol/dm³ solution?
A. 0.0100 mol.
B. 0.00400 mol.
C. 10.0 mol.
D. 0.250 mol. [1]

(9) What volume does 0.100 mol gas occupy at room temperature and pressure using 24 dm³/mol?
A. 0.00417 dm³.
B. 24.0 dm³.
C. 2.40 dm³.
D. 240 dm³. [1]

(10) A compound has empirical formula CH2 and Mr=42. Ar: C 12, H 1. What is its molecular formula?
A. C2H4.
B. C3H6.
C. CH2.
D. C42H84. [1]

(11) What percentage of the mass of H2O is hydrogen? Ar: H 1, O 16.
A. 88.9%.
B. 11.1%.
C. 66.7%.
D. 5.56%. [1]

(12) What is the percentage yield when 6.0 g pure product is obtained against a theoretical 8.0 g?
A. 133%.
B. 25%.
C. 75%.
D. 48%. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) D. One twelfth of a carbon-12 atom’s mass. Ar compares average atomic mass with the carbon-12 reference.

(2) C. The summed relative atomic masses. Each atom contributes its Ar according to the formula.

(3) D. Approximately 6.022 × 10²³ H2O molecules. The mole counts the specified particles, here water molecules.

(4) A. 44 g. Molar mass is numerically 44 g/mol.

(5) B. The simplest whole-number atom ratio. An empirical formula states the simplest ratio.

(6) A. The relative mass sum for the simplest formula unit. It sums Ar values for the empirical formula.

(7) D. 4.0 g. 2.4/24=0.10 mol Mg gives 0.10 mol MgO; 0.10×40=4.0 g.

(8) A. 0.0100 mol. 0.200×(50.0/1000)=0.0100 mol.

(9) C. 2.40 dm³. V=0.100×24=2.40 dm³ at room conditions.

(10) B. C3H6. Empirical mass 14; 42/14=3, giving C3H6.

(11) B. 11.1%. 2/18≈11.1% approximately.

(12) C. 75%. 6.0/8.0=75%.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Ar compares average atomic mass with the carbon-12 reference. Distractor explanations: A: not the stated reference. B: confuses relative mass with sample mass. C: neutron count is not relative atomic mass.

Part 2: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Each atom contributes its Ar according to the formula. Distractor explanations: A: all atom contributions are included. D: charge is a different quantity. B: Mr is not a particle count.

Part 3: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: The mole counts the specified particles, here water molecules. Distractor explanations: A: water has molar mass about 18 g/mol. C: one molecule is far less than a mole. B: each water molecule contains two H atoms.

Part 4: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Molar mass is numerically 44 g/mol. Distractor explanations: D: one mole does not mean one gram. C: this is an amount unit. B: confuses particle count with mass.

Part 5: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: An empirical formula states the simplest ratio. Distractor explanations: A: shape is not given. C: electrons are not counted by it. D: that description concerns molecular formula.

Part 6: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: It sums Ar values for the empirical formula. Distractor explanations: B: sample size is irrelevant. D: coefficients are not formula mass. C: volume is a different quantity.

Part 7: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: 2.4/24=0.10 mol Mg gives 0.10 mol MgO; 0.10×40=4.0 g. Distractor explanations: A: ignores oxygen mass added. B: gives only the oxygen mass contribution. C: uses one mole rather than 0.10 mol.

Part 8: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: 0.200×(50.0/1000)=0.0100 mol. Distractor explanations: C: omits cm³-to-dm³ conversion. D: divides volume by concentration. B: divides concentration by the unconverted volume.

Part 9: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: V=0.100×24=2.40 dm³ at room conditions. Distractor explanations: A: divides instead of multiplying. B: assumes one mole. D: divides by 0.100 instead of multiplying.

Part 10: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Empirical mass 14; 42/14=3, giving C3H6. Distractor explanations: C: ignores the multiplier. A: uses multiplier two. D: uses Mr itself as the multiplier.
Part 11: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: 2/18≈11.1% approximately. Distractor explanations: D: counts only one H. C: uses atom-count percentage. A: is the oxygen percentage.
Part 12: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: 6.0/8.0=75%. Distractor explanations: B: reports the percentage shortfall. A: reverses the ratio. D: multiplies masses without forming a percentage.

items.prompt:
(a) State the meaning of amount concentration in mol/dm³. [1]

(b) Calculate the concentration of a solution containing 0.0100 mol solute in a total volume of 250 cm³. [3]

(c) Explain why adding water to a solution lowers its concentration if no solute is lost or reacts. [2]

(d) Explain why equal volumes of 0.100 mol/dm³ and 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH require different volumes of the same HCl solution for complete neutralisation. HCl and NaOH react 1:1. [3]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Moles of dissolved substance per dm³ of solution.

(b) V=250/1000=0.250 dm³. c=n/V=0.0100/0.250=0.0400 mol/dm³.

(c) The solute amount stays constant while total solution volume increases, so amount per unit volume decreases.

(d) At equal volume, the 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH contains twice as many moles. It requires twice the amount of HCl by the 1:1 ratio, and therefore twice the volume of a fixed-concentration HCl solution.
marking_guidance: Award marks for the distinct chemical point and reason below; accept equivalent accurate reasoning.
Part a: Moles of solute per dm³ of solution (1).
Part b: 0.250 dm³ (1).
Part b: c=n/V (1).
Part b: 0.0400 mol/dm³ (1).
Part c: Unchanged solute amount (1).
Part c: Larger volume lowers amount per volume (1).
Part d: Twice the NaOH amount at equal volume (1).
Part d: Twice the HCl amount from 1:1 ratio (1).
Part d: Twice the same-concentration HCl volume (1).

items.prompt:
(a) Name the apparatus used to deliver a measured, variable volume of HCl during a titration. [1]

(b) State the initial and final readings from the magnified burette panels in visuals/VIS-6117-4-readings.svg. The scale increases downwards and each small division is 0.1 cm³. [2]

(c) Calculate the titre and amount of HCl delivered from initial reading 0.40 cm³ and final reading 25.40 cm³. The HCl concentration is 0.100 mol/dm³. [3]

(d) Calculate the NaOH concentration if that HCl neutralises a 25.0 cm³ NaOH aliquot exactly. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. The HCl amount is 0.00250 mol; correct follow-through from part (c) is also allowed. [2]

(e) Explain why a rough titre should be followed by repeated careful titrations before choosing a mean. A rough trial used large additions near the endpoint. [2]

(f) State two conditions to keep constant across repeat titrations: one involving the NaOH sample and one involving endpoint detection. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Burette.

(b) Initial 0.40 cm³; final 25.40 cm³, reading the bottom of each meniscus.

(c) Titre=25.40−0.40=25.00 cm³=0.02500 dm³. n(HCl)=cV=0.100×0.02500=0.00250 mol.

(d) The 1:1 ratio gives n(NaOH)=0.00250 mol. c=0.00250/0.0250=0.100 mol/dm³.

(e) Large additions can overshoot the endpoint, making the rough titre too high. Repeat with small additions near the endpoint, then use a mean of suitably close concordant titres rather than including the rough overshoot.

(f) Keep the NaOH aliquot volume at 25.0 cm³ and use the same indicator and endpoint criterion.
marking_guidance: Apparatus and method, recorded data, then conclusion and improvement are assessed by the points below.
Part a: Burette (1).
Part b: Initial 0.40 cm³ (1).
Part b: Final 25.40 cm³ (1); accept each within ±0.05 cm³.
Part c: Final minus initial gives 25.00 cm³ (1).
Part c: Conversion to 0.02500 dm³ (1).
Part c: n=cV gives 0.00250 mol (1); follow through permitted readings.
Part d: 1:1 ratio gives 0.00250 mol NaOH (1).
Part d: Divide by 0.0250 dm³ to give 0.100 mol/dm³ (1); follow through part (c).
Part e: Rough large additions can overshoot/increase uncertainty (1).
Part e: Repeat carefully and average concordant titres, excluding the rough result (1).
Part f: Constant 25.0 cm³ aliquot (1).
Part f: Same indicator/endpoint criterion (1).

items.prompt:
(1) Why is a sawn timber plank still classed as a natural material?
A. Sawing changes cellulose into polythene.
B. Sawing reshapes the existing natural material.
C. Every manufactured object is synthetic.
D. Wood contains no chemical substances. [1]

(2) Which statement explains a useful property and a limitation of window glass?
A. It conducts current well but dissolves in rain.
B. It is opaque but can be drawn into wire.
C. It has no bonds and behaves as a flexible fibre.
D. It transmits light but can fracture under impact. [1]

(3) Why is concrete not the same material as cement?
A. All concrete is a single molecule.
B. Concrete contains only water.
C. Concrete includes cement binder and aggregate.
D. Cement is a metal. [1]

(4) Why can a nylon strand be described both as a fibre and as a synthetic polymer?
A. The descriptions are contradictory.
B. Nylon has no covalent bonds.
C. They describe different aspects of nylon.
D. A fibre must be natural. [1]

(5) Why can concrete contain both ionic and covalent bonding?
A. Its constituents are several substances with different structures.
B. Every bond alternates between ionic and covalent each second.
C. Water removes every covalent bond.
D. All concrete particles are metal ions. [1]

(6) Which statement correctly relates cellulose and its origin?
A. It has no molecular structure because it comes from plants.
B. It is a natural polymer with covalent bonds.
C. It is synthetic because it has bonds.
D. It is metallic because wood is solid. [1]

(7) Which building-material choice is linked to an appropriate property?
A. Glass for a transparent window.
B. Thatch because it is a metal.
C. Steel for a transparent pane.
D. Concrete for a flexible electrical cable. [1]

(8) Why does concrete harden after water is added to cement and aggregate?
A. Water is chemically irrelevant.
B. The stones become sodium chloride.
C. Hydration of cement binds the aggregate.
D. All the ingredients melt. [1]

(9) Which arrangement helps disperse a grease droplet in water?
A. Heads in grease and tails in water.
B. Every molecule becomes a metal ion.
C. Both regions permanently outside both liquids.
D. Tails in grease and hydrophilic heads facing water. [1]

(10) Which statement correctly describes soap preparation from oil?
A. Freezing the oil converts it into soap.
B. Any oil mixed with water instantly becomes soap.
C. No chemical change is involved.
D. Alkaline hydrolysis produces soap and glycerol. [1]

(11) Why can soap clean less efficiently in hard water?
A. Soap becomes a noble gas.
B. Insoluble scum consumes some of the soap.
C. Hard water contains no particles.
D. All detergents are insoluble in water. [1]

(12) Which approximate dimensional range is used for nanomaterials here?
A. 1–100 nm.
B. 1–100 mm.
C. 1–100 cm.
D. 1–100 m. [1]
items.canonical_answer:
(1) B. Sawing reshapes the existing natural material. Mechanical shaping does not change the natural origin of the wood.

(2) D. It transmits light but can fracture under impact. Transparency suits windows; brittleness limits impact resistance.

(3) C. Concrete includes cement binder and aggregate. Cement is one ingredient of the concrete mixture.

(4) C. They describe different aspects of nylon. Classification can use different criteria.

(5) A. Its constituents are several substances with different structures. Concrete is a mixture, so its constituents need not share one bonding type.

(6) B. It is a natural polymer with covalent bonds. Natural origin is compatible with a covalent polymer structure.

(7) A. Glass for a transparent window. Glass transmits light.

(8) C. Hydration of cement binds the aggregate. Hydration produces the hardened binder.

(9) D. Tails in grease and hydrophilic heads facing water. The different molecular regions interact with grease and water respectively.

(10) D. Alkaline hydrolysis produces soap and glycerol. Hydrolysis changes the fat or oil chemically.

(11) B. Insoluble scum consumes some of the soap. Calcium/magnesium ions form insoluble soap salts.

(12) A. 1–100 nm. The nanoscale range is approximately 1–100 nanometres in at least one dimension.
marking_guidance: Part 1: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Mechanical shaping does not change the natural origin of the wood. Distractor explanations: C: manufacture of an object is not necessarily chemical synthesis. D: wood contains chemical substances. A: sawing does not produce a different polymer.

Part 2: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Transparency suits windows; brittleness limits impact resistance. Distractor explanations: A: ordinary glass is insulating and does not simply dissolve in rain. B: these are not window-glass properties. C: glass is bonded and generally rigid.

Part 3: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Cement is one ingredient of the concrete mixture. Distractor explanations: B: it contains several solid constituents. D: cement is not metallic. A: concrete is not one molecule.

Part 4: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Classification can use different criteria. Distractor explanations: D: fibres can be synthetic. A: the criteria are compatible. B: nylon has covalent polymer structures.

Part 5: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Concrete is a mixture, so its constituents need not share one bonding type. Distractor explanations: B: that is not the meaning of mixed bonding types. D: the constituents are not all metallic. C: adding water does not eliminate covalent bonding.

Part 6: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Natural origin is compatible with a covalent polymer structure. Distractor explanations: C: bonding does not establish synthetic origin. D: solidity does not establish metallic bonding. A: plant materials contain molecules.
Part 7: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Glass transmits light. Distractor explanations: D: concrete is not a ductile wire conductor. C: steel is opaque. B: thatch is plant material.

Part 8: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Hydration produces the hardened binder. Distractor explanations: A: water participates in the process. B: the aggregate does not transform into salt. D: setting is not melting.

Part 9: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: The different molecular regions interact with grease and water respectively. Distractor explanations: A: reverses the interactions. C: gives no grease–water interface arrangement. B: emulsification does not create metal ions.

Part 10: Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Hydrolysis changes the fat or oil chemically. Distractor explanations: A: freezing is a physical change. B: water alone does not perform the stated preparation. C: the process is a chemical reaction.

Part 11: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Calcium/magnesium ions form insoluble soap salts. Distractor explanations: C: hard water contains dissolved ions. A: no such nuclear change occurs. D: the statement about detergents is false.

Part 12: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: The nanoscale range is approximately 1–100 nanometres in at least one dimension. Distractor explanations: B: millimetres are much larger. C: centimetres are much larger. D: metres are bulk dimensions.
