blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-51 — Carbon dioxide in exhaled air
blocks.text:
Aim: compare exhaled air with room air using a carbon dioxide test. A teacher-controlled arrangement uses fresh limewater and a suitable one-way gas delivery or collection system that prevents liquid being drawn into the mouth. Do not share mouthpieces or suck through a tube into limewater. An alternative is teacher-collected gas samples delivered from clean gas syringes.

Pass comparable gas volumes through equal fresh limewater portions. Exhaled air commonly makes limewater milky sooner because it contains more carbon dioxide than room air. The milkiness is a calcium carbonate precipitate. Room air also contains some CO2, so the comparison is not 'CO2 present versus absent'. Keep gas volume, flow rate and limewater concentration comparable.

A limitation is that time to visible cloudiness is an approximate endpoint. Large excess CO2 can eventually dissolve the precipitate, so compare the initial appearance rather than treating a long exposure as a simple stronger result. Connect the exhaled gas to aerobic respiration, not to the claim that oxygen changes into carbon atoms.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-52 — Carbon dioxide from fermentation
blocks.text:
Aim: identify the gas released by a fermenting sugar mixture. Use teacher-prepared glucose or fruit-juice mixture with yeast in a suitable warm environment, a gas outlet and fresh limewater. The vessel must have a safe gas escape route rather than becoming a sealed pressure vessel. A control without active yeast helps distinguish biological gas production from effects of the apparatus or warming.

Collect or pass the evolved gas through limewater; initial milkiness supports CO2 formation. The mixture may show bubbles, but bubbles alone do not identify the gas. Fermentation also forms ethanol, as taught in Topic 10. Keep sugar concentration, mixture volume and temperature comparable across trials. Excessive heat can denature enzymes, while low temperature slows the process.

Record observations over a stated time and avoid interpreting unequal temperatures as evidence for different yeast activity. Do not taste the fermented laboratory mixture. The original equation C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 conserves atoms and links the gas test to a specific chemical process.

topics/11/content-units/CU-6117-11.3.jso.title: 11.3 — describe the commercial preparation of oxygen, nitrogen (from liquid air by fractional distillation) and carbon dioxide

blocks.heading: Oxygen from liquid air
blocks.text:
Commercial oxygen can be separated from air by fractional distillation of liquid air. Water vapour and carbon dioxide are removed before deep cooling so they do not freeze and block equipment. Air is compressed, cooled and expanded through an appropriate refrigeration process until it liquefies. Fractional distillation then separates components using their different boiling temperatures.

Oxygen boils at about −183 °C at atmospheric pressure, while nitrogen boils at about −196 °C. Nitrogen is the more volatile of the two and is removed more readily; oxygen is collected as the higher-boiling component. These figures describe boiling temperatures and are not a request for gas-law calculations. The separation does not create oxygen atoms or split nitrogen into oxygen. It separates gases already present in air. Purification and process control determine the product grade; a classroom flow diagram shows the essential chemistry rather than every piece of industrial equipment. Avoid claiming that filtering ordinary air alone separates its oxygen molecules from nitrogen molecules.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxygen from liquid air
blocks.text:
Describe why an air-liquefaction plant must remove water before cooling, and why ordinary filtration of warm air cannot separate oxygen from nitrogen.

Water would freeze and block cold equipment; dissolved/mixed gases are not separated by an ordinary particle filter, so liquefaction and boiling-point separation are needed.

Checking the response: Remove water to prevent ice blockage (1). Particle filtration cannot replace separation by differing boiling points (1).

blocks.heading: Nitrogen from liquid air
blocks.text:
Nitrogen is the most abundant component of dry air and can be obtained commercially by separating liquid air. Pretreatment removes water vapour and carbon dioxide, then compression and cooling prepare liquid air for fractionation. Nitrogen's lower boiling temperature makes it more volatile than oxygen. On controlled warming, a nitrogen-rich fraction is obtained before the higher-boiling oxygen fraction.

The approximate boiling temperatures, −196 °C for nitrogen and −183 °C for oxygen at atmospheric pressure, must be compared correctly: −196 is the lower temperature. A common mistake is to compare only the magnitudes 196 and 183 and reverse the order. The process is physical separation, so nitrogen remains N2. It does not become single nitrogen atoms during ordinary fractional distillation. Nitrogen's abundance makes air a useful source for the Haber process, but a useful industrial feed requires separation and purity control rather than simply feeding untreated air with all its oxygen into every reaction system.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nitrogen from liquid air
blocks.text:

Nitrogen has the lower boiling point and preferentially vaporises first.

Checking the response: Nitrogen is more volatile because −196 °C is below oxygen’s −183 °C boiling point (1). Nitrogen preferentially vaporises before oxygen during warming/distillation of the liquid mixture (1).

blocks.heading: Commercial carbon dioxide
blocks.text:
Carbon dioxide can be recovered from industrial processes that produce it, including fermentation and suitable combustion or chemical-manufacturing streams. The gas must be separated from unwanted material and purified for its intended use. It can then be dried and compressed or cooled for storage and supply. Recovering a by-product is different from assuming raw exhaust gas is already suitable for food or laboratory use.

A laboratory acid–carbonate reaction illustrates carbon dioxide formation, but it is not necessarily the economical source for a large commercial supply. A process answer should distinguish production from purification and storage. Fermentation produces a gas stream containing carbon dioxide, while impurities, moisture and process conditions determine subsequent treatment. A source does not guarantee a particular purity grade. Carbon dioxide is not obtained as a major fraction of ordinary liquid-air separation in the same way as nitrogen and oxygen; it is removed before deep cooling because of freezing concerns. This links the separate preparation routes without suggesting all three gases are collected by the same column.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Commercial carbon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe why CO2 recovered from an industrial exhaust cannot be sent directly to a drinks plant merely because it turns limewater milky.

The test supports CO2 identity but does not prove purity; contaminants must be removed and the recovered gas checked against the intended use.

Checking the response: Positive identity test does not establish purity (1). Purification and suitability checks are required (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Commercial carbon dioxide
blocks.text:
Suggest why carbon dioxide recovered from an industrial exhaust cannot be assumed suitable for drinks without treatment.

The stream may contain harmful impurities that must be removed and checked.

Checking the response: The stream may contain harmful impurities that must be removed and checked (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Uses of oxygen
blocks.text:
Oxygen is used in medical oxygen supplies, in steelmaking and in high-temperature cutting or welding systems where appropriate. Its role is linked to supporting oxidation and combustion. In steelmaking, oxygen helps oxidise unwanted elements in the molten material. In a suitable fuel–oxygen torch, the fuel provides the combustible substance and oxygen supports a high-temperature reaction.

Medical use depends on controlled equipment and professional management; the chemistry point is oxygen's role in respiration, not instructions for treatment. Oxygen does not itself replace the fuel in a welding flame. A use–property answer should connect the use to the required oxidation or physiological role. Increased oxygen availability can intensify burning, so oxygen-handling systems require appropriate materials and precautions. Do not describe it as inert because it is colourless. Colour and reactivity are separate properties. The same molecular gas can serve different purposes because the surrounding reactants and conditions determine what happens.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of oxygen
blocks.text:
Describe two uses of oxygen.

It is supplied for medical respiratory support and used to oxidise impurities during steelmaking.

Checking the response: Medical respiratory support (1). Oxidising impurities in steelmaking (1). Accept other distinct valid uses, such as supporting oxy-fuel combustion; maximum two marks, no repeated use.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of oxygen
blocks.text:
Describe oxygen’s role in a fuel–oxygen cutting flame.

It supports rapid combustion of the fuel, producing the high temperature needed for the process.

Checking the response: Oxygen supports rapid combustion of the fuel (1). The combustion releases enough heat to raise the metal to the high temperature needed for the cutting process (1).
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Uses of carbon dioxide
blocks.text:
Carbon dioxide is used to carbonate drinks and in suitable fire extinguishers; solid carbon dioxide, dry ice, can provide cooling. In an extinguisher it can displace oxygen around certain fires. That does not make it suitable for every burning material or every enclosed space. A school answer should state a recognised use and its relevant property without giving emergency operating instructions.

Carbonation involves carbon dioxide dissolved under pressure. On opening a container, some gas leaves solution and forms bubbles. Dry ice changes directly from solid to gas under ordinary atmospheric conditions, providing cooling without a liquid-water residue. Cold and asphyxiation hazards mean it is handled with suitable controls. Carbon dioxide is denser than air under comparable conditions, but density alone does not guarantee that a gas forms a perfectly unmixed permanent layer. In a chemistry explanation, link the chosen use to dissolution, cooling or limited support of combustion as appropriate. It is a greenhouse gas, so usefulness does not remove the need to consider emissions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of carbon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe two uses of carbon dioxide.

Carbonating drinks and extinguishing suitable fires.

Checking the response: Carbonating drinks (1). Extinguishing suitable fires by displacing oxygen around the flame (1). Accept other distinct valid uses, such as dry-ice cooling; maximum two marks.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of carbon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe how carbon dioxide helps extinguish an appropriate ordinary fire.

It displaces oxygen around the burning material and does not support that combustion, reducing the oxygen supply.

Checking the response: Oxygen displaced/reduced (1). Combustion no longer sustained under suitable conditions (1).

blocks.heading: Uses of nitrogen
blocks.text:
Nitrogen is used as a feedstock for ammonia manufacture and as a relatively unreactive atmosphere in suitable food packaging or industrial operations. Liquid nitrogen is also used for cooling. Its low reactivity under ordinary conditions is useful where oxygen-driven changes are unwanted. This does not mean nitrogen cannot react: the Haber process uses conditions and a catalyst that allow reaction with hydrogen.

A packaging explanation should say that replacing much of the oxygen can slow oxidation, not that nitrogen automatically sterilises food. The package, hygiene and storage conditions still matter. In ammonia manufacture, nitrogen supplies the nitrogen atoms that later enter fertilisers and other compounds. Liquid nitrogen's very low boiling temperature makes it useful for cooling but also requires specialised handling; it is not an ordinary classroom liquid to touch. Distinguish a use based on the molecular gas's low reactivity from a use in which nitrogen becomes chemically combined. The same substance can be unreactive in one set of conditions and a reactant in another.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of nitrogen
blocks.text:
Describe two uses of nitrogen.

As a reactant in ammonia manufacture and as a relatively unreactive atmosphere in food packaging.

Checking the response: Ammonia feedstock (1). Packaging/inert-atmosphere use or liquid-nitrogen cooling (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of nitrogen
blocks.text:
Describe why nitrogen can help protect a packaged food from oxidation.

It replaces much of the oxygen and is relatively unreactive under storage conditions, slowing oxidation.

Checking the response: Reduced oxygen availability (1). Low-reactivity atmosphere slows oxidation (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-11-P01 (7)
blocks.text:
Why is oxygen used in steelmaking?
A. It coats steel with unreactive air
B. It prevents every chemical reaction
C. It oxidises impurities in molten material
D. It acts as a carbon fuel

C. It oxidises impurities in molten material Controlled oxidation helps remove impurities.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Controlled oxidation helps remove impurities. Distractor explanations: A does not describe the process; D confuses oxidant and fuel; B contradicts its intended reactivity.

blocks.text: Connect environmental observations to reactions, separation methods and controlled comparisons. Distinguish concentration from total emissions, treatment from purity, and a local measurement from a national claim.

topics/7/content-units/CU-6117-7.3.json.title: 7.3 — describe the reaction of a base/alkali with an acid as neutralisation

blocks.heading: Neutralisation
blocks.text:
Neutralisation is the reaction of an acid with a base. In the common acid–metal oxide or acid–hydroxide examples, a salt and water form. The acid's hydrogen ions are consumed through reaction with the base. Neutralisation is a chemical reaction; it is not simply diluting an acid by adding water.

Distinguish the reaction from the final pH. Adding a small base amount to excess acid gives neutralisation while leaving an acidic solution. For the familiar strong-acid/strong-alkali pair, a correctly matched endpoint can give a neutral salt solution, but matching volumes alone does not establish matching reacting amounts. Concentration and the balanced ratio also matter. Record a temperature change or indicator transition as an observation, then explain it using the acid–base process rather than assuming that every neutralisation mixture must have the same colour or final temperature.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Neutralisation
blocks.text:
Describe why adding a small amount of metal hydroxide can neutralise some acid without making the whole solution neutral.

Some H⁺ is consumed by the base, but excess unreacted acid can remain.

Checking the response: Acid–base reaction consumes a portion of acid (1). Remaining excess acid explains non-neutral final solution (1).
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Neutralisation
blocks.text:
Describe why adding base to acid can be neutralisation even if the final solution remains acidic.

Some acid reacts and is consumed, but acid left in excess still makes the mixture acidic.

Checking the response: Acid consumption occurs (1). Excess acid explains final pH (1).

blocks.heading: The neutralisation ionic equation
blocks.text:
For an aqueous acid reacting with an alkali, the key ionic equation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H2O(l). One hydrogen ion combines with one hydroxide ion to form one water molecule. Atoms and charge balance: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom occur on each side, and the positive and negative charges sum to zero.

Spectator ions are omitted because they do not change in this ionic step. In hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ remain in solution before and after neutralisation. They form the dissolved salt's ions rather than disappearing. An ionic equation therefore gives a focused account of the chemical change, not a claim that the whole beaker contains water alone afterwards. Keep the 1:1 H⁺:OH⁻ ratio separate from molecular acid-to-base ratios, which can differ when a formula supplies more than one reacting ion.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The neutralisation ionic equation
blocks.text:
Describe why equal amounts in moles of H⁺ and OH⁻ combine in aqueous neutralisation.

One proton combines with one hydroxide ion to form one water molecule; this balances both atoms and charge.

Checking the response: One of each ion gives the water composition (1). Opposite single charges cancel in the 1:1 combination (1).
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The neutralisation ionic equation
blocks.text:
Describe why Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are absent from the net ionic equation for HCl reacting with NaOH in water.

They remain unchanged in solution as spectator ions; the net chemical change is H⁺ combining with OH⁻.

Checking the response: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ remain unchanged in solution and are spectator ions (1). H⁺ and OH⁻ react to make water: H⁺+OH⁻→H2O (1).
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Preparing a soluble salt by neutralisation
blocks.text:
Neutralisation can prepare a soluble salt from a suitable acid and base. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide produce sodium chloride solution. Because both reagents are soluble, an unmeasured excess of either remains in the solution and cannot be removed by simple filtration. A titration first finds the volumes that react accurately.

Use a suitable indicator for the endpoint, then repeat the measured reaction without indicator when a pure salt is required. Concentrate the resulting solution carefully and allow crystals to form, rather than assuming the initial dilute solution will immediately crystallise. Collect and dry the crystals appropriately. The indicator is useful for measuring the endpoint but would become an impurity if retained. Accurate apparatus and repeat titres therefore support chemical purity, not merely neat volume readings.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Preparing a soluble salt by neutralisation
blocks.text:
Describe why a salt preparation can determine reacting volumes using indicator and then repeat the reaction without indicator.

The first titration fixes the neutralising proportions; repeating these without indicator avoids contaminating the salt product with indicator.

Checking the response: First titration establishes reacting volumes (1). Indicator-free repeat avoids indicator contamination (1).
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Preparing a soluble salt by neutralisation
blocks.text:
Describe why excess sodium hydroxide cannot be removed from sodium chloride solution by ordinary filtration.

Both are dissolved; dissolved ions pass through filter paper with the solution.

Checking the response: Excess remains dissolved (1). Filter does not separate dissolved ions (1).

blocks.heading: Choosing a soluble-salt route
blocks.text:
Choose a preparation method from reagent solubility and reactivity. Copper(II) sulfate can be prepared by adding excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid. The acid is consumed while some black oxide remains; filtration removes the excess insoluble solid, leaving a blue salt solution. Concentrating and cooling that filtrate then gives crystals.

Sodium chloride needs a different control when prepared from sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid, because both reagents dissolve. A titration establishes the required amounts, followed by an indicator-free repeat. Do not choose an unreactive metal and an acid simply because the desired salt contains that metal: copper with dilute sulfuric acid is not an appropriate hydrogen-producing route. A proposed method must give the correct ions, remove excess reagent and provide a workable separation. Use supplied solubility information to explain why each stage is possible.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Choosing a soluble-salt route
blocks.text:
Suggest the suitable base to add in excess to warm dilute sulfuric acid to prepare CuSO4 when the available choices are insoluble CuO and soluble NaOH.

Copper(II) oxide, CuO.

Checking the response: Copper(II) oxide, CuO (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Choosing a soluble-salt route
blocks.text:
State which separation removes excess insoluble CuO after reaction with sulfuric acid, given that the CuSO4 product remains dissolved.

Filtration.

Checking the response: Filtration (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Oxides and hydroxides with acids
blocks.text:
Metal oxides and metal hydroxides can neutralise acids, forming salts and water. Copper(II) oxide with sulfuric acid gives CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O. Sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid gives NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O. Name the acid and basic reactant to determine the salt, then balance the equation.

The visible behaviour depends on solubility. An insoluble oxide may disappear as it reacts, while two colourless solutions can react without an obvious visual change unless an indicator or thermometer is used. Do not invent bubbling as a general neutralisation observation: gas is not a product of these oxide/hydroxide equations. Excess solid remaining after adequate stirring and warming can indicate that the acid has been used up, but insufficient mixing could also leave solid temporarily. Completion should be judged with the method conditions in mind.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxides and hydroxides with acids
blocks.text:
Describe why calcium oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid forms calcium chloride rather than sodium chloride.

The base supplies calcium ions and the acid supplies chloride; there is no sodium source in the reactants.

Checking the response: Salt ions traced to the stated acid and base (1). Element conservation excludes sodium chloride (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxides and hydroxides with acids
blocks.text:
Describe why excess CuO can be used up to the acid endpoint and then removed during CuSO4 preparation.

CuO reacts while acid remains; unreacted insoluble CuO left after completion can be filtered off.

Checking the response: Reaction consumes acid (1). Excess insoluble solid removable (1).

blocks.heading: Carbonate reaction and gas test
blocks.text:
An acid–carbonate reaction produces carbon dioxide in addition to salt and water. The test reagent is limewater, an aqueous calcium hydroxide solution. Carbon dioxide passing through it produces a white calcium carbonate precipitate, making the initially clear liquid look milky. The observation belongs to the test liquid, not to a colour change of the carbon dioxide gas.

Record reagent and result together: gas bubbled through limewater makes it milky. A statement such as it turns cloudy is incomplete unless the reader knows which liquid was used. Prolonged passage of excess carbon dioxide can eventually clear the cloudiness, so the initial positive observation is the relevant test at this level. Compare gas tests carefully: hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint, while oxygen relights a glowing splint. Choosing the correct test prevents a gas merely being guessed from bubbling.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbonate reaction and gas test
blocks.text:
Describe why limewater becomes cloudy rather than the carbon dioxide itself turning white during the carbonate gas test.

CO2 reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, whose suspended solid scatters light.

Checking the response: Insoluble calcium carbonate is formed in the liquid (1). Suspended precipitate accounts for cloudiness rather than gas colour (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbonate reaction and gas test
blocks.text:
Describe why limewater becomes milky when carbon dioxide first passes through it.

Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble white calcium carbonate suspended in the liquid.

Checking the response: Calcium carbonate formed (1). Insoluble solid gives cloudiness (1).

blocks.heading: Acid–oxide equations
blocks.text:
A word equation identifies the chemical substances before a symbol equation accounts for atoms. For magnesium oxide and hydrochloric acid: magnesium oxide + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water. The balanced symbol equation is MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O. Magnesium's +2 charge requires two chloride ions in the salt formula.

Write correct formulae first and change coefficients to balance; do not change formula subscripts to force a count. The coefficient 2 before HCl provides two hydrogen atoms for water and two chlorine atoms for MgCl2. Check oxygen as well as metal and hydrogen. For a different acid, the anion changes: magnesium oxide plus sulfuric acid makes magnesium sulfate and water. The general salt-and-water pattern helps predict products, but the formula and ratio still need independent checking.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acid–oxide equations
blocks.text:
State the balanced equation for magnesium oxide reacting with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and water.

MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O.

Checking the response: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acid–oxide equations
blocks.text:
Explain the coefficient 2 before HCl in MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O.

Two HCl supply the two chloride ions in MgCl2 and the two hydrogen atoms in water.

Checking the response: Two HCl supply the two chloride ions in MgCl2 and the two hydrogen atoms in water (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Acid–hydroxide equations
blocks.text:
Group I hydroxides such as NaOH contain one hydroxide ion per formula unit, whereas a Group II hydroxide such as Ca(OH)2 contains two. Their acid requirements reflect those counts. Hydrochloric acid reacts as NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O, but calcium hydroxide needs Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + 2H2O.

Read brackets correctly: Ca(OH)2 has two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms in its hydroxide groups. The coefficient before water then balances both oxygen atoms and the hydrogen supplied by hydroxide and acid. The word equation calcium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water names the substances but does not state these quantities. State symbols may be added where known: solutions are aqueous and water is liquid. Keep the aqueous neutralisation relationship H⁺ + OH⁻ → H2O visible beneath the formula-unit ratio.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acid–hydroxide equations
blocks.text:
State the balanced equation for calcium hydroxide reacting with hydrochloric acid.

Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + 2H2O.

Checking the response: Ca(OH)2 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + 2H2O (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acid–hydroxide equations
blocks.text:
Explain why one formula unit of Ca(OH)2 needs two H⁺ ions for neutralisation.

It contains two hydroxide ions, each accepting one H⁺ to form water.

Checking the response: It contains two hydroxide ions, each accepting one H⁺ to form water (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Acid–carbonate equations
blocks.text:
For an acid and carbonate, include salt, water and carbon dioxide before balancing. Calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide becomes CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The carbonate's three oxygen atoms appear as one in water and two in carbon dioxide.

A common mistake is to omit water because the bubbles draw attention to the gas. Check hydrogen: the two H atoms from two HCl must appear in a product. For sodium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. The sodium coefficient changes because the carbonate formula contains two sodium ions, while the acid requirement remains two H⁺ per carbonate ion. Count each element explicitly rather than copying coefficients from a superficially similar equation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acid–carbonate equations
blocks.text:
State the balanced equation for sodium carbonate reacting with hydrochloric acid.

Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.

Checking the response: Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2 (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acid–carbonate equations
blocks.text:
Explain why water must appear along with carbon dioxide in CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

Water accounts for the acid hydrogen and the remaining carbonate oxygen after CO2 forms.

Checking the response: Water accounts for the acid hydrogen and the remaining carbonate oxygen after CO2 forms (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-7-P01 (7)
blocks.text:
Why can a neutralisation mixture remain acidic?
A. All acids have pH 7 after mixing.
B. Water is a strong acid.
C. Some acid may remain in excess.
D. No reaction can have occurred.

C. Some acid may remain in excess. Neutralisation can consume only part of the initial acid.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Neutralisation can consume only part of the initial acid. Distractor explanations: D: partial consumption is possible. A: depends on quantities. B: false explanation.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-7-P01 (8)
blocks.text:
A learner must prepare CuSO4 from warm dilute H2SO4. CuO is insoluble; NaOH is soluble. Which route is appropriate?
A. React excess CuO, filter, then crystallise.
B. Mix NaCl and water.
C. Add NaOH and label the product CuSO4.
D. Add copper metal and assume rapid hydrogen formation.

A. React excess CuO, filter, then crystallise. CuO supplies copper, neutralises acid, and excess solid can be removed.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: CuO supplies copper, neutralises acid, and excess solid can be removed. Distractor explanations: C: no copper source. D: copper does not react that way with dilute sulfuric acid. B: wrong ions.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-7-P01 (9)
blocks.text:
Which equation correctly represents magnesium oxide with hydrochloric acid?
A. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O
B. MgO + HCl → MgCl2 + H2
C. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + CO2
D. MgO + HCl → MgCl + OH

A. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O Correct formulae and atom balance give salt and water.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Correct formulae and atom balance give salt and water. Distractor explanations: B: unbalanced and wrong gas. C: introduces carbon. D: wrong salt formula and products.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-7-P02 (credit-group-1)
blocks.text:
Describe the reaction and separation used to obtain CuSO4 solution from warm dilute sulfuric acid and excess CuO.

Add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid with stirring; filter away the unreacted solid to obtain CuSO4 solution.

Excess CuO added to warm dilute H2SO4 (1). Filter excess solid (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-7-P02 (credit-group-2)
blocks.text:
Explain why the CuO is added in excess and why that excess can then be removed.

Excess oxide consumes the acid, and its insolubility allows the remaining oxide to be removed by filtration.

Excess oxide consumes acid (1). Insoluble excess can be filtered away (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-33 — Comparing acid reactions
blocks.text: In teacher-supervised small-scale tests, compare dilute hydrochloric acid reacting with a suitable metal oxide, metal hydroxide and carbonate. Record solid disappearance, temperature change where measured, and any gas separately. The oxide and hydroxide give salt and water; the carbonate also evolves carbon dioxide. Test the carbonate gas with limewater and record its milky appearance. Do not invent gas production for every acid–base reaction. Keep reagent identities explicit, avoid excess heating and use eye protection. Where starting solids differ in solubility or particle size, the observations are reaction descriptions rather than a controlled ranking of reaction rates.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-35 — Titration for salt preparation
blocks.text: Measure an alkali aliquot with a pipette and filler into a conical flask. Under supervision, add acid from a burette using a suitable indicator and a white tile to recognise the endpoint. Record initial and final burette readings and calculate their difference. A rough trial locates the endpoint; careful repeats with small additions near it give concordant titres. Repeat the established reacting quantities without indicator to prepare an uncontaminated salt solution. Remove a filling funnel before reading the burette, keep the meniscus at eye level, and rinse apparatus appropriately. Equal liquid volumes are not assumed to mean equal reacting amounts.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-36 — Two neutralisation routes
blocks.text: Prepare sodium chloride solution from accurately measured hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide volumes established by titration, repeating without indicator. Separately, add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid, stir until reaction is complete and filter excess oxide from the blue solution. Concentrate the appropriate solutions and allow crystallisation, then collect and dry the crystals suitably. Compare why one route needs measured soluble reactants while the other tolerates removable excess solid. Do not boil copper(II) sulfate solution to dryness. Record observations at each stage, and explain which fraction is retained after filtration rather than treating filtration as a universal salt-recovery step.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Connect acid–base chemistry to ionic formulae, reacting amounts and separation techniques. Check strength separately from concentration, and identify the desired product fraction before filtering or crystallising.

topics/7/content-units/CU-6117-7.2.json.title: 7.2 — classify oxides as basic (e.g. Na2O and MgO), acidic (e.g. SO2, SO3 and NO2) or amphoteric (e.g. Al2O3), related to the metallic, non-metallic or metalloid character of the element forming the oxide

blocks.heading: Basic oxides
blocks.text:
A basic oxide reacts with an acid to form a salt and water. Many metal oxides, including sodium oxide and magnesium oxide, show this behaviour. Some react with water to form alkaline solutions; others are insoluble and react directly at the surface when acid is added. Water solubility is therefore not the defining test for basic oxide character.

Use the reaction to justify the classification. MgO + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2O shows magnesium oxide neutralising hydrochloric acid. A sample's pH cannot be read directly if it is a dry solid; an indicator tests an appropriate aqueous mixture. Metal character gives a useful trend but not an exception-free rule, because aluminium oxide is amphoteric. State the particular oxide and its observed reaction rather than calling every metal oxide a soluble alkali.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Basic oxides
blocks.text:
State the acid–base classification of magnesium oxide.

Basic oxide.

Checking the response: Basic oxide (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Basic oxides
blocks.text:
Explain why adding an insoluble basic oxide can raise the pH of an acidic solution even though the oxide is not an alkali.

The oxide reacts with and consumes H⁺ at its surface; lower hydrogen-ion concentration raises pH without requiring the oxide to dissolve as an alkali first.

Checking the response: Consumption of H⁺ lowers its concentration and therefore raises pH; both cause and consequence required (1).
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Factual teaching retained; linked worked example updated.

blocks.heading: Acidic oxides
blocks.text:
An acidic oxide reacts with a base to form a salt, often with water. Many non-metal oxides, including sulfur dioxide and sulfur trioxide, are acidic. Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide solution to form calcium carbonate and water, which is the chemical basis of the limewater test. Some acidic oxides form acidic solutions on reacting with water.

Classify by chemical behaviour rather than by the state or colour of the oxide. A gas is not necessarily acidic, and some non-metal oxides are neutral. For the syllabus examples SO2, SO3 and NO2, retain the acidic classification while avoiding the blanket statement that every non-metal oxide is acidic. Aqueous indicator evidence can support the classification where the oxide reacts with or dissolves in water, but reaction with a base is the defining comparison used here.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acidic oxides
blocks.text:
State the acid–base classification of sulfur dioxide.

Acidic oxide.

Checking the response: Acidic oxide (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Amphoteric oxides
blocks.text:
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis. Aluminium oxide is the specified example: it can show basic behaviour towards an acid and acidic behaviour towards an alkali. Amphoteric does not mean neutral or chemically inactive. It describes two types of acid–base reactivity depending on the reaction partner.

The broader trend from metallic to non-metallic character helps organise oxide behaviour, but exceptions and intermediate behaviour matter. Aluminium is a metal, yet its oxide is amphoteric, so metal identity alone cannot settle the classification. Use supplied reaction observations to justify the category: reaction with an acid and with an alkali together supports amphoterism. Detailed complex-ion formulae are not needed here. Compare the behaviours without adding advanced product structures that the syllabus excludes.

For a supplied comparison, oxide X reacts with acid but not with alkali, while oxide Y reacts with both. X shows basic behaviour in those tests; Y shows amphoteric behaviour. The conclusion uses the pair of observations, not a guess from colour. A test giving no visible change may need adequate time or a suitable measurement before being treated as no reaction. Record the tested conditions and distinguish a negative observation from proof of chemical inactivity under every possible condition.

topics/7/content-units/CU-6117-7.4.json.title: 7.4 — describe the preparation, separation and purification of soluble and insoluble salts as examples of the application of some of the techniques specified in section 1.5 and the reactions specified in section 7.3

blocks.heading: Separating and purifying salts
blocks.text:
For a soluble salt prepared with excess insoluble reactant, filter the mixture and retain the filtrate. Concentrate the filtrate gently, allow it to cool for crystallisation, then collect the crystals. A small cold-water rinse can remove adhering mother liquor while limiting dissolution, followed by suitable drying. Evaporation to complete dryness is not the intended method for hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals.

For an insoluble salt made by precipitation, the product is the solid residue on the filter, not the filtrate. Wash the precipitate with distilled water to remove soluble impurities and dry it appropriately. These routes reverse which fraction contains the desired product. Before each separation, identify the product's physical state and solubility. A method that says filter but never states which fraction to keep leaves a crucial decision unresolved. Purification removes unwanted material; it is different from simply collecting the largest possible mass, which may include excess reactants or retained solution.

blocks.text:

Stop after sufficient concentration and cool to crystallise; wash separated crystals with only a small amount of cold water.

Checking the response: Concentrate and cool without drying out (1). Use a small cold rinse to reduce dissolution (1).

blocks.heading: Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts
blocks.text:
The school solubility rules classify the familiar sodium, potassium and ammonium salts as soluble in water. This makes their solutions useful sources of anions in precipitation preparations. Sodium carbonate solution can supply carbonate ions, for example, while sodium ions generally remain in solution when an insoluble carbonate is formed with another metal ion.

Soluble does not mean that unlimited solid dissolves in a fixed amount of water. A solution can become saturated, and temperature affects solubility. Use the rule to decide whether a reagent can be supplied as a solution and whether a predicted product is likely to precipitate in the stated classroom conditions. When two soluble solutions are mixed, inspect the new ion combinations rather than assuming they remain soluble because the starting salts were soluble. The rule is an organising tool for the specified salts, not a claim about every imaginable compound under every condition.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sodium, potassium and ammonium salts
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Nitrates
blocks.text:
The nitrate salts used in this syllabus are soluble in water. Silver nitrate and lead(II) nitrate can therefore provide dissolved metal ions for a precipitation reaction. Their nitrate ions remain in the solution when the metal forms an insoluble chloride, sulfate or carbonate with another reagent.

Identify nitrate as NO3⁻ and distinguish it from a metal ion. In AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3, the silver chloride is the precipitate, while sodium nitrate remains dissolved. Ordinary filtration can separate the solid from the liquid but cannot remove dissolved nitrate from the liquid itself. Washing the collected precipitate removes solution carrying nitrate and other soluble impurities. This explains why the solubility rule matters for both the choice of starting reagent and the purification stage.

blocks.heading: Lead salts
blocks.text:
Many familiar lead(II) salts are insoluble or sparingly soluble, but lead(II) nitrate is soluble. Lead(II) chloride, sulfate and carbonate are important exceptions to broader soluble-salt patterns or examples of insoluble products at ordinary classroom conditions. State the named salt rather than treating the metal name lead as sufficient to predict every case.

Lead(II) nitrate solution can supply Pb²⁺ for a precipitation example because it dissolves. The resulting insoluble lead salt is collected as a solid and soluble spectator ions are washed away. These are conceptual or teacher-controlled examples because lead compounds are hazardous; do not propose unrestricted learner handling. Lead(II) chloride is more soluble in hot water than in cold water, so solubility conditions matter. A simplified rule for cold aqueous mixtures should not be extended to every temperature or concentration.

blocks.heading: Hydroxides
blocks.text:
Most familiar metal hydroxides are insoluble, while sodium and potassium hydroxides are soluble. Calcium hydroxide is slightly soluble and produces limewater; the dissolved portion supplies hydroxide ions. Aqueous ammonia is a weak alkaline solution and should not be treated as proof that every named metal hydroxide dissolves.

The rule helps predict precipitates in qualitative tests, but observations should distinguish an insoluble solid from a coloured solution. Mixing a metal-ion solution with a soluble hydroxide can form an insoluble metal hydroxide, which appears as a precipitate. Some precipitates dissolve in excess reagent; those specific tests are taught in Qualitative Analysis. Here the task is to identify whether the initial hydroxide product is expected to remain dissolved. Keep limited solubility separate from weak base behaviour: dissolution and ion formation are different questions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydroxides

blocks.heading: Carbonates
blocks.text:
Most familiar metal carbonates are insoluble in water. Sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates are soluble exceptions in the school rules. A soluble carbonate solution can therefore supply CO3²⁻ ions to precipitate an insoluble carbonate of another metal, such as calcium carbonate.

A carbonate's reaction with acid is different from its solubility in plain water. An insoluble carbonate can disappear when acid is added because it chemically reacts, producing a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Do not describe that disappearance as evidence that it was water-soluble all along. When selecting a precipitation reagent, choose a soluble source of carbonate ions; adding two insoluble powders to water does not provide the same controlled mixing of dissolved ions. The intended product must then be retained on the filter and washed.

blocks.heading: Chlorides
blocks.text:
Most familiar chlorides are soluble in water, with silver chloride and lead(II) chloride important insoluble or sparingly soluble exceptions under ordinary classroom conditions. Silver nitrate solution mixed with sodium chloride solution produces white silver chloride. The net ionic equation is Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl, with a solid product.

The white appearance is a precipitate in the mixture, not a white solution of dissolved silver chloride. Filter and wash the solid to separate it from soluble spectator ions. Protect silver chloride from strong light when appropriate because it can darken through photochemical change. Lead(II) chloride has temperature-dependent solubility, so a cold-water rule needs that boundary. A correctly named exception is more useful than the inaccurate blanket statement that every chloride dissolves.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chlorides
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Sulfates
blocks.text:
Most familiar sulfates are soluble, but barium sulfate and lead(II) sulfate are insoluble, and calcium sulfate is only slightly soluble. These exceptions matter when choosing an acid for salt preparation. Adding sulfuric acid to a calcium-containing solid may form a poorly soluble coating rather than providing the clean soluble-product route expected from a different acid.

Barium sulfate forms when suitable soluble barium and sulfate solutions are mixed. A soluble sodium sulfate reagent can provide sulfate while sodium remains a spectator ion. The solid product is recovered by filtration, washing and drying. Do not collect a sulfate precipitate by crystallising the filtrate; that liquid contains the soluble species left after the desired solid has been removed. Read both ion identities before applying the rule, because a soluble nitrate starting material does not make the newly formed sulfate soluble.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sulfates
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Selecting starting materials
blocks.text:
A precipitation preparation starts with suitable soluble reagents that supply the two ions of an insoluble product. For silver chloride, silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions provide Ag⁺ and Cl⁻. Mix measured amounts, allow the solid to form, filter it, wash away soluble impurities and dry it appropriately. The net ionic reaction identifies the product independently of the spectator ions.

For a soluble salt, choose a different route: neutralise an acid with an appropriate base, carbonate or reactive metal, then separate any excess solid and crystallise the solution. If both reacting substances are soluble, measured reacting quantities are needed because filtration cannot remove a dissolved excess. A method choice is justified by solubility, chemical reactivity and purification, not just by matching words in the product name. Use any supplied solubility table to check the proposed starting substances and final product before describing the apparatus.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-7-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Plan a teacher-supervised preparation of a clean, dry sample of insoluble silver chloride from suitable soluble starting salts. Include measured mixing, separation, washing, drying and a practical check that precipitation is complete. Collect silver-containing waste separately.

Use silver nitrate solution and sodium chloride solution in measured suitable amounts. Mix with stirring to precipitate AgCl; a slight excess of chloride can be used. After settling, test a separate small clear portion with an additional drop of chloride solution: no further cloudiness supports completion of silver precipitation. Filter the main mixture and keep the white AgCl residue. Wash with small portions of distilled water to remove dissolved salts, then dry between clean filter papers or by a suitable low-temperature method while protecting from strong light. The visual completion check does not prove full purity; careful washing and uncontaminated apparatus support it.

Suitable soluble silver salt (1). Suitable soluble chloride (1). Measured mixing with stated completion check (1). Filter and retain precipitate (1). Wash to remove soluble impurities (1). Appropriate drying and distinguish completion evidence from proof of purity (1). Accept equivalent safe preparation; maximum six marks.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-34 — Observing crystals
blocks.text: Examine teacher-prepared salt crystals using a magnifying glass. Record colour, shape and size with labelled sketches, distinguishing separate crystals from clumps and wet mother liquor. Compare crystals from slow cooling with those from faster concentration where samples are available, while avoiding an unsupported claim that one shape proves purity. Blue copper(II) sulfate crystals provide a familiar example. Handle with appropriate tools, not bare fingers, and do not taste the samples. A visible crystal is a solid with an ordered arrangement; a clear solution can contain the same salt dissolved even though crystals are absent.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-37 — Preparing an insoluble salt
blocks.text: Use teacher-approved soluble reagents that supply the desired product ions. For AgCl, mix measured silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions, observe the white precipitate, filter and retain the solid, wash with distilled water and dry appropriately. Protect the product from strong light and collect silver waste for controlled disposal. In the model explanation, Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ form AgCl while Na⁺ and NO3⁻ remain dissolved. A small separate completion test can check whether adding more precipitating reagent causes further cloudiness; it does not by itself prove purity. Washing removes soluble impurities but cannot separate an unrelated insoluble contaminant, so suitable clean starting materials matter.

topics/7/content-units/CU-6117-7.1.json.title: 7.1 — define acids and bases in terms of proton transfer (limited to aqueous solutions)

blocks.heading: Acids as proton donors
blocks.text:
An acid is a proton donor in the aqueous proton-transfer model used here. A proton is represented by H⁺. Hydrochloric acid donates protons in water, giving the characteristic reactions of its aqueous solution. The definition concerns transfer to another species, rather than a sour taste or a hazard label. Tasting chemicals is not an identification method.

Keep acid strength separate from concentration. A strong acid ionises completely in aqueous solution; a weak acid ionises partially. Concentrated and dilute describe the amount of dissolved acid per solution volume. A strong acid can be dilute, and a weak acid can be concentrated. The pH depends on the resulting hydrogen-ion concentration, which is influenced by both strength and total acid concentration. Define the acid by proton donation first, then state these separate descriptors where the question supplies them.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acids as proton donors
blocks.text:
Define an acid in the aqueous proton-transfer model.

A proton donor.

Checking the response: A proton donor (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Bases as proton acceptors
blocks.text:
A base is a proton acceptor in the aqueous proton-transfer model used here. Hydroxide ions accept protons to form water: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H2O. Ammonia can also accept a proton in water to form ammonium, showing that a base need not have OH written in its original molecular formula. Identify the species accepting the proton rather than treating every hydrogen-containing substance as an acid.

The acid and base roles belong to a particular proton-transfer reaction. In the familiar neutralisation of aqueous hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide solution, the relevant reacting species are H⁺ and OH⁻. Sodium and chloride ions remain in solution as spectators. Writing the ionic change helps distinguish proton transfer from an unrelated reaction such as a metal losing electrons. Keep this lesson within aqueous examples; more general solvent chemistry is unnecessary for the stated syllabus model.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bases as proton acceptors
blocks.text:

Checking the response: A proton acceptor (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Bases and alkalis
blocks.text:
An alkali is a water-soluble base that gives hydroxide ions in aqueous solution. Sodium hydroxide is an example. Base is the broader category: an insoluble basic oxide such as copper(II) oxide can react with acid but is not an alkali. Solubility therefore distinguishes an alkali from a base that does not dissolve sufficiently to make the corresponding alkaline solution.

Do not infer solubility from the ability to neutralise an acid. An acid can react with an insoluble solid at its surface, gradually using it up. This distinction determines salt-preparation methods: excess insoluble base can be filtered away, whereas an excess soluble alkali cannot be removed by ordinary filtration. State the water-solubility condition when explaining the category. A comparison between copper(II) oxide and sodium hydroxide should connect the naming difference to practical behaviour rather than merely memorising two examples.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bases and alkalis
blocks.text:

Dissolution provides mobile ions, including hydroxide ions; OH⁻ makes the solution alkaline while mobile ions carry current.

Checking the response: Mobile dissolved ions carry current and the presence of OH⁻ accounts for alkalinity; both links required for the single mark (1).

It accepts protons/reacts as a base, but lacks the water solubility required for an alkali.

blocks.heading: Indicators
blocks.text:
Indicators give different colours under different acid–alkali conditions. An acidic solution turns blue litmus red, while an alkaline solution turns red litmus blue. A neutral solution does not produce either of those opposite-colour changes. Litmus identifies broad categories, whereas Universal Indicator provides an approximate pH by comparison with the colour chart supplied for that indicator.

Use separate small samples and clean equipment so the indicator test does not contaminate the main preparation. Record the observed colour before inferring acidic or alkaline. A coloured sample may obscure the indicator, and Universal Indicator gives an estimate rather than an exact concentration. Its familiar progression is red/orange/yellow in acidic regions, green near neutral and blue/purple in alkaline regions, with exact shade boundaries checked against the supplied chart. Do not use indicator colour alone to identify a particular acid or prove its degree of ionisation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Indicators

An acid turns blue litmus red; an alkali turns red litmus blue.

Checking the response: An acid turns blue litmus red; an alkali turns red litmus blue (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: The pH scale
blocks.text:
For the usual room-temperature school scale, pH 7 is neutral, values below 7 are acidic and values above 7 are alkaline. Within the stated 0–14 range, a lower pH indicates greater acidity and a higher pH greater alkalinity. This syllabus uses whole-number readings, so match a Universal Indicator colour to the nearest supported whole-number value rather than inventing decimal precision.

A pH comparison describes the solutions as tested. It does not by itself give the total amount of acid available for reaction or identify the acid species. Two samples with the same pH can have different total acid concentrations if their ionisation behaviour differs. Similarly, a large volume of dilute acid can contain more total acid than a small concentrated sample. Keep pH, concentration and total amount as separate quantities. Compare colours with the relevant chart under suitable lighting and acknowledge ambiguous matches.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The pH scale

pH 7 is neutral; below 7 is acidic and above 7 alkaline.

Checking the response: pH 7 is neutral at the stated room-temperature convention (1). Below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline; both directions required (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The pH scale
blocks.text:

The chart relates colour to a range or approximate whole-number pH; visual matching lacks the resolution to justify arbitrary decimal precision.

Checking the response: Colour-to-pH comparison depends on the chart (1). Limited colour resolution prevents unsupported decimal precision (1).

blocks.heading: Comparing alkaline samples
blocks.text:
Universal Indicator can compare the alkalinity of supplied soap solution, limewater and sodium hydroxide samples. A sample matching pH 10 is alkaline, while one matching pH 13 has a higher hydroxide-ion concentration under the comparison conditions. This is a comparison of measured solutions, not proof that the lower-pH substance is partially ionised. Concentration and solubility can affect the result as well as intrinsic base strength.

Limewater is aqueous calcium hydroxide. Its limited solubility must not be mistaken for weak dissociation of the dissolved portion. The syllabus groups it with weakly alkaline examples, but this should be read as a classroom comparison of samples rather than a chemically precise definition of weak base. Sodium hydroxide solution itself can have a lower pH when sufficiently diluted. Report the actual indicator observation and pH, then explain the limits of what that evidence establishes. Ammonia solution is a clearer example of a weak base when teaching partial formation of ions in water.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing alkaline samples
blocks.text:

Checking the response: Both above neutral (1). pH 13 sample more alkaline (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing alkaline samples
blocks.text:
Suggest why a limewater sample giving a lower pH than a sodium hydroxide sample does not by itself prove partial dissociation of calcium hydroxide.

The samples may have different dissolved concentrations; calcium hydroxide has limited solubility.

Checking the response: The samples may have different dissolved concentrations; calcium hydroxide has limited solubility (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Comparing acidic samples
blocks.text:
A supplied lemon-juice sample and hydrochloric acid can both give acidic Universal Indicator colours. Lemon juice contains weak acids, whereas hydrochloric acid is a strong acid. At a suitable matched acid concentration, a strong acid generally produces a higher hydrogen-ion concentration than a weak acid, giving a lower pH. The comparison needs the concentration condition; the names alone do not fix the pH of an arbitrary sample.

For observed samples at pH 3 and pH 1, both are acidic and the pH 1 sample is more acidic as tested. It is not valid to conclude from that observation alone that every pH 3 solution contains a weak acid. A dilute strong-acid solution can have that reading. Distinguish evidence about pH from evidence about ionisation, and do not assign an invariant pH to lemon juice, whose composition and dilution vary. Use whole-number readings consistent with the indicator chart.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing acidic samples
blocks.text:
Distinguish supplied lemon juice at pH 3 from hydrochloric acid at pH 1 in terms of measured acidity.

Both are acidic; the pH 1 hydrochloric acid sample is more acidic as tested.

Checking the response: Both acidic (1). pH 1 sample more acidic (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing acidic samples
blocks.text:
Suggest why a hydrochloric acid sample can have pH 3 even though hydrochloric acid is strong.

It can be sufficiently dilute; strong describes ionisation, not concentration.

blocks.heading: Acids and reactive metals
blocks.text:
A suitable reactive metal reacts with a dilute non-oxidising acid to form a salt and hydrogen. Magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid gives magnesium chloride and hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2. Bubbles indicate gas evolution, while an appropriate small-sample hydrogen test gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint under supervision.

The conditions matter. Copper does not produce hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid in the same way, so avoid writing that every metal reacts with every acid. Nitric acid has different oxidising behaviour and is not the basis of this general hydrogen pattern. Describe the metal disappearing and gas forming as observations, then identify the products from the reaction and test. Keep hydrogen away from ignition sources during collection; the controlled test uses a separate small sample. The salt name follows the acid's anion and the reacting metal.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acids and reactive metals
blocks.text:
Describe why hydrogen from a magnesium–acid reaction is tested as a small separate sample rather than with a flame at the generating flask.

Hydrogen mixed with air is flammable; ignition at the generator could spread into gas there, whereas a small separated sample limits the amount ignited.

Checking the response: Hydrogen–air ignition hazard (1). Separate small sample limits ignition and avoids flame at the generator (1).

blocks.text:

H2: two hydrogen atoms remain after zinc and chlorine are assigned to ZnCl2.

Checking the response: H2 supported by conserving the two remaining hydrogen atoms (1).

blocks.heading: Acids and bases
blocks.text:
An acid reacts with a suitable base to form a salt and water. A metal oxide such as copper(II) oxide consumes acid as the solid reacts, while a soluble hydroxide supplies hydroxide ions directly in solution. For hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. The aqueous hydrogen and hydroxide ions combine to form water.

A neutralisation reaction can occur without the final mixture being neutral. If acid or alkali is left in excess, the mixture retains its corresponding acidic or alkaline character. Even at a stoichiometric endpoint, the salt can affect pH outside the simple strong-acid/strong-alkali example. For this level, identify the reactants and products and avoid saying that adding any amount of base instantly makes any acid pH 7. Controlled quantities and an appropriate endpoint matter when preparing a pure soluble salt.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Acids and bases
blocks.text:
Describe why an acid–alkali neutralisation can produce water while leaving a conducting solution.

H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to water; dissolved salt ions remain mobile and can carry current.

Checking the response: Reacting ions form water (1). Remaining mobile salt ions explain conduction (1).

blocks.heading: Acids and carbonates
blocks.text:
An acid reacting with a metal carbonate forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide. Calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid gives CaCO3 + 2HCl → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Effervescence accompanies gas production, but identify carbon dioxide using a test rather than calling every colourless gas carbon dioxide.

Bubble a small gas sample through limewater; it turns milky or cloudy as a white calcium carbonate precipitate forms. Name both the reagent and observation. Carbon dioxide itself is colourless, so saying the gas turns white confuses the gas with the precipitate in the test solution. A carbonate sample may dissolve as it is consumed, but any excess solid or insoluble impurities can remain. The acid selected determines the salt anion, and the product solubility influences whether this reaction is convenient for preparing a particular salt.

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Recognising proton transfer
blocks.text:
To explain a supplied aqueous reaction as acid–base, identify the proton donor and the proton acceptor. In H⁺ + OH⁻ → H2O, the proton is accepted by hydroxide. In NH3 + H⁺ → NH4⁺, ammonia accepts a proton to become ammonium. These examples show the transfer directly without requiring a metal hydroxide formula in every base.

Check atoms and charge in the ionic description. The hydroxide example has total charge zero on each side, while ammonia plus H⁺ has total charge +1, matching NH4⁺. Proton transfer is different from electron transfer: a species becoming positively charged does not by itself prove oxidation. Ammonia gaining H⁺ is an acid–base event in this model, not a loss of an electron. Use the stated reacting species to support the classification and avoid deciding solely from the word hydrogen appearing somewhere in the equation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Recognising proton transfer
blocks.text:

NH3, ammonia.

Checking the response: NH3, ammonia (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

OH⁻ accepts a proton, so the reaction involves proton transfer.

Checking the response: OH⁻ accepts a proton, so the reaction involves proton transfer (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Strength and ion formation
blocks.text:
A strong acid ionises completely in aqueous solution, while a weak acid ionises only partially. For bases, a strong soluble hydroxide such as sodium hydroxide gives its dissolved ions essentially completely; a weak base such as ammonia reacts with water only partly to produce hydroxide ions. The central distinction is the extent of ion formation under the relevant conditions, not the amount placed in a bottle.

Use matched concentrations when comparing the effect of strength on pH or electrical conductivity. A weak acid solution contains both un-ionised acid and ions; it is not an ion-free liquid. Diluting it reduces the total acid amount per unit volume even though the fraction ionised may change. At this level, qualitative particle descriptions are enough. Do not confuse a sparingly soluble strong hydroxide with a weak molecular base: limited dissolution and partial ionisation are different limitations on the ion concentration.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Strength and ion formation

Partial ionisation supplies some mobile ions even though many acid molecules remain un-ionised.

Checking the response: Partial ionisation supplies some mobile ions even though many acid molecules remain un-ionised (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:

Its partial ionisation still produces mobile ions that carry charge.

Checking the response: Its partial ionisation still produces mobile ions that carry charge (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Concentration and dilution
blocks.text:
Concentration describes dissolved substance per unit volume of solution. For comparable samples of the same strong acid, a more concentrated sample contains more H⁺ ions per dm³; for the same strong alkali it contains more OH⁻ ions per dm³. This comparison holds the substance and ionisation behaviour fixed. Across different acids or bases, total dissolved concentration cannot be replaced by an ion count without considering strength.

Dilution adds water and increases total solution volume without adding solute. The same solute amount is spread through a larger volume, lowering concentration. A dilution does not turn hydrochloric acid from a strong acid into a weak acid, because those words describe ionisation rather than amount per volume. State the species and comparison conditions when linking concentration to hydrogen or hydroxide ions. A claim about the total number of ions in a whole container also requires the container volume, not just the concentration.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentration and dilution
blocks.text:
Explain why dilution changes the concentration of a strong acid without turning it into a weak acid.

Amount per volume decreases, but acid strength concerns extent of ionisation rather than that concentration.

Checking the response: Amount per volume decreases, but acid strength concerns extent of ionisation rather than that concentration (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:

The amount of solute remains unchanged while volume doubles; amount per volume therefore halves.

Checking the response: Unchanged solute amount divided by twice the volume gives half the concentration (1).

blocks.heading: Why pH needs two descriptors
blocks.text:
The pH of an acid or alkali solution depends on both its strength and its concentration. Strength determines how extensively the dissolved species produces ions, while concentration describes how much dissolved substance is present per volume. The resulting H⁺ or OH⁻ concentration controls the acid–alkali condition being measured. Either factor can therefore change an indicator reading.

A lower pH cannot identify a stronger acid unless concentration and other relevant conditions are controlled. Compare a dilute strong acid with a concentrated weak acid cautiously: the names strong and weak alone do not establish which has the lower pH. Conversely, equal pH does not imply equal total acid concentrations or equal quantities needed for neutralisation. A sound answer states what information is available and what further comparison is needed. Use these distinctions to check claims about household samples, whose concentrations are often unspecified.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Why pH needs two descriptors
blocks.text:
Explain why both acid strength and concentration affect pH.

They jointly determine the hydrogen-ion concentration: extent of ionisation and amount of acid per volume both matter.

Checking the response: They jointly determine the hydrogen-ion concentration: extent of ionisation and amount of acid per volume both matter (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

The pH difference could result from concentration differences rather than acid strength.

Checking the response: The pH difference could result from concentration differences rather than acid strength (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-31 — Placing samples on a pH scale
blocks.text: Under teacher supervision, test separate small samples of labelled solutions using Universal Indicator and its supplied chart. Use clean droppers and wells, record the colour first, then assign a supported whole-number pH and place the sample on a 0–14 scale. Include a neutral reference and known acidic and alkaline references. Compare samples without tasting or touching them. A strongly coloured sample may obscure the indicator, and the chart match is approximate. A pH ranking describes the tested solutions; it does not identify their chemical names or total acid amounts.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-32 — Comparing strength at matched concentration
blocks.text: Compare teacher-prepared strong and weak acid samples with the same stated total molar concentration and comparable proton stoichiometry. Record pH under the same conditions and connect a lower pH to greater hydrogen-ion formation in the matched comparison. A similar comparison can use sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia at stated comparable concentrations. Do not use arbitrary household samples with unknown dilution as evidence of intrinsic strength. Calcium hydroxide solubility is a separate issue and must not be presented as partial ionisation. Keep temperature, indicator method and sample contamination controlled. The conclusion needs both the measurement and the concentration information.

topics/6/content-units/CU-6117-6.6.json.title: 6.6 — define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen gain/loss and in terms of the transfer of electrons

blocks.heading: Oxidation
blocks.text:
Oxidation can be defined as gain of oxygen or loss of electrons. The electron definition applies to reactions where oxygen is absent, such as Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. Magnesium loses two electrons, so it is oxidised. When magnesium burns to form magnesium oxide, it gains oxygen and loses electrons; both definitions identify oxidation in that example.

Write electrons on the product side of an oxidation half-equation and check the total charge. Mg on the left is neutral; Mg²⁺ and two electrons on the right have a total charge of zero. Do not confuse losing negative electrons with becoming more negative: electron loss makes the resulting ion more positive. Oxygen gain is a useful visible chemical pattern, but a reaction need not contain oxygen to be redox. The wider electron definition connects this topic to electrode reactions and displacement.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxidation
blocks.text:
Define oxidation in terms of oxygen and electrons.

Gain of oxygen or loss of electrons.

Checking the response: Gain of oxygen or loss of electrons (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Reduction
blocks.text:
Reduction can be defined as loss of oxygen or gain of electrons. Copper(II) ions are reduced in Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu because they gain electrons. Copper(II) oxide can be reduced by removing oxygen to form copper. In a suitable reaction, the oxygen removed is accepted by another substance, linking reduction with oxidation of that substance.

Place electrons on the reactant side of a reduction half-equation and verify charge balance. A positive ion gaining enough electrons may form a neutral atom, but not every reduction produces a neutral substance: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺ is also reduction. Its ionic charge decreases because a negative electron has been gained. Relate charge changes to actual electron transfer rather than assuming that a smaller positive number means fewer electrons. This makes unfamiliar ionic examples easier to classify.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reduction
blocks.text:
Define reduction in terms of oxygen and electrons.

Loss of oxygen or gain of electrons.

Checking the response: Loss of oxygen or gain of electrons (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Recognising redox from charge
blocks.text:
Changes in ionic charge can show electron transfer. An increase from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ represents loss of an electron and oxidation; a decrease from Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ represents gain and reduction. In a complete redox reaction, electrons lost by one species are gained by another, so the electron transfers balance overall.

Compare the same element before and after reaction and distinguish its ionic charge from a formula subscript. The 2 in MgCl2 counts chloride ions in a formula unit; it is not a charge on magnesium written by itself. Where half-equations are supplied, locate the electrons and check atoms as well as charge. A reaction such as ion exchange without a change in the relevant ionic charges is not identified as redox simply because ions are present. The evidence must be a transfer of electrons.

For the supplied reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, separate the changes. Zinc becomes Zn²⁺ by losing two electrons: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Copper(II) ions gain those electrons: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Adding the half-equations cancels two electrons on each side and gives the stated overall equation. There is one zinc atom and one copper atom on both sides, and total charge is +2 on both sides. These checks establish balanced transfer; a half-equation with just one electron for Zn²⁺ would fail the charge check.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Recognising redox from charge
blocks.text:
Identify which supplied change is oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻, or Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺.

Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation because an electron is lost.

Checking the response: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation because an electron is lost (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
