blocks.heading: Oxidising and reducing agents
blocks.text:
An oxidising agent causes another substance to be oxidised and is itself reduced. It accepts electrons in the electron-transfer description. A reducing agent causes another substance to be reduced and is itself oxidised, donating electrons. Name the agent from what it does to its reaction partner, while checking the change it undergoes itself.

For CuO + H2 → Cu + H2O, hydrogen removes oxygen from copper(II) oxide and is the reducing agent; hydrogen is oxidised to water. Copper(II) oxide supplies oxygen to hydrogen and is the oxidising agent; it is reduced to copper. In a supplied ionic displacement, the metal losing electrons is the reducing agent and the ion gaining them is the oxidising agent. Do not label the final metal product as the reducing agent merely because it was formed by reduction. The agent belongs to the reacting substance that causes the partner's change.

In that zinc–copper example, zinc is the reducing agent because it provides the electrons that reduce Cu²⁺. The Cu²⁺ ion is the oxidising agent because it accepts the electrons lost by zinc. Name the reacting ion rather than the spectator sulfate ion if the solution happens to be copper(II) sulfate. A useful answer sequence is to identify the electron loss, identify the matching gain, and then assign the agents. This prevents the common reversal between the agent name and the change the agent itself undergoes. The reducing agent is oxidised; the oxidising agent is reduced. These paired descriptions are consistent, not contradictory.

Checking the response: Hydrogen, H2 (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

topics/6/content-units/CU-6117-6.1.json.title: 6.1 — distinguish between chemical and physical changes

blocks.heading: Physical and chemical changes
blocks.text:
A physical change alters a state, shape or arrangement without forming a different chemical substance. Ice melting remains water: the particles move differently, but the molecular identity stays H2O. A chemical change forms one or more new substances. Burning magnesium forms magnesium oxide, so the product has a different chemical composition from the starting metal. Classify by substance identity rather than by how dramatic the event looks.

Reversibility alone is not a reliable classification rule. Some chemical reactions can be reversed by changing conditions, and a physical change such as breaking a glass may be difficult to reverse in practice. Likewise, bubbles can arise from boiling or from a reaction; they do not prove chemical change without evidence of the gas identity and process. Compare properties before and after, identify a new product where possible, and explain the inference. A supplied observation should support the conclusion rather than merely repeat the word change.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Physical and chemical changes
blocks.text:
Distinguish a physical change from a chemical change.

A physical change retains chemical identity; a chemical change forms new substances.

Checking the response: No new substance in a physical change (1). New substance formed chemically (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Physical and chemical changes
blocks.text:
Suggest whether heating ice until it becomes liquid water is a physical or chemical change, given that both samples consist of H2O molecules.

Physical: the substance remains H2O.

Checking the response: Physical: the substance remains H2O (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Energy accompanies reaction
blocks.text:
Chemical reactions involve an energy change. Energy may pass from the reacting system to its surroundings or enter the reacting system from them. A temperature rise or fall is one possible observation, but energy may also be transferred as light or electrical work. A change too small for a classroom thermometer to detect does not establish that no energy change occurred.

Decide what belongs to the system before describing the energy direction. In a simple reaction mixture, a thermometer measures the mixture temperature, while the chemical process changes the energy stored in the substances. Insulation reduces transfer to the wider room and makes a temperature change easier to interpret. The distinction between the reaction and the warming water will matter when using calorimetry: heat gained by the water corresponds approximately to heat lost by an exothermic reaction, with opposite signs.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Energy accompanies reaction

An energy change.

topics/6/content-units/CU-6117-6.3.json.title: 6.3 — describe the production of heat energy by burning fuels

blocks.heading: Burning fuels
blocks.text:
A fuel releases useful energy when it reacts, commonly by burning in oxygen. Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon forms carbon dioxide and water and transfers energy to the surroundings. A stove or heater directs some of this transfer into an intended use, such as warming water. The useful fraction is less than the total release because surrounding air and apparatus also warm.

Fuel choice involves more than whether a flame is visible. Compare energy delivered, supply, cost and unwanted products under the same purpose and conditions. Limited oxygen can lead to incomplete combustion and hazardous carbon monoxide, while solid soot may indicate incomplete burning. Do not infer a fuel's energy content from flame colour alone. In a calorimetry comparison, measure mass consumed as well as water temperature change; burning twice as much fuel does not establish that it releases more energy per gram.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Burning fuels
blocks.text:
Describe why complete combustion of a hydrocarbon increases the mass of the collected products compared with the hydrocarbon alone.

Oxygen from the surroundings is incorporated into carbon dioxide and water, so the products include that additional reactant mass.

Checking the response: Oxygen is an additional reactant from outside the fuel (1). Its atoms enter CO2 and water, increasing collected product mass relative to fuel alone (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Burning fuels
blocks.text:
Describe why a water-heating fuel experiment measures less useful heat than the fuel releases in total.

Some energy warms the air and apparatus instead of the water; heat lost to these surroundings is not included in the water calculation.

Checking the response: Other energy recipients (1). Water measurement omits that transfer (1).

blocks.heading: Nuclear energy sources
blocks.text:
Radioactive isotopes can be sources of energy through changes in their nuclei. Uranium-235 is used as a nuclear fuel: controlled nuclear fission releases energy that heats a working system, which can be used to generate electricity. This is a nuclear process, not combustion of uranium in oxygen and not a rearrangement of outer electrons in chemical bonds.

A description at this level identifies the isotope, the nuclear origin of the energy and its useful transfer. Compare it with a chemical fuel without claiming that both release energy by the same bond changes. Nuclear generation does not require burning a carbon fuel during the energy-releasing process, but radioactive materials and waste require controlled management. Do not use the absence of carbon dioxide from the fission step to conclude that construction, fuel preparation and the whole energy system have no environmental effects.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nuclear energy sources
blocks.text:
Describe why a nuclear power station can heat water without burning uranium in oxygen as its main energy-releasing process.

Uranium fission releases energy through nuclear changes; that energy heats the water without requiring combustion as the source.

Checking the response: Nuclear rather than chemical-combustion energy release (1). Released energy transfers as heat to water (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nuclear energy sources
blocks.text:
Describe why uranium-235 energy release is different from burning a hydrocarbon.

Its energy comes from changes in nuclei; combustion involves chemical reactions and rearrangement of bonds.

Checking the response: Nuclear change (1). Chemical bond change contrasted (1).

blocks.heading: Simple chemical cells
blocks.text:
A simple chemical cell can produce electrical energy from a spontaneous chemical reaction using two suitable different electrodes in an electrolyte. The electrode materials and electrolyte must support complementary reactions. Electrons travel through the external connection, while ions carry charge in the electrolyte. A complete circuit permits current to flow through a load, such as a small suitable meter.

This arrangement differs from an electrolytic cell driven by an external power supply. In a generating cell, the chemical reaction supplies the energy for electron flow; in electrolysis, electrical energy drives a chemical change. Both involve oxidation and reduction, but do not transfer an electrode-sign rule from one case without checking the cell type. Electrolysis products also depend on an aqueous or molten electrolyte and on whether an inert electrode or an active copper electrode is used. Comparing different metals in an identical electrolyte can show that the electrode pair matters. Keep immersion depth, contact quality and solution conditions consistent; a weak or unstable reading can reflect the apparatus rather than prove no chemical change is possible.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Simple chemical cells
blocks.text:
Describe why a simple cell cannot sustain current through an external wire if the ionic path between its electrodes is interrupted.

Both external electron flow and internal ionic charge transport are needed; interruption prevents a complete sustained circuit.

Checking the response: Internal ionic transport completes the charge path (1). Interruption prevents sustained external electron flow (1).

X converts chemical energy to electrical output; Y uses electrical input to drive chemical change.

blocks.heading: Cleaner energy sources
blocks.text:
Solar, wind and hydroelectric generation can provide useful energy without burning a fuel at the point of generation. Solar cells convert light to electricity, wind turbines use moving air, and hydroelectric systems use moving water. Calling a source cleaner usually compares particular emissions or impacts; it does not mean the system has no materials, land or maintenance requirements.

Match a source to the conditions needed for operation. Solar output depends on available light, wind output on wind conditions, and hydroelectric output on suitable water flow and infrastructure. Storage or a combination of sources may help when output varies. A comparison should name both the benefit and its boundary: reduced combustion emissions during generation do not quantify the full lifecycle impact. Avoid treating renewable and continuously available as synonyms. A renewable flow can vary through a day or season.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Cleaner energy sources
blocks.text:
Describe why a wind turbine and a hydroelectric generator can produce electricity without fuel combustion at the generator.

Moving air or water transfers kinetic energy to machinery that drives a generator; the energy input is motion, not a burning fuel.

Checking the response: Wind or water transfers motion to the generator system (1). Electrical energy derives from that motion rather than local combustion (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Cleaner energy sources
blocks.text:
Describe why solar electricity can reduce combustion emissions while still needing planning for variable supply.

Solar cells do not burn fuel during generation, but output varies with available sunlight.

Checking the response: No fuel combustion during generation (1). Variable light means variable output (1).

blocks.heading: Solar cells
blocks.text:
Solar cells produce electrical energy from sunlight. The input is light, and the useful output is electrical energy. A solar water heater has a different immediate output, transferring energy to water as heat. Both may use sunlight, so identify the device by its conversion rather than by the general word solar.

A small classroom cell connected to a meter can show how output changes with illumination. Compare exposure while keeping the circuit, orientation and load consistent, and distinguish a qualitative demonstration from an efficiency measurement. No fuel is consumed by combustion in the cell during generation, but energy conservation still applies: the electrical output comes from the incoming light. At night without another light source, the same device cannot generate from absent sunlight; a system providing power then must draw on storage or another supply.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Solar cells
blocks.text:
State the useful energy conversion made by a solar cell in sunlight.

Light energy to electrical energy.

Checking the response: Light energy to electrical energy (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Hydrogen fuel cells
blocks.text:
A hydrogen fuel cell reacts hydrogen with oxygen to generate electricity, producing water overall. The summary equation is 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. It is useful to distinguish this electrochemical conversion from simply burning a hydrogen flame to heat water. At this level, the reactants, useful electrical output and water product explain its role; internal construction detail is unnecessary.

Hydrogen is an energy carrier whose environmental impact depends partly on how it was produced and transported. Water as the product at the fuel cell does not establish that producing the hydrogen emitted no greenhouse gases. A balanced evaluation names the point-of-use benefit and the production limitation without introducing an unsupported numerical efficiency. Compare a hydrogen fuel cell with a fossil-fuel combustion source for a specified purpose, retaining the boundary of the comparison. Both require an available supply of suitable reactants to continue operating.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen fuel cells
blocks.text:
Describe why a hydrogen fuel cell needs a continuing supply of both hydrogen and oxygen rather than hydrogen alone.

Both reactants participate in forming water; a continuing reaction and electron transfer require both supplies.

Checking the response: Water formation requires both H and O reactants (1). Sustained reaction/electron flow stops when a required reactant is unavailable (1).

Describe why water as a fuel-cell product does not prove the entire hydrogen supply has no environmental impact.

Water is the point-of-use product, but hydrogen production and transport may require energy and cause emissions.

Checking the response: Point-of-use boundary (1). Upstream energy/emission limitation (1).

blocks.text:

B. Energy disappears from the surroundings.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Net reaction energy is transferred to the surroundings. Distractor explanations: D: material transfer is not the explanation. A: bond breaking absorbs energy. B: energy is transferred, not destroyed.

topics/6/content-units/CU-6117-6.2.json.title: 6.2 — explain the meanings of the terms exothermic and endothermic

blocks.heading: Exothermic changes
blocks.text:
An exothermic reaction transfers energy from the reacting system to the surroundings. In a simple insulated experiment, the mixture or surrounding water usually warms, providing evidence of released thermal energy. The reaction enthalpy change is negative because the products are at a lower enthalpy than the reactants under the comparison conditions. Burning a fuel and many neutralisation reactions provide familiar examples.

Exothermic does not mean a reaction needs no starting energy. A fuel may require ignition because particles must overcome an activation-energy barrier before the reaction proceeds rapidly. After initiation, energy release may sustain further reaction. Keep this starting requirement separate from the net energy change between reactants and products. A hot starting mixture alone does not prove a reaction is exothermic: compare the observed temperature change with appropriate controls and account for external heating.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Exothermic changes
blocks.text:
Explain why an exothermic reaction can warm a surrounding water bath even when no heater is switched on.

The reaction transfers energy out of its reacting system into the surrounding water.

Checking the response: The reaction transfers energy out of its reacting system into the surrounding water (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Exothermic changes
blocks.text:
Explain why a reaction that warms an initially unheated insulated mixture from 21 °C to 29 °C is classified as exothermic. Assume no other heat source.

Energy released by the reaction warms the mixture.

Checking the response: Energy released by the reaction warms the mixture (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Endothermic changes
blocks.text:
An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings. The products have a higher enthalpy than the reactants, giving a positive enthalpy change. If the reaction draws thermal energy from an initially unheated mixture, its temperature can fall. Energy has not vanished: it has been transferred into the chemical change. Some endothermic reactions require continued heating to maintain a useful rate.

A temperature observation needs its conditions. Evaporation and other physical changes can also cool a sample, so cooling alone does not prove that a chemical reaction occurred. Establish the chemical change independently, then use the temperature evidence to infer the direction of energy transfer. An insulated container reduces exchange with the room but does not make measurement perfect; the container, thermometer and surrounding air may still exchange energy. Describe the observed change before assigning an energy sign.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Endothermic changes
blocks.text:
Explain why an endothermic reaction can cool its surroundings while proceeding.

It absorbs energy from the surroundings, reducing their thermal energy.

Checking the response: It absorbs energy from the surroundings, reducing their thermal energy (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Endothermic changes
blocks.text:
Explain why an identified chemical reaction that cools an insulated mixture from 24 °C to 18 °C, with no evaporation, is endothermic.

The reaction absorbs thermal energy from the mixture, lowering its temperature.

Checking the response: The reaction absorbs thermal energy from the mixture, lowering its temperature (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Energy profiles and activation energy
blocks.text:
An energy profile plots energy vertically against reaction progress horizontally; the horizontal axis is not time. Label reactants and products at their respective levels. Their vertical difference is the enthalpy change, ΔH: product level minus reactant level. For an exothermic change the products lie lower and ΔH is negative; for an endothermic change they lie higher and ΔH is positive. The zero of the vertical scale may be chosen arbitrarily, so differences matter.

The profile rises to a peak representing the activation barrier. Forward activation energy is measured from the reactant level to the peak, not from zero on the page. A catalyst provides a pathway with a lower barrier but does not change the reactant or product levels and therefore does not change ΔH. In an original illustrative profile with reactants at 40, peak at 100 and products at 10 kJ/mol, forward activation energy is 60 kJ/mol and ΔH is −30 kJ/mol. Label both arrows separately and do not mistake the peak height for the net reaction change.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Energy profiles and activation energy
blocks.text:
Draw an energy profile from these illustrative levels: reactants 30, products 10, peak 80 kJ/mol. Label both axes, forward activation energy and ΔH.

Products lie below reactants; Ea = 50 kJ/mol upwards from reactants to peak, ΔH = −20 kJ/mol from reactants to products.

Checking the response: Profile matches the three levels with energy and progress axes (1). Correct 50 kJ/mol activation and −20 kJ/mol reaction-energy arrows (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Energy profiles and activation energy
blocks.text:
Describe the energy change and forward activation energy from an illustrative profile with reactants at 40, products at 10 and peak at 100 kJ/mol.

ΔH=10−40=−30 kJ/mol, exothermic. Forward activation energy=100−40=60 kJ/mol.

Checking the response: −30 kJ/mol and exothermic (1). 60 kJ/mol activation energy (1).

blocks.heading: Breaking and forming bonds
blocks.text:
Breaking a chemical bond requires energy input and is endothermic. Forming a chemical bond releases energy and is exothermic. A reaction usually involves both processes, so its overall energy change depends on the balance. It is incorrect to describe fuel combustion as releasing energy simply because fuel bonds break: bond breaking consumes energy, while formation of product bonds releases it.

For an exothermic reaction, the energy released on forming product bonds exceeds the energy required to break reactant bonds. For an endothermic reaction, the required input exceeds the release. Draw a clear boundary around the balanced reaction when counting bonds, because a coefficient multiplies every bond in that molecule. The separate steps are an accounting model for the overall change; they are not a claim that a reacting mixture first becomes a container of isolated atoms and then reforms all its bonds.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Breaking and forming bonds
blocks.text:
Describe why breaking reactant bonds alone cannot account for an exothermic reaction.

Bond breaking requires energy; net release occurs only if forming product bonds releases more energy than was absorbed.

Checking the response: Breaking requires energy input (1). Greater product-bond release accounts for net exothermic change (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Breaking and forming bonds
blocks.text:
Describe why a reaction can release energy overall even though reactant bonds must be broken.

Product bond formation releases more energy than reactant bond breaking requires, giving a net release.

Checking the response: Energy input for breaking (1). Larger release on forming produces net release (1).

blocks.heading: Simple calorimetry
blocks.text:
For a substance changing temperature without changing state, q=mcΔT relates transferred thermal energy to mass m, specific heat capacity c and temperature change ΔT. With mass in grams and c in J/(g °C), q is in joules. Subtract initial temperature from final temperature before substituting. Use the mass of the material being warmed, not automatically the mass of the fuel or a reactant added to it.

In simple calorimetry, heat gained by water or solution is used to estimate the reaction energy released. State assumptions: negligible heat loss, negligible heat absorbed by apparatus, and the stated heat capacity. A measured water temperature rise gives positive q for the water; the corresponding exothermic reaction has negative energy change. Converting joules to kilojoules requires division by 1000. If a temperature rise is requested instead, rearrange to ΔT=q/(mc). Report the quantity the prompt requests and avoid attaching a per-mole unit unless an amount of reaction has actually been used.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Simple calorimetry
blocks.text:
Calculate the thermal energy gained by 80.0 g water warming from 20.0 °C to 26.0 °C. Take c=4.20 J/(g °C) and q=mcΔT.

ΔT=6.0 °C. q=80.0×4.20×6.0=2016 J, approximately 2.02 kJ.

Checking the response: ΔT=26.0−20.0=6.0 °C and q=80.0×4.20×6.0 (1). 2016 J, or 2.02 kJ to three significant figures (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Simple calorimetry
blocks.text:
Calculate the temperature rise of 100 g water that gains 2.10 kJ. Take c=4.20 J/(g °C) and q=mcΔT; assume no state change.

q=2100 J; ΔT=q/(mc)=2100/(100×4.20)=5.00 °C.

Checking the response: Convert energy and rearrange correctly (1). 5.00 °C (1).

blocks.heading: Bond-energy estimates
blocks.text:
Estimate a reaction energy change as total energy required to break reactant bonds minus total energy released when product bonds form. Both supplied bond-energy values are positive magnitudes, so the subtraction determines the final sign. Count bonds from displayed formulae and multiply by equation coefficients. A double bond uses its supplied double-bond energy; it is not automatically twice a single-bond value.

For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, one H–H and one Cl–Cl bond are broken and two H–Cl bonds form. With supplied values 436, 243 and 431 kJ/mol respectively, the estimate is 436+243−2×431=−183 kJ/mol of reaction as written. Average bond energies are estimates and need not reproduce a precise experimental enthalpy. A reverse question may give ΔH and ask for a missing bond energy: retain the coefficient multiplying that unknown when rearranging. Check that the final result has the requested sign and refers to the stated reaction amount.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bond-energy estimates
blocks.text:
Calculate ΔH for H2 + Br2 → 2HBr using supplied bond energies H–H 436, Br–Br 193 and H–Br 366 kJ/mol. Apply broken minus formed.

ΔH=436+193−2×366=−103 kJ/mol of reaction as written.

Checking the response: Broken minus formed: 436+193−2×366 (1). −103 kJ/mol of reaction as written (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bond-energy estimates
blocks.text:
Calculate the H–Cl bond energy from H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl, ΔH=−183 kJ/mol, H–H=436 and Cl–Cl=243 kJ/mol. Let the H–Cl value be E; the relationship is total energy broken minus formed.

−183=436+243−2E; 2E=862, so E=431 kJ/mol.

Checking the response: −183=436+243−2E, hence 2E=862 (1). E=431 kJ/mol (1).

blocks.heading: Light as an energy source
blocks.text:
Light can supply energy needed for a chemical reaction. Photosynthesis uses light to support chemical synthesis, and silver chloride can decompose in light to form silver. A colour change in exposed silver chloride can therefore provide evidence of a light-sensitive reaction when compared with a protected sample. Light supplies energy; it is not a chemical element added to the product formula.

A controlled comparison separates light from other changes. Use equal samples, equal exposure time and comparable temperature, protecting one from light. If an intense lamp also heats one sample, the experiment cannot attribute the entire difference to light alone. Some reactions respond to particular wavelengths and conditions, so the statement does not imply that illumination speeds up every chemical reaction. Use supervised observations or supplied results for light-sensitive chemical tests, and describe the light condition alongside the outcome.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Light as an energy source
blocks.text:

Light energy.

Checking the response: Light energy (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Photosynthesis
blocks.text:
Photosynthesis produces glucose from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight. A balanced summary is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, with light and chlorophyll shown as conditions rather than reactants consumed in the equation. The process stores energy in chemical products and provides organic material used by living organisms.

Distinguish the energy input from the material inputs. Carbon in glucose comes from carbon dioxide, while water provides hydrogen and participates in the overall change. Sunlight supplies energy rather than matter. Chlorophyll enables light absorption; it is not written as a coefficient-bearing glucose ingredient. In an answer naming the requirements, include both starting substances and the light/chlorophyll conditions. This chemical summary does not require a detailed biological pathway or a claim that all absorbed light is converted into glucose.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Photosynthesis
blocks.text:
State the starting substances, product sugar and conditions for photosynthesis.

Carbon dioxide and water form glucose in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight.

Checking the response: Carbon dioxide and water form glucose in the presence of chlorophyll and sunlight (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-26 — Estimating energy from a spirit fuel
blocks.text: A teacher-controlled spirit burner can heat a measured water mass in a suitable metal calorimeter. Record the water temperature before and after and the burner mass before and after a short heating period, with the burner extinguished and safely cooled for weighing. Stir the water gently for a representative reading and use q=mcΔT to estimate energy gained by the water. Divide by fuel mass lost for an approximate energy transferred per gram. Keep the flame-to-container distance and water mass comparable across trials. Heat lost to the room, warming of apparatus and fuel evaporation limit the estimate. A shield must not restrict ventilation. Methylated spirits are flammable and harmful: trained supervision handles fuel, and a hot or burning burner must not be refilled. This gives a calorimetry estimate, not a claim that all combustion energy reached the water.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-30 — Light and silver chloride
blocks.text: Compare equal small teacher-prepared silver chloride samples, one exposed to light and the other protected, while keeping temperature and observation time comparable. Record initial appearance and the extent of darkening. Silver forms during photochemical decomposition, explaining the colour change; the protected sample provides a control for changes unrelated to illumination. A covered sample can also have a different temperature, so check that limitation rather than assuming the covering changes light alone. Use approved handling and waste collection under supervision. The conclusion is that this reaction responds to light, not that illumination increases the rate of every chemical process.

topics/6/content-units/CU-6117-6.5.json.title: 6.5 — describe the idea that some chemical reactions can be reversed by changing the reaction conditions (including the effects of heat on hydrated salts, e.g. hydrated copper(II) sulfate and hydrated cobalt(II) chloride (cross reference to 11.1.1)

blocks.heading: Reversible reactions
blocks.text:
Some chemical reactions can proceed in either direction when conditions change. Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate removes water of crystallisation and leaves white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. Adding water can restore the blue hydrated form. Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is pink, while the anhydrous form is blue. These changes demonstrate chemical reversibility, not simply a solid melting and freezing.

Use a reversible arrow when representing the forward and reverse changes. For copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4·5H2O ⇌ CuSO4 + 5H2O summarises hydration and dehydration under appropriate conditions. Gentle teacher-controlled heating is needed; excessive heating can produce further chemical changes outside the intended comparison. Reversibility does not mean both directions proceed at the same rate under every condition. It means the reverse chemical process is possible, while equilibrium requires a suitable closed system and stable conditions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reversible reactions
blocks.text:
Describe why blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate can return after the white anhydrous solid is cooled and water is added.

Heating removed water of crystallisation; adding water allows hydration to reverse the earlier change.

Checking the response: Dehydration accounts for the white solid (1). Rehydration restores the blue hydrated form (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reversible reactions
blocks.text:
Describe why the hydrated-to-anhydrous copper(II) sulfate change is reversible.

Heating removes water of crystallisation; adding water reforms the hydrated substance.

Checking the response: Forward water removal (1). Reverse hydration restores starting form (1).

blocks.heading: Dynamic equilibrium
blocks.text:
Dynamic equilibrium is the state in a closed system where forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so reactant and product concentrations remain constant. The word dynamic matters: both reactions continue. Constant concentrations do not imply that the amounts of reactants and products are equal, nor that particles have stopped reacting.

Imagine a reversible reaction initially containing mostly reactants. The forward reaction creates products, which can then react in reverse. At equilibrium, the two rates balance. If a molecule changes into product, another event can convert product back, maintaining the macroscopic composition. The equality concerns rates, not individual particle identities. A graph of concentrations can therefore flatten while molecular changes continue. State the closed-system condition because loss of a gaseous component can prevent the required balance from being maintained.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Dynamic equilibrium
blocks.text:
Define dynamic equilibrium for a reversible reaction.

In a closed system, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations remain constant.

Checking the response: In a closed system, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations remain constant (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Why a closed system matters
blocks.text:
A reversible reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium in a closed system, where relevant substances cannot escape or enter. Stable temperature and other conditions permit a steady balance between the forward and reverse processes. If a gas product escapes, its removal changes the composition and can keep driving further forward reaction rather than preserving the original equilibrium.

A closed system is not the same as an insulated system. Closed concerns material exchange, while insulation concerns energy transfer. A closed reaction vessel may still exchange heat with its surroundings. This distinction helps separate equilibrium reasoning from calorimetry. A sealed classroom vessel must not be improvised for a gas-generating reaction; equilibrium descriptions are conceptual or use appropriate controlled equipment. When explaining a constant composition, refer to equal reaction rates rather than claiming that the reaction has ceased.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Why a closed system matters
blocks.text:
Describe why constant concentrations at dynamic equilibrium do not mean the particles have stopped reacting.

Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so gains and losses balance and concentrations remain constant.

Checking the response: Both reaction directions continue (1). Equal rates balance concentration changes (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Why a closed system matters
blocks.text:
Describe why continuous escape of a gaseous product can prevent the original dynamic equilibrium from being maintained.

Product is removed, changing its concentration and reducing its availability for reverse reaction.

Checking the response: Escape lowers the concentration of gaseous product (1). Reverse/forward balance disturbed (1).
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.

blocks.heading: Changing concentration at equilibrium
blocks.text:
Changing the concentration of a component disturbs a chemical equilibrium. The system responds in the direction that tends to oppose the imposed concentration change. Adding a reactant commonly favours its consumption and increases the equilibrium amount of product; removing a product also favours further product formation. State temperature as fixed when isolating a concentration effect.

The response is partial rather than magical cancellation. Adding reactant does not mean every added particle is consumed, and the new equilibrium need not have the same concentrations as before. Identify the species changed, the side on which it appears and the direction that uses it up or replaces it. In a supplied symbolic reaction A + B ⇌ C, adding B at fixed temperature favours C formation, while removing A favours the reverse direction. The reasoning follows the stated equation, not the left-to-right layout of a memorised example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changing concentration at equilibrium
blocks.text:
Predict the equilibrium shift for A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq) when B is added at fixed temperature without a substantial volume change. Give the reason.

It shifts towards C, tending to consume the added B.

Checking the response: Towards products (1). Consumes increased B (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changing concentration at equilibrium
blocks.text:
State the direction of the equilibrium response when C is removed from A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq) at fixed temperature.

Towards C, the forward direction.

Checking the response: Towards C, the forward direction (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Changing temperature at equilibrium
blocks.text:
Increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction of a reversible reaction, while decreasing it favours the exothermic direction. Establish which direction the supplied ΔH describes before predicting a shift. For a forward exothermic reaction, warming favours the reverse reaction and can reduce the equilibrium product proportion even though reactions proceed faster.

This distinction between rate and equilibrium yield is essential. A hotter process may reach equilibrium sooner but have a less favourable equilibrium composition for a desired product. Conversely, cooling can favour an exothermic product while making approach to equilibrium slow. A prediction should specify the temperature change, the favoured thermal direction and the resulting composition change. Do not use the sign of ΔH without explaining that negative means the forward direction releases energy and positive means it absorbs energy.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changing temperature at equilibrium
blocks.text:
Predict the equilibrium response when temperature rises for A(g) ⇌ B(g), whose forward reaction has ΔH=−40 kJ/mol. Explain your choice.

It shifts towards A because warming favours the endothermic reverse direction.

Checking the response: Towards A (1). Endothermic reverse direction favoured (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changing temperature at equilibrium
blocks.text:
State how cooling affects the equilibrium amount of B in A(g) ⇌ B(g) when the forward direction is exothermic.

The equilibrium amount of B increases.

Checking the response: The equilibrium amount of B increases (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Changing pressure at equilibrium
blocks.text:
For a gaseous equilibrium, increasing pressure by compression favours the side with fewer moles of gas. Decreasing pressure favours the side with more moles of gas. Count the gas coefficients in the balanced equation; solid and liquid amounts do not enter this simple gas-count comparison. If both sides contain equal gas amounts, compression produces no equilibrium shift in this model.

For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), four moles of gaseous reactants correspond to two moles of gaseous product. Increased pressure at fixed temperature therefore favours ammonia. Explain both the direction and gas-count basis, rather than saying pressure always favours products. Reversing how the equation is written reverses the words left and right but not the physical conclusion. Pressure questions must retain the gas-state condition and distinguish equilibrium composition from the separate collision-frequency effect on rate.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changing pressure at equilibrium
blocks.text:
Predict the effect of compression at constant temperature on N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), initially at equilibrium. Explain using gas amounts.

The equilibrium shifts towards ammonia because that side has two moles of gas compared with four on the reactant side.

Checking the response: Towards NH3 (1). Fewer gas moles, two versus four (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changing pressure at equilibrium
blocks.text:
State the effect of increasing pressure by compression at constant temperature on the equilibrium composition of H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).

No shift: each side has two moles of gas.

Checking the response: No shift: each side has two moles of gas (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-6-P01 (10)
blocks.text:
Why can adding water restore blue colour to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate?
A. The copper atoms become a different element.
B. Water removes all copper ions.
C. The solid burns.
D. The hydrated salt reforms.

D. The hydrated salt reforms. Hydration reverses the intended dehydration change.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Hydration reverses the intended dehydration change. Distractor explanations: A: no element change. B: ions are not all removed. C: this is not combustion.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-6-P01 (11)
blocks.text:
A(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ C(aq) is at equilibrium. What response follows removal of some C at fixed temperature?
A. No response because equilibrium is permanent.
B. Shift towards C.
C. Both reactions stop.
D. Shift towards A and B.

B. Shift towards C. The response tends to replace removed product.

Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The response tends to replace removed product. Distractor explanations: D: further removes B. C: dynamic reactions continue. A: changed composition disturbs the balance.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-28 — Dehydration and rehydration
blocks.text: Use teacher demonstrations or recorded observations of small hydrated-salt samples. Gentle heating changes hydrated copper(II) sulfate from blue to white; adding water to the cooled anhydrous salt restores blue. Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride changes from pink to blue on dehydration, with the reverse colour change on hydration. Record the starting colour, change during heating and change after water addition in separate columns. Avoid excessive heating, which may introduce further changes. Cobalt salts require controlled handling and disposal, so this is not an unsupervised learner procedure. Explain the observations by loss and return of water of crystallisation, and distinguish reversibility from evidence of equilibrium in an open test tube.

blocks.heading: Closed-system equilibrium
blocks.text:
![Equal forward and reverse rates do not require equal reactant and product amounts.](visuals/VIS-6117-6-03.svg)

Equal forward and reverse rates do not require equal reactant and product amounts. These labelled diagrams are answer and teaching references; attempt drawing tasks before consulting them.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Connect this topic to particle models, stoichiometry and electrochemistry. Keep energy direction, collision rate and equilibrium composition distinct; interpret each using the stated conditions and measured quantity.

topics/6/content-units/CU-6117-6.4.json.title: 6.4 — explain the meaning of the term rate of reaction

blocks.heading: Rate is change per time
blocks.text:
Rate of reaction measures the change in a reactant or product quantity per unit time. Depending on the observation, it can be expressed as gas volume per second, mass lost per second or concentration change per second. An average rate uses a stated interval: change in the measured quantity divided by elapsed time. A total gas volume alone measures an amount of product, not a rate.

On a product-volume against time graph, gradient represents the rate of volume production. A steeper curve indicates faster production at that time. A flattening curve has a declining rate, and a plateau means no further measured gas is being collected. Distinguish the curve's final height from its steepness: two reactions may give the same final gas amount but reach it at different times. Conversely, a larger final volume need not imply a larger initial rate. State both the measured quantity and time interval when comparing results.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Rate is change per time
blocks.text:
Explain why two trials producing the same gas volume need not have the same average reaction rate.

They may take different times; rate compares quantity change with elapsed time.

Checking the response: They may take different times; rate compares quantity change with elapsed time (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Rate is change per time
blocks.text:
Explain which of two trials has the greater average gas-production rate in the first 10 s: X produces 20 cm³ and Y produces 30 cm³.

Y: 3.0 cm³/s exceeds X at 2.0 cm³/s over the same interval.

Checking the response: Y: 3.0 cm³/s exceeds X at 2.0 cm³/s over the same interval (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Rate is change per time
blocks.text:
Explain the error in calling 50 cm³ of gas a reaction rate without giving any time information.

It is a gas volume, not a change per unit time; a time interval is needed.

Checking the response: It is a gas volume, not a change per unit time; a time interval is needed (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Catalysts
blocks.text:
A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction and is chemically unchanged at the end. It participates in the reaction pathway rather than standing outside the process, but is regenerated overall. It may change physically, for example through a change in particle size, without having been consumed as a reactant. A small amount can therefore influence the conversion of a larger amount of reactant.

A catalyst is specific to a useful pathway and does not make every reaction faster. It changes how rapidly equilibrium is approached but does not alter the equilibrium position or the energy difference between reactants and products. In a comparison, keep other conditions fixed and measure rate rather than assuming a larger final amount means catalytic action. Recovery of the catalyst helps test the definition, but unchanged mass alone is not proof of unchanged chemical identity. Link the observation to both rate increase and regeneration.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Catalysts
blocks.text:
Define a catalyst.

A substance that increases reaction rate and is chemically unchanged at the end, although it may change physically.

Checking the response: A substance that increases reaction rate and is chemically unchanged at the end, although it may change physically (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Lower activation energy
blocks.text:
A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. At the same temperature, a greater fraction of particle encounters can lead to successful reaction along that pathway. It does not increase the particles' average kinetic energy by definition; heating and catalysis are different ways to change reaction rate.

On an energy profile, represent the catalysed pathway with a lower peak while leaving the reactant and product levels unchanged. Both pathways connect the same starting and ending substances. The vertical distance from reactants to the lower peak is the reduced activation energy. The energy change ΔH remains the same, so a catalyst cannot turn an endothermic reaction into an exothermic one. When explaining an observed speed increase, name the alternative pathway and lower barrier instead of claiming that the catalyst simply adds heat.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Lower activation energy
blocks.text:
State how a catalyst increases reaction rate in terms of activation energy.

It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

Checking the response: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Inhibitors
blocks.text:
An inhibitor is a substance that reduces the rate of a chemical reaction. The term describes its effect on the rate, not a claim that it permanently stops every reaction. Some applications seek slower unwanted change, such as reducing a damaging reaction during storage. Whether an inhibitor is useful depends on the specified reaction and conditions.

Distinguish an inhibitor from dilution or cooling, which are changes in conditions rather than necessarily added inhibiting substances. In an investigation, compare the same reacting system with and without the candidate substance while keeping other variables constant. If addition also changes concentration or temperature, those changes may explain a lower rate. Measure the rate consistently and use a control before concluding that inhibition occurred. Do not infer the detailed molecular mechanism simply from the word inhibitor; that would require further evidence.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Inhibitors
blocks.text:
Define an inhibitor.

A substance that reduces the rate of a chemical reaction.

Checking the response: A substance that reduces the rate of a chemical reaction (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Concentration and collisions
blocks.text:
For a reaction involving dissolved particles, increasing concentration commonly increases rate when other relevant conditions are fixed. More reactant particles occupy each unit volume, increasing the frequency of encounters with other reacting particles or a reacting surface. More frequent successful collisions can produce more product per second. The explanation is about particle number per volume, not particles becoming larger or necessarily moving faster.

Compare concentration effects at the same temperature, with the same solid mass and exposed area where a solid reacts. If more concentrated solution also contains more total limiting reactant, the final product amount may change as well as the rate. Separate those consequences: use excess solution with a fixed limiting solid to compare rates while keeping the theoretical total gas similar. Concentrated and dilute describe amount per volume; strong and weak acids describe ionisation extent. Compare concentrations of the same acid, rather than confusing acid strength with concentration. The concentration rule is conditional and does not imply direct proportionality for every chemical system.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentration and collisions
blocks.text:
Describe why increasing dissolved reactant concentration can increase rate at fixed temperature.

More reactant particles per unit volume produce more frequent successful collisions.

Checking the response: More particles per volume (1). More frequent successful collisions (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentration and collisions
blocks.text:
Suggest why trial Y produces gas faster than X when identical carbonate chips react with excess acid at the same temperature, but Y has a higher acid concentration.

Y has more acid particles per volume, causing more frequent successful collisions at the chips.

Checking the response: Y has more acid particles per volume, causing more frequent successful collisions at the chips (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Gas pressure and rate
blocks.text:
Increasing the pressure of gaseous reactants by compressing them at constant temperature brings more particles into each unit volume. Their collision frequency increases, which can increase the reaction rate. This explanation applies to reacting gases; increasing pressure around a solid does not automatically create the same concentration effect. The temperature condition prevents a separate kinetic-energy change from being confused with compression.

Distinguish the effect on rate from the effect on equilibrium composition. Compression may speed reactions through more frequent gas collisions, while an equilibrium shift depends on the numbers of gaseous particles on the two sides of the equation. An equation with equal gas amounts on both sides can have no pressure-driven equilibrium shift even though collision rates change. When answering a rate question, state the gas-concentration and collision link; do not replace it with a yield argument unless equilibrium composition is actually requested.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Gas pressure and rate
blocks.text:
Describe why compressing gaseous reactants at constant temperature can increase reaction rate.

Gas particles become more concentrated, so successful collisions occur more frequently.

Checking the response: Increased particles per volume (1). Increased successful collision frequency (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Gas pressure and rate
blocks.text:
Suggest why a gas reaction proceeds faster in a smaller vessel containing the same reactant amounts at the same temperature.

The gases have a higher concentration and collide more frequently.

Checking the response: The gases have a higher concentration and collide more frequently (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Particle size and exposed area
blocks.text:
Breaking a solid into smaller pieces increases its total exposed surface area without changing its total mass. For a reaction occurring at the solid surface, more reactant can contact the solid at once, increasing the frequency of successful surface collisions. Powder can therefore react faster than the same mass of large chips under otherwise comparable conditions.

Do not describe the solid's individual atoms as becoming smaller. The pieces contain fewer particles each, and more of the original particles are exposed at surfaces. A fair test keeps solid composition and mass, liquid concentration and volume, and temperature fixed. Where the solid is the limiting reactant and reacts completely, changing size need not change the final gas amount. It changes the time taken to reach that amount. Settling, clumping or incomplete mixing may complicate a real powder comparison and should be considered when observations depart from the simple model.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Particle size and exposed area
blocks.text:
Describe why powder can react faster than equal-mass chips of the same solid in excess solution at equal temperature.

Powder exposes a larger total surface, allowing more frequent successful collisions with dissolved reactant.

Checking the response: Larger exposed area (1). More frequent successful surface collisions (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Particle size and exposed area
blocks.text:
Suggest one change to a fixed mass of carbonate that should increase its reaction rate with excess acid without changing its composition.

Break it into smaller pieces to expose more surface area.

Checking the response: Break it into smaller pieces to expose more surface area (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Catalysts and successful collisions
blocks.text:
A catalyst changes the available reaction pathway so that the activation-energy barrier is lower. At the same temperature, more collisions have enough energy to lead to reaction along this pathway. The resulting increase is in successful reaction events per unit time, not necessarily in the total number of collisions between particles.

A suitable inorganic catalyst or an enzyme can show this effect, but suitability depends on the reaction and conditions. Keep catalyst identity separate from concentration and temperature. A demonstration with a catalyst and a hotter uncatalysed mixture cannot isolate the catalyst effect without additional controls. The catalyst is regenerated chemically and does not change the overall energy difference between reactants and products. For a reversible reaction it accelerates both directions, helping equilibrium be reached sooner without shifting the equilibrium composition at a fixed temperature.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Catalysts and successful collisions
blocks.text:
Describe the collision-theory explanation for a suitable catalyst increasing rate at fixed temperature.

It lowers activation energy by an alternative pathway, so more collisions are successful.

Checking the response: Lower barrier/pathway (1). Greater fraction of successful collisions (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Catalysts and successful collisions
blocks.text:
Suggest why adding a suitable catalyst speeds a reaction even when the measured temperature stays constant.

Its lower-activation-energy pathway allows more successful collisions without heating the particles.

Checking the response: Its lower-activation-energy pathway allows more successful collisions without heating the particles (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Temperature and collision energy
blocks.text:
Raising temperature increases particles' average kinetic energy. They move faster and collide more frequently, but the especially important effect is that a greater fraction of collisions have enough energy to overcome the activation barrier. Together these changes commonly increase the reaction rate. Lowering temperature reverses these tendencies under comparable conditions.

An explanation should not say that every collision becomes successful or that activation energy itself falls when a mixture is heated. The barrier belongs to the pathway; heating changes the distribution of particle energies. A catalyst, by contrast, changes the pathway. In a controlled experiment, warm reactants to a measured starting temperature and maintain comparable conditions during the reaction. If heat is released or absorbed, the mixture may not stay at its initial temperature, and that is a limitation when comparing trials.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Temperature and collision energy
blocks.text:
Describe why increasing temperature commonly increases reaction rate in collision theory.

Particles move faster, and a larger fraction of collisions exceeds activation energy.

Checking the response: Higher speed/collision frequency (1). Greater fraction above activation energy (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Temperature and collision energy
blocks.text:
Suggest why identical reactant mixtures react faster at 35 °C than at 20 °C under otherwise matched conditions.

At 35 °C a greater fraction of collisions has enough energy to react.

Checking the response: At 35 °C a greater fraction of collisions has enough energy to react (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Light-sensitive reactions
blocks.text:
For a light-sensitive reaction, absorbed light can provide energy needed to initiate chemical change. Increasing suitable illumination may increase the rate when other factors are fixed. Silver chloride darkening in light is an example. This is not simply the same claim as increasing the temperature: absorbed photons can drive a light-dependent process even when bulk temperature is controlled.

Apply the condition explicitly. Light does not accelerate every reaction, and increasing illumination may cease to be the limiting factor. A comparison should control temperature, sample size, exposed area and observation time. Shield one sample as a reference and record the change consistently. If the light source heats the sample, separate that thermal effect before attributing a faster change to illumination. Do not force every rate factor into the phrase more collisions; for light, explain the energy supplied to the relevant photochemical process.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Light-sensitive reactions
blocks.text:
Describe how light can affect a light-sensitive chemical reaction while temperature is controlled.

Absorbed light supplies energy to initiate reaction; suitable stronger illumination can increase the rate.

Checking the response: Light energy input (1). Conditional rate increase for light-sensitive system (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Light-sensitive reactions
blocks.text:
Suggest why a silver chloride sample darkens more quickly in light than an equal sample protected from light at the same temperature.

Light supplies energy for its photochemical decomposition to silver.

Checking the response: Light supplies energy for its photochemical decomposition to silver (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Enzymes
blocks.text:
Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts in organic reactions. They increase rate while being regenerated chemically, but their activity depends on suitable conditions. Their protein structure gives them a functional shape, so the response to temperature cannot be extended indefinitely from the simple rule that heating increases rate.

At sufficiently high temperatures, an enzyme can lose its functional structure and activity. This differs from an inorganic catalyst merely operating faster at a higher temperature. A classroom enzyme investigation should keep enzyme amount, substrate amount and pH comparable when testing temperature. Use controlled observations to distinguish an initial rate change from a loss of activity. The term enzyme identifies a protein catalyst, not the reactant consumed to make the product, and not a source of extra product atoms.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Enzymes
blocks.text:
State the name for proteins that catalyse organic reactions.

Enzymes.

Checking the response: Enzymes (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Combustible dust
blocks.text:
A combustible material dispersed as fine powder has a large exposed surface compared with an equal mass in a compact piece. If suspended in air, much of that surface can contact oxygen. Ignition can then lead to rapid combustion and energy release, creating an explosion hazard in settings such as flour handling or coal dust accumulation. The hazard requires a combustible dust and suitable conditions; not every powder burns.

The chemical explanation connects exposed area, contact with oxygen and rapid reaction. Do not attempt to demonstrate a dust explosion in ordinary learner work. Use teacher-provided observations or diagrams and discuss prevention conceptually, such as avoiding dust accumulation and ignition sources. A pile and a suspended cloud of the same substance need not behave alike because oxygen access differs. This example applies collision reasoning to a real consequence without suggesting that changing particle size changes the chemical identity of the fuel.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Combustible dust
blocks.text:
Describe why a cloud of fine combustible dust can be an explosion hazard when ignited in air.

It exposes a large surface to oxygen, allowing very rapid combustion and energy release.

Checking the response: Large oxygen-contact surface (1). Rapid combustion/energy release (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Combustible dust
blocks.text:
Describe why an equal mass of compact combustible material may burn less rapidly than a dispersed fine powder.

The compact mass exposes less surface to oxygen, so fewer surface reaction events occur per second under comparable conditions.

Checking the response: Smaller exposed area (1). Less rapid surface reaction (1).

blocks.heading: Investigating rate
blocks.text:
Choose a measurable change that follows reaction progress, such as gas collected or mass lost, and record it against time. To investigate acid concentration with carbonate, change concentration while keeping carbonate mass and particle size, acid volume and temperature constant. Use enough acid in each trial to remain in excess if the aim is to compare rates at the same limiting solid amount.

Start timing consistently at mixing, minimise gas lost during assembly, and ensure a collection syringe moves freely. Record several points, repeat trials and compare gradients or average rates over equivalent intervals. A final volume alone cannot establish a rate difference. Identify leaks, timing delay and changing temperature as possible limitations. Eye protection and teacher supervision are needed, and gas must have an unobstructed path into the collection device rather than a rigid sealed container. A fair method explains both what changes and what is held constant.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Investigating rate
blocks.text:
Describe why a final gas volume alone cannot establish reaction rate, even when the measuring cylinder is accurately calibrated.

Rate is volume change per time; accurate final volume says nothing about how long collection took.

Checking the response: Rate requires an elapsed-time measurement (1). Accurate quantity alone cannot distinguish fast and slow production (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Investigating rate
blocks.text:
Describe why carbonate mass and particle size are held constant when investigating acid concentration effects on rate.

Mass can change the total available reactant, while particle size changes exposed area and hence rate independently of concentration.

Checking the response: Mass/amount control (1). Size/surface-area control (1).

blocks.heading: Interpreting rate data
blocks.text:
Read the axis labels before interpreting a rate graph. On a gas-volume against time graph, gradient measures gas production per time, while height measures gas collected. For a mass-remaining graph, the gradient may be negative; its magnitude indicates the speed of loss. Use the physical quantity and unit to explain what the slope means rather than applying a memorised shape without context.

For supplied observations of 18 cm³ at 20 s and 38 cm³ at 60 s, average gas-production rate is (38−18)/(60−20)=0.50 cm³/s. This is an interval average, not necessarily the instantaneous rate at either endpoint. A plateau can support completion of the measured gas evolution, but check for leaks or a blocked collection device before concluding the reaction itself stopped. Compare final amounts only after the curves have levelled off. When one curve is still rising, its latest reading is not yet proven to be its final yield.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Interpreting rate data
blocks.text:
Suggest why a gas-volume curve becomes less steep as a fixed carbonate sample is consumed in excess acid.

Less reactive solid surface remains available, so gas production slows.

Checking the response: Less reactive solid surface remains available, so gas production slows (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-6-P01 (6)
blocks.text:
What does a steeper gradient on a gas-volume against time curve mean?
A. A larger final product amount.
B. The gas is denser.
C. Time has stopped.
D. A higher gas-production rate.

D. A higher gas-production rate. Gradient is change in volume per unit time.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Gradient is change in volume per unit time. Distractor explanations: A: endpoint need not differ. B: density is not shown. C: neither axis indicates stopped time.

Describe two shared features of the chip and powder gas-volume curves in visuals/VIS-6117-6-02.svg. Original synthetic observations: time / s: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120. blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-6-P03 (b)

Average rate=(38−18)/(60−20)=20/40=0.50 cm³/s.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-6-P03 (c)
blocks.text:
State a suitable apparatus for measuring the volume of gas produced by carbonate reacting with excess acid.

A gas syringe with a freely moving plunger.

Gas syringe (1); accept a suitable graduated water-displacement arrangement.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-6-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Plan a teacher-supervised investigation of how dilute hydrochloric acid concentration affects the initial rate of CO2 production from carbonate chips. Include the changed variable, controls, measurements and a comparison supporting a conclusion.

Connect a carbonate reaction flask by a bung and unobstructed delivery tube to a freely moving gas syringe. Vary dilute hydrochloric acid concentration over several stated values, keeping acid volume fixed and acid in excess in every trial. Keep carbonate mass and particle-size range fixed and maintain the same starting temperature. Start the clock consistently on mixing and record gas volume at the same short time intervals. Repeat each concentration and compare mean initial gradients or mean gas volume per equal early interval, with units, to conclude how concentration affects rate. Check for leaks and timing delay; wear eye protection under teacher supervision.

Workable gas-collection method (1). Vary acid concentration explicitly (1). Control carbonate mass and size (1). Control temperature (1). Gas volumes at fixed timed intervals (1). Compare initial rates to form conclusion (1). Accept an equivalent safe mass-loss method with timed measurements and appropriate controls; maximum six marks.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-27 — Comparing rates with dilute acid
blocks.text: Under teacher supervision, react equal masses of carbonate chips with equal volumes of dilute acid at several concentrations, each chosen to leave acid in excess. Collect carbon dioxide in a gas syringe and record volume at fixed intervals, starting consistently at mixing. Keep particle-size range and temperature constant. Plot volume against time and compare early gradients; the larger gradient indicates faster measured gas production. Repeat trials to judge spread and check for leakage or delayed collection. A metal–acid alternative produces hydrogen, so ignition sources must be excluded and product identity distinguished. Keep the gas outlet unobstructed. Explain a concentration effect by particle encounters rather than claiming that a larger endpoint alone proves a faster reaction.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-29 — Two catalyst demonstrations
blocks.text: In a teacher-supervised comparison, manganese(IV) oxide increases oxygen evolution from hydrogen peroxide compared with a matched control. Record gas production over equal intervals; the catalyst is regenerated, and the reaction is 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. A separate teacher demonstration uses a cobalt(II) salt to catalyse oxidation of tartaric acid or tartrate by hydrogen peroxide. A pink-to-green-to-pink sequence and faster gas evolution illustrate temporary participation followed by regeneration; the returning colour supports, but alone does not prove, chemical regeneration. This needs peroxide as a reacting substance rather than heating tartaric acid alone. Compare matched starting mixtures and temperatures; use recorded observations where suitable facilities are unavailable. The cobalt demonstration includes carbon dioxide and oxygen evolution, so bubbling is not a specific gas test. The observation sequence is checked against the [University of Western Australia teaching guide](https://www.uwa.edu.au/science/-/media/Faculties/Science/Docs/Teacher-Guide---Controlling-reactions.pdf). Detailed intermediate structures are outside this lesson.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Connect this topic to particle models, stoichiometry and electrochemistry. Keep energy direction, collision rate and equilibrium composition distinct; interpret each using the stated conditions and measured quantity.

blocks.heading: Choosing measuring apparatus
blocks.text:
Choose apparatus by the quantity, required precision and practical conditions. Use a stopwatch for time, a suitable thermometer for temperature and a balance for mass. A measuring cylinder is useful for approximate liquid volumes over a range; a volumetric pipette delivers one specified volume more precisely when used correctly. A burette delivers variable volumes found from the difference between its initial and final readings.

A beaker can hold, mix or heat a liquid, but its coarse markings usually make it unsuitable for an accurate titration volume. Read a burette with its tip filled and free of air bubbles, and use the bottom of the meniscus for a clear aqueous solution. The scale usually increases downwards. Use a pipette filler, not mouth suction. Choosing a more precise instrument is useful only if the technique matches it: an incorrectly read burette can still give a poor result. Gas volume can be measured with a suitable gas syringe or collected over water when the gas does not dissolve significantly under the collection conditions.

blocks.heading: Temperature ranges and mixtures
blocks.text:
A pure substance has a characteristic melting point and, at a stated pressure, a characteristic boiling point. Many mixtures melt or boil over a range because their components do not all change state under the same conditions. A sample beginning to melt at 78 °C and finishing at 84 °C behaves differently from a pure reference that melts sharply near 80 °C.

Use the range as evidence rather than assuming that one observed temperature settles identity. The heating rate, thermometer position, pressure and instrument uncertainty affect the measurement. A mixture's boiling behaviour can change as its composition changes during distillation; the more volatile component may be removed first. A narrow range supports purity, but experimental resolution limits what can be detected, and some mixtures have special behaviour. At this level, use the general distinction without claiming that a sharp reading proves the absence of every impurity. Compare like conditions and record both the start and completion of melting where relevant.

blocks.heading: Using melting and boiling points as evidence
blocks.text:
Compare a measured melting or boiling point with an appropriate reference under the same conditions. A sharp melting point close to the reference supports the conclusion that the sample is relatively pure and may be that substance. A shifted or broadened melting range can indicate impurities. For boiling measurements, pressure matters, so a reference at a different pressure may not be directly comparable.

Identity and purity are related questions but not identical. Two substances can have similar physical constants; further tests may be needed to distinguish them. A poorly positioned thermometer can also produce an inaccurate reading, so investigate apparatus before attributing every difference to the sample. Record the full observation rather than selecting the temperature closest to the expected value. In a simple identification problem, choose the candidate whose characteristic value and state-change behaviour match the evidence, but avoid claiming proof beyond the available tests.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Using melting and boiling points as evidence
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Why purity matters in everyday substances
blocks.text:
Purity matters when the composition of a substance affects its purpose or safety. An unwanted substance in food or medicine can introduce harmful material, change taste or stability, or alter the intended dose. A medicine containing less active ingredient than its labelled amount may not provide the expected treatment; a harmful contaminant creates a different problem. This is why composition needs checking rather than assuming that a clean appearance proves purity.

In laboratory work, impurities can change measured melting points, cause unexpected reactions or distort a mass used in a calculation. The required purity depends on the use: drinking water contains dissolved minerals and is not chemically pure water, yet it can meet its intended safety requirements. Distinguish chemical purity from suitability for use. A substance need not be a single pure chemical to be useful, but its composition and contaminants must be appropriate for the application. Purification methods are chosen using the physical properties of both the wanted substance and the impurities.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Why purity matters in everyday substances
blocks.text:

They help confirm the intended amount of active ingredient and detect harmful contaminants.

Checking the response: Credit correct active-ingredient content as one required property (1). Credit absence or controlled level of harmful contamination as the second (1).

blocks.heading: Filtration and selective dissolving
blocks.text:
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a fluid using a porous barrier. The liquid and dissolved substances pass through as the filtrate; the insoluble solid is retained as the residue. This distinction is essential: filtering a salt solution does not normally remove the dissolved salt. The dissolved particles pass through with the solvent.

To separate a mixture of soluble salt and insoluble sand, add a suitable amount of water and stir to dissolve the salt. Filter the mixture so that sand remains on the paper and salt solution passes into a clean vessel. Washing the residue with a little water can transfer remaining salt solution into the filtrate. If the salt is wanted, recover it from the filtrate by a suitable crystallisation method. If the sand is wanted, wash and dry the residue. State which substance is being collected; otherwise a technically correct method can end with the wrong fraction. The choice of solvent depends on differential solubility, not simply on which liquid is most convenient.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Filtration and selective dissolving
blocks.text:

Keep the filtrate because the salt remains dissolved; evaporate some water and cool the concentrated filtrate to obtain crystals.

Checking the response: Retain salt-containing filtrate rather than sand residue (1). Concentrate then cool that filtrate to crystallise salt (1).
