blocks.heading: Crystallisation and re-crystallisation
blocks.text:
Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid by forming crystals from its solution. Gently evaporate some solvent to concentrate the solution, then allow it to cool so that crystals form. Separate the crystals from the remaining solution and dry them appropriately. Do not assume that heating to complete dryness is suitable: some substances decompose or lose water from their crystal structure when overheated.

Re-crystallisation uses a suitable solvent in which the wanted solid is more soluble when hot than when cold. Dissolve the impure solid in a small amount of hot solvent, remove insoluble impurities by filtration when appropriate, then cool the solution. The wanted material crystallises while some soluble impurities remain in the mother liquor. Wash crystals with a small amount of cold solvent to remove adhering solution while limiting product loss. Using too much solvent may leave too much product dissolved. Purification and yield can compete, so describe both the purpose of the steps and which fraction contains the product.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Crystallisation and re-crystallisation
blocks.text:

Cool the concentrated solution to crystallise the salt; separate crystals and rinse with a small amount of cold water.

Checking the response: Cool rather than boil completely dry (1). Small cold rinse limits dissolution, rather than a large hot rinse (1).

blocks.heading: Paper chromatography of coloured mixtures
blocks.text:
Paper chromatography separates dissolved components because they move at different rates with a solvent through the paper. Draw a pencil baseline near the bottom and place a small concentrated sample spot on it. Let the spot dry. Stand the paper in a small depth of solvent with the starting spot above the solvent surface, and cover the container where appropriate to limit evaporation.

As the solvent rises, components distribute differently between the paper and the moving solvent, so their spots travel different distances. Remove the paper before the solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front promptly, before it evaporates. A sample giving several separated spots contains several detectable components under those conditions. One spot is not absolute proof of purity, because components can overlap or fail to be visible. Pencil is used because an ink baseline might itself dissolve and separate. Compare samples and references on the same chromatogram or under closely matched solvent and paper conditions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Paper chromatography of coloured mixtures
blocks.text:

Raise the spotted baseline above the solvent and replace the ink line with pencil.

Checking the response: Baseline/sample above solvent to avoid loss into the reservoir (1). Pencil instead of soluble ink to avoid extra spots (1).

blocks.heading: Simple distillation
blocks.text:
Simple distillation can recover a volatile solvent from a solution containing a non-volatile dissolved solid. Heat the solution so that solvent vapour leaves the flask, then cool that vapour in a condenser and collect the liquid distillate. The dissolved solid remains mainly in the original vessel under the intended conditions. Evaporation alone would lose the solvent to the surroundings rather than collect it.

Place the thermometer bulb where it measures the vapour entering the condenser, rather than immersing it unnecessarily in the boiling mixture. Run cooling water into the lower condenser port and out through the upper port so the jacket fills effectively. Keep the apparatus open to the atmosphere through its normal outlet; a sealed heated system can build pressure. Use controlled heating and suitable anti-bumping precautions under supervision. Distillation separates by volatility; it does not guarantee that every volatile impurity has been removed. Choosing the method requires knowing whether the wanted material is the solvent, a solute or one of several volatile liquids.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Simple distillation
blocks.text:

Checking the response: Vaporisation followed by condensation accounts for recovered liquid (1). Non-volatile salt remains in the original vessel (1).

blocks.heading: Fractional distillation
blocks.text:
Fractional distillation separates a mixture of miscible liquids with different volatilities more effectively than simple distillation when their boiling points are relatively close. A fractionating column provides repeated vaporisation and condensation. Vapour travelling up the column becomes richer in the more volatile component, while less volatile material tends to condense and return towards the flask.

Collect fractions over appropriate temperature ranges rather than assuming that the first drop is completely pure. The temperature and composition change as distillation proceeds. The column increases separation through repeated equilibrations; it is not a filter that catches larger molecules. The method is used in contexts such as separating products from fermented mixtures and separating crude-oil fractions, which are taught in Organic Chemistry. Crude-oil fractions are themselves mixtures with boiling ranges. Choose fractional distillation when the task requires separating volatile miscible components, and use a suitable safe heating method when flammable liquids are involved.

blocks.heading: Selecting a separation method from properties
blocks.text:
Choose a separation method by identifying the physical difference that can be used. Insolubility supports filtration; a difference in solubility in a chosen solvent supports selective dissolving; formation of crystals on cooling supports crystallisation; different movement through paper supports chromatography; and different volatility supports distillation. The method must also recover the material that the task actually asks for.

For a salt-and-sand mixture, filtration alone is not enough before a solvent is added: both components begin as solids. Dissolve the salt, filter away sand and recover the salt from solution if it is wanted. If water is the wanted product, distillation is more appropriate than evaporating it away. A multi-step method should follow the changing state and location of each substance. State the assumptions given by the task, such as salt being soluble in water and sand being insoluble. A method name without this connection can hide the wrong reasoning. Purification is an application of properties rather than a list of interchangeable procedures.

blocks.heading: Choosing gas-collection and rate apparatus
blocks.text:
A gas syringe measures gas volume directly if it moves freely, has sufficient capacity and is connected without leaks. Collection over water can be suitable when the gas is not appreciably soluble in water under the experiment's conditions. A gas that dissolves readily in water would give a misleadingly small collected volume by that method. Choose a method using the stated gas properties rather than using the same setup for every gas.

Rate measurements can follow gas volume against time, mass loss against time or a visible endpoint, depending on the reaction. The selected quantity must change detectably and relate to the process being investigated. Read the syringe at fixed intervals using a stopwatch and record the initial volume. Keep tubing secure without blocking the outlet, and avoid a sealed rigid system in which gas pressure can build. A balance can monitor mass loss when gas escapes, but splashing or evaporation of other material can confuse the result. The apparatus choice therefore includes both a measurable response and control of competing effects.

blocks.heading: Locating colourless chromatogram spots
blocks.text:
A colourless substance may separate on chromatography paper without producing visible spots. After the chromatogram is developed and the solvent front is marked, a suitable locating agent can reveal the positions of the separated substances. The locating treatment makes the pattern visible; it does not replace the separation stage or change the distances already measured from the baseline.

Use only a locating procedure appropriate to the substances and the supervised method. The syllabus does not require the identities of particular locating agents, so the important reasoning is when they are used and why. Mark the solvent front promptly because it can become invisible as solvent evaporates. Once spots have been revealed, measure from the same baseline to the spot centres and the front. Do not infer that no substance was present merely because the untreated paper appeared blank. Visibility depends on the detection method, while movement depends on the chromatography conditions. Compare unknown spots with suitable references under the same conditions.

Mark the solvent front before it disappears, then apply a suitable locating treatment to reveal colourless components.

Checking the response: Mark the wet solvent front promptly (1). Locate colourless spots with a suitable treatment (1).

blocks.heading: Interpreting spots and calculating Rf
blocks.text:
The retention factor Rf is the distance travelled by the substance divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front, both measured from the same baseline. Measure to the centre of a spot and use compatible distance units. A spot 3.0 cm above the baseline with a solvent front 6.0 cm above it has Rf = 0.50. The units cancel, so Rf has no unit.

Use the actual distance travelled, not the spot's height above the bottom edge of the paper. If the baseline is 1 cm above the bottom, that offset must be excluded from both travel distances. Under the intended chromatography conditions, a spot carried by the solvent front has an Rf between zero and one. A calculated value above one suggests a distance or reference error. Matching Rf values support identification when the same paper, solvent and conditions are used, but do not give an unconditional identity guarantee. Several components may overlap. Comparing unknown and known samples on the same sheet provides a stronger controlled comparison than comparing values from different solvent systems.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Interpreting spots and calculating Rf
blocks.text:

Spot travel = 3.6 cm and front travel = 6.0 cm; Rf = 0.60.

Checking the response: Subtract baseline height from both readings (1). Rf = 3.6/6.0 = 0.60, no unit (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical — Crystallisation from solution
blocks.text: Under teacher supervision, gently concentrate a salt solution without boiling it dry. Allow it to cool, then separate and dry the crystals. Record when crystals first appear and compare their appearance with the starting solution. Use a small cold-solvent wash to reduce adhering impurities; explain why a large hot wash could reduce yield.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical — Distillation of a fermented sample
blocks.text: Use a teacher-prepared fermented sample with supervised apparatus and a suitable non-flame heating method. Record vapour temperature as distillate is collected. Explain the roles of the condenser and fractionating column where used. Do not taste the distillate or assume it is pure or safe; the task is to interpret separation by volatility.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical — Filtration of muddy water
blocks.text: Stir a prepared water-and-sand mixture, then filter it through paper in a funnel. Record the retained residue and clarity of the filtrate. Explain why removing suspended solid does not establish that water is safe to drink: dissolved material and microorganisms may remain.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical — Chromatography of coloured substances
blocks.text: Place small coloured-sample spots and a reference on a pencil baseline. Keep the starting spots above the solvent and develop the chromatogram under supervision. Mark the solvent front, count separated spots and measure their baseline distances. Calculate Rf values and compare references under the same conditions; avoid claiming that a single spot proves complete purity.

blocks.heading: Precision, accuracy and uncertainty
blocks.text:
Precision describes how closely repeated results agree; accuracy describes closeness to an accepted value. Uncertainty expresses the range within which a measurement is reasonably judged to lie. A fine scale division may reduce reading uncertainty, but it does not guarantee that the instrument is correctly calibrated. Three readings near 10.5 g can be precise while inaccurate if the accepted mass is 10.0 g.

Record measured values to a resolution justified by the instrument. A scale marked every 1 cm³ does not normally justify a reading with many decimal places. Keep enough intermediate digits in calculations, then round the final result appropriately. Leading zeros locate the decimal point but are not significant figures; in 0.00450, the digits 4, 5 and the final zero express three significant figures. Do not confuse significant figures with decimal places. When comparing results, consider whether a small difference is meaningful relative to uncertainty. A difference smaller than the measurement uncertainty does not justify a strong claim of a real physical change.

blocks.heading: Processing results and investigating anomalies
blocks.text:
Process results in a way that answers the question: calculate changes, means or rates only after preserving the original readings. An anomalous result lies unexpectedly far from a consistent pattern or cluster. It is a reason to investigate the method and repeat a measurement, not a reason to delete an inconvenient value without explanation.

Suppose repeated times are 30, 31, 58 and 30 s. The 58 s result deserves attention, but the list alone does not prove its cause. A delayed start, a changed reactant quantity or a genuine variable effect may need checking. Record what was found and state whether the suspect result was retained or excluded when calculating a mean. Repeating under controlled conditions provides evidence for that decision. Keep uncertainty and precision in view: a difference of 0.1 s is not necessarily anomalous when manual timing varies by much more. A trend can also be non-linear, so a point should be compared with the appropriate pattern rather than an assumed straight line.

Check the method and original record for a possible error, then repeat the measurement under the same controlled conditions before deciding how to treat the result.

Checking the response: Credit investigating the anomalous result rather than silently deleting it (1). Credit a controlled repeat as the next method step (1).

blocks.heading: Drawing a conclusion that the data support
blocks.text:
A conclusion connects the results to the investigation's aim or hypothesis. State the observed relationship, refer to the relevant measurements and explain it using chemistry where possible. If increasing a controlled solution temperature reduces the time to collect a fixed gas volume, the data support a faster reaction over the tested range. They do not prove that the same relationship holds at every possible temperature.

Check whether alternative explanations remain. If particle size changed alongside temperature, the effect cannot confidently be attributed to temperature alone. Repeats and uncertainty help judge how strong the evidence is. A conclusion can report that the data are insufficient or inconsistent; it need not force agreement with the original prediction. Separate what the measurements show from the model used to explain them. “The time fell from 60 to 35 s” is evidence; a collision-based explanation interprets that evidence. A valid conclusion should not claim a finer difference or wider scope than the experiment can support.

Checking the response: Credit comparison of the measured results (1). Credit the shorter-time/higher-rate interpretation with a fair method (1).

blocks.heading: Random and systematic errors
blocks.text:
Random errors cause results to vary unpredictably around a value. Manual reaction timing can vary because the observer starts or stops slightly differently on each trial. Repeats can reveal this scatter and averaging can reduce its influence on the estimated result. A systematic error shifts results consistently, as when a balance reads 0.3 g with nothing on it or a scale is incorrectly calibrated.

Identify an error in relation to the actual measurement. “Human error” is too vague to explain a result or propose a repair. State which action or instrument feature affects which reading and whether it tends to increase, decrease or scatter the values. A consistent viewing angle can introduce a directional parallax bias; variable viewing can contribute to scatter. Some errors depend on conditions, so distinguish the observed symptom from an assumed cause. Repeating a biased procedure does not remove the bias. Correct the zero, calibrate against an appropriate reference or improve the method, then repeat to evaluate the change.

blocks.heading: Choosing an improvement that addresses the error
blocks.text:
An improvement should remove or reduce a named limitation in the method. If results scatter because of manual timing, repeat trials or use a more consistent timing trigger. If a gas syringe leaks, repair the connection and test its seal; averaging more leaking trials will not recover the lost gas. If an instrument has a zero offset, zero or calibrate it rather than merely repeating the measurement.

Explain why the proposed change improves the particular quantity. Reading a meniscus at eye level reduces parallax; using an instrument with finer divisions can reduce reading uncertainty. A larger sample may reduce the percentage uncertainty of a fixed absolute uncertainty, but the method must still be safe and within the apparatus capacity. Improvements can affect different qualities: repeats mainly assess repeatability and random scatter, while calibration addresses accuracy. Do not promise that a change makes a measurement exact. State the limitation it reduces and how the revised results would be checked.

blocks.heading: Observing and handling apparatus safely
blocks.text:
An observation records what is detected or measured; an inference explains what it might mean. “Bubbles formed” is an observation. “Hydrogen formed” is an inference that requires an appropriate gas test or other evidence. Record colour, state, temperature and changes with enough detail to distinguish possibilities. A blue solid settling in a liquid is not the same observation as a blue solution.

Choose a technique that matches the quantity. Put a measuring cylinder upright on a level surface and view a concave meniscus at eye level. Read the bottom of the meniscus rather than the top edge. A sloping view gives parallax error. Support hot apparatus securely, use eye protection where required, and follow the teacher's instructions for reagents and heating. Never taste a laboratory sample or use a mouth to fill a pipette. Safety is part of a valid method: a badly supported vessel can spill material and invalidate the measurement as well as cause injury. Record the observation immediately rather than reconstructing it from memory after later steps.

blocks.heading: Separating the variables in a fair comparison
blocks.text:
The independent variable is deliberately changed. The dependent variable is the response measured. Control variables are other factors kept sufficiently constant to make the comparison meaningful. In a rate investigation, solution temperature might be the independent variable and the volume of gas produced in 30 s the dependent variable. Reactant quantities, concentration, chip size and apparatus could need controlling.

Naming a variable is not the same as explaining how it is controlled. “Keep temperature constant” becomes a workable instruction when the method says to use a water bath at a stated temperature and allow the solutions to reach that temperature before mixing. Choose a measurable response: “amount of reaction” is too vague unless it is defined as gas volume, mass change or another quantity. A control variable can become the independent variable in a different investigation; these labels describe its role in the particular method, not an unchanging property of the quantity. Changing temperature and concentration together makes it difficult to decide which caused an observed rate difference.

blocks.heading: Aims, hypotheses and predictions
blocks.text:
An aim states the question that the investigation will answer. A hypothesis proposes a testable relationship or explanation. A prediction states an expected observation if that hypothesis is correct. For example, the aim could be to investigate how powder size affects reaction rate. A hypothesis could link greater exposed surface to more frequent reacting collisions. The prediction would be that a fine powder produces a fixed gas volume in less time than equal-mass large chips under otherwise matched conditions.

Write a prediction before examining the results. It should name the quantities and the direction of change, so that the measurements can support or challenge it. “The reaction will be better” cannot be tested clearly; “the time to collect 20 cm³ will decrease” can. A result that differs from the prediction is useful evidence, not permission to rewrite the original hypothesis unnoticed. First consider method limitations and repeatable results, then revise the explanation where justified. The aim, chosen measurements and final conclusion should address the same relationship.

blocks.heading: Fairness, repeats and zero readings
blocks.text:
A fair comparison changes the intended factor while controlling other influential conditions. Repeatability asks whether the same method gives similar results when repeated. Accuracy concerns closeness to an accepted or true value. These ideas support each other but are not interchangeable: a balance with a zero error can give repeated readings that agree closely yet are all too high.

Before measuring, check the instrument's initial reading. An empty balance should read zero or be tared with the sample container in place. If the empty container is not tared, subtract its mass from the combined reading. A gas syringe can start above zero, provided that the initial reading is recorded and subtracted from the final one. Do not silently assume zero. Repeating the same biased measurement does not remove its bias. If a measuring instrument shows a consistent offset, correct its setup or apply a justified correction. Controls establish comparability, repeats reveal random variation, and zero checks help prevent systematic error.

blocks.heading: Length, area and volume scale differently
blocks.text:
Length measures one dimension, area measures two and volume measures three. Their units therefore change differently. Because 1 m = 100 cm, a square metre is 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm². A cubic metre is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = 1 000 000 cm³. Applying a length conversion factor just once to an area or volume gives a large error.

For similarly shaped objects, multiplying every length by a factor k multiplies area by k² and volume by k³. A cube with twice the edge length has four times the surface area but eight times the volume. The surface-area-to-volume ratio therefore decreases as the cube becomes larger. This helps explain why breaking a solid into smaller pieces can expose more surface for reaction without increasing its total mass. Keep geometric reasoning separate from changing the amount of substance: cutting a cube creates extra exposed surfaces, whereas increasing its edge length creates a larger object.

blocks.heading: SI units and metric prefixes
blocks.text:
Use the unit appropriate to the quantity. The SI units relevant here include metre for length, kilogram for mass, second for time, kelvin for temperature and mole for amount of substance. Derived units combine these: volume is measured in m³ and speed in m/s. Laboratory measurements also commonly use g, cm³ and dm³, provided the unit is stated and conversions are made correctly.

Prefixes multiply a unit by a power of ten: tera T is 10¹²; giga G, 10⁹; mega M, 10⁶; kilo k, 10³; deci d, 10⁻¹; centi c, 10⁻²; milli m, 10⁻³; micro μ, 10⁻⁶; nano n, 10⁻⁹; and pico p, 10⁻¹². Letter case matters: M and m indicate different factors. A milligram is 0.001 g, not 0.001 kg. First convert the prefixed quantity to its stated base unit, then make any further conversion. A cubic prefix applies in three dimensions: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³. The conversion of solution volumes is especially important in concentration calculations.

blocks.heading: Writing numbers in scientific notation
blocks.text:
Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient between one and ten multiplied by an integer power of ten. Thus 4500 is 4.5 × 10³ and 0.0045 is 4.5 × 10⁻³. Count how far the decimal point moves and choose the sign that reproduces the original size. A positive exponent describes a large multiplier; a negative one a fraction.

Scientific notation makes significant figures clearer. The expression 4.50 × 10³ explicitly gives three significant figures, whereas a bare 4500 may be ambiguous about the significance of the trailing zeros. For a calculation, combine the coefficients and powers separately, then adjust the final coefficient if it is outside the standard range. For instance, 12 × 10³ becomes 1.2 × 10⁴. Do not discard the unit: 4.5 × 10⁻³ g and 4.5 × 10⁻³ kg are different masses. A calculator's E display is a compact power-of-ten notation, not a separate physical unit.

blocks.heading: Writing compound units
blocks.text:
A compound unit shows how quantities combine. Metres per second can be written m/s or m s⁻¹. The exponent −1 means “per second”, not a negative time. Similarly, cm³/s is a volume-production rate, whereas cm³ alone is a volume. Use spacing and brackets to make the meaning clear when several units are involved.

In table and graph labels, a form such as distance / cm says that the numerical entries are distances expressed in centimetres. A rate axis might read gas-production rate / cm³ s⁻¹. Do not write cm/s when the measured response is a gas volume: the missing cube changes the physical quantity. Unit checking can expose an incorrect relationship even when the arithmetic looks tidy. Dividing a volume by a time produces a volume-per-time unit; multiplying the same quantities would not give a rate. Keep symbols consistent across a task so that a reader does not have to guess whether different labels describe the same quantity.

blocks.heading: Absolute zero and the Kelvin scale
blocks.text:
Absolute zero is the zero point of the thermodynamic temperature scale: 0 K corresponds to −273.15 °C. A temperature interval of one kelvin is the same size as an interval of one degree Celsius, but the two scales have different zero points. The kelvin is written K, without a degree symbol.

A room temperature near 20 °C is therefore near 293 K, not 20 K. Celsius temperatures below zero are common, but a negative Celsius reading is not a negative Kelvin reading. At this level, use absolute zero as the lower endpoint of the Kelvin scale; do not describe it as every kind of microscopic motion completely stopping. The scale is useful because it refers temperatures to an absolute zero rather than to the Celsius reference point. Temperature is distinct from heat transferred: an amount of energy is measured in joules, not kelvin. Converting a temperature scale changes the numerical label, not the physical state or warmth of the sample.

Checking the response: 0 K (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Converting between Celsius and kelvin
blocks.text:
Add 273.15 to a Celsius temperature to obtain the corresponding Kelvin temperature. Subtract 273.15 to convert in the other direction. Thus 20.00 °C corresponds to 293.15 K. The conversion is an offset, not multiplication by a scale factor. Writing the formula before the substitution helps avoid multiplying by 273.15 or choosing the wrong direction.

The temperature change between two states has the same numerical value on both scales. Heating a sample from 20 °C to 30 °C is an increase of 10 °C or 10 K. The initial temperatures are not numerically the same, but the offset cancels when taking their difference. Follow the precision of the supplied data: adding a conversion constant does not create extra experimental accuracy. If a question specifies the approximate conversion 273, use that stated convention; otherwise retain the syllabus value 273.15. These conversions are mathematical temperature-scale work and do not require gas laws.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these methods when calculating solution quantities in Stoichiometry, interpreting reactions in Chemical reactions, and evaluating laboratory methods in Practical skills and investigation planning.

blocks.heading: Arithmetic with measured quantities
blocks.text:
Choose the operation from the physical meaning of the quantities. Add portions to obtain a total, subtract a starting reading from a final reading to obtain a change, multiply a rate by its duration to obtain an amount, and divide an amount by a duration to obtain an average rate. For example, a gas syringe changes from 8 cm³ to 32 cm³: the gas collected during that interval is 24 cm³, not 32 cm³. If the interval lasts 12 s, the average production rate is 2 cm³/s. A rate is a ratio; it is not an extra volume.

Convert quantities to compatible units before adding or subtracting them. Adding 0.050 dm³ to 20 cm³ means adding 50 cm³ to 20 cm³. Keep the working line with the numbers and their units so that another person can reconstruct the calculation. Brackets preserve the intended order: subtract the two syringe readings before dividing by time. Intermediate values should retain enough digits to avoid introducing rounding errors. Check the magnitude: a collected volume cannot exceed the final reading if the initial reading is positive. These arithmetic habits support reacting quantities, concentration and experimental rates later in the course.

Checking the response: Subtract initial reading and injected air: (34.0 − 7.0) − 3.0 (1). 24.0 cm³ reaction gas (1).

blocks.heading: Means, fractions, percentages and ratios
blocks.text:
An arithmetic mean is the sum of comparable readings divided by their number. Three volumes of 19.8, 20.0 and 20.2 cm³ give a mean of 20.0 cm³. Repeated measurements should refer to the same conditions; averaging results from different temperatures would conceal the effect being investigated. A mean can reduce the influence of random variation, but it cannot repair an instrument that reads too high on every trial.

A fraction compares a part with a whole. Convert it to a percentage by multiplying by 100. If 18 g of a 24 g sample is the wanted substance, the fraction is 18/24 = 0.75 and the percentage is 75%. State what the denominator represents: using impurity mass instead of total sample mass answers a different question. A ratio such as 2:3 specifies relative amounts; five equal shares make the total. The reciprocal of a value x is 1/x, so the reciprocal of 4 s is 0.25 s⁻¹. Reciprocals reverse the unit as well as the number. Decimals, fractions and percentages can describe the same proportion, but they must not be interchanged without conversion.

blocks.heading: Direct and inverse proportion
blocks.text:
Two quantities are directly proportional when multiplying one by a factor multiplies the other by the same factor, with the other relevant conditions unchanged. The ratio y/x is then constant. At fixed solution concentration, doubling the solution volume doubles the dissolved amount. A graph of y against x for direct proportion is a straight line through the origin; a straight line with a non-zero intercept represents a different relationship.

For inverse proportion, increasing one quantity by a factor decreases the other by that factor, so their product is constant. If a fixed quantity of material is processed at twice the constant rate, the required time is halved. Do not assume that every decreasing graph is inverse proportion: the product must remain constant. First identify the fixed quantity, then write the relationship and substitute the new value. A useful direction check is whether the result moves as expected. Requiring more time at a faster rate, while the amount remains unchanged, signals that the proportional relationship has been reversed. These examples concern numerical reasoning, not gas-law calculations outside the syllabus.

blocks.heading: Powers of ten and indices
blocks.text:
An index tells us how many times a factor is multiplied by itself. Thus 10³ is 1000, while 10⁻³ is 1/1000. A negative index does not make a quantity negative: 2 × 10⁻³ g is a small positive mass. For the same base, multiplication adds indices and division subtracts them. Therefore 10³ × 10⁻² = 10¹, while 10³/10⁻² = 10⁵. The coefficient is handled separately from the power of ten.

Brackets matter when a whole quantity is raised to a power: (2 × 10³)² is 4 × 10⁶. The square applies to both the coefficient and the power. The zeroth power of a non-zero number is one. Scientific calculators may show E−3 instead of ×10⁻³; these are alternative displays of the same numerical value. Enter a negative exponent using the calculator's exponent controls rather than interpreting it as subtraction from the coefficient. Estimate the size before accepting a display: multiplying two small positive quantities should not produce a very large answer.

blocks.heading: Estimating before calculating
blocks.text:
An estimate is a deliberately simplified calculation used to check order of magnitude. Round awkward values to nearby convenient values, perform the arithmetic mentally, and compare the estimate with the detailed calculation. For example, 19.7/4.9 is close to 20/5, which is 4. An exact calculator result near 4 is plausible; one near 40 suggests an entry or decimal-place error. An estimate is not a replacement for a requested precise calculation.

Choose rounding that preserves the overall size. Rounding every value upward does not necessarily round the result upward, because a larger denominator makes a quotient smaller. State the rounded expression so that the approximation is visible. When estimating a product, each coefficient and power of ten still contributes: 0.020 × 300 is approximately 6, not 6000. The unit remains attached to the physical quantity even though its value is approximate. Use estimates to catch errors before rounding a final answer. A final answer with many decimal places can still be wrong if its scale is implausible.

blocks.heading: Rearranging a relationship
blocks.text:
In x = yz, x is the product of y and z. To find y, divide both sides by z; to find z, divide both sides by y. The operation must be applied to the whole side, not just one term chosen from it. For a laboratory example, mass = density × volume gives volume = mass/density. Substituting units gives g/(g/cm³) = cm³, which checks the rearrangement.

Write the symbolic rearrangement before inserting numbers. This makes it easier to see whether the unknown belongs in a numerator or denominator and avoids a calculator sequence hiding an algebra mistake. If mass is 15 g and density is 3 g/cm³, volume is 5 cm³. Multiplying mass by density would produce neither the right number nor the right unit. After solving, substitute the result into the original relationship: 3 × 5 gives the stated mass of 15. The original equation, worked substitution and unit together provide a more reliable check than the number alone.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Use these methods when calculating solution quantities in Stoichiometry, interpreting reactions in Chemical reactions, and evaluating laboratory methods in Practical skills and investigation planning.

blocks.heading: Selecting and organising evidence
blocks.text:
Use information that answers the investigation question. A table of temperatures and reaction times is relevant to a temperature-rate investigation; a list of apparatus prices is not evidence of the rate. Keep sources, conditions and units attached for traceability. Data from different methods should not be combined without checking whether they measure the same thing under comparable conditions.

When selecting information, distinguish a direct measurement from a calculated value or someone else's interpretation. Organise comparable results into a consistent table rather than copying them into an unstructured paragraph. For example, convert all volumes to the same unit before comparing samples. Keep unusual readings in the original record even if they are later investigated as anomalies. A transparent record explains why each source was selected or rejected. Do not select just results agreeing with the prediction.

Checking the response: Dataset A: temperature is varied while the other stated factors are controlled (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Recording complete experimental results
blocks.text:
A results record should preserve the measurements needed to answer the question. Write the readings as they are made, including the independent-variable setting, response, units and repeat number. A table is useful for exact values; a graph helps reveal a trend or compare patterns. Record the original readings before calculating means, changes or rates. Otherwise a later arithmetic mistake may be impossible to trace.

Units tell the reader which physical quantity a number represents and how large it is. A bare value of 25 could mean seconds, degrees Celsius or cubic centimetres. Use a consistent number of decimal places for repeated readings from the same instrument when its resolution supports that convention. Record a qualitative observation clearly alongside the relevant trial, such as cloudiness or a persistent precipitate. Do not replace an unexpected measurement with the value that seems more likely. Make a note, investigate and repeat if needed; retain the original evidence.

blocks.heading: Quantity-and-unit headings
blocks.text:
A table heading names the quantity and its unit, for example time / s or mass / g. The numerical entries then contain values without repeating the unit in each cell. This makes the table easier to scan and avoids ambiguous mixtures of notation. Use specific names such as initial burette reading / cm³ and final burette reading / cm³ rather than two columns both labelled volume.

A column of calculated values also needs a heading: average rate / cm³ s⁻¹ distinguishes a rate from a collected volume. Do not confuse the solidus in a heading with an instruction to divide each recorded measurement again. It expresses the unit in which the numerical values are given. State a changed unit in the heading before entering converted data. If a time column is labelled min, a value of 30 s must appear as 0.50 rather than 30. An unambiguous heading is part of the evidence, not decorative formatting.

blocks.heading: Turning a table into a graph
blocks.text:
Use the table headings to label graph axes with quantities and units. The independent variable normally goes on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis. Choose scales that spread the data across a substantial part of the grid and use equal numerical intervals at equal distances. A graph scale must not change halfway along an axis simply to fit an inconvenient point.

Plot each pair of values as a small clear cross or point. Decide whether the pattern supports a straight best-fit line or a smooth curve; joining every point with sharp segments may exaggerate random variation. A best-fit line is not required to pass through every point, and an intercept should not be forced to zero unless the relationship supports that choice. To read an intermediate value, move from the specified horizontal coordinate to the line and then to the vertical scale. Marking the two read-off directions helps distinguish interpolation from simply quoting the nearest measured point.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.4.jso.title: 10.4 — describe alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n

blocks.heading: Alkenes and unsaturation
blocks.text:
Alkenes in this course are open-chain hydrocarbons containing one carbon–carbon double bond. Their general formula is CnH2n. Ethene CH2=CH2 is the smallest member; one carbon cannot make a carbon–carbon double bond by itself. Propene CH2=CHCH3 and the butenes extend the same family. Unsaturation refers to the C=C bond and the possibility of addition reactions, not to a shortage of solvent.

A double bond counts twice toward carbon's valency of four. In ethene each carbon is bonded twice to the other carbon and once to each of two hydrogens. In propene the middle carbon has a double bond, a single carbon bond and one hydrogen bond. Draw those connections explicitly when asked for a displayed formula. Replacing a double bond by a single bond makes one further bond available at each of its two carbons; this is the structural basis for addition. Do not leave the double bond in an addition product while also attaching extra atoms: that would give some carbons too many bonds. The general formula should be applied only within the stated open-chain, single-double-bond family.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Alkenes and unsaturation
blocks.text:
Describe why an open-chain hydrocarbon with one C=C bond has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the corresponding alkane with the same carbon count.

The additional C–C bond uses one further bonding position on each carbon involved, leaving two fewer positions for H.

Checking the response: Double bond uses two additional carbon bonding positions (1). Two fewer C–H bonds explain the hydrogen difference (1).

blocks.heading: Addition reactions of alkenes
blocks.text:
Ethene reacts with bromine by addition: CH2=CH2 + Br2 → CH2BrCH2Br. The C=C bond becomes C–C and one bromine atom attaches to each carbon. Bromine water is decolourised under the usual test conditions. With hydrogen and a suitable nickel catalyst, ethene forms ethane: C2H4 + H2 → C2H6. With steam and a suitable acid catalyst under industrial conditions, it forms ethanol: C2H4 + H2O → C2H5OH.

In each example the atoms of the added substance become part of the product. Hydrogenation adds H and H; hydration adds H and OH; bromination adds Br and Br. Keep these reagent–product pairs separate. Steam is gaseous water, not oxygen, and hydration is not fermentation. The overall equations and conditions are sufficient here; reaction mechanisms are outside this topic's required scope. Where a diagram is given, first locate C=C, then change it to C–C and place the added groups on those two carbons. Count valencies before naming the product. Reaction conditions matter: a statement that ethene simply becomes ethanol whenever it meets cold water would be misleading.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Addition reactions of alkenes
blocks.text:
Describe why adding hydrogen across ethene’s double bond produces a saturated molecule.

One part of the double bond is replaced by bonding to one extra H on each carbon; the carbon–carbon bond is then single with valency four maintained.

Checking the response: One extra H bonds to each carbon as C=C becomes single (1). No C=C remains, so the product is saturated (1).

blocks.heading: Catalytic cracking
blocks.text:
Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbon molecules into smaller molecules. Heating hydrocarbon vapour over a suitable hot catalyst can produce a mixture of shorter alkanes and alkenes. This is a chemical change because carbon–carbon bonds are broken and new molecules form. It is different from fractional distillation, which separates molecules already present according to boiling range. Cracking helps convert less useful heavy fractions into more useful fuels and alkene feedstocks.

An illustrative balanced equation is C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4. It conserves ten carbons and twenty-two hydrogens. It represents one possible overall split, not the unique product mixture from every industrial cracking process. To complete a simple cracking equation, subtract the atoms in a named product from those in the original molecule, then check whether the remaining formula fits the proposed family. The appearance of an alkene explains why a cracked product mixture can decolourise bromine water. Laboratory demonstrations need controlled heating, appropriate collection and precautions against liquid being drawn back into hot apparatus; students should interpret the model or supervised demonstration rather than improvise a setup.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Catalytic cracking
blocks.text:

Cooling condenses existing molecules; cracking needs chemical bond breaking, for example hot vapour passing over a suitable hot catalyst.

Checking the response: Condensation does not change molecular size (1). Hot catalytic cracking breaks molecules into smaller products (1).

blocks.heading: Testing for unsaturation
blocks.text:
A simple test compares a saturated hydrocarbon with an alkene under the same conditions. Add a small amount of bromine water and mix. In ordinary conditions away from ultraviolet light, an alkene decolourises the orange-brown reagent, whereas an alkane does not produce that reaction. Keep the test conditions explicit because alkanes can react with chlorine or bromine by substitution under suitable light. A disappearing colour is an observation; the inference is that the sample contains a reactive unsaturated bond in the stated comparison.

Cold dilute potassium manganate(VII) provides another test. In acidified solution, an alkene removes the purple colour, giving a colourless solution under the usual test conditions. In neutral or alkaline conditions a brown manganese dioxide product can appear, so the reagent conditions should be stated before predicting a final colour. Other reducing substances can also react with these reagents. Therefore the test distinguishes the given hydrocarbon alternatives rather than proving the identity of every unknown organic liquid. Fresh portions prevent one reagent contaminating the other test. In a written response distinguish 'colourless' from 'clear': a coloured solution may still be clear because it contains no suspended solid.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-46 — Comparing saturated and unsaturated samples
blocks.text:
Aim: distinguish a supplied alkane from an alkene using their chemical responses. Use teacher-approved small hydrocarbon samples in labelled tubes, separate droppers, bromine water and cold dilute acidified potassium manganate(VII). Work under the teacher's supervision with protection and ventilation appropriate to the reagents; this is not an unsupervised home test. Keep both hydrocarbon samples away from flames and ultraviolet illumination.

Add the same small volume of bromine water to equal sample portions and mix consistently. An alkene decolourises the orange-brown reagent; the alkane retains the reagent colour under the stated conditions. On fresh sample portions, the purple acidified manganate(VII) is decolourised by the alkene. State that the reagent is acidified: neutral or alkaline manganate conditions can produce a brown solid instead. Record the initial reagent colour and the final observation separately from the inferred identity.

Controls include equal reagent quantities, equal sample volumes, mixing time and light conditions. A reagent blank helps distinguish a reaction from a faded or contaminated reagent. The conclusion is restricted to the given hydrocarbon alternatives; other reducing compounds can also remove reagent colours. Do not conclude that a colourless final liquid is pure water. Separate droppers and fresh portions avoid carrying one reagent into another test.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.2.1.j.title: 10.2.1 — name the fuels coal, natural gas and petroleum (crude oil)

blocks.heading: Three fossil fuels
blocks.text:
Coal, natural gas and petroleum are important fossil fuels. They formed from ancient organic material over geological time. Coal is a carbon-rich solid with other substances present; natural gas is a gaseous fuel mixture; petroleum, also called crude oil, is a liquid mixture of hydrocarbons. A fuel releases useful energy during combustion. It is not the same as an oxidising agent: oxygen normally comes from the air and supports burning, while the fuel supplies the material that is oxidised.

These fuels are non-renewable on a human timescale. Consuming a store rapidly does not allow geological processes to replace it rapidly. A school comparison can separate physical form, ease of transport, useful energy and emissions instead of declaring one fuel best in every setting. Solid coal must be handled and may leave ash. Gas can be supplied through pipes or appropriate containers. Petroleum is commonly separated before its fractions are used. Combustion chemistry also depends on oxygen supply; changing the source of fuel alone does not guarantee complete combustion. Do not confuse natural gas with refinery gas: they are related fuel mixtures obtained from different sources.

blocks.heading: Methane in natural gas
blocks.text:
Methane, CH4, is the main constituent of natural gas. It is a hydrocarbon because it contains only carbon and hydrogen. Its carbon atom forms four single bonds to hydrogen, making it the smallest alkane. A sample described as natural gas need not be pure methane: the term identifies a naturally occurring gas mixture with methane as its major component, rather than a formula for a pure substance.

With a sufficient oxygen supply, methane burns to form carbon dioxide and water: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. Count one carbon, four hydrogen and four oxygen atoms on each side. With insufficient oxygen, carbon monoxide and sometimes carbon particles can form instead. Carbon monoxide is poisonous; a clean-looking flame is not a complete safety test for a fuel system. Distinguish the formula of the fuel from the formulae of its combustion products. Methane is CH4, whereas carbon dioxide is CO2. Naming methane as the major constituent is more precise than answering simply 'a gas' or 'a hydrocarbon'.

blocks.heading: Fractional distillation of petroleum
blocks.text:
Petroleum is a mixture of many hydrocarbons with different boiling ranges. Fractional distillation separates this mixture by physical changes, not by breaking carbon–carbon bonds. Crude oil is heated and vapours enter a fractionating column. The column is hotter near the bottom and cooler near the top. As vapours rise, components condense in regions where the temperature is low enough for them to become liquid. Fractions containing smaller molecules generally have lower boiling ranges and are collected higher in the column; larger-molecule fractions condense lower down or remain as residue.

A fraction is still a mixture, containing hydrocarbons with similar boiling ranges. It is not one pure compound with a single molecular formula. For a homologous family, increasing molecular size generally increases intermolecular attractions and boiling temperature. Distillation overcomes attractions between molecules; it does not turn an alkane into an alkene. Repeated evaporation and condensation in the column improve separation compared with collecting all vapour together in one receiver. The order of fractions is more useful here than memorising exact boiling temperatures, which vary with how a refinery defines its cuts. Refinery gas leaves near the top; bitumen is obtained from the heavy residue. Cracking is a different process that changes molecules chemically and is considered later.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Fractional distillation of petroleum
blocks.text:

Different components vaporise and condense at different temperatures; these are physical changes that preserve the molecules.

Checking the response: Different boiling behaviour separates fractions (1). Phase changes preserve molecular identities rather than breaking molecules (1).

blocks.heading: Refinery gas and its use
blocks.text:
Refinery gas is a petroleum fraction used for cooking and heating. The use is linked to the physical and chemical properties of the material, not just to its position in a list. Fractional distillation sorts a mixture into boiling ranges so that each collected mixture is more suitable for particular purposes. The molecules in a fraction do not all have identical chain lengths. Different refinery operations can produce somewhat different mixtures while retaining the same broad fraction name.

Its small hydrocarbon molecules remain gaseous at ordinary conditions. A burner mixes fuel with air; useful combustion depends on an adequate oxygen supply. Do not call the gas ‘air’, because air supplies the oxidant rather than the hydrocarbon fuel. To answer a one-mark use question, give one precise accepted use, then stop. For a longer explanation, connect an appropriate property to that use: a fuel supplies energy through combustion, while a heavy waterproof residue provides a barrier. Do not describe distillation itself as the use of the fraction; it is the separation process used to obtain it. Compare neighbouring fractions by their broad boiling ranges and molecule sizes without inventing fixed values. The trend from lighter to heavier fractions helps reconstruct the sequence: refinery gas, gasoline, naphtha, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil and bitumen. A fraction can have more than one industrial application, but a clear familiar example is sufficient for the stated recall task.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.5.jso.title: 10.5 — describe alcohols as saturated compounds with a hydroxyl functional group and the general formula CnH2n+1OH

blocks.heading: Alcohol structure
blocks.text:
The saturated monohydric alcohols considered here contain one hydroxyl group, –OH, and follow CnH2n+1OH. 'Saturated' refers to the carbon skeleton having single carbon–carbon bonds. The oxygen has two bonds, one to carbon and one to hydrogen. Ethanol is CH3CH2OH, with six hydrogen atoms in total. The hydroxyl group should be drawn as part of the molecule rather than as a separate hydroxide ion.

Alcohol molecules are electrically neutral compounds; writing OH in an alcohol formula does not make the substance an alkali. Sodium hydroxide contains hydroxide ions in solution, whereas ethanol contains covalent C–O and O–H bonds. This distinction links organic formula reading to the earlier distinction between molecules and ions. The position of OH can matter: propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol have the same atom totals but different connectivity. In a displayed structure include the O–H bond, and make sure the carbon bearing oxygen still has four bonds. For the family formula, n counts carbon atoms in the hydrocarbon part, while the OH is shown separately to emphasise the functional group.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Alcohol structure
blocks.text:
Describe what follows from these observations: solution X contains an OH-bearing organic molecule but is neutral; solution Y contains sodium hydroxide and is alkaline. Can the letters OH alone establish alkalinity?

No: X is a counterexample. In Y hydroxide ions account for alkalinity; OH written within a molecular formula need not represent free hydroxide ions.

Checking the response: Neutral X disproves the proposed OH-letter rule (1). Distinguish molecular OH from the hydroxide ions in Y (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Alcohol structure
blocks.text:
Describe why ethanol is not sodium hydroxide despite both formulae containing OH.

Ethanol has a covalently bonded hydroxyl group in a neutral molecule; sodium hydroxide supplies hydroxide ions in water.

Checking the response: Covalent OH in neutral ethanol molecule (1). OH− ions in sodium hydroxide solution (1).

blocks.heading: Two routes to ethanol
blocks.text:
Fermentation converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide using enzymes from yeast: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2. Conditions are warm rather than boiling, commonly about 30–40 °C, with oxygen excluded after preparation. Excessive temperature damages the enzymes; low temperature slows the process. The product is a dilute aqueous mixture, and ethanol is separated and concentrated by fractional distillation. Fermentation uses a renewable sugar feedstock when the crop is replenished, but that does not remove energy and land-use considerations.

The industrial hydration route reacts ethene with steam using an acid catalyst, commonly phosphoric acid, at elevated temperature and pressure. C2H4 + H2O ⇌ C2H5OH gives the overall transformation. A typical account uses approximately 300 °C and high pressure; the essential distinction is a catalytic addition process rather than biological conversion of sugar. Ethene can be obtained from petroleum cracking. Compare feedstocks, reaction speed, purity and process conditions rather than simply calling one method 'natural' and therefore superior. Fermentation releases carbon dioxide as a reaction product, whereas the hydration equation incorporates water into ethene. Both routes produce the same ethanol molecule.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Two routes to ethanol
blocks.text:
Describe two corrections to a fermentation trial in which glucose and yeast are boiled in an open container with a constant air supply.

Keep the mixture warm rather than boiling to preserve enzymes, and use anaerobic conditions with gas able to escape safely.

Checking the response: Avoid boiling; suitable warmth preserves yeast/enzyme activity (1). Exclude continuing air supply while allowing safe gas escape (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Two routes to ethanol
blocks.text:
Suggest why a glucose and yeast mixture heated to boiling fails to produce ethanol by fermentation.

Boiling denatures the yeast enzymes needed for fermentation.

Checking the response: Boiling denatures the yeast enzymes needed for fermentation (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Burning ethanol
blocks.text:
Ethanol burns in a sufficient supply of oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water: C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O. The oxygen already present in ethanol must be included when balancing the equation. On the product side there are seven oxygen atoms: four in carbon dioxide and three in water. One comes from the ethanol and six from three oxygen molecules.

Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, so ethanol can be used as a fuel. A classroom comparison of fuels must control factors such as water mass, starting temperature and burner-to-container distance. A measured temperature rise does not capture all the energy released because heat is lost to air and apparatus. Burning an alcohol is not the same transformation as oxidising it to a carboxylic acid under controlled laboratory conditions. Complete combustion breaks down the carbon framework to carbon dioxide; controlled oxidation can retain the two-carbon framework. Ethanol is flammable, so heating ethanol mixtures for separation or reactions requires an appropriate controlled heat source rather than an exposed flame near vapour.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Burning ethanol
blocks.text:
Describe why a well-aerated ethanol flame can heat a container while its collected gaseous products include both water vapour and CO2.

Product bond formation releases more energy than reactant bond breaking absorbs; oxidation transfers the fuel’s H and C into water and CO2.

Checking the response: Net bond-energy release accounts for heating (1). Complete oxidation conserves H and C in water and CO2 (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Burning ethanol
blocks.text:
Describe how C2H5OH + 3O2 → 2CO2 + 3H2O conserves oxygen.

The ethanol provides one oxygen atom and three O2 provide six, matching four in CO2 and three in water.

Checking the response: Seven oxygen atoms in reactants, including ethanol oxygen (1). Seven oxygen atoms in products (1).

blocks.heading: Uses of ethanol
blocks.text:
Ethanol is used as a solvent, as a fuel and as a constituent of alcoholic drinks. As a solvent it can dissolve many substances used in preparations such as fragrances. As a fuel it releases energy by combustion. In drinks it is the ethanol formed by fermentation that is relevant to the chemistry; laboratory ethanol is not suitable for tasting or drinking.

Match the use to the property. A solvent provides a medium in which a solute dissolves; a fuel is consumed in an energy-releasing reaction. These are different roles even though the same substance can perform both. Ethanol mixes with water, so separating a fermented solution is not a matter of filtering out solid ethanol. Fractional distillation exploits volatility and produces an ethanol-enriched distillate. A use question normally needs a concise specific response. 'It is useful in industry' does not name a use, whereas 'solvent in a fragrance preparation' does. Where a product contains several substances, do not assume the whole product is pure ethanol or assign it ethanol's exact physical properties.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of ethanol
blocks.text:
Name one use of ethanol other than in alcoholic drinks.

As a solvent or as a fuel.

Checking the response: As a solvent or as a fuel (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P01 (7)
blocks.text:
Which pair forms during complete combustion of ethanol?
A. Carbon monoxide and carbon
B. Ethene and hydrogen
C. Carbon dioxide and water
D. Ethanoic acid and hydrogen

C. Carbon dioxide and water Complete oxidation gives CO2 and H2O.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Complete oxidation gives CO2 and H2O. Distractor explanations: B is not combustion; D is not the complete-combustion products; A lists incomplete-combustion carbon products.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-44 — Fractionating a fermented mixture
blocks.text:
Aim: separate an ethanol-rich fraction from a teacher-prepared fermented sugar solution. Use a distillation flask, fractionating column, thermometer with its bulb at the vapour outlet, condenser, receiver and controlled electric heater or water bath appropriate to the setup. Condenser water enters at the lower connection and leaves at the upper connection. The apparatus remains open to pressure relief through the receiver; it is not a sealed heated system. Avoid exposed flames because ethanol vapour is flammable.

The teacher heats the mixture gently, allowing repeated evaporation and condensation within the column. Record vapour temperature and collect successive small fractions as directed. An early fraction is enriched in the more volatile ethanol compared with the starting mixture; later fractions contain relatively more water. Do not infer that one distillation gives chemically pure ethanol, and do not taste any fraction. Cloudiness or colour in the original mixture need not carry into the distillate because non-volatile material remains in the flask.

Interpretation: the separation is physical and uses different volatilities. It does not convert glucose into ethanol during distillation; fermentation has already occurred. A useful limitation is imperfect separation of miscible liquids and changes in temperature as composition changes. Keep the thermometer position and heating rate appropriate, and compare fractions using a suitable teacher-selected measurement rather than a smell test. Cross-reference the fractional-distillation apparatus in Topic 1 and fermentation in this unit.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.3.jso.title: 10.3 — describe alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula CnH2n+2

blocks.heading: Saturated hydrocarbons
blocks.text:
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: they contain only carbon and hydrogen, and their carbon–carbon bonds are single. Saturated means that the carbon skeleton has no carbon–carbon double bond available for the addition reactions studied here. For open-chain alkanes, CnH2n+2 gives the atom counts. Methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8 and butane C4H10 illustrate the pattern.

The word saturated does not mean dissolved to a solubility limit in this context. Chemistry uses the same word in different settings; here it describes bonding within molecules. Carbon has four bonds in the displayed structure. An internal carbon in a straight alkane chain normally bonds to two other carbons and two hydrogens; an end carbon bonds to one carbon and three hydrogens. Methane is a special one-carbon case with four hydrogens. Counting available bonds explains why an alkene with one double bond has two fewer hydrogens than the corresponding alkane. The bonds within a molecule should also be distinguished from attractions between separate molecules, which control many physical properties.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Saturated hydrocarbons
blocks.text:
Describe why a saturated open-chain hydrocarbon with three carbon atoms has eight hydrogen atoms when carbon makes four bonds and hydrogen one.

The two C–C single bonds use four carbon bonding positions in total; eight of the twelve positions remain for H.

Checking the response: Twelve carbon bonding positions minus four used by C–C links (1). Eight remaining C–H bonds give C3H8 (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Saturated hydrocarbons
blocks.text:
Describe how the carbon bonding in ethane gives the formula C2H6.

The two carbons share one single bond; each carbon then bonds to three hydrogens to have four bonds.

Checking the response: One C–C bond (1). Three H on each carbon completes valency four (1).

blocks.heading: Complete and incomplete combustion
blocks.text:
Alkanes are relatively unreactive under many ordinary conditions, but they burn when ignited with oxygen. Complete combustion of methane is CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. The products contain all the carbon as carbon dioxide and all the hydrogen as water. Combustion is exothermic; energy is transferred to the surroundings. A balanced equation conserves atoms and does not imply that oxygen is part of the fuel before reaction.

An insufficient oxygen supply leads to incomplete combustion. One possible equation is 2CH4 + 3O2 → 2CO + 4H2O; very oxygen-poor conditions can also produce carbon particles, seen as soot. Real flames can produce mixtures of carbon products. Carbon monoxide is poisonous and cannot be identified safely by smell or by tasting combustion gases. A practical explanation should connect poor air supply to incomplete oxidation rather than saying that the fuel somehow 'turns into oxygen'. Improving air mixing can promote complete combustion in suitable equipment. Carbon dioxide still contributes to greenhouse warming even when combustion is complete, so complete combustion reduces some hazards without making fossil-fuel use environmentally neutral.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Complete and incomplete combustion
blocks.text:
Describe why restricting the oxygen supply can change methane combustion products without changing the elements originally present.

Less oxygen permits incomplete oxidation to CO or carbon instead of CO2; only the bonding and oxygen amount in products change, not element identities.

Checking the response: Limited oxygen explains incompletely oxidised carbon products (1). Products still contain only elements from the reactants (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Complete and incomplete combustion
blocks.text:
Suggest why a methane burner produces soot when its air inlet is restricted.

Insufficient oxygen causes incomplete combustion, producing carbon particles.

Checking the response: Insufficient oxygen causes incomplete combustion, producing carbon particles (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Substitution with chlorine
blocks.text:
Methane reacts with chlorine in suitable light, commonly stated as ultraviolet light, to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride: CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. This is substitution because a hydrogen atom in the alkane is replaced by a chlorine atom. The carbon skeleton remains saturated. It is different from addition across C=C, since methane has no carbon–carbon double bond.

The equation describes one substitution stage. Further substitution can occur, so conditions and reactant proportions affect the mixture obtained. For this course, name the reaction type, give the required light condition and show the appropriate overall product rather than introducing a stepwise mechanism. Chlorine is hazardous, so this is a teacher-controlled demonstration or a paper model, not an invitation to mix gases. Counting atoms catches a frequent error: Cl2 supplies one chlorine for CH3Cl and one for HCl. Writing CH4Cl2 as though both chlorine atoms simply attach without replacement would violate the intended chemistry and the carbon valency. A colour change by itself must be interpreted with the light and reactants stated.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Substitution with chlorine
blocks.text:
Describe why CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl is substitution and why the equation cannot instead produce CH4Cl plus HCl.

One H on methane is replaced by Cl; the proposed alternative would exceed carbon valency and fail hydrogen balance.

Checking the response: Replacement of one H by Cl identifies substitution (1). Proposed alternative violates carbon valency or hydrogen conservation (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Substitution with chlorine
blocks.text:
Describe why CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl is substitution rather than addition.

One hydrogen attached to carbon is replaced by chlorine; the removed hydrogen forms HCl instead of both chlorine atoms joining the carbon.

Checking the response: H is replaced by Cl (1). HCl forms / no addition across a C=C bond (1).

Why can restricting a methane burner’s air supply lead to carbon monoxide?
A. Nitrogen supplies carbon atoms
B. Methane becomes saturated
C. Water changes into carbon
D. Less oxygen allows incomplete combustion

D. Less oxygen allows incomplete combustion Incomplete oxidation occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Incomplete oxidation occurs when oxygen supply is insufficient. Distractor explanations: C violates element conservation; B methane is already saturated; A nitrogen contains no carbon.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.8.1.j.title: 10.8.1 — describe polymers in terms of large molecules built up from small units (monomers), different polymers having different units and/or different linkages

blocks.heading: Monomers and polymers
blocks.text:
A polymer is a very large molecule built from many smaller units derived from monomers. A monomer is a small molecule capable of joining with other molecules to form the polymer. 'Polymer' describes the resulting large molecule, not a loose pile of unconnected monomer molecules. The chemical bonds linking units give the material properties different from those of the starting monomer.

Different polymers can have different units, different linkages, or both. Poly(ethene) has a carbon backbone derived from ethene. A polyester contains ester linkages, while a polyamide contains amide linkages. The repeat unit is the smallest section whose repetition represents the chain; it is not necessarily identical in bonding to the original monomer. In addition polymerisation the monomer's double bond changes to single bonds in the backbone. A bracket with n outside indicates many repetitions, not a charge or a fixed small atom count. Chain ends are often omitted in a repeat-unit drawing, but continuation bonds must show how the unit joins to its neighbours.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Monomers and polymers
blocks.text:
Describe why joining many small monomers can give a large polymer while leaving some structural features of each monomer recognisable.

New covalent links join the units into one extended molecule; portions not involved in forming those links remain in the repeat units.

Checking the response: New inter-unit bonds create one larger chain (1). Unreacted portions of monomer structures remain within repeat units (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Monomers and polymers
blocks.text:
Describe why two polymers can have different properties even if both are long chains.

Their monomer-derived units and linkages may differ, changing molecular interactions and chain behaviour.

Checking the response: Different units/linkages despite shared chain form (1). Those structural differences affect interactions or chain behaviour and hence properties (1).

blocks.heading: Addition and condensation polymerisation
blocks.text:
Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers by changing their carbon–carbon double bonds into single bonds in a long chain. No small molecule is eliminated in this overall process. All the monomer atoms appear in the polymer. Ethene forming poly(ethene) is the simplest example. The word addition here describes joining many monomers, not the addition of bromine to one alkene molecule.

Condensation polymerisation joins monomers with reactive groups at more than one position. Each joining step forms a linkage and can eliminate a small molecule such as water. A diol and a dicarboxylic acid can form a polyester; a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid can form a polyamide. The resulting chain contains ester or amide links. Bifunctional monomers can continue joining at both ends, whereas a simple esterification between monofunctional molecules produces a small ester rather than an extended chain. Compare the processes by the monomer features, linkage and small-molecule product. Avoid the false rule that all polymers are made by addition just because molecules are being joined in ordinary language.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Addition and condensation polymerisation
blocks.text:
Describe why condensation polymerisation can release water without violating conservation of mass.

Atoms removed from monomer functional groups form water; the mass of polymer plus eliminated water equals total reactant mass.

Checking the response: Eliminated H/O atoms accounted for in water (1). Including water in total product mass preserves mass balance (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Addition and condensation polymerisation
blocks.text:
Describe why a diol and a dicarboxylic acid can produce a long polyester chain.

Each monomer can react at both ends, allowing repeated ester links rather than stopping after one joining step.

Checking the response: Each monomer has two reactive ends (1). Repeated ester link formation allows chain extension (1).

blocks.heading: From alkene to repeat unit and back
blocks.text:
To draw an addition-polymer repeat unit, identify the two carbons of the monomer's C=C bond. Change that bond to a single bond, retain every attached atom or group, and extend a bond from each of those carbons through the repeat-unit brackets. Put n outside the brackets. Ethene gives [–CH2–CH2–]n. Chloroethene CH2=CHCl gives [–CH2–CHCl–]n, with chlorine attached to a backbone carbon, not inserted into the backbone.

To recover a monomer from a suitable two-carbon repeat unit, remove the continuation bonds and restore C=C between those carbons, preserving the substituents. For [–CH2–CH(CH3)–]n, the monomer is CH2=CHCH3. Check carbon valency in both forms. Leaving C=C inside the polymer while retaining both continuation bonds would overbond the backbone carbons. A polymer drawing represents repeated connectivity; it is not an instruction to join the end hydrogen atoms. The task can require interpretation rather than recall when an unfamiliar substituent arrangement is supplied, so show how the atoms have been preserved rather than naming a memorised polymer unrelated to the given structure.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — From alkene to repeat unit and back
blocks.text:
Draw the repeating unit formed from CH2=CHCl, with continuation bonds and n.

[–CH2–CHCl–]n, with single backbone bonds and Cl attached to the second carbon.

Checking the response: Correct CH2–CHCl single-bond backbone with Cl substituent (1). Brackets, continuation bonds and n (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — From alkene to repeat unit and back
blocks.text:
Deduce the monomer for the repeat unit [–CH2–CH(CH3)–]n.

CH2=CHCH3, propene.

Checking the response: CH2=CHCH3, propene (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Poly(ethene)
blocks.text:
Poly(ethene) forms when many ethene molecules join by addition polymerisation. The overall representation is n CH2=CH2 → [–CH2–CH2–]n. Each carbon retains two hydrogen atoms, but its double bond becomes part of the single-bonded chain. Suitable industrial conditions and a catalyst or initiator are used; merely storing ethene does not imply that it instantly becomes a solid polymer.

The polymer is a different substance with much larger molecules and different physical properties. Ethene is a small gaseous molecule at ordinary conditions; poly(ethene) is used as a solid plastic. Different grades can have different properties, so a bag and a rigid bottle need not behave identically even when both are described as polyethylene products. For a reaction classification, identify the alkene monomer and the absence of an eliminated small molecule. For a drawing, maintain the two-carbon repeat unit and continuation bonds. Do not write a water product simply because many molecules have joined: water elimination belongs to appropriate condensation reactions, not this addition process.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Poly(ethene)
blocks.text:
Describe why an ethene polymer model cannot retain a C=C bond within every repeat while also adding continuation bonds to neighbouring repeats.

Keeping the double bond and both continuation connections would give carbon too many bonds; addition polymerisation replaces C=C with single backbone bonding.

Checking the response: Excess carbon valency identified in the proposed model (1). Single-bond backbone restores carbon valency four (1).

blocks.text:
Suggest the error in the equation n C2H4 → poly(ethene) + n H2O.

Addition polymerisation of ethene does not eliminate water; ethene contains no oxygen to supply it.
