blocks.heading: Nylon and amide links
blocks.text:
Nylon is a synthetic polyamide. In a simplified condensation model, a diamine H2N–R–NH2 reacts with a dicarboxylic acid HOOC–R′–COOH. The joining reaction forms amide linkages, –C(=O)–NH–, and eliminates water. R and R′ represent carbon-containing sections; their detailed structures are not needed to recognise the linkage. A general repeating section can be written [–NH–R–NH–C(=O)–R′–C(=O)–]n.

Follow the boundary of the repeat unit: the terminal carbonyl carbon joins the NH of the next unit. This creates another amide link when repetitions are connected. The carbonyl double bond is retained; the nitrogen is not an oxygen atom. Condensation uses functional groups at both ends of the monomers so the chain can continue. A drawing of one small amide molecule without continuation bonds does not show the polymer adequately. Nylon's strong fibres are used in textiles and ropes, but its identity is established by the polyamide structure, not by a particular colour or use. Proteins also contain amide links, yet their units differ from the units used in nylon.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nylon and amide links
blocks.text:
Draw a continuing chain by joining the supplied fragments –NH–R–NH– and –C(=O)–R′–C(=O)– alternately. Mark the new linkage type.

…–NH–R–NH–C(=O)–R′–C(=O)–NH–R–NH–…; the links are amide links.

Checking the response: Alternating supplied fragments joined without breaking their internal structure (1). Correct C(=O)–NH connectivity and continuation (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nylon and amide links
blocks.text:
Describe the linkage and polymer type in the supplied chain …–C(=O)–NH–R–NH–C(=O)–R′–….

It contains amide links, –C(=O)–NH–, so it is a polyamide.

Checking the response: Identify amide linkage from supplied chain (1). Classify as polyamide (1).

blocks.heading: Terylene and ester links
blocks.text:
Terylene is a polyester made by condensation polymerisation. A diol and a dicarboxylic acid join to form repeated ester links, –C(=O)–O–, with water eliminated. A schematic chain is [–O–R–O–C(=O)–R′–C(=O)–]n. The symbols represent the internal carbon-containing portions of the relevant monomers. This schematic emphasises the repeated linkage without requiring every atom of the commercial monomers.

Compare the schematic with nylon: an ester link contains oxygen where the amide link contains NH. Both retain a carbonyl double bond. A polyester is not the same as the small ester ethyl ethanoate, although the linkage is related. Monomers with two reactive ends allow an extended chain, whereas ethanol and ethanoic acid form a small ester under the ordinary reaction described earlier. Terylene fibres are used in fabrics and other materials. To identify a supplied polymer structure, locate the connecting groups first and classify by those groups rather than guessing from its trade name. Continuation bonds and brackets make clear that the structure repeats beyond the displayed fragment.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Terylene and ester links
blocks.text:
Draw a segment containing two ester links by connecting HO–R–OH between the supplied carbonyl-ended fragments …–C(=O)– and –C(=O)–…. Remove each hydroxyl hydrogen when connecting its oxygen to a carbonyl carbon.

…–C(=O)–O–R–O–C(=O)–…

Checking the response: One correctly connected ester link on each side of R (1). Single continuous segment with correct oxygen/carbonyl valencies (1).

blocks.text:
Describe the linkage and polymer type in …–O–R–O–C(=O)–R′–C(=O)–….

The chain contains ester links, –C(=O)–O–, and is a polyester.

blocks.heading: Choosing a plastic
blocks.text:
Plastics are used in packaging, containers, electrical insulation, pipes and many other products. Useful properties can include low density, resistance to water, electrical insulation and the ability to be shaped. These are not universal properties of every plastic under every condition. A material chosen for a flexible bag needs different mechanical behaviour from a material chosen for a rigid water pipe.

Link a use to a relevant property. An insulating covering on an electrical wire must resist electrical conduction and remain suitable under the expected temperature and mechanical conditions. A drinks container needs to retain liquid and withstand handling. A lightweight package can reduce transport mass, but disposal and recycling remain separate considerations. Naming 'plastic' does not by itself identify a chemical structure or establish whether it is biodegradable. Different polymer units, chain arrangements and additives can change performance. A reasoned selection states the requirement, names a matching property and recognises an important limitation when the context calls for it.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Choosing a plastic
blocks.text:
Outline two uses of plastics with an appropriate property for each.

Water containers use resistance to water; wire coverings use electrical insulation.

Checking the response: Water container: water resistance prevents the container being damaged by its contents (1). Wire covering: electrical insulation prevents current passing through the covering to the user (1). Accept other distinct scientifically valid use–property pairs; one mark per complete pair.

blocks.text:
Explain why an electrically insulating plastic can be useful around a metal wire.

It prevents contact with the conducting metal and restricts current passing to a person or another conductor.

Checking the response: It prevents contact with the conducting metal and restricts current passing to a person or another conductor (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:
Which monomer matches [–CH2–CHCl–]n?
A. CH3CH2Cl
B. CH2ClCH2Cl
C. CH2=CHCl
D. CHCl=CHCl

C. CH2=CHCl Restoring C=C between backbone carbons retains one chlorine substituent.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Restoring C=C between backbone carbons retains one chlorine substituent. Distractor explanations: A is saturated; D has two chlorines per unit; B is saturated and has two chlorines.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P01 (10)
blocks.text:
Why is an electrically insulating plastic useful as a wire covering?
A. It supplies extra electrons to the circuit
B. It restricts unwanted current paths from the metal
C. It replaces the conducting core with air
D. It turns the metal into a gas

B. It restricts unwanted current paths from the metal The coating separates people and other conductors from the conducting metal.

Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The coating separates people and other conductors from the conducting metal. Distractor explanations: A invents an electron source; D is irrelevant chemical change; C would break the intended conducting path.

blocks.heading: Addition repeat units

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.8.2.j.title: 10.8.2 — name proteins, fats and carbohydrates as the main constituents of food

blocks.heading: Food constituents
blocks.text:
Proteins, fats and carbohydrates are major chemical constituents of food. They are not interchangeable names for one kind of molecule. Proteins are polymers of amino-acid-derived units joined by amide links. Fats are esters formed from glycerol and fatty acids. Carbohydrates include simple sugars and larger molecules assembled from sugar units. Water, minerals and other substances can also be present in food; the three named classes are not a claim that every food contains nothing else.

A chemical classification concerns structure and composition. A food sample is usually a mixture, so a positive test or a stated nutrient content does not imply a pure substance. The same food can contain more than one of the major classes. Hydrolysis breaks suitable linkages using water: proteins yield amino acids, and complex carbohydrates can yield simple sugars. Fats contain ester linkages, but a fat molecule is not automatically a long-chain polymer like a polyester. Keep the class, linkage and hydrolysis product as separate pieces of information. This helps prevent assigning protein products to carbohydrate hydrolysis simply because both processes involve breaking large molecules into smaller ones.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Food constituents
blocks.text:
Name the three main classes of food constituents studied in this organic section.

Proteins, fats and carbohydrates.

Checking the response: Proteins, fats and carbohydrates (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Protein and nylon: same link, different units
blocks.text:
Proteins contain amide linkages, also called peptide links in the protein context. The characteristic section is –C(=O)–NH–. Nylon is also a polyamide, so the link type is shared. This structural similarity does not make nylon a protein. The repeating units and their arrangement differ, and the resulting substances have different biological and material properties.

When comparing two chain drawings, isolate the joining group from the larger blocks on either side. A shared C(=O)–NH section supports a statement about the linkage. It does not establish that the entire chains have the same composition or function. The protein chain contains units derived from amino acids, while the nylon model uses its own monomer units. A generic representation is sufficient here; names and detailed structures of individual amino acids are not required. Carbonyl oxygen should be shown with a double bond, and nitrogen must retain chemically appropriate bonding. Replacing NH with O changes the link to an ester and therefore changes the chemical classification.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Protein and nylon: same link, different units
blocks.text:
Describe which evidence supports identifying fibre X as protein rather than nylon: both fibres contain amide links, but hydrolysis of X produces amino acids and hydrolysis of Y produces a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid.

The amino-acid products support protein for X. The shared amide links alone do not distinguish X from Y; Y’s different products support a different polyamide.

Checking the response: X produces amino acids, the building units of proteins, supporting protein identification (1). Both X and nylon contain amide links, so that observation alone cannot distinguish them (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Protein and nylon: same link, different units
blocks.text:
Describe why a chain containing amide links is not necessarily a protein.

Nylon also contains amide links, but its units differ from amino-acid-derived protein units.

Checking the response: Nylon also contains amide links, so amide links alone do not identify protein (1). Protein units derive from amino acids; nylon has different monomer-derived units (1).

blocks.heading: Representing a protein chain
blocks.text:
A simplified protein chain can be represented with generic units joined through –C(=O)–NH– links. One convenient schematic is …–NH–U–C(=O)–NH–V–C(=O)–NH–W–C(=O)–…, where U, V and W stand for the appropriate carbon-containing portions of different units. The letters are placeholders, not element symbols or named amino acids. Their purpose is to show that different units can occur within the same chain.

Draw the linkage accurately even when the rest is schematic. Carbonyl carbon has a double bond to oxygen and single bonds connecting it into the chain. The NH group lies between the carbonyl carbon and the next unit. A protein is not represented by isolated boxes touching without any indication of the joining chemistry. Conversely, the course does not require an atom-by-atom structure of every amino-acid unit. A labelled schematic can show the requested relationship clearly. Hydrolysis later breaks these links to release smaller units; it does not merely stretch the chain or change its drawing orientation. Use the structure to explain the process rather than relying on a remembered biological function.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Representing a protein chain
blocks.text:
Draw a schematic protein-chain section containing two amide links, with generic units U, V and W.

U–C(=O)–NH–V–C(=O)–NH–W.

Checking the response: Two correctly connected C(=O)–NH links (1). Generic units connected into one chain (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Representing a protein chain
blocks.text:
Describe the two linkage sites in U–C(=O)–NH–V–C(=O)–NH–W that hydrolysis can break.

They are the two amide C(=O)–NH linkages connecting U to V and V to W.

Checking the response: Locate the C(=O)–NH connection between U and V (1). Locate the C(=O)–NH connection between V and W (1).

blocks.heading: Protein hydrolysis
blocks.text:
Hydrolysis uses water to break chemical linkages. Hydrolysis of proteins breaks amide links and produces amino acids. Suitable acid conditions and heating can be used in a laboratory account. The process is a chemical change: the large molecule is converted into smaller molecules. Dissolving a protein or simply cutting a piece of food into smaller pieces is not the same transformation.

The required product class is amino acids; individual names and structures are outside this outcome. A useful explanation follows the chain representation: breaking multiple links separates the monomer-derived units and adds the elements of water at the broken connections. Hydrolysis is related to the reverse of condensation, although actual reaction conditions and complete biological processes need not be symmetrical. A partially hydrolysed sample may still contain shorter chains, so a claim of complete conversion requires appropriate conditions or evidence. Chromatography can help separate and compare products with reference substances. A single unresolved spot is not proof that every link has broken or that the original protein had one type of unit.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Protein hydrolysis
blocks.text:
Describe why a protein solution is not evidence of complete hydrolysis, and the product observation that would support that claim.

Dissolution need not break peptide bonds; evidence of amino-acid products would support hydrolysis.

Checking the response: Physical dissolution does not establish bond cleavage (1). Amino-acid product evidence supports hydrolysis (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Protein hydrolysis
blocks.text:
Suggest why merely dissolving a protein in water does not demonstrate complete hydrolysis.

Dissolving does not establish that its amide links have been broken into amino-acid products.

Checking the response: Dissolving does not establish that its amide links have been broken into amino-acid products (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Fats and ester links
blocks.text:
Fats are esters with linkages of the same chemical type as those in Terylene: –C(=O)–O–. Their units are different. A typical fat molecule contains glycerol joined to three fatty-acid-derived groups. It is not an indefinitely repeating polyester chain. This is an important limit to the analogy: a shared linkage does not imply the same molecular size, shape or material properties.

The carbonyl double bond is part of the ester group. Do not identify an ester simply by seeing a C–O single bond, because alcohols and other compounds also contain such bonds. Hydrolysis of fats can break ester links. With an alkali, the products include glycerol and salts of the fatty acids; these salts form soaps. The soap-making practical connects this structural idea to Topic 3. The detailed structures of every fatty acid are unnecessary for recognising the relationship. A schematic should show the glycerol-derived part connected through ester groups to the carbon chains, with correct oxygen bonding. A fat is neither a protein nor a carbohydrate simply because all three occur in food.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Fats and ester links
blocks.text:
Describe why a fat molecule and Terylene can both undergo ester-link hydrolysis without being the same kind of molecular structure.

Both contain ester links that can break on hydrolysis; their constituent units and arrangement differ, with Terylene forming repeating polymer chains.

Checking the response: Shared ester links account for hydrolysis (1). Different units/chain arrangement explain distinct structures (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Fats and ester links
blocks.text:
Describe why a fat molecule is classified as an ester rather than a polyamide.

It contains C(=O)–O connections, not the C(=O)–NH connections characteristic of amides.

Checking the response: Fat contains ester C(=O)–O connections (1). A polyamide instead contains C(=O)–NH connections (1).

blocks.heading: Complex carbohydrates
blocks.text:
Complex carbohydrates such as starch contain many sugar-derived units joined together. A schematic can represent each sugar unit by a box and show oxygen-containing links between boxes. The boxes are a model of the units, not literal square molecules. Condensation joins units with elimination of water, producing a much larger molecule than an individual sugar.

Keep the model at the required level: many sugar units, covalent linking and the relationship between condensation and hydrolysis. Detailed ring structures are unnecessary for this task. A chain diagram should connect the units rather than draw an unconnected collection of sugar boxes. If the drawing uses a joining oxygen explicitly, show its two bonds to neighbouring units. Complex carbohydrate is not a synonym for any substance containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen: fats also contain these elements but have different units and linkages. A supplied diagram with three boxes usually represents part of a much larger chain. It should not be interpreted as a claim that starch contains exactly three sugar units.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Complex carbohydrates
blocks.text:
Draw a schematic section of a complex carbohydrate using three boxes for sugar units and O for each joining oxygen.

[sugar]–O–[sugar]–O–[sugar], continuing beyond the displayed section.

Checking the response: Three sugar units linked through oxygen (1). Connected chain with continuation indicated (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Complex carbohydrates
blocks.text:
Describe what the model …[S]–O–[S]–O–[S]… represents and how the links form.

S represents sugar-derived units in a complex carbohydrate; the units join by condensation with water eliminated.

Checking the response: Many sugar-derived units / complex carbohydrate (1). Condensation with water elimination (1).

blocks.heading: Hydrolysing starch
blocks.text:
Heating starch with a suitable dilute acid can hydrolyse the complex carbohydrate to simple sugars. Water participates in breaking the linkages, while the acid provides conditions that promote the reaction. The large molecule is converted into smaller sugar molecules. This process differs from simply dispersing starch in water or melting a material; the chemical connectivity changes.

A teacher-prepared hydrolysate can be compared with the starting material and with reference sugars. When interpreting results, separate evidence for disappearance of the original material from evidence for formation of a particular product. A chromatogram can show spots matching reference substances under the same conditions. Complete hydrolysis should not be inferred from colour or clarity alone. The familiar relationship is condensation joining sugar units and hydrolysis separating them. Do not transfer the protein product class to this case: starch yields sugars, whereas proteins yield amino acids. Any practical involving hot acid requires controlled preparation, suitable cooling and the appropriate treatment of the sample before later tests.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrolysing starch
blocks.text:
Describe why two starch trials may differ if one is mixed with cold water and the other heated with dilute acid.

Cold water alone does not establish hydrolysis; heated dilute acid can break carbohydrate links and produce simple sugars.

Checking the response: Heating with dilute acid promotes hydrolysis unlike simple cold mixing (1). Link breaking yields smaller sugar units (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrolysing starch
blocks.text:
Suggest the product class expected when a starch sample is fully hydrolysed.

Simple sugars.

Checking the response: Simple sugars (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Chromatography of hydrolysis products
blocks.text:
Chromatography separates components of a mixture because they move at different rates between the moving solvent and the stationary material. For a hydrolysed food sample, place small sample and reference spots on a pencil baseline above the solvent level. Develop them together under the same conditions. Mark the solvent front when the paper is removed, and make colourless spots visible by a suitable method; the identity of a specific locating agent is not required here.

Compare sample spots with reference spots on the same run. A matching position supports a possible identification, but different substances can sometimes travel similar distances. Additional evidence can be needed for a firm conclusion. Rf equals the distance from baseline to spot centre divided by the distance from baseline to solvent front. Both distances must use the same units, so Rf has no unit. For original practice data, a spot travelling 2.4 cm while the front travels 8.0 cm has Rf = 0.30; another at 4.8 cm has Rf = 0.60. Two resolved sample spots indicate at least two detected components, not necessarily every component originally present. Keep the baseline above the solvent to stop the sample dissolving directly into the reservoir.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chromatography of hydrolysis products
blocks.text:
Describe why a hydrolysate spot with Rf 0.40 cannot securely be matched to a reference with Rf 0.40 measured using another solvent, and give a better comparison.

Rf depends on the separation conditions; run sample and reference together with the same solvent and paper.

Checking the response: Different solvent makes the numerical match inconclusive (1). Same-run sample/reference comparison (1).

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P01 (11)
blocks.text:
Which change describes protein hydrolysis?
A. Sugars join into starch
B. Protein chains become longer without reacting
C. Amide links form while water leaves
D. Water breaks amide links, releasing amino acids

D. Water breaks amide links, releasing amino acids Hydrolysis breaks the links and gives smaller amino-acid products.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Hydrolysis breaks the links and gives smaller amino-acid products. Distractor explanations: A is carbohydrate condensation; C reverses hydrolysis; B does not describe bond breaking.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P01 (12)
blocks.text:
Why should hydrolysate and reference spots be developed in the same chromatography run?
A. Matching conditions permit meaningful comparison
B. All substances must travel equal distances
C. The paper dissolves each component into the same substance
D. The reference converts the sample into glucose

A. Matching conditions permit meaningful comparison Same solvent and stationary conditions support a valid positional comparison.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Same solvent and stationary conditions support a valid positional comparison. Distractor explanations: B denies separation; D invents a reaction; C confuses separation with conversion.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P03 (a)
blocks.text:
Plan chromatography to compare the components of a teacher-prepared carbohydrate hydrolysate with glucose and reference sugar B. Include preparation, apparatus, development, observation and a defensible conclusion. No specific locating-agent identity is required.

Filter a suitable diluted portion of the teacher-prepared hydrolysate if suspended solids remain. Draw a pencil baseline above a shallow solvent reservoir in a covered chamber. Apply small hydrolysate, glucose and B spots in separate lanes, drying between applications. Develop all lanes on the same paper in the same solvent, with the paper upright and solvent initially below the baseline. Remove the paper before the front reaches the top, mark the solvent front immediately, and visualise the spots by a suitable supervised method. Compare positions or Rf values with references: in the original DATA-10 example the two detected sample spots match glucose and B, supporting their possible presence rather than proving unique identities.

Prepare an appropriate sample, including filtration if needed (1). Pencil baseline above solvent with suitable chamber/paper arrangement (1). Small dried sample and reference spots in separate lanes (1). Develop together in covered chamber under the same solvent conditions (1). Mark front promptly and visualise spots suitably (1). Compare reference positions/Rf for a qualified conclusion (1). Accept equivalent sound sequencing; no named locating chemical required.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P03 (b)
blocks.text:
State the distances travelled by the lower sample spot and the solvent front from the pencil baseline in the learner panel of VIS-6117-10-04. Read the ruler, whose marks are heights above the paper bottom.

Lower sample spot: 2.4 cm from baseline. Solvent front: 8.0 cm from baseline. Subtract the baseline height, 1.0 cm, from the ruler heights 3.4 and 9.0 cm.

2.4 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1). 8.0 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1). Reject uncorrected heights from paper bottom.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P03 (c)
blocks.text:
Calculate Rf for the lower sample spot. For this part, the measured baseline-to-spot distance is 2.4 cm and baseline-to-front distance is 8.0 cm.

Rf = distance travelled by spot / distance travelled by solvent front = 2.4/8.0 = 0.30. It has no unit.

Correct spot/front ratio (1). 0.30 without units (1). Accept 0.28–0.32 from permitted visual readings, with correct follow-through.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Explain why a wide, wet starting spot can make the chromatogram hard to interpret, and how the spotting procedure should be improved.

A large wet spot spreads and can make neighbouring component spots overlap. Apply smaller spots with a capillary and dry each application before adding more, so starting spots remain compact.

Broad/wet spots spread or overlap, obscuring components (1). Smaller applications dried between additions (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-45 — Preparing soap from oil and alkali
blocks.text:
Aim: connect ester hydrolysis to soap formation. A teacher-controlled preparation uses a measured oil or fat portion, an appropriate alkali solution, a beaker or reaction vessel, stirring equipment and a controlled warming bath. Alkali can damage skin and eyes; wear the specified protection and follow the teacher's quantities and handling procedure. If any flammable solvent is included in the approved method, avoid flames and control vapour exposure.

Warm and stir the prescribed mixture so the fat's ester links react with alkali. The products include glycerol and fatty-acid salts, the soap. An approved procedure may add concentrated salt solution to separate the soap, then filter and wash it. A separated solid is evidence of product isolation, but its appearance alone does not establish purity or absence of residual alkali. The product is a laboratory sample, not a cosmetic for use on skin.

Compare a small appropriately prepared soap solution with an unreacted oil control using the same water volume and mixing procedure. Soap can help disperse oil and produce lather, whereas oil alone is not a soluble soap. Hard-water ions can affect the test, so use the same water for both samples. Explain the result through chemical conversion and soap behaviour, not by saying that stirring made the oil disappear. Cross-reference Topic 3 for the cleaning action and hard-water limitation.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.1.jso.title: 10.1 — use the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) system to name and draw the structures of the unbranched alkanes, alkenes (not cis and trans), alcohols and carboxylic acids containing up to four carbon atoms per molecule and ethyl ethanoate and the products of the reactions stated in section 10.4 to 10.5

blocks.heading: Reading and building organic names
blocks.text:
An organic name is a compact description of a structure. Start with the number of carbon atoms: meth- means one, eth- two, prop- three and but- four. The ending identifies the family. For the unbranched alkanes, methane, ethane, propane and butane have condensed structures CH4, CH3CH3, CH3CH2CH3 and CH3CH2CH2CH3. Each carbon makes four bonds. A single line counts as one bond, a double line as two. In a displayed structure show every atom and every bond, including C–H and O–H bonds; a condensed formula groups those bonds to save space.

An alkene needs at least two carbons because it contains C=C. Ethene is CH2=CH2 and propene is CH2=CHCH3. But-1-ene is CH2=CHCH2CH3; but-2-ene is CH3CH=CHCH3. Number the chain from the end giving the double bond the smaller number. Alcohols include methanol CH3OH, ethanol CH3CH2OH, propan-1-ol CH3CH2CH2OH and propan-2-ol CH3CH(OH)CH3. The four-carbon unbranched alcohols are butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol. Their OH group belongs to an alcohol when it is not part of COOH. Methanoic acid HCOOH, ethanoic acid CH3COOH, propanoic acid CH3CH2COOH and butanoic acid CH3CH2CH2COOH each include the carboxyl carbon in the chain count. Ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH2CH3, has two carbon fragments joined by an ester linkage. Check the functional group before counting: an oxygen between two fragments does not join them into a single uninterrupted carbon chain.

blocks.heading: Functional groups and endings
blocks.text:
A functional group is the atom or group of atoms responsible for a family's characteristic chemical reactions. In a simple alkene it is the carbon–carbon double bond, C=C. In an alcohol it is the hydroxyl group, –OH, bonded to a saturated carbon. A carboxylic acid contains the complete –COOH group, written more explicitly as –C(=O)–OH. An alkane contains carbon and hydrogen with single carbon–carbon bonds; it has no separate reactive functional group of the kinds just listed. The ending -ane therefore identifies the saturated hydrocarbon family.

Names ending in -ene, -ol and -oic acid usually identify the alkene, alcohol and carboxylic-acid families studied here. Use the full structure if one is supplied. Seeing OH somewhere in a formula is not sufficient to call the compound an alcohol: ethanoic acid contains an OH within COOH, and its reactions are those of a carboxylic acid. Similarly an ester contains –C(=O)–O– between carbon-containing groups, not a free carboxyl OH. Classification should explain the relevant bond or group rather than rely on how the whole molecule looks on the page. A rotated drawing represents the same compound when its connections are unchanged.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.8.3.j.title: 10.8.3 — classify fibre polymers as natural or synthetic, give examples of both and observe the different types of fibres used in the home

blocks.heading: Natural and synthetic fibres
blocks.text:
Natural fibres include cotton and wool. Cotton is a plant fibre based mainly on cellulose, a carbohydrate polymer; wool is an animal fibre containing proteins. Synthetic fibres include nylon and polyester such as Terylene. Their polymers are manufactured through chemical processes. A textile can contain a blend, so its label may name more than one fibre class.

Classify by source and chemical type rather than appearance alone. A soft fibre is not necessarily natural, and a shiny one is not necessarily synthetic. In the home, clothing labels provide evidence for identifying fibre mixtures; the feel of a fabric is a useful observation but not a definitive chemical test. The polymer structure contributes to behaviour, while weaving, fibre thickness and finishes also affect the fabric. A comparison should therefore state whether it concerns individual fibres or finished textiles. Natural does not mean identical or suitable for every use: cotton and wool differ chemically and physically. Synthetic does not automatically mean waterproof, because water uptake depends on the particular material and construction.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Natural and synthetic fibres
blocks.text:
State whether nylon and cotton are synthetic or natural fibres.

Nylon is synthetic; cotton is natural.

Checking the response: Nylon is synthetic; cotton is natural (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Natural and synthetic fibres
blocks.text:
Explain why softness alone cannot reliably identify a fibre as natural.

Both natural and synthetic fibres can be made into soft fabrics, so softness is not unique to natural origin.

Checking the response: Both natural and synthetic fibres can be made into soft fabrics, so softness is not unique to natural origin (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Fibres become textiles
blocks.text:
Fibres are spun or assembled into yarns and fabrics. A textile's useful properties include insulation, water absorption, strength and flexibility. Insulating fabrics reduce heat transfer, often partly by trapping air. An absorbent fabric takes up water, making it suitable for a towel but not necessarily for an outer rain barrier. The intended use determines which property matters.

A fair comparison controls specimen size, thickness, initial dryness and test conditions. Water absorption can be compared by weighing equal dry samples, applying a defined soaking and draining method, and calculating the mass of water retained. Insulation can be compared by wrapping identical warm-water containers with equal layers of fabric and recording temperature against time. A smaller temperature drop suggests better insulation under those conditions. It does not prove that fibre chemistry alone caused the difference if weave or thickness also varied. State that limitation and improve the design. Repeating measurements helps reveal variation rather than relying on one convenient result.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Fibres become textiles
blocks.text:
Outline how fabric properties suit a towel and a warm blanket.

A towel needs high water absorption; a blanket needs thermal insulation to reduce heat loss.

Checking the response: A towel absorbs water so it removes water from a wet surface or body (1). A blanket provides thermal insulation, reducing heat loss from the body (1).

blocks.text:
Explain why comparing one thin fabric with a much thicker fabric cannot isolate the effect of fibre type on insulation.

Thickness also changes heat transfer, so it is a confounding variable.

Checking the response: Thickness also changes heat transfer, so it is a confounding variable (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Persistent plastic and fibre pollution
blocks.text:
Many conventional plastics and synthetic fibres are not readily biodegradable. They can persist in the environment, accumulate as litter and fragment into smaller pieces. Wildlife can be harmed by entanglement or ingestion. Persistent does not mean chemically indestructible: sunlight and physical wear can break an object into fragments without rapidly converting it into harmless simple substances through biological action.

Waste management should distinguish reduction, reuse, recycling and disposal. Reducing unnecessary material prevents waste at source. Reuse extends the service of an item. Recycling can recover material but depends on collection, sorting and suitable processing. Mixed materials and contamination can make recycling difficult. Burning mixed plastic waste can release harmful products and is not a suitable classroom solution. Synthetic fibres shed from textiles can contribute small particles to water systems. An explanation should connect slow biodegradation to accumulation, not claim that a material disappears merely because its pieces become too small to see. Compare benefits during use with the persistence and management of the resulting waste.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Persistent plastic and fibre pollution
blocks.text:
Describe the limitation of a waste-treatment trial that reports a plastic bag disappeared from sight after shredding but measures neither polymer breakdown nor the resulting fragments.

Loss of visibility establishes fragmentation, not chemical biodegradation. Without collecting or tracking the fragments the trial cannot show removal of persistent plastic from the environment.

Checking the response: Visual disappearance does not demonstrate chemical breakdown (1). Missing fragment tracking prevents a claim of environmental removal (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Persistent plastic and fibre pollution
blocks.text:
Describe why a plastic bag breaking into tiny fragments does not solve the pollution problem.

Fragmentation makes smaller pieces without necessarily biodegrading the material; the persistent pieces can spread and enter organisms.

Checking the response: Fragmentation is not biodegradation (1). Persistent small pieces disperse/cause harm (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-47 — Testing fabric absorption and insulation
blocks.text:
Aim: compare fabric properties with a controlled measurement. For absorption, use equal-area, comparable-thickness dry fabric pieces, a balance, water, a timer and a standard draining arrangement. Weigh each dry sample, soak for the same time, then drain for the same time without arbitrary squeezing and reweigh. Original practice data: sample X has dry mass 2.00 g and drained mass 5.60 g; sample Y has dry mass 2.00 g and drained mass 3.20 g. X retains 3.60 g water and Y retains 1.20 g under this procedure.

For insulation, wrap identical containers with equal layers of the fabrics, add equal masses of water at the same initial temperature, and record temperature at fixed times in the same surroundings. Use comfortably warm teacher-prepared water rather than an unnecessary scalding temperature. Original practice data after ten minutes: from 50 °C initially, X ends at 43 °C and Y at 39 °C. The drops are 7 and 11 °C, suggesting better insulation by X in this arrangement.

Repeat trials and compare averages. Do not infer natural or synthetic origin from these results alone. Fibre chemistry, weave, thickness and trapped air all affect the outcome. If thickness cannot be matched, identify it as a limitation and describe the result as a comparison of the fabrics as supplied. A good conclusion distinguishes water absorption from thermal insulation; one property does not logically prove the other.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.6.jso.title: 10.6 — describe carboxylic acids as compounds with the carboxyl functional group (COOH)

blocks.heading: Carboxylic acids
blocks.text:
Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group, –COOH. This combines a carbonyl bond, C=O, with an O–H group on the same carbon: –C(=O)–OH. Ethanoic acid is CH3COOH. The carboxyl carbon is one of the two carbon atoms, so the prefix eth- is consistent with its formula. Methanoic acid HCOOH has one carbon, while propanoic and butanoic acids contain three and four respectively.

The full group controls classification. An alcohol also has an O–H bond, but that OH is not attached as part of COOH. A carboxylic acid can show acid reactions in aqueous solution, such as reacting with a carbonate to release carbon dioxide. Ethanoic acid is a weak acid: it partially ionises in water. Weak is different from dilute; strong/weak describes ionisation, while concentrated/dilute describes the amount per volume. The carbonyl carbon has four bonds in total: two to one oxygen, one to the hydroxyl oxygen and one to the rest of the molecule, or to hydrogen in methanoic acid. A structural drawing that gives that carbon five bonds is incorrect even if its atom totals seem plausible.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carboxylic acids
blocks.text:
Describe how to distinguish the functional groups in CH3CH2OH and CH3C(=O)OH by tracing the carbon attached to oxygen.

In CH3CH2OH the OH-bearing carbon has no C=O bond, giving an alcohol. In CH3C(=O)OH the OH is attached to a carbonyl carbon, giving a carboxylic acid.

Checking the response: First displayed connectivity identifies an alcohol group (1). Second connectivity identifies the complete carboxyl group (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carboxylic acids
blocks.text:
Describe why an OH group in ethanol does not give the same characteristic chemistry as the OH within a carboxyl group.

In a carboxyl group the OH is connected to a carbonyl carbon; the complete functional group, not the isolated OH letters, determines the characteristic reactions.

Checking the response: Carbonyl connectivity distinguishes COOH from alcohol OH (1). Whole functional-group arrangement explains different characteristic chemistry (1).

blocks.heading: Oxidation of ethanol
blocks.text:
Ethanol can be oxidised to ethanoic acid. One route uses microorganisms in the presence of oxygen, as in the formation of vinegar from an alcoholic liquid. This oxygen-dependent stage differs from the oxygen-excluding fermentation used to produce ethanol from sugar. A liquid left exposed to air may therefore change from containing mainly the alcohol product to containing more acid under suitable biological conditions.

A laboratory route uses an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium manganate(VII), with appropriate controlled warming. Its purple colour is lost as the oxidising agent reacts. This observation alone is not a unique test for ethanol, since other reducing substances also react. Keep the transformation at the required level: ethanol is converted to ethanoic acid, with the oxidising conditions stated. Detailed equations and mechanisms for this conversion are not needed. Compare it with combustion carefully. Both are oxidation processes, but complete combustion forms carbon dioxide and water, while this controlled conversion retains the two-carbon skeleton. Acidified oxidant and flammable alcohol require a teacher-controlled procedure and appropriate heating arrangements.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxidation of ethanol
blocks.text:
Describe why ethanol mixed with an oxidising reagent and ethanol merely diluted with water can give different chemical products. The first mixture is gently warmed under teacher supervision.

A suitable oxidising reagent can convert ethanol to ethanoic acid; dilution changes concentration without producing that oxidation.

Checking the response: Oxidation can produce ethanoic acid (1). Dilution alone does not cause this chemical conversion (1).

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.2.2.j.title: 10.2.2 — describe the concept of homologous series as a ‘family’ of similar compounds with similar chemical properties due to the presence of the same functional group and a trend in physical properties

blocks.heading: What a homologous series means
blocks.text:
A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group, a common general formula and similar chemical reactions. Successive members differ by CH2. Their physical properties show a gradual trend as the chain becomes longer. For example, the boiling temperatures of the unbranched alkanes generally rise with increasing chain length. Similar reactions do not mean that all members have identical boiling points, densities or physical states.

Separate a chemical similarity from a physical trend. Alcohols share reactions associated with their hydroxyl group. Differences in molecular size change attractions between molecules and therefore affect physical properties. A family definition should contain both ideas when requested: common chemical behaviour because of the common functional group, and a systematic variation in physical behaviour. A molecule with a different functional group belongs to a different family even when it happens to have the same number of carbon atoms. Ethane and ethanol both have two carbons, but their functional groups and characteristic reactions differ. A molecular formula by itself may not reveal the functional group, so inspect the structural formula when classification is uncertain.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — What a homologous series means
blocks.text:
Describe why a homologous series can show similar reactions while its boiling points change as molecules grow.

The shared functional group gives similar chemistry; larger molecules generally have stronger intermolecular attractions and need more energy to separate.

Checking the response: The shared functional group gives similar characteristic reactions (1). Larger molecules generally have stronger intermolecular attractions, requiring more energy and a higher temperature to separate them (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — What a homologous series means
blocks.text:
Describe why members of one homologous series can react similarly but have different boiling points.

The shared functional group gives similar reactions, while increasing molecular size changes intermolecular attractions and boiling temperature.

Checking the response: Shared functional group explains similar chemistry (1). Molecular size/intermolecular attraction changes explain physical trend (1).

blocks.heading: General formulae
blocks.text:
A general formula expresses the atom-number pattern for a family. For unbranched or branched open-chain alkanes it is CnH2n+2. The open-chain alkenes considered here, with one carbon–carbon double bond, follow CnH2n. Saturated monohydric alcohols follow CnH2n+1OH; writing the OH separately makes the functional group visible. The symbol n is a positive whole number representing the number of carbon atoms, not a chemical element.

Substitution into a general formula is a check, not a substitute for reading bonds. At n = 3, the alkane formula gives C3H8, the alkene formula gives C3H6 and the alcohol formula gives C3H7OH. Count the OH hydrogen when comparing total hydrogen atoms. The alcohol has eight hydrogen atoms in total. A formula pattern applies within its stated family: matching CnH2n without any structural information is not proof of an alkene in every possible organic compound. In the syllabus cases, inspect C=C or the name ending as well. Confusing general formula with molecular formula is another common mistake: CnH2n is general, whereas C2H4 describes a particular molecule's atom counts.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — General formulae
blocks.text:
State the relationship between the general formulae of members of one homologous series.

They follow the same general formula.

Checking the response: They follow the same general formula (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Structural isomers
blocks.text:
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different arrangements of bonds between atoms. Drawing a chain in a curved shape instead of a straight line does not create an isomer if its connections are unchanged. Butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3, and 2-methylpropane, CH3CH(CH3)CH3, are the two structural isomers of C4H10. Both contain four carbons and ten hydrogens, but one has an unbranched carbon chain and the other has a branched carbon skeleton.

For C5H12 the required examples are pentane CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3, 2-methylbutane CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH3 and 2,2-dimethylpropane C(CH3)4. Check the central carbon of the last structure: it has four carbon neighbours and no hydrogen. Propan-1-ol CH3CH2CH2OH and propan-2-ol CH3CH(OH)CH3 are positional isomers with the same formula C3H7OH. The OH group occupies a different position on the same three-carbon skeleton. Numbering from the other end must not duplicate an existing structure. The alcohols have different connectivity, not merely a different orientation on the page. These named isomers extend beyond the unbranched naming set, but that does not require a general study of all branched organic compounds.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Structural isomers
blocks.text:
Identify the term for compounds with the same molecular formula but different atom connectivity.

Structural isomers.

Checking the response: Structural isomers (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

Why do alcohols in one homologous series show similar characteristic reactions?
A. Their molecules have equal lengths
B. They have identical molecular formulae
C. Their boiling points are equal
D. They share the hydroxyl functional group

D. They share the hydroxyl functional group The common functional group governs similar chemistry.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: The common functional group governs similar chemistry. Distractor explanations: B confuses general with molecular formula; C ignores physical trends; A ignores increasing chain length.

topics/10/content-units/CU-6117-10.7.jso.title: 10.7 — describe the formation of ethyl ethanoate by the reaction of ethanoic acid with ethanol

blocks.heading: Making ethyl ethanoate
blocks.text:
Ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid to form ethyl ethanoate and water. This esterification is commonly carried out with an acid catalyst and gentle warming in a controlled water bath. Ethyl ethanoate has the structure CH3C(=O)OCH2CH3. The ethyl part of its name comes from ethanol and the ethanoate part from ethanoic acid. The ester linkage is –C(=O)–O– between the carbon-containing parts.

Condensation describes joining molecules with elimination of a small molecule, here water. Esterification is reversible, so a simple reaction mixture need not be pure ester. Do not identify a product by smell alone or directly inhale laboratory vapours. A structural answer should preserve the carbonyl double bond and oxygen's two bonds. When applying the naming pattern to a supplied different alcohol, keep the acid-derived part separate: propan-1-ol with ethanoic acid gives propyl ethanoate. That extension uses the same naming relationship; it does not require a new reaction mechanism. Distinguish ethyl ethanoate from ethanol: their names share letters, but their functional groups and molecular structures differ.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Making ethyl ethanoate
blocks.text:
Describe the corrections to a proposed ethyl-ethanoate preparation that combines methanol with ethanoic acid and claims water is a reactant in ester formation.

Replace methanol with ethanol; water is formed along with the ester during acid-catalysed esterification.

Checking the response: Ethanol provides the ethyl group (1). Water is a product, not the stated esterification reactant (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Making ethyl ethanoate
blocks.text:
Suggest the missing reactant for making ethyl ethanoate from ethanol.

Ethanoic acid.

Checking the response: Ethanoic acid (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Uses of esters
blocks.text:
Many esters are used in flavours and fragrances because they have characteristic smells. The name of the chemical family is not a guarantee that every member smells pleasant or is safe to ingest. Commercial food or fragrance use requires the appropriate substance and formulation. In this course, flavours and fragrances are sufficient named applications of esters.

An ester use should not be confused with an alcohol use. Ethanol can act as a solvent carrying a fragrance, while an ester can contribute a particular fragrance. The roles may occur in the same product but belong to different substances. A named use earns more useful credit than 'making chemicals'. For a structure question, identify the –COO– linkage rather than assuming that any substance with a fruity smell must have a particular formula. Observations such as odour can support an account of a known preparation but are not a substitute for structural evidence or controlled identification. Do not taste laboratory products, and vapour exposure is controlled by the teacher.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of esters
blocks.text:
State one use of esters.

In flavours or fragrances.

Checking the response: In flavours or fragrances (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-10-P01 (8)
blocks.text:
Which account describes formation of ethyl ethanoate?
A. Alcohol + acid → ester + water
B. Ethanoic acid loses its entire carbon group
C. Ethanol becomes an ester by filtration
D. Ethene and bromine form an ester

A. Alcohol + acid → ester + water An alcohol and carboxylic acid form an ester plus water.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: An alcohol and carboxylic acid form an ester plus water. Distractor explanations: D gives a brominated addition product; B does not conserve the required ester skeleton; C physical filtration cannot cause esterification.

topics/8/content-units/CU-6117-8.1.json.title: 8.1 — describe the use of the following tests to identify

blocks.heading: Ammonium ions
blocks.text:
To test for ammonium ions, add aqueous sodium hydroxide to a small sample and warm carefully under supervision. Ammonia is released if ammonium ions are present. Test the gas with damp red litmus paper held clear of the liquid; it turns blue. State the reagent, warming condition and gas-test observation rather than writing that a smell proves ammonium.

The gas is ammonia, NH3, while the ion being identified is ammonium, NH4⁺. Confusing those names loses the distinction between original sample and product of the test. Sodium hydroxide droplets can also make litmus blue, so keep the paper out of contact with the liquid and avoid vigorous boiling or spray. Use separate clean samples for other tests. A nitrate reduction test also produces ammonia, but it requires additional aluminium and different interpretation; warming with alkali alone is the relevant ammonium comparison.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ammonium ions
blocks.text:
Describe two corrections to an ammonium test in which cold NaOH is added and dry red litmus is held in the alkaline liquid.

Warm carefully and hold damp red litmus in the gas above the liquid, avoiding contact with liquid or spray.

Checking the response: Careful warming to release gas (1). Damp paper in gas, not alkaline liquid/spray (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ammonium ions
blocks.text:
State the cation indicated when an aqueous sample gives a gas turning damp red litmus blue on warming with NaOH, without added aluminium.

Ammonium, NH4⁺.

Checking the response: Ammonium, NH4⁺ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Aluminium ions
blocks.text:
Aluminium ions give a white precipitate when aqueous sodium hydroxide is added gradually. The precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide, leaving a colourless solution. With aqueous ammonia on a fresh portion, a white precipitate forms but does not dissolve in excess. Record the initial solid and the final behaviour separately.

The sodium hydroxide result alone does not distinguish aluminium from zinc, because both give white precipitates soluble in excess NaOH. The ammonia comparison distinguishes them in the syllabus set: aluminium's precipitate remains, whereas zinc's dissolves in excess ammonia. Do not call the final colourless sodium hydroxide mixture a white solution. White described the precipitate that was present before excess reagent. A colourless solution may contain dissolved aluminium species even though no solid is visible; detailed complex-ion formulae are not required for the observation-based identification.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Aluminium ions
blocks.text:
Describe how a record for a suspected Al³⁺ solution should be corrected: “white solution after a little NaOH; the precipitate disappeared in excess”.

Record an initial white precipitate, followed by a colourless solution when the solid dissolves in excess.

Checking the response: Initial white material is a precipitate, not a solution (1). After dissolution record a colourless solution, not a white precipitate (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Aluminium ions
blocks.text:
State which ion, Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺, gives a white precipitate soluble in excess NaOH but insoluble in excess aqueous ammonia on a fresh portion.

Al³⁺.

Checking the response: Al³⁺ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Zinc ions
blocks.text:
Zinc ions give a white precipitate with a small amount of aqueous sodium hydroxide. It dissolves in excess to give a colourless solution. A fresh portion treated with aqueous ammonia also gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess, again leaving a colourless solution. Both the initial and excess-reagent observations are needed for the full test pattern.

Compare the two reagents rather than stopping after white precipitate. Aluminium and calcium can also give white solids under suitable tests, but their excess behaviour differs. Aluminium's precipitate does not dissolve in excess ammonia, and calcium's does not dissolve in excess NaOH. Use clean labelled portions so a previous reagent does not alter the next test. The conclusion is strongest when the complete observed pattern agrees with the candidate ion, not when one colour is treated as a unique fingerprint.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Zinc ions
blocks.text:
Describe the evidence that rejects Al³⁺ in this two-candidate test: Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ both give white precipitates with NaOH; only the Zn²⁺ precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia. X gives a white precipitate that dissolves in excess ammonia.

The excess-ammonia result matches Zn²⁺ and contradicts the stated Al³⁺ behaviour.

Checking the response: Zn²⁺ selected from excess-ammonia dissolution (1). Al³⁺ rejected because its precipitate would remain (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Zinc ions
blocks.text:
State which ion, Al³⁺ or Zn²⁺, is supported by white precipitates that dissolve in excess of both NaOH and aqueous ammonia on separate portions.

Zn²⁺.

Checking the response: Zn²⁺ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Calcium ions
blocks.text:
Calcium ions give a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, insoluble in excess. With aqueous ammonia there is no precipitate or only a very slight white precipitate under the syllabus test conditions. Preserve this qualification rather than treating every slight cloudiness as evidence against calcium.

A flame test can add a brick-red observation, distinguishing calcium from ions with other flame colours. The wet and flame tests provide different kinds of evidence and should be recorded separately. With a very dilute sample, a weak precipitate may be difficult to see; compare against a clean reagent blank where appropriate. A white solid by itself is not a unique calcium test. The useful combination is NaOH insolubility, the limited ammonia response and a suitable confirming observation. Do not invent a deeply coloured solution for a colourless calcium-ion sample.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Calcium ions
blocks.text:
Describe which candidate fits X and why: supplied references say Ca²⁺ gives a white precipitate with NaOH but no or very slight precipitate with ammonia; Zn²⁺ gives a white precipitate with both. X follows the first pattern on separate portions.

Ca²⁺ fits; the absence or near absence of an ammonia precipitate distinguishes it from Zn²⁺.

Checking the response: Ca²⁺ selected (1). Ammonia result distinguishes the candidates (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Calcium ions
blocks.text:
State the ion supported by a brick-red flame and a white precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH: Ca²⁺ or Zn²⁺.

Ca²⁺.

Checking the response: Ca²⁺ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Copper(II): solid and solution colours
blocks.text:
Copper(II) ions give a light-blue precipitate with a small amount of aqueous sodium hydroxide. That precipitate remains insoluble in excess NaOH. With aqueous ammonia on a separate portion, the initial precipitate is also light blue, but excess ammonia dissolves it to form a dark or deep-blue solution. The final liquid is a solution, not a deeper-coloured precipitate.

Record which reagent was used and whether it was in excess. A statement that copper turns blue is ambiguous because an initial copper(II) solution may already be blue and the test can produce both a blue solid and a different blue solution. Use the words precipitate forms, remains or dissolves to describe the change. The copper(II) ion is also distinct from copper metal and from copper(II) carbonate: a green carbonate solid is not made blue simply because it contains copper. These distinctions prevent a memorised colour from being attached to the wrong substance or physical state.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Copper(II): solid and solution colours
blocks.text:
Describe the change of physical state in this Cu²⁺ test record: a light-blue solid appears after a little ammonia; after excess ammonia, no solid remains and the liquid is deep blue.

A light-blue precipitate forms first; it dissolves to give a deep-blue solution.

Checking the response: Initial precipitate correctly distinguished from liquid (1). Dissolution gives deep-blue solution, not deep-blue precipitate (1).

blocks.text:

Cu²⁺.

blocks.text:
Explain why a learner cannot call a supplied green copper(II) carbonate solid blue just because many copper(II) test results involve blue colours.

The colour belongs to the specific substance and state; the given carbonate solid is green, not the blue hydroxide precipitate or solution.

Checking the response: The colour belongs to the specific substance and state; the given carbonate solid is green, not the blue hydroxide precipitate or solution (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Copper(II): solid and solution colours
blocks.text:
Explain the error in recording a deep-blue precipitate after excess ammonia has dissolved the light-blue solid in a copper(II) test.

The final deep-blue material is a solution; the precipitate has dissolved.

Checking the response: The final deep-blue material is a solution; the precipitate has dissolved (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Iron(II) ions
blocks.text:
Iron(II) ions give a green precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, insoluble in excess. Aqueous ammonia on a fresh portion also gives a green precipitate insoluble in excess. State the initial green observation, because exposure to air can change the appearance as iron(II) material is oxidised.

Iron(II) and iron(III) are different ions of the same element, with different charges and test colours. A delayed brown appearance does not justify rewriting the original green observation as if it never occurred. Record timing and any subsequent change separately. In a supplied candidate set containing Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, a fresh green precipitate supports Fe²⁺, whereas a red-brown precipitate supports Fe³⁺. Avoid identifying every green solution as iron(II); reagent, precipitate formation and excess behaviour provide the relevant evidence.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Iron(II) ions
blocks.text:
Describe the supported identification and one limit: reference Fe²⁺ gives green precipitate and Fe³⁺ red-brown with NaOH, both insoluble in excess. A fresh sample gives green precipitate remaining in excess.

Fe²⁺ is supported by the green colour. Insolubility alone cannot distinguish the two ions.

Checking the response: Fe²⁺ inferred from green colour (1). Shared excess-reagent behaviour alone is not diagnostic (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Iron(II) ions
blocks.text:
State which iron ion is indicated by a freshly formed green precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH: Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺.

Fe²⁺.

blocks.heading: Iron(III) ions
blocks.text:
Iron(III) ions give a red-brown precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide. It remains insoluble in excess. Aqueous ammonia gives a red-brown precipitate with the same excess-reagent behaviour on a separate sample. The observation distinguishes iron(III) from the initial green precipitate of iron(II) in the specified tests.

Write iron(III) or Fe³⁺ rather than just iron, because the oxidation state is the target of the comparison. A sample containing a mixture may produce less straightforward observations than a single-ion exercise; do not invent certainty beyond the supplied evidence. In a clean candidate comparison, the reddish-brown solid and its persistence in excess reagent support the inference. Distinguish colour of the original solution from colour of the precipitate. The reagent can create a new solid whose colour is the observation being recorded.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Iron(III) ions
blocks.text:
Describe why a learner cannot identify Fe³⁺ solely from “precipitate remains in excess ammonia” if the candidate table shows this for both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. State the further observation needed; reference colours are green and red-brown respectively.

The excess-reagent result is shared. Record the precipitate colour: red-brown supports Fe³⁺, green Fe²⁺.

Checking the response: Shared persistence is inconclusive (1). Colour comparison using the supplied references resolves the candidates (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Iron(III) ions
blocks.text:
State the cation among Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ indicated by a red-brown precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH.

blocks.heading: Lithium flame test
blocks.text:
Lithium salts give a red flame in the syllabus test. Use a clean suitable wire loop, a small sample and a non-luminous flame under teacher supervision. The observed colour is the flame colour, not the original salt's appearance. Record the red observation before identifying lithium from the candidate set.

A wire carrying residue from a previous sample can give a mixed or misleading colour. Clean it and check the blank flame before introducing the next sample. Compare lithium red with calcium brick-red rather than treating the two verbal descriptions as identical. A flame colour is useful evidence in the defined test, but a contaminated or mixed sample may need repeat testing. Do not introduce advanced electron-transition calculations; the practical aim is a reliable observation and identification under the stated conditions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Lithium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe the lithium flame-test colour and name the object whose colour is observed.

The flame appears red; the observation refers to the flame, not the salt solution.

Checking the response: Red flame (1). The colour belongs to the flame, not the test solution (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Lithium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe how to investigate a suspected lithium sample when the cleaned wire produces a yellow flame before any sample is added.

Reclean or replace the wire and check a colourless blank; repeat with the sample and look for its own flame colour.

Checking the response: Remove contamination and verify blank (1). Repeat sample test only after a clean blank (1).

blocks.heading: Sodium flame test
blocks.text:
Sodium salts give a bright-yellow flame. Its strong colour can mask weaker colours from other ions when contamination is present. Use a clean wire and a blank check before testing the sample, and avoid transferring solution with a dropper already used for another reagent.

Distinguish the observed yellow flame from the inference sodium present. A dirty wire giving yellow before the sample is added does not establish sodium in the sample itself. Repeat after cleaning and compare the blank with the test. The flame test is not a quantitative sodium-concentration measurement: brightness depends on sample size and conditions as well as composition. In a simple pure-salt exercise, the characteristic bright yellow supports sodium identification; in mixed or contaminated samples, state the limitation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sodium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe the characteristic sodium flame-test colour and one limitation from contamination.

Bright yellow; sodium contamination can produce yellow even when it did not originate from the sample.

Checking the response: Bright yellow (1). Contamination limitation (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sodium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe how to check that a yellow flame comes from a test sample rather than the wire.

Clean the wire and check that its blank flame lacks yellow, then add the sample and look for bright yellow.

Checking the response: Clean-wire blank (1). Sample comparison for yellow (1).

blocks.heading: Potassium flame test
blocks.text:
Potassium salts give a lilac flame. The colour can be harder to see than sodium's bright yellow, so a clean sample holder and suitable flame are especially useful. A teacher-supervised test should use a small sample and compare the observed hue with a known reference or the stated observation guide.

If yellow appears with a faint lilac component, contamination is a plausible explanation and a clean repeat is justified. Do not conclude that potassium is absent merely because a sodium colour dominates the first attempt. State the action and reason: clean the wire, test a blank and repeat so the sample's lilac observation can be distinguished from carry-over. No chemical identity should be inferred from an artist's colour patch alone; schematic colours support the written observations and are not a replacement for controlled testing.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Potassium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe the potassium flame-test observation and how sodium contamination can interfere.

Potassium gives lilac; bright-yellow sodium contamination may mask it.

Checking the response: Lilac (1). Yellow masking/carry-over (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Potassium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe why a suspected potassium result cannot be accepted when the wire alone gives yellow, and the sequence needed before retesting.

The blank proves contamination; clean or replace the wire and confirm a clean blank before adding the sample again.

Checking the response: Contaminated blank invalidates attribution to sample (1). Clean-blank check followed by sample retest (1).

blocks.heading: Calcium flame test
blocks.text:
Calcium salts give a brick-red flame. This observation complements the wet-test pattern of a white precipitate with NaOH that remains in excess, and little or no precipitate with aqueous ammonia. The flame and wet tests should be performed on appropriate separate material and recorded independently.

Compare brick-red with lithium's red in a controlled candidate exercise; colour names are useful but human perception and contamination can make a single observation uncertain. A clean-wire repeat and a supporting wet test improve the inference. Do not say that calcium metal must be burned directly to perform the ion test: the classroom test uses a suitable small salt sample under supervision. The colour is associated with the tested calcium-containing sample and is not a claim that its solution is red.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Calcium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe the calcium flame-test colour and distinguish it from the colour of the test solution.

The flame is brick-red; the observation does not mean the solution is red.

Checking the response: Brick-red flame (1). The flame colour does not establish that the solution is brick-red (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Calcium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe the conclusion and repeat needed if a calcium sample gives a brick-red flame but the same colour was seen with the wire before sampling.

The blank means the colour cannot yet be attributed to the sample; clean or replace the wire, check the blank, and repeat.

Checking the response: Contaminated blank prevents valid attribution (1). Clean-blank repeat before identification (1).

blocks.heading: Barium flame test
blocks.text:
Barium salts give a green flame in the syllabus test. Use teacher-approved small samples because soluble barium compounds require controlled handling and disposal. A clean wire and non-luminous flame make the colour easier to recognise than an already yellow luminous flame.

The green flame supports barium identification within the specified candidate set; it is not a universal proof that any green light comes from barium. Distinguish a flame colour from a green precipitate such as an iron(II) test result. The physical observation and the reagent context matter together. Record the flame colour promptly, compare a blank and repeat if contamination is suspected. Do not use tasting or uncontrolled sample burning to distinguish salts. A well-recorded negative or ambiguous test is more useful than a forced identification.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Barium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe the barium flame-test colour and the physical observation it refers to.

A green flame is observed; it is not the colour of a precipitate or solution.

Checking the response: Green (1). Flame identified as observation (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Barium flame test
blocks.text:
Describe which observation supports barium in a sample: the clean-wire blank is colourless, sample P gives green and sample Q gives yellow. Supplied references: barium green, sodium yellow.

P supports barium; the blank rules out colour already present on the wire, whereas Q fits sodium.

Checking the response: P matched to supplied barium reference (1). Clean blank supports attribution to P, or Q distinguished as sodium (1).

blocks.heading: Carbonate ions
blocks.text:
Add dilute acid to a small carbonate-containing sample. Effervescence occurs as carbon dioxide forms. Pass the gas through limewater to obtain a milky appearance, confirming the gas test. The carbonate inference relies on the reaction with acid plus the carbon dioxide observation, not bubbling alone.

Limewater is the reagent in the second stage, not the reagent that starts the carbonate reaction. Keep the sequence clear: dilute acid releases a gas, then limewater tests that gas. The white material is a precipitate in the limewater, while carbon dioxide is colourless. Use an unobstructed gas path and avoid drawing liquid back into a hot reaction tube. Strong and weak describe acid ionisation, whereas concentrated and dilute describe amount per volume; the test instruction specifies a suitable dilute acid rather than requiring a concentrated acid.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbonate ions
blocks.text:
Describe why bubbles alone cannot confirm carbonate, and the next test on the collected gas. A separate metal–acid reaction also gives bubbles.

Effervescence does not identify the gas; pass a separate gas sample through limewater and look for milkiness.

Checking the response: Bubbles are non-specific, as the comparison demonstrates (1). Limewater milkiness confirms CO2 in this context (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbonate ions
blocks.text:
State the anion indicated by effervescence with dilute acid and a gas that turns limewater milky.

Carbonate, CO3²⁻.

Checking the response: Carbonate, CO3²⁻ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Chloride ions
blocks.text:
Acidify a fresh solution sample with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. Chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride. The precipitate dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia, providing a further distinction from the cream bromide precipitate under the stated conditions.

Nitric acid is chosen because it does not add the chloride ions being tested. Hydrochloric acid would contaminate the test and could produce a false positive. Acidification also removes carbonate interference before silver nitrate is added. Record the order, white precipitate and any ammonia follow-up separately. Do not use a portion already treated with another chloride-containing reagent. The test identifies chloride ions in solution; a white solid forming after arbitrary reagents is not sufficient evidence without the correct procedure.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chloride ions
blocks.text:
Describe why a chloride test must be repeated on a fresh sample if hydrochloric acid was used before silver nitrate. Specify the replacement acid.

Hydrochloric acid adds chloride and could cause the white precipitate itself; repeat with dilute nitric acid.

Checking the response: Introduced chloride makes the original result ambiguous (1). Fresh portion acidified with dilute nitric acid (1).

blocks.text:
State the halide indicated by a white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that dissolves in dilute ammonia.

blocks.heading: Bromide ions
blocks.text:
Bromide ions give a cream precipitate when aqueous silver nitrate is added after acidification with dilute nitric acid. The silver bromide precipitate is insoluble in dilute ammonia in the syllabus comparison. Use the cream colour and stated ammonia concentration together rather than replacing them with a vague pale solid description.

Chloride gives a white precipitate and iodide a yellow one, so consistent lighting and clean separate samples help compare the three. A coloured starting solution can obscure small colour differences, making the full test sequence more useful. Do not add hydrochloric acid for acidification because chloride contamination would create another silver precipitate. Interpret only the stated reagent concentration: dilute ammonia behaviour is the comparison specified here, and it need not be replaced by a detailed study of concentrated-reagent chemistry.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bromide ions
blocks.text:
Describe the identity supported by X and the role of a follow-up: reference chloride gives white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia; bromide gives cream precipitate insoluble in dilute ammonia. X gives a cream precipitate that remains in dilute ammonia.

Bromide is supported by both observations; the follow-up distinguishes it from the stated chloride reference.

Checking the response: Bromide from matching supplied observations (1). Insolubility contrasts with the supplied chloride follow-up (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bromide ions
blocks.text:
State the halide indicated by a cream precipitate after dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate, remaining insoluble in dilute ammonia.

Bromide, Br⁻.

Checking the response: Bromide, Br⁻ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
