blocks.heading: Iodide ions
blocks.text:
Iodide ions give a yellow precipitate after the sample is acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with aqueous silver nitrate. The product is silver iodide. In the syllabus colour comparison, chloride is white, bromide cream and iodide yellow. Describe the solid as a precipitate rather than a yellow solution.

Use a fresh portion and add the reagents in the stated order. A previous sodium hydroxide test or another added ion can interfere if the same tube is reused indiscriminately. The test concerns the iodide ion I⁻, not iodine I2; their names, charges and physical observations differ. No complex-ion formula is needed to identify the yellow precipitate. If observations are mixed or unclear, report that limitation and repeat with clean apparatus instead of assuming one idealised colour proves a pure single-ion sample.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Iodide ions
blocks.text:
Describe a valid conclusion when acidified X gives a yellow precipitate with AgNO3, a reagent blank gives none, and the reference table lists chloride white, bromide cream and iodide yellow.

Iodide is supported by the colour match; the negative blank makes reagent contamination less likely.

Checking the response: Iodide matched to supplied reference (1). Blank supports sample rather than reagent origin (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Iodide ions
blocks.text:
State the halide indicated by a yellow precipitate when an acidified sample is treated with silver nitrate.

Iodide, I⁻.

Checking the response: Iodide, I⁻ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Nitrate ions
blocks.text:
For the syllabus nitrate test, add aqueous sodium hydroxide and then aluminium foil to the sample, warming carefully under supervision. Nitrate is reduced to ammonia. The evolved gas turns damp red litmus blue. Include the aluminium step: warming with alkali alone is the ammonium-ion test rather than the full nitrate test.

An existing ammonium ion can also release ammonia with warm alkali, so it can interfere with interpretation. Use a separate preliminary ammonium check or a suitably prepared sample before attributing ammonia produced after aluminium addition to nitrate. Keep litmus clear of the liquid so alkaline spray is not mistaken for ammonia. The inference is nitrate initially in solution, not ammonia as the original anion. Detailed reduction balancing is unnecessary for this practical identification objective; the required elements are reagents, warming, gas test and careful interpretation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nitrate ions
blocks.text:
Describe why ammonia after warming a sample with NaOH and aluminium cannot by itself prove nitrate, and give a comparison that addresses the ambiguity.

Ammonium already in the sample can also release ammonia. Test a fresh portion with NaOH and warming but without aluminium.

Checking the response: Pre-existing ammonium is an alternative explanation (1). No-aluminium comparison tests that alternative (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nitrate ions
blocks.text:
State the anion indicated when a sample confirmed free of ammonium gives ammonia on warming with NaOH and aluminium foil.

Nitrate, NO3⁻.

Checking the response: Nitrate, NO3⁻ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Sulfate ions
blocks.text:
Acidify a fresh sample with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate. Sulfate ions produce a white precipitate of barium sulfate. Acidification removes carbonate interference, which could otherwise also form an insoluble barium salt. The procedure therefore makes the white-precipitate inference more specific.

Do not acidify with sulfuric acid, because it supplies the sulfate being tested and can cause a false positive. A fresh portion also avoids contamination from previous reagents. State which barium reagent is used and describe the white solid explicitly as a precipitate. The observation is not a white solution. Handle soluble barium reagents only under appropriate supervision and collect waste as directed. The conclusion identifies sulfate in the original sample, not nitrate introduced by the test reagents.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sulfate ions
blocks.text:
Describe why a sulfate test is invalid if sulfuric acid is added before barium nitrate, and how to repeat it.

The acid introduces sulfate; repeat on a fresh portion using dilute nitric acid before barium nitrate.

Checking the response: Added sulfate can cause the precipitate independently of the sample (1). Fresh sample with nitric-acid pretreatment (1).

State the anion indicated by a white precipitate after dilute nitric acid and barium nitrate are added to a fresh sample.

Why should the wire be checked in a blank flame before a lithium sample is added?
A. It makes every flame red.
B. It detects contamination on the wire.

B. It detects contamination on the wire. A blank distinguishes carry-over from sample evidence.

Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: A blank distinguishes carry-over from sample evidence. Distractor explanations: D: elements are not converted. C: no mass measurement. A: colour still depends on sample and contamination.

Suggest a method and reason for checking a suspected potassium flame result that appears mainly yellow with a faint lilac component.

Clean the wire, check its blank flame and repeat the test. This removes possible sodium carry-over so a persistent lilac potassium colour can be distinguished from yellow contamination.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-8-P03 (a)
blocks.text:
Describe the NaOH procedure and the initial and excess-reagent observations for X. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate.

Add aqueous NaOH dropwise to a small portion, then add excess. A light-blue precipitate forms initially and remains insoluble in excess.

NaOH gradually then excess (1). Light-blue precipitate (1). Remains insoluble in excess (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-8-P03 (b)
blocks.text:
Deduce the cation in X from these observations. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate.

Copper(II), Cu²⁺.

Cu²⁺/copper(II) (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-8-P03 (c)
blocks.text:
Describe the halide-test procedure on a fresh portion of X and its observation. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate.

Acidify a fresh portion with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate. A white precipitate forms.

Fresh portion with dilute nitric acid (1). Aqueous silver nitrate added (1). White precipitate (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-8-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Explain why separate portions and nitric-acid pretreatment are used, and identify the anion by comparing the white precipitate with the chloride, bromide and iodide alternatives. Original synthetic results for unknown X. Cation candidates: Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺. Anion candidates: Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. NaOH added gradually gives a light-blue precipitate; excess NaOH leaves the precipitate. A separate portion acidified with dilute nitric acid and treated with AgNO3 gives a white precipitate.

Separate portions prevent earlier reagents carrying over into a different test. Nitric-acid pretreatment removes carbonate interference without adding halide. White silver precipitate supports chloride rather than the cream bromide or yellow iodide alternatives.

Prevents reagent carry-over (1). Acidification removes carbonate interference (1). Cl⁻ identified by white versus cream/yellow alternatives (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-8-P03 (e)
blocks.text:
State two apparatus choices that help keep unknown-solution tests organised and control reagent addition.

Clean labelled test tubes and separate droppers for controlled addition.

Clean labelled test tubes (1). Dropper(s) for controlled addition (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-39 — A systematic test record
blocks.text: In a supervised sequence covering the Annexe B tests, use labelled small portions for each reagent. Record reagent identity, addition order, initial observation and behaviour in excess where relevant. Keep sodium hydroxide and ammonia results in separate columns, and distinguish precipitate colour from final solution colour. Include clean-wire flame tests and the specified gas tests. Compare observations with known reference samples before interpreting unknowns. Do not taste chemicals or smell gases directly. Controlled handling and waste collection are needed for silver, barium, lead and other hazardous reagents. A complete test record is more useful than a list of ion names without the observations that support them.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-40 — Identifying both ions in an unknown
blocks.text: Take separate labelled portions of a soluble unknown. Use sodium hydroxide and, where needed, aqueous ammonia to investigate the cation; use a fresh portion for the appropriate anion test. An original practice sample gives a light-blue precipitate insoluble in excess NaOH, and a white precipitate after dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate. These observations support copper(II) and chloride within the stated candidate set. Infer copper(II) chloride only after both ion conclusions are justified. Do not identify the anion from solution colour or use a previously contaminated portion. Report an ambiguous observation rather than forcing a unique answer when the evidence does not distinguish candidates.

blocks.text: Connect these tests to ionic charges, solubility rules and reliable observations. Name the reagent, its order and amount condition, the physical change, and only then the inferred ion or gas.

topics/8/content-units/CU-6117-8.2.json.title: 8.2 — describe the use of the following tests to identify

blocks.heading: Ammonia gas
blocks.text:
Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue. The paper must be damp so the gas can dissolve and produce an alkaline condition at the indicator. Hold the paper in the gas region without touching the generating liquid. Direct contact with alkaline liquid or spray could turn it blue without establishing that ammonia gas was present.

Use the chemical test rather than deliberately smelling the gas. Ammonia is not ammonium: ammonia is the gas NH3, while ammonium is the ion NH4⁺ that can release ammonia when warmed with alkali. In a supplied unknown-gas exercise, red-to-blue litmus supports ammonia among the specified gases. It is different from chlorine's bleaching and from the splint tests for oxygen and hydrogen. Record the initial paper colour, the damp condition and the final colour to make the observation unambiguous.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ammonia gas
blocks.text:
Describe the litmus observation for ammonia gas, including the paper condition.

Damp red litmus turns blue.

Checking the response: Damp red paper (1). Blue result (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ammonia gas
blocks.text:
Describe how to investigate a litmus change seen only when droplets from a warm alkaline mixture hit the paper, but not when paper is held in the gas above it.

Liquid contact can cause the change directly; repeat with damp paper in the gas while shielding it from spray.

Checking the response: Liquid-contact result does not establish ammonia gas (1). Gas-only exposure with spray excluded tests the alternative (1).

blocks.heading: Carbon dioxide gas
blocks.text:
Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Passing the gas into initially clear limewater forms a suspension of white calcium carbonate. The cloudiness is a solid precipitate dispersed in liquid; the gas itself has not turned white. Name limewater rather than simply water when describing the test.

Use a small gas sample and observe the initial change. Passing a large excess of carbon dioxide can eventually clear the precipitate, so a later clear tube does not erase an earlier positive result. Record observations in order. A gas extinguishing a flame is not a specific confirmation of carbon dioxide because several gases do not support combustion. The limewater result is the characteristic test required here. Keep the delivery path open and avoid suck-back when a generating apparatus cools.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbon dioxide gas
blocks.text:
Describe the carbon dioxide test and positive observation.

Pass the gas through limewater; it becomes milky.

Checking the response: Limewater (1). Milky/cloudy result (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbon dioxide gas
blocks.text:
Describe the corrections to “white carbon dioxide gas formed” when the actual observation was a colourless gas entering clear limewater and making the liquid cloudy.

The gas is colourless; the white appearance is a solid precipitate in the limewater.

Checking the response: Colourless gas recorded separately (1). Cloudiness assigned to precipitate in the liquid (1).

blocks.heading: Chlorine gas
blocks.text:
Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. With damp blue litmus, an initial acidic red change may be seen before bleaching, but the characteristic identifying observation is loss of colour. Moisture is needed for the usual test chemistry, so a dry-paper negative result cannot be interpreted as equivalent.

Chlorine is hazardous; use a teacher-controlled demonstration or supplied observations, not deliberate inhalation or unrestricted learner generation. Distinguish bleaching from ammonia turning red litmus blue. An answer naming just litmus without its damp condition and colour loss is incomplete. Also distinguish the gas's appearance from the indicator response: the test establishes an observed chemical effect on damp paper. Test a separate small sample with suitable containment and supervision, and never propose combining unknown gases to see whether they react.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chlorine gas
blocks.text:
Describe the characteristic litmus test for chlorine gas.

It bleaches damp litmus paper, removing its colour.

Checking the response: Damp litmus (1). Bleaching (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chlorine gas
blocks.text:

A fits ammonia and B fits chlorine.

Checking the response: A matched to ammonia using the key (1). B matched to chlorine using the key (1).

blocks.heading: Hydrogen gas
blocks.text:
A small hydrogen sample gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint in the controlled test. Lighted means a visible flame, unlike the glowing splint used to identify oxygen. The pop is evidence of rapid reaction with oxygen from the air at the test boundary.

Testing must use a separate small sample under teacher supervision, with the generating mixture kept away from ignition sources. Do not apply a flame to a large accumulated unknown gas volume. Record the pop rather than writing merely that the gas burns, because burning is not unique to hydrogen. A positive test identifies the gas, not the metal ion left in the generating solution. If hydrogen was made by a reactive metal and dilute acid, the salt in solution is a separate product with its own identification evidence.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen gas
blocks.text:
Describe the hydrogen splint test and positive observation.

A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop with a small hydrogen sample.

Checking the response: Lighted splint (1). Squeaky pop (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen gas
blocks.text:
Describe the errors in a proposed hydrogen test that puts a glowing splint into the gas-generating flask while gas is still being produced.

Use a separately collected small sample and a lighted splint under teacher supervision; do not ignite the generating apparatus.

Checking the response: Separate small sample avoids ignition at the generator (1). Lighted rather than glowing splint (1).

blocks.heading: Oxygen gas
blocks.text:
Oxygen relights a glowing splint. A glowing splint has a hot ember but no visible flame when introduced; renewed flame is the positive observation. Oxygen supports combustion, but the test does not mean oxygen is itself a fuel. A lighted splint simply burning more vigorously is not the precise confirmation required by this test.

Distinguish gas tests from flame tests for metal ions. A lilac flame identifies potassium in a suitable salt test, while a glowing splint relighting identifies oxygen gas in the specified gas comparison. A hydrogen test instead uses a lighted splint and a pop. Keep these three procedures separate in both words and drawings. Record the starting condition of the splint and the observed change, because saying a splint was used leaves the key distinction unresolved.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxygen gas
blocks.text:

A glowing splint relights.

Checking the response: Glowing splint (1). Relights (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Oxygen gas
blocks.text:

The observation does not show relighting; blow out the flame to leave a glowing splint, then test a separate sample for renewed flame.

Checking the response: Continuing flame is not the specified relighting observation (1). Repeat with a glowing, non-flaming splint (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-38 — Obtaining three gas samples
blocks.text: Use teacher-supervised small-scale preparations: carbonate with dilute acid for carbon dioxide, hydrogen peroxide with a suitable catalyst for oxygen, and a suitable reactive metal with dilute hydrochloric acid for hydrogen. Keep samples labelled and separate. Choose a collection method appropriate to the gas and apparatus, leaving an unobstructed outlet. Test carbon dioxide with limewater, oxygen with a glowing splint and a separate small hydrogen sample with a lighted splint. Keep bulk hydrogen generation away from ignition. Record starting materials, collection and test observations separately; a preparation label is a prediction, while the positive gas test is confirming evidence.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-41 — An unknown-gas decision
blocks.text: Use teacher-provided small samples or recorded observations to distinguish the specified gases. A glowing splint relighting supports oxygen; a lighted splint producing a squeaky pop supports hydrogen; limewater turning milky supports carbon dioxide. Damp red litmus becoming blue supports ammonia, while bleaching of damp litmus supports chlorine. Select a suitable test rather than applying ignition to a large unknown gas volume. Keep the observed change separate from the inferred gas name and include the damp or glowing condition explicitly. A negative or unclear test may reflect wet apparatus, contamination or collection error; repeat safely with appropriate controls instead of claiming every gas has been excluded.

topics/4/content-units/CU-6117-4.1.json.title: 4.1 — define relative atomic mass, Ar , of an element as the ratio of the average mass of the atoms of the naturally occurring element to 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom

blocks.heading: Relative atomic mass
blocks.text:
Relative atomic mass, Ar, is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. It has no unit because it is a ratio of masses. The average reflects the naturally occurring isotopic mixture rather than requiring every atom of the element to have identical mass. This is why a Periodic Table value can be non-integer even though a particular isotope's nucleon number is a whole number.

Distinguish Ar from proton number and nucleon number. Proton number counts protons and identifies the element. Nucleon number counts protons plus neutrons in one isotope. Ar is an average mass comparison used in chemical calculations. A table entry such as 35.5 must not be described as thirty-five and a half protons in an atom. When a calculation supplies rounded Ar values, use those values consistently throughout it. An answer in grams belongs to a calculated sample mass, not to Ar itself. The unit distinction prevents errors later when converting between mass and amount.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Relative atomic mass
blocks.text:
Define relative atomic mass, Ar.

The average mass of an atom of an element relative to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

Checking the response: The average mass of an atom of an element relative to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Relative formula mass
blocks.text:
Relative formula mass, Mr, is the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms represented by a chemical formula. It has no unit. For water, using Ar(H) = 1 and Ar(O) = 16 gives Mr = 2 × 1 + 16 = 18. For an ionic compound, the formula represents the simplest ion ratio rather than a separate molecule, but the same mass-summing method applies. Sodium chloride has Mr = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 using those supplied values.

Brackets multiply the complete group within them. In Ca(NO3)2, count one Ca, two N and six O, so Mr = 40 + 2 × 14 + 6 × 16 = 164. Do not multiply only the oxygen or forget the two nitrogen atoms. A useful method is to write the atom counts first, multiply each by its Ar, then add. Keep the distinction between a dimensionless relative formula mass and a molar mass expressed in g/mol, even though their numerical values correspond in the calculations used here.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Relative formula mass
blocks.text:

The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms represented in a chemical formula.

Checking the response: The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms represented in a chemical formula (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Amount of substance and the mole
blocks.text:
A mole is an amount of substance containing approximately 6.022 × 10²³ specified particles. The particle must be named: atoms, molecules, ions or formula units may be counted in different contexts. One mole of oxygen molecules contains one mole of O2 molecules but two moles of oxygen atoms. Both statements describe the same sample from different particle-counting viewpoints.

The mole is not itself a mass or a particle. Equal amounts of two different substances contain equal numbers of their specified particles but can have different masses. One mole of carbon atoms and one mole of water molecules therefore contain the same number of specified particles without weighing the same. If an equation shows a reacting ratio of 1:2, it compares amounts of the stated substances. It does not mean their Avogadro constants differ. Distinguish the number of moles from the number of particles: multiply amount in moles by the Avogadro constant to obtain a particle count, and divide a particle count by that constant to obtain amount.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Amount of substance and the mole
blocks.text:

An amount containing approximately 6.022 × 10²³ of the specified particles.

Checking the response: An amount containing approximately 6.022 × 10²³ of the specified particles (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Amount of substance and the mole
blocks.text:

The Avogadro constant is unchanged; two moles contain twice its numerical particle count, about 1.2044 × 10²⁴ specified particles.

Checking the response: The Avogadro constant is unchanged; two moles contain twice its numerical particle count, about 1.2044 × 10²⁴ specified particles (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: The Avogadro constant
blocks.text:
The Avogadro constant is approximately 6.022 × 10²³ particles per mole. It connects an amount of substance with a number of specified particles. In N = nNA, N is particle number, n is amount in moles and NA is the Avogadro constant. The constant does not change with the element, compound or sample size. What changes is the amount and therefore the total number of particles.

For 0.50 mol of water molecules, the particle count is 0.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ molecules. Each molecule contains three atoms, so a question asking for total atoms would require a further factor of three. Read the requested entity before calculating. The unit mol⁻¹ describes the constant, whereas a particle count is a number of named entities. Confusing those quantities can produce an answer numerically similar to a familiar constant but chemically meaningless. In reacting calculations, use the balanced equation to find the amount first, then convert to a particle count if requested.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The Avogadro constant
blocks.text:

6.022 × 10²³ specified particles per mole.

Checking the response: 6.022 × 10²³ specified particles per mole (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Mass and molar mass
blocks.text:
One mole has a mass in grams numerically equal to the relative mass of the specified substance. Molar mass M expresses this as grams per mole. Using Ar(Mg) = 24 gives M(Mg) = 24 g/mol; using Mr(H2O) = 18 gives M(H2O) = 18 g/mol. The relationship n = m/M converts mass m in grams to amount n in moles. Rearranging gives m = nM.

For 9.0 g of water, n = 9.0/18 = 0.50 mol. For 0.20 mol of magnesium, m = 0.20 × 24 = 4.8 g. These examples show why equal mole amounts need not have equal masses. Be precise about molecules: the molar mass of O2 is 32 g/mol when Ar(O) = 16, while the molar mass of oxygen atoms is 16 g/mol. A balanced reaction involving oxygen gas requires O2. Check that the formula used to calculate M matches the substance named in the equation and question.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Mass and molar mass
blocks.text:

44 g.

Checking the response: 44 g (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Empirical formula
blocks.text:
An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound. It describes composition without necessarily identifying the number of atoms in a molecule. For C6H12O6, dividing all subscripts by six gives the empirical formula CH2O. For C2H6, dividing by two gives CH3. The simplification must apply the same factor to every element.

Some molecular formulae are already in their simplest ratio. H2O cannot be reduced further, so its empirical and molecular formulae are the same. By contrast, different molecular formulae can share an empirical formula; CH2O alone does not prove a molecule is glucose. An empirical formula also does not provide the detailed arrangement of bonds. To determine a molecular formula, additional relative molecular mass information is needed. In calculations from composition by mass, first convert masses to amounts, then find the simplest ratio. Directly copying a mass ratio into subscripts would ignore differences in atomic mass.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Empirical formula
blocks.text:

The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound.

Checking the response: The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the elements in a compound (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Empirical formula mass
blocks.text:
Empirical formula mass is the sum of the relative atomic masses in one empirical-formula unit. It is a relative quantity and has no unit. For CH2O, using C = 12, H = 1 and O = 16 gives 12 + 2 + 16 = 30. A molecule with this empirical formula can contain one or several of these simplest-ratio units.

Divide the given relative molecular mass by the empirical formula mass to obtain the whole-number multiplier. If Mr is 180 and the empirical formula mass is 30, the multiplier is six and the molecular formula is C6H12O6. Multiply every subscript, including any implied one. Multiplying only the carbon count would destroy the empirical ratio. A result far from a sensible whole number indicates that the formula, mass data or arithmetic needs checking; do not round an arbitrary value to force a convenient molecule. Rounded experimental data can produce a value very close to an integer, which should be interpreted with the stated precision.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Empirical formula mass
blocks.text:

Checking the response: The sum of the relative atomic masses in the simplest whole-number formula of a compound (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Concentration
blocks.text:
Concentration is mass or amount of dissolved substance per unit solution volume. Mass concentration is commonly expressed in g/dm³ and amount concentration in mol/dm³. For amount concentration, c = n/V, where V is solution volume in dm³. Thus n = cV and V = n/c. One dm³ equals 1000 cm³, so divide a volume in cm³ by 1000 before using these equations with c in mol/dm³.

The volume is the total solution volume, not the volume of solvent before dissolving. Adding solute to a measured volume of water does not necessarily leave the final volume unchanged. In dilution, the same amount of solute occupies a larger solution volume, so concentration decreases. Strong and weak describe the extent of ionisation of an acid, while concentrated and dilute describe amount per volume; these pairs are not interchangeable. A dilute strong acid can have lower amount concentration than a concentrated weak acid. Stoichiometric calculations use the stated concentration and balanced equation rather than guessing from the word strong.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentration
blocks.text:

Checking the response: Amount of dissolved substance per unit solution volume, expressed in mol/dm³ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

What is empirical formula mass?
A. The relative mass sum for the simplest formula unit.
B. The mass of the whole laboratory sample.
C. The volume of one mole of gas.
D. The sum of all coefficients in an equation.

A. The relative mass sum for the simplest formula unit. It sums Ar values for the empirical formula.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: It sums Ar values for the empirical formula. Distractor explanations: B: sample size is irrelevant. D: coefficients are not formula mass. C: volume is a different quantity.

topics/4/content-units/CU-6117-4.2.json.title: 4.2 — calculate stoichiometric reacting masses of pure substances

blocks.heading: Reacting masses
blocks.text:
A balanced equation supplies ratios of amounts, not direct ratios of masses. Convert the known mass to moles using n = m/M, apply the coefficient ratio, then convert the required amount to mass using m = nM. For 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO, magnesium and magnesium oxide have a 1:1 amount ratio, while oxygen gas has half as many moles. The different molar masses mean their reacting masses are not equal.

Read limiting conditions before applying the ratio. If one reactant is stated to be in excess, the specified other reactant controls the maximum product amount. If amounts of both are given, compare n divided by the respective coefficient; the smaller value identifies the limiting reactant. A theoretical mass assumes the stated reaction completes without losses. Show each stage with its substance label so a correct number is not attached to the wrong material.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reacting masses
blocks.text:
Calculate the theoretical MgO mass when 4.8 g Mg reacts completely with excess oxygen: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Ar: Mg 24, O 16.

n(Mg)=4.8/24=0.200 mol. The Mg:MgO ratio is 1:1, so n(MgO)=0.200 mol. M(MgO)=40 g/mol; mass=0.200×40=8.00 g.

Checking the response: 0.200 mol Mg (1). 1:1 amount transfer to MgO (1). 8.00 g, accepting 8.0 g (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reacting masses
blocks.text:
Calculate the magnesium mass required to produce 10.0 g MgO at complete conversion with excess oxygen: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. Ar: Mg 24, O 16.

M(MgO)=40 g/mol; n(MgO)=10.0/40=0.250 mol. n(Mg)=0.250 mol; mass=0.250×24=6.00 g.

Checking the response: 0.250 mol MgO (1). 1:1 ratio gives 0.250 mol Mg (1). 6.00 g Mg (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reacting masses
blocks.text:
Calculate the CaO mass from complete decomposition of 25.0 g pure CaCO3: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. Molar masses: CaCO3 100 g/mol, CaO 56 g/mol.

n(CaCO3)=25.0/100=0.250 mol. Ratio CaCO3:CaO=1:1, so mass(CaO)=0.250×56=14.0 g.

Checking the response: 0.250 mol CaCO3 (1). 1:1 amount transfer (1). 14.0 g CaO (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reacting masses
blocks.text:
Calculate the water mass formed when 3.2 g O2 reacts completely with excess H2: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. Molar masses: O2 32 g/mol, H2O 18 g/mol.

n(O2)=3.2/32=0.100 mol. n(H2O)=2×0.100=0.200 mol; mass=0.200×18=3.60 g.

Checking the response: 0.100 mol O2 (1). 2:1 ratio gives 0.200 mol water (1). 3.60 g, accepting 3.6 g (1).

blocks.heading: Solutions and reacting amounts
blocks.text:
For a solution with concentration c in mol/dm³ and volume V in dm³, the dissolved amount is n = cV. Convert cm³ to dm³ first. For example, 40.0 cm³ becomes 0.0400 dm³, not 40.0 dm³. A missed conversion causes a factor-of-1000 error. If concentration is given in g/dm³, multiplying by volume gives mass, which must then be divided by molar mass before using a mole ratio.

At a complete reaction endpoint, use the balanced equation to connect the reacting amounts. HCl and NaOH react 1:1, whereas two moles of HCl react with one mole of Na2CO3. Equal volumes therefore do not automatically mean equal reacting amounts. In a limiting-reactant calculation, calculate each available amount separately and compare it with the required ratio. Name the limiting substance before calculating product mass or the amount left over.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Solutions and reacting amounts
blocks.text:
Calculate the amount of HCl in 40.0 cm³ of a 0.150 mol/dm³ HCl solution.

V=40.0/1000=0.0400 dm³. n=cV=0.150×0.0400=0.00600 mol.

Checking the response: 0.0400 dm³ (1). n=cV with correct substitution (1). 0.00600 mol HCl (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Solutions and reacting amounts
blocks.text:
Calculate the amount concentration of a solution containing 0.0100 mol solute in a total volume of 25.0 cm³. Show the volume conversion in your working.

V=25.0/1000=0.0250 dm³. c=n/V=0.0100/0.0250=0.400 mol/dm³. Treating 25 cm³ as 25 dm³ makes the answer 1000 times too small.

Checking the response: 0.0250 dm³ conversion (1). c=n/V with corrected volume (1). 0.400 mol/dm³ (1); diagnostic explanation confirms the same unit correction rather than earning an extra mark.

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Gas volume at room conditions
blocks.text:
Use a molar gas volume of 24 dm³/mol at room temperature and pressure in these calculations. Then Vgas = n × 24 and n = Vgas/24 when volume is in dm³. Convert cm³ to dm³ before division, or use the equivalent 24 000 cm³/mol consistently. The condition belongs with the numerical value: do not apply 24 dm³/mol to an unspecified high-temperature or different-pressure situation without justification.

Combine gas volume with the balanced-equation ratio where needed. If one mole of a carbonate produces one mole of carbon dioxide, calculate carbonate amount and transfer that amount to CO2 before finding volume. Gas volume ratios equal the equation's mole ratios when the gases are compared at the same temperature and pressure. State whether a calculated product volume is theoretical, especially for a reversible reaction. The question must supply enough conditions and completion assumptions to support the requested result.

blocks.text:

Amount remaining = 0.250 mol; volume = 6.00 dm³ at room temperature and pressure.

Checking the response: Subtract to obtain 0.250 mol (1). 6.00 dm³ at the stated room conditions (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Gas volume at room conditions

The N2:NH3 amount and volume ratio is 1:2 at the same conditions. V(NH3)=2×1.20=2.40 dm³.

Checking the response: 1:2 gas-volume ratio at the same conditions (1). 2.40 dm³ theoretical NH3 (1).

blocks.heading: Empirical formula from mass data
blocks.text:
Convert each element's mass to an amount by dividing by its relative atomic mass. Then divide all amounts by the smallest to obtain a ratio. If percentages by mass are supplied, choose a notional 100 g sample, so each percentage becomes the corresponding mass in grams. The choice does not change the ratio. Round only after examining the complete ratio, because early rounding can obscure a simple relationship.

A ratio such as 1:1.5 should be multiplied throughout by two to give whole numbers, not rounded to 1:2. The final formula uses the same element order as the working and has no mole unit. Check it by calculating the approximate mass percentages it would imply. Small differences from rounded input percentages are expected; large differences suggest an incorrect ratio or an omitted element. If a product gains oxygen during a reaction, determine the oxygen mass separately before constructing the amount ratio.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Empirical formula from mass data
blocks.text:
Calculate the empirical formula of a compound with mass percentages C 40.00%, H 6.67%, O 53.33%. Ar: C 12, H 1, O 16.

For 100 g: n(C)=40.00/12=3.3333 mol; n(H)=6.67 mol; n(O)=53.33/16=3.333125 mol. Divide by the smallest: approximately 1:2:1. Empirical formula CH2O.

Checking the response: Mass/Ar amounts for all elements (1). Approximately 1:2:1 ratio (1). CH2O (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Empirical formula from mass data
blocks.text:
Calculate the empirical formula when 0.480 g Mg combines with 0.320 g O. Ar: Mg 24, O 16.

n(Mg)=0.480/24=0.0200 mol; n(O)=0.320/16=0.0200 mol. Ratio 1:1; empirical formula MgO.

Checking the response: Both amounts (1). Simplest ratio 1:1 (1). MgO (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Empirical formula from mass data
blocks.text:
Calculate the empirical formula from C 52.18%, H 13.04%, O 34.78% by mass. Ar: C 12, H 1, O 16.

For 100 g: amounts are 4.34833, 13.04 and 2.17375 mol respectively. Divide by 2.17375 to obtain approximately 2:6:1; formula C2H6O.

Checking the response: Mass/Ar amounts (1). Ratio approximately 2:6:1 (1). C2H6O (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Empirical formula from mass data
blocks.text:
Calculate the empirical formula from C 54.55%, H 9.09%, O 36.36% by mass. Ar: C 12, H 1, O 16.

For 100 g: amounts are 54.55/12=4.54583, 9.09 and 36.36/16=2.2725 mol. Divide by 2.2725: approximately 2:4:1; formula C2H4O.

Checking the response: Mass/Ar amounts (1). Ratio approximately 2:4:1 (1). C2H4O (1).

blocks.heading: Molecular formula from an empirical formula
blocks.text:
Calculate the empirical formula mass, then divide the supplied relative molecular mass by it. The resulting multiplier tells how many simplest-ratio units occur in one molecule. Multiply every empirical-formula subscript by that integer. For an empirical formula CH2 and Mr = 56, empirical mass 14 gives multiplier four, producing C4H8.

The molecular formula must preserve the empirical atom ratio and have the stated relative molecular mass. These are independent checks. A formula can have the correct ratio but the wrong total mass if the multiplier is wrong. Conversely, a guessed formula with the right mass may not preserve the measured composition. Keep implied subscripts of one visible in the working when that helps. A molecular formula specifies atom counts but does not necessarily identify one unique structure; different compounds can share a formula. Do not add a structural claim that the calculation cannot establish.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Molecular formula from an empirical formula
blocks.text:

Empirical formula mass=30. Multiplier=180/30=6. Multiply every subscript by 6: C6H12O6.

Checking the response: Empirical formula mass 30 (1). Multiplier 6 (1). C6H12O6 (1); formula has no unit.

blocks.heading: Percentage composition
blocks.text:
Percentage by mass of an element in a compound equals its total mass contribution in the formula divided by the relative formula mass, multiplied by 100. Include every atom of that element, including those in repeated bracketed groups. In NH4NO3 there are two nitrogen atoms, not one, so nitrogen contributes 28 when Ar(N) = 14.

The denominator is the mass contribution of the complete formula. A numerator and denominator must refer to the same formula unit or sample. Do not divide an atom count by a mass, and do not confuse the percentage of atoms with the percentage by mass. The percentages for all elements should sum to approximately 100%, allowing for rounding. A percentage is dimensionless, written with %, whereas the intermediate mass contributions are based on the supplied relative atomic masses. Preserve unrounded working until the final percentage to avoid unnecessary rounding errors.

blocks.text:

Formula mass=100; calcium contributes 40. Mass fraction=40/100=0.4. Percentage by mass=40.0%.

Checking the response: Correct ratio 40/100 and ×100 (1). 40.0% (1); accept appropriate rounding.

blocks.heading: Percentage yield
blocks.text:
Percentage yield compares the actual product obtained with the theoretical maximum: actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100. Both yields must use compatible units and refer to the same product. The theoretical yield comes from the balanced equation and limiting reactant, assuming complete conversion by the stated reaction. It is not necessarily the starting reactant mass.

An actual yield can be lower because reaction is incomplete, competing reactions occur, or product is lost during separation and transfer. An apparent yield above 100% suggests a problem such as retained solvent, contamination or measurement error, rather than extra matter being created. Rearrange the percentage relationship when actual or theoretical mass is unknown. For a 75% yield, use the fraction 0.75; multiplying by 75 without dividing by 100 gives the wrong scale. State whether the measured product was dry and pure when those assumptions matter.

Checking the response: Subtract container mass to obtain 8.00 g product (1). 80.0% using product mass/theoretical mass (1).

blocks.heading: Percentage purity
blocks.text:
Percentage purity is the mass of the desired pure substance divided by the total sample mass, multiplied by 100. It concerns sample composition, whereas percentage yield concerns how much product was obtained relative to a theoretical amount. A sample may have high purity but low recovery yield, so the two percentages answer different questions.

A reaction can determine the amount of a component if the other sample constituents do not contribute to the measured product. For limestone, carbon dioxide volume can indicate calcium carbonate content when carbonate reacts completely and the impurities do not also generate gas. Calculate gas amount, use the reaction ratio, convert the carbonate amount to mass, then divide by the whole sample mass. State those assumptions in the question rather than letting the answer invent them. If purity is given and pure mass is required, multiply total mass by the purity fraction, such as 0.90 for 90%.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: 2.4/24=0.10 mol Mg gives 0.10 mol MgO; 0.10×40=4.0 g. Distractor explanations: A: ignores oxygen mass added. B: gives only the oxygen mass contribution. C: uses one mole rather than 0.10 mol.

blocks.text:
What is the percentage yield when 6.0 g pure product is obtained against a theoretical 8.0 g?
A. 133%.
B. 25%.
C. 75%.
D. 48%.

C. 75%. 6.0/8.0=75%.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: 6.0/8.0=75%. Distractor explanations: B: reports the percentage shortfall. A: reverses the ratio. D: multiplies masses without forming a percentage.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-4-P02 (b)
blocks.text:
Calculate the concentration of a solution containing 0.0100 mol solute in a total volume of 250 cm³.

V=250/1000=0.250 dm³. c=n/V=0.0100/0.250=0.0400 mol/dm³.

Explain why equal volumes of 0.100 mol/dm³ and 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH require different volumes of the same HCl solution for complete neutralisation. HCl and NaOH react 1:1.

At equal volume, the 0.200 mol/dm³ NaOH contains twice as many moles. It requires twice the amount of HCl by the 1:1 ratio, and therefore twice the volume of a fixed-concentration HCl solution.

Twice the NaOH amount at equal volume (1). Twice the HCl amount from 1:1 ratio (1). Twice the same-concentration HCl volume (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-4-P03 (a)

Initial 0.40 cm³; final 25.40 cm³, reading the bottom of each meniscus.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-4-P03 (c)

Final minus initial gives 25.00 cm³ (1). Conversion to 0.02500 dm³ (1). n=cV gives 0.00250 mol (1); follow through permitted readings.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-4-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Calculate the NaOH concentration if that HCl neutralises a 25.0 cm³ NaOH aliquot exactly. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O. The HCl amount is 0.00250 mol; correct follow-through from part (c) is also allowed.

The 1:1 ratio gives n(NaOH)=0.00250 mol. c=0.00250/0.0250=0.100 mol/dm³.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-4-P03 (e)
blocks.text:
Explain why a rough titre should be followed by repeated careful titrations before choosing a mean. A rough trial used large additions near the endpoint.

Large additions can overshoot the endpoint, making the rough titre too high. Repeat with small additions near the endpoint, then use a mean of suitably close concordant titres rather than including the rough overshoot.

topics/3/content-units/CU-6117-3.4.json.title: 3.4 — state that nanotechnology is used to produce nano-materials such as graphene and fullerenes

blocks.heading: Nanotechnology and carbon materials
blocks.text:
Nanotechnology works with materials at very small length scales to obtain useful properties. Graphene and fullerenes are carbon-based examples associated with this field. Graphene is a single sheet of carbon atoms in a connected arrangement, while fullerenes contain cage-like molecular structures. They are not interchangeable names for any small piece of carbon. The arrangement as well as the scale affects the properties.

Producing or organising a material at a small scale can change how it interacts with its surroundings. The term nanotechnology does not mean that ordinary atoms have been made smaller; it concerns structures and particles assembled from atoms. A sample may contain many atoms while still being nanoscale in one dimension. This distinction helps separate a nanoparticle from an individual atom and from a large bulk piece of material. At this level, recognise examples and the link between scale and properties rather than memorising a manufacturing process or assuming every nanoscale material has the same use.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nanotechnology and carbon materials
blocks.text:
State two carbon-based materials associated with nanotechnology.

Graphene and fullerenes.

Checking the response: Graphene and fullerenes (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: The nanoscale
blocks.text:
The approximate nanoscale range used here is 1–100 nanometres in at least one dimension. One nanometre is 10⁻9 metres. A particle can therefore contain many atoms while being far smaller than an ordinary visible grain. A thin sheet can have a nanoscale thickness even if its length and width are much greater. Do not assume that every dimension must be identical or that a material is nanoscale merely because its packaging uses the word small.

Compare units carefully: 1 micrometre is 1000 nanometres, while 1 millimetre is one million nanometres. A 50 nm particle lies within the stated range; a 5000 nm particle does not on that dimension. A logarithmic size ladder gives equal spacing to equal multiplication factors, not equal differences in size. Label that scale explicitly so that a drawing does not falsely suggest 1 nm and 1 mm differ by only a few times. For example, a stated thickness of 0.050 micrometres converts to 0.050 × 1000 = 50 nm, within the stated nanoscale range. A thickness of 0.50 micrometres gives 500 nm, outside that range on the measured dimension. Check the decimal place before classifying a size: a tenfold error can reverse the conclusion. These conversions describe size; they do not establish toxicity, usefulness or chemical identity by themselves.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The nanoscale
blocks.text:
State the approximate size range used to describe a nanomaterial in at least one dimension.

1–100 nm.

Checking the response: 1–100 nm (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Why small size changes behaviour
blocks.text:
Nanomaterials can have properties different from a bulk sample of the same substance and from individual atoms or molecules. As a particle becomes smaller, a greater fraction of its atoms can be associated with the surface. Surface interactions can therefore become particularly important. The relevant change is in scale and arrangement, not a change in the element's proton number. Silver nanoparticles provide the syllabus example of antimicrobial behaviour.

An observed useful property does not justify a universal claim about safety or performance. Antimicrobial means acting against microorganisms under appropriate conditions; it does not mean that a silver-containing product sterilises anything it touches or is suitable for every medical use. The amount, surrounding material, particle size and exposure conditions all matter. A comparison should identify the measured property and the particle sizes being compared. A bulk piece of silver, a silver nanoparticle and an isolated silver atom are three distinct physical descriptions, even though each involves the same element. Treat any application claim as specific to the tested material and conditions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Why small size changes behaviour
blocks.text:
State one property of silver nanoparticles that makes them useful in some products.

Antimicrobial activity.

Checking the response: Antimicrobial activity (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Applications of nanotechnology
blocks.text:
Nanotechnology has applications in medicine, electronics, environmental technologies, consumer products and sporting goods. Examples include nanoscale materials in some antimicrobial coatings, miniaturised electronic structures, high-surface-area materials used in filtration or treatment, and lightweight reinforced composites used in some sports equipment. The useful property must be named alongside the application: small size, surface behaviour or reinforcement can serve different purposes.

These are application categories rather than a promise that any nanoparticle will work in every product. A filter must be tested for the substance it is meant to remove, and a reinforced material must be tested for the load and conditions of use. Describing a material as nano does not replace such evidence. For a school answer, give one concrete pairing of application and relevant property without inventing a product brand or a guaranteed health benefit. Environmental assessment considers both benefits during use and what happens when the material is released or discarded. Size alone is not a complete risk assessment.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Applications of nanotechnology
blocks.text:

Lightweight reinforced composite materials in some sports equipment.

Checking the response: Lightweight reinforced composite materials in some sports equipment (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

topics/3/content-units/CU-6117-3.2.json.title: 3.2 — describe the use of different building materials in the local environment: bricks (mud or ceramic), concrete, wood, metal, thatch and glass

blocks.heading: Building materials in the local environment
blocks.text:
Buildings combine materials with different jobs. Mud or fired ceramic bricks form walls; concrete forms foundations and other load-bearing components; wood can form doors, frames and roof supports; metal can provide roofing sheets, fasteners or reinforcement; thatch provides a roof covering; and glass admits light through windows. The examples identify possible uses, not a rule that every building should use the same combination.

Survey a local building by recording each component, its material and the property that makes it useful. Windows transmit light, foundations support loads, and roofs resist weather. Distinguish the visible finish from the underlying material: paint or plaster can hide concrete, brick or wood. A roof's insulation depends on thickness, trapped air, arrangement and ventilation as well as material identity. Comparisons should therefore specify conditions. Link each component to its material and purpose.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Building materials in the local environment
blocks.text:
Describe why ordinary window glass suits a light-admitting pane while a ductile metal suits a bent load-bearing bracket.

Glass transmits light; a ductile metal can be shaped without brittle fracture and support the bracket load.

Checking the response: Glass transmits light through the window pane (1). The metal can be bent without brittle fracture and is strong enough to support the bracket’s load (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Building materials in the local environment
blocks.text:
Describe why glass and concrete are normally selected for different building components.

Glass transmits light for windows; concrete withstands compression for foundations or other suitable supports.

Checking the response: Glass transmits light, making it suitable for a window (1). Concrete withstands compression, making it suitable for foundations or compressive supports (1).

blocks.heading: Selecting by properties
blocks.text:
Selecting a building material begins with the required performance. Compressive strength concerns resistance to being crushed; tensile strength concerns resistance to being pulled apart. A material that performs well in one test may be weaker in the other. Thermal conductivity concerns heat transfer, while water absorption concerns uptake of moisture. These properties are related to different demands and should not be replaced by the vague statement that a material is strong.

For a window, transparency and resistance to ordinary weather matter, while for a cooking-area roof, heat transfer, durability and fire behaviour may matter. Use supplied test data to justify a choice and state a relevant limitation. Equal sample dimensions, comparable moisture conditions and consistent test procedures are needed for fair comparisons. A thicker sample may appear a better insulator simply because heat travels farther through it. Cost and availability can affect practical selection, but they do not establish chemical properties. These comparisons are not structural certification.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Selecting by properties
blocks.text:
Explain why high compressive strength is useful for a building foundation material.

The material must resist being crushed by the load transmitted through the building.

Checking the response: The material must resist being crushed by the load transmitted through the building (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:

X, because lower thermal conductivity means a lower rate of heat transfer under those conditions.

Checking the response: X, because lower thermal conductivity means a lower rate of heat transfer under those conditions (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Making concrete
blocks.text:
Concrete is prepared by mixing cement, sand and crushed stone or other suitable aggregate, then adding a controlled amount of water. Water allows the cement to undergo hydration reactions that form a hardened binder around the aggregate. Setting is therefore not simply the evaporation of all the water. Appropriate curing maintains conditions that allow the binder to develop. The precise proportions and treatment depend on the intended material specification.

Too much mixing water can leave a more porous, weaker hardened material after excess water leaves. Too little or poorly distributed water can prevent proper mixing and hydration. These relationships explain why preparation must be controlled rather than altered casually to make pouring easier. Distinguish cement, the binding ingredient, from concrete, the complete mixture. Sand and crushed stone provide different aggregate sizes; they are not alternative names for cement. In a school study, use teacher-prepared samples or a controlled small demonstration and avoid skin contact with wet cement, which is alkaline and can cause injury.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Making concrete
blocks.text:
Explain why water is required when cement, sand and crushed stone are mixed to make concrete.

Water reacts with the cement during hydration, forming a hardened binder that holds the aggregate together.

Checking the response: Water reacts with the cement during hydration, forming a hardened binder that holds the aggregate together (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Making concrete
blocks.text:
Explain why adding a large unmeasured excess of water to a concrete mixture can reduce the strength of the hardened sample.

Checking the response: Excess water can leave greater pore space, weakening the material (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Raw materials for cement
blocks.text:
Clay and limestone are the principal raw materials named here for making cement. They are processed and heated to produce the cement-making material, which is then prepared as a fine powder. Cement is subsequently mixed with water and aggregate to make concrete. The two stages must remain separate: producing cement from raw minerals is not the same operation as preparing concrete at a building site.

Limestone is rich in calcium carbonate, while clay supplies other mineral components. For this objective, identify the raw materials rather than inventing a detailed industrial recipe. A bag of cement does not contain ready-made concrete because it lacks the intended sand and coarse aggregate mixture. Similarly, adding only water to cement produces a paste, not the full concrete mixture described in the preceding section. Reading a process diagram from left to right helps distinguish raw mineral extraction, cement manufacture, concrete mixing and curing. Each stage changes either composition, physical form or both.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Raw materials for cement

Checking the response: Clay and limestone (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-19 — Comparing strength
blocks.text: Use teacher-approved small samples and guarded apparatus to compare resistance to compression or tension. Record sample dimensions, the applied load and the chosen endpoint. Compare equal cross-sectional areas and change one material at a time; otherwise size may explain the result. Keep people away from possible falling loads or sharp fragments. Supplied data are an appropriate alternative to breaking samples. A compression result cannot be silently reused as a tensile-strength result, and a classroom comparison does not certify a material for a real building.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-20 — Surveying local materials
blocks.text: Survey an accessible building without disturbing its structure. Record component, apparent material, supporting evidence and likely purpose in a table. Check uncertain identifications using reliable information rather than appearance alone. Compare a window, roof covering, wall and frame. Link each use to a property such as light transmission, strength or weather resistance. Note concealed layers or coatings as limitations; a painted surface may not reveal the underlying material. The survey identifies uses and hypotheses, not a structural safety verdict.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-21 — Comparing insulation
blocks.text: Under teacher supervision, compare equal-thickness roofing-material samples in the same small model enclosure using safe warm-water containers as a heat source. Record temperatures at equal times with the same starting temperature, exposed area and room conditions. A slower temperature change can support better insulation under those conditions. Repeat and compare results; gaps around samples or unequal thickness are alternative explanations. Do not use an open flame or high-temperature heater to test unknown materials. The model simplifies ventilation and weather conditions found in real roofs.

topics/3/content-units/CU-6117-3.3.json.title: 3.3 — outline and sketch the generalised structure of a soap or detergent

blocks.heading: The structure of a cleaning molecule
blocks.text:
A soap or detergent molecule can be represented by a water-attracting head and a long water-repelling tail. The head is hydrophilic and the tail hydrophobic. The tail interacts with grease or oil, while the head interacts with water. A simple sketch uses a circle for the head and a long line or zigzag for the tail, with a key explaining both symbols. The sketch is a model of different interactions, not a claim that the molecule has a literal spherical head and rigid stick.

Keep the orientation clear when drawing cleaning action. Tails enter a grease droplet and heads face the surrounding water. Reversing the labels would predict the wrong arrangement. The general model applies to both soap and many synthetic detergents even though their detailed chemical groups differ. It explains how one molecule can connect an oily region with a watery environment. Exact structural formulae are unnecessary for a generalised sketch; the important features are the two different regions and their interactions.

A hydrophobic region associates with grease while a hydrophilic region faces water, allowing grease droplets to disperse.

Checking the response: Grease association by hydrophobic region (1). Water interaction by hydrophilic region supports dispersion (1).

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Removing grease by emulsification
blocks.text:
Grease does not mix readily with water. Soap or detergent helps disperse grease into small droplets by placing hydrophobic tails in the grease and hydrophilic heads towards the water. Agitation helps detach and break up the grease, while the surrounding cleaning molecules help keep droplets dispersed. The resulting emulsion can be carried away during rinsing. This is dispersion of droplets, not necessarily conversion of grease into a new water-soluble chemical compound.

In a drawing, show a central grease droplet, tails directed inward and heads at the water-facing surface. Name the surrounding water so the direction has meaning. Saying only that soap dissolves dirt leaves out the mechanism and can be inaccurate for oily droplets. The cleaning action also depends on amount, temperature, agitation and water composition. A comparison of two cleaning products should hold these conditions steady before attributing a difference to the product. More foam does not automatically prove that more grease has been removed; foam and cleaning performance are different observations.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Removing grease by emulsification
blocks.text:

Its tails enter the grease and its heads face water, helping keep the droplet dispersed for rinsing.

Checking the response: Its tails enter the grease and its heads face water, helping keep the droplet dispersed for rinsing (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Removing grease by emulsification
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Recognising cleaning materials
blocks.text:
Soap and synthetic detergents are common cleaning materials. A soap bar may contain soap together with perfume, colourants and other ingredients. Washing-up liquids and laundry formulations commonly contain detergents and additional components. A product's everyday name does not establish its exact composition, so use a supplied ingredient description when a question distinguishes soap from a synthetic detergent.

Cleaning products are mixtures designed for particular purposes. Abrasive particles can scrub a surface, while surfactant molecules help disperse greasy material. These functions should not be confused with disinfection, which concerns microorganisms. A product that removes visible grease is not automatically proven to kill every microorganism. Likewise, an antimicrobial label does not explain emulsification. In a simple classroom comparison, identify the cleaning agent and the measured outcome before drawing conclusions. Do not mix household products to investigate them; the chemistry task can use prepared solutions or supplied labels and observations under teacher supervision.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Recognising cleaning materials
blocks.text:
Identify the cleaning agent, soap or soapless detergent, that forms lather without scum in both distilled water and hard water under the same test conditions.

Detergent.

Checking the response: Detergent (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Preparing soap
blocks.text:
Soap can be prepared by alkaline hydrolysis of a fat or oil. Heating the fat or oil with an appropriate alkali breaks it down to produce soap and glycerol. The process is commonly called saponification. The alkali is a reactant, not merely a neutral mixing liquid. A school description should identify the fat or oil, the alkali, controlled heating and the separation of the soap product without implying that ordinary mixing at any temperature gives an instantly finished product.

In a supervised demonstration, the mixture is heated using appropriate equipment and the soap is separated, for example by salting out, then collected and washed. Excess alkali must be removed or checked; an experimental product should not be used on skin simply because it looks like a soap bar. Hot alkaline mixtures can damage skin and eyes. The learning task is to relate the chemical change to the raw material and products, and to understand why separation and washing matter. Detailed industrial recipes and unsupervised manufacture are not needed.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Preparing soap
blocks.text:
Outline why a classroom soap preparation is incomplete if oil is merely stirred with cold water and the mixture is labelled pure soap.

Water alone under these conditions does not carry out the required alkaline hydrolysis; even a reacted mixture needs separation and washing to remove excess alkali and other soluble material.

Checking the response: Alkaline hydrolysis, not simple mixing with water, is needed (1). Separate and wash the product rather than call the mixture pure (1).

blocks.heading: Biodegradability and persistence
blocks.text:
Biodegradable means capable of being broken down by microorganisms. A non-biodegradable material does not undergo such breakdown readily under the relevant conditions and can persist. The distinction concerns a biological process, not simply whether a substance dissolves, breaks into small pieces or becomes invisible. A detergent can dissolve in water yet remain chemically present until a breakdown process acts on it.

Interpret environmental claims with conditions and timescales. Microorganisms, temperature, oxygen availability and treatment systems affect breakdown. Biodegradable does not mean instant disappearance or harmlessness at any dose. If two supplied samples lose 80% and 20% of their original material during the same controlled biodegradation test, the first breaks down more extensively under those conditions; that comparison does not prove its behaviour in every river or soil. State what the data support and identify the limitation. Responsible product comparisons also consider the amount released, toxicity and wastewater treatment rather than relying on one favourable label.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Biodegradability and persistence
blocks.text:
Suggest which sample is less persistent under a controlled microbial test: P loses 80% of its original material and Q loses 20% in the same time.

P is less persistent under those test conditions because more of it has been broken down.

blocks.text:
State the conclusion supported when a cleaning agent dissolves but its molecules remain unchanged during a microbial test.

Dissolving alone has not demonstrated biodegradation.

blocks.heading: Comparing soaps and detergents
blocks.text:
Soaps can remove grease and are generally biodegradable, but calcium and magnesium ions in hard water form insoluble soap salts, commonly called scum. This consumes soap and can leave less available for cleaning. Many synthetic detergents remain effective in hard water because they do not form the same insoluble precipitate under comparable conditions. A fair comparison uses equal amounts, the same water, similar grease deposits and consistent agitation.

Environmental performance varies between detergent formulations. Some are readily biodegradable, while persistent ingredients can remain in the environment; additional formulation components may also matter. Do not state that every detergent is non-biodegradable or that natural soap has no environmental effects. Use the data supplied for the specific products. A recommendation may favour a detergent for hard-water cleaning while noting a persistence disadvantage, or favour a biodegradable product where comparable cleaning is achieved. State the criterion, evidence and trade-off rather than calling one category universally better. Increasing dose can compensate for some loss but increases material use and discharge.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing soaps and detergents
blocks.text:
Outline one limitation of soap in hard water and one resulting consequence for cleaning.

Soap forms insoluble scum with calcium or magnesium ions, leaving less soap available to clean grease.

Checking the response: Scum formation (1); reduced available soap/cleaning efficiency (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing soaps and detergents
blocks.text:
Suggest a reason for choosing detergent D rather than soap S when supplied tests show D cleans at a lower dose in the same hard water and neither product has a demonstrated persistence advantage.

D achieves the required cleaning using less material under the stated hard-water conditions.

Checking the response: D achieves the required cleaning using less material under the stated hard-water conditions (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-3-P02 (credit-group-1)
blocks.text:
An original controlled washing trial uses equal grease deposits and the same water volume, temperature and agitation. The volume required to reach the same cleaning endpoint is: soap S, 2 cm³ in soft water and 8 cm³ in hard water; detergent D, 2 cm³ in soft water and 2 cm³ in hard water. S forms scum in hard water; D does not. In a separate seven-day microbial test under identical conditions, each product starts at 5.0 g of the measured cleaning ingredient. The remaining masses are S 1.0 g and D 4.0 g. These are synthetic teaching data, not product claims.

Describe the orientation of cleaning molecules around grease.

Hydrophobic tails enter the grease and hydrophilic heads face the surrounding water, allowing dispersed droplets to be rinsed away.

Tails enter grease (1). Heads face water (1).

Mass broken down = initial − remaining: S = 5.0 − 1.0 = 4.0 g; D = 5.0 − 4.0 = 1.0 g.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-3-P02 (credit-group-6)
blocks.text:
Explain a balanced recommendation and an evidence limitation.

D achieves the cleaning endpoint with less product in hard water, but S shows more extensive microbial breakdown in this test. A defensible choice weighs those two findings; neither is unconditionally best. Seven-day results under one set of conditions do not establish behaviour in every environment, and no toxicity data are supplied.

Recommendation linked to D’s lower required dose (1). Acknowledges S’s greater measured breakdown as a competing benefit (1). Relevant limitation: one time/condition set, absent toxicity data, or equivalent specific limitation (1). Either product choice can earn full marks when justified.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-22 — Comparing emulsification
blocks.text: Place equal small volumes of water and cooking oil in teacher-approved stoppered tubes. Add a fixed amount of soap solution to one, detergent solution to another and no cleaning agent to a control. Shake each in the same way and record the appearance and time taken for layers to separate. More persistent fine droplets support emulsification. Keep temperature and amounts comparable; foam alone is not a measure of grease removal. Draw heads towards water and tails towards oil to explain the observation.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-23 — Observing soap preparation
blocks.text: Use a teacher demonstration of alkaline hydrolysis of a fat or oil, with eye protection and controlled heating. Record the starting materials, formation of a soap-containing mixture, separation by salting out, and washing of the collected product. Explain that excess alkali can affect both safety and test results. Do not use the unverified product on skin. Compare a small teacher-prepared solution with water for emulsification rather than assuming appearance alone proves purity. This is a chemical preparation followed by separation, not simply drying an oil.

blocks.text: Connect material properties to Matter and bonding, Organic chemistry and Environmental and industrial chemistry. Distinguish a measured observation from an inferred structure or environmental claim.

topics/3/content-units/CU-6117-3.1.json.title: 3.1 — classify materials into categories such as wood, metals, glasses, ceramics, concrete, plastics and fibres and identify examples of these materials in the local environment

blocks.heading: Wood as a material
blocks.text:
Wood is a natural material obtained from trees. It contains cellulose, a natural polymer, together with other substances, and commonly shows a grain that reflects its growth structure. Timber doors, roof supports and furniture are familiar uses in Namibia. A wooden chair is an object; wood is the material from which parts of it are made. An object may contain several materials, such as a wooden seat with steel screws and plastic feet.

Properties vary with species, grain direction, moisture and treatment. Wood is relatively easy to shape and generally conducts heat poorly compared with metals, making it useful for handles and some building components. It can absorb moisture, decay or burn, so suitability depends on conditions rather than the label natural alone. Painted wood remains wood even if its surface resembles plastic. To classify a sample, use its stated composition, visible grain and relevant observations together, without damaging an unknown object. Classification identifies the material; selection for a job also requires evidence about performance and durability.

Checking the response: Wood (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Metals as materials
blocks.text:
Metal materials include elemental metals and alloys. Copper electrical wiring, aluminium cooking vessels and steel roofing sheets illustrate different uses. Most familiar metals conduct heat and electricity well and can be shaped without immediately shattering. Their composition and processing affect hardness, corrosion resistance and strength, so a property of one metal should not be assumed for another without evidence. Steel is an alloy, but still belongs to the broad metal-material category.

When identifying a material, distinguish appearance from composition. A shiny coating can conceal plastic or wood, and a magnet does not attract every metal. Aluminium and copper are metals even though an ordinary magnet does not strongly attract them. Use electrical conduction, stated composition and other suitable observations alongside appearance. The metal's role also matters: copper is selected for conducting wire, while an insulating coating around it serves the opposite electrical purpose. A complete object may therefore combine conducting metal with non-conducting materials. Naming the object alone does not identify the material in each component.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Metals as materials
blocks.text:

Checking the response: Metal (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Glasses
blocks.text:
Glass is commonly used for windows, bottles and laboratory containers. Familiar window glass transmits visible light, resists many everyday substances and forms a rigid barrier. It is brittle: a sufficient impact can make it fracture rather than bend permanently. Different glass compositions provide different properties, so a window pane and a heat-resistant laboratory vessel are not automatically interchangeable.

Glass has an extended structure with mainly covalent bonding, but lacks the regular long-range arrangement of a crystal. Transparency alone does not identify it, because some plastics are also transparent. Classify a known window sample using composition or reliable product information rather than a hazardous breakage test. Distinguish the material glass from the object a drinking glass: a similarly shaped drinking vessel can be made from plastic. In selecting glass for a purpose, connect transparency with visibility, chemical resistance with containment, and brittleness with the risk of impact damage. A useful property and a limitation can belong to the same material without contradiction.
