blocks.heading: Ceramics
blocks.text:
Ceramics include fired clay bricks, pottery and many tiles. Heating suitable mineral materials during manufacture changes them into hard solids that retain their shape. Familiar ceramics often resist heat and wear but are brittle, meaning they can crack under an impact or tensile stress. A glazed tile has a surface coating that may change water absorption and appearance; the coating does not turn the whole object into a metal or plastic.

A mud brick dried without firing and a fired ceramic brick have different processing histories and may respond differently to water. Do not infer identical performance just because both are rectangular building blocks. A ceramic mug can withstand normal use while still breaking when dropped. Classification and suitability are therefore separate questions: first identify the material and then examine the loads, temperature and moisture it will encounter. Controlled observations can include surface appearance, porosity information and manufacturer-provided composition. Do not use unsafe heating or impact tests on unknown glazed items to identify them.

blocks.heading: Concrete
blocks.text:
Concrete is a mixture made using cement, sand, larger aggregate such as crushed stone, and water. Cement acts as a binder as it reacts with water and hardens around the aggregate. Concrete is therefore not the same material as dry cement powder. Pavements, foundations and structural components provide local examples. It can be cast into a mould while fresh and becomes rigid as it sets and cures.

Concrete generally withstands compression better than tension. Steel reinforcement can help a concrete structure carry tensile loads, but the combination must be designed appropriately; adding an arbitrary piece of metal does not guarantee a safe structure. Here the aim is to link material properties with uses, not to prescribe building designs. Composition, water content, curing and defects all affect performance. A concrete sample can contain several kinds of bonding because it contains several substances, rather than one molecule with a single formula. The visible stones do not mean the cement has failed to mix: aggregate is an intended component.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concrete
blocks.text:

Checking the response: Concrete (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Plastics
blocks.text:
Plastics are materials based on polymers that can be formed into useful shapes during manufacture. Examples include polythene packaging, nylon components and melamine-based moulded products. They contain long covalently bonded molecular structures, but different polymer structures and additives produce different properties. Some plastics are flexible, others rigid; some soften readily on heating, while others do not. “Plastic” is therefore a category, not one substance with one melting point.

Many familiar plastics are lightweight and poor electrical conductors, making them useful for packaging and insulation. Heat resistance, weathering and disposal must also be considered. A plastic coating can protect a metal or provide electrical insulation without changing the material of the underlying core. Identify a component from reliable information or appropriate observations; burning an unknown plastic is not an acceptable identification method because fumes may be harmful. A natural-looking colour or texture does not make a synthetic polymer natural wood. Conversely, natural polymers such as cellulose show that the word polymer is broader than the everyday category plastic.

blocks.heading: Fibres
blocks.text:
Fibres are thin, elongated strands that can be spun into yarn or incorporated into other materials. Cotton and wool are natural examples; nylon and polyester are synthetic examples. Fabrics are made by arranging or joining fibres, often by weaving or knitting. A fibre describes the material's strand-like form as well as its practical use, so it can overlap with chemical categories: a nylon fibre is also a synthetic polymer.

Different fibres have different strengths, flexibility and water uptake. A fabric suitable for an absorbent towel may be unsuitable where rapid drying or low water absorption is required. Compare controlled samples rather than assuming every natural fibre is absorbent and every synthetic one is waterproof. A blended fabric contains more than one fibre type and may combine properties. When interpreting a label, distinguish the percentage composition from the weave or colour. An experiment on equal-sized fabric samples should also consider thickness and mass, because these can affect apparent absorption independently of the fibre chemistry.

blocks.heading: Natural and synthetic materials
blocks.text:
Natural materials originate in living organisms or natural deposits, while synthetic materials are made through deliberate chemical manufacture. Wood, cotton and wool provide natural examples. Polythene and nylon are synthetic polymers. Processing a natural material does not automatically make it synthetic: cutting timber, washing wool or spinning cotton changes form without synthesising a new polymer. A manufactured object can therefore be made from a natural material.

The categories do not rank safety, quality or environmental impact by themselves. A natural material can burn, decay or require substantial processing, and a synthetic material can be durable or recyclable in an appropriate system. Compare the actual use, lifetime and disposal conditions. A label stating natural origin does not prove biodegradation will occur rapidly under every condition. If a sample combines natural and synthetic components, name both rather than forcing the whole object into one category. For example, cotton fabric with a synthetic coating has a natural fibre base and a manufactured polymer surface.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Natural and synthetic materials
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Bonding in metals
blocks.text:
Metallic bonding is attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons. This model applies to the metal structure in familiar copper, aluminium and steel components. The delocalised electrons can move and carry electric current, while the positive ions form the structural framework. In a solid metal, conduction does not require the ions themselves to travel along the wire.

The model also helps explain shaping. Layers can move while remaining attracted to the electron population, so metals can often be hammered or drawn into wire. Alloys may resist sliding more strongly because atoms of different sizes disturb the regular arrangement. Do not replace this explanation with ionic bonding merely because the metallic model contains ions: ionic bonding involves attraction between positive and negative ions, whereas the negative component here is delocalised electrons. A material choice such as copper for a cable depends on the resulting properties as well as the bonding label.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bonding in metals
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Bonding in concrete
blocks.text:
Concrete contains several substances, so its bonding cannot be represented by one small molecular formula. Its constituents involve both ionic and covalent bonding. Aggregate and the hardened cement binder contribute different structures and roles. The binder forms through reactions involving cement and water and holds the aggregate together; the stones are not converted into a single enormous concrete molecule.

When asked to identify bonding in concrete, state both ionic and covalent contributions rather than choosing metallic bonding because a structure may contain steel reinforcement. Reinforced concrete combines concrete with metal, but that metal is a distinct reinforcing component. The overall behaviour depends on composition and arrangement as well as bond types. Hardness alone cannot identify a unique bonding type because ionic, covalent and metallic solids can each be hard in different circumstances. Treat the material as a composite mixture and connect any property claim to the particular constituent or structure being discussed.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bonding in concrete
blocks.text:

Both ionic and covalent bonding.

Checking the response: Both ionic and covalent bonding (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Bonding in glass
blocks.text:
Common silica-based glass has a giant structure with mainly covalent bonding. The network extends through the solid rather than forming many separate small glass molecules. Its arrangement is not a regular crystal lattice over long distances. This distinguishes glass from a molecular liquid frozen into a simple array and also from a metal with mobile delocalised electrons.

Strong bonding contributes to rigidity, but a glass can still be brittle. Bond strength and resistance to impact are different questions: a rigid network can crack instead of allowing layers to slide as in a ductile metal. Ordinary glass is usually an electrical insulator because it lacks the mobile charge carriers characteristic of metals. Its transparency is useful for windows, but transparency alone does not prove covalent bonding; the structure must come from chemical knowledge or supplied evidence. Composition changes can alter thermal and chemical performance, so avoid assigning identical properties to every product called glass.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bonding in glass
blocks.text:

A giant structure with mainly covalent bonding.

Checking the response: A giant structure with mainly covalent bonding (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Cellulose in wood
blocks.text:
Cellulose is a natural polymer in wood and other plant materials. A polymer contains large molecules built from many linked units; in cellulose, covalent bonds join atoms within the long chains. Wood also contains other substances and structural features, so describing it as pure cellulose would be inaccurate. The chains and their organisation contribute to the mechanical behaviour of the plant material.

Natural origin does not imply the absence of chemical bonds or molecules. Cellulose is a chemical substance even though a plant produces it. Distinguish covalent bonds within its molecular structure from the larger-scale arrangement of fibres and cells in wood. Changes in moisture can alter practical behaviour without changing the statement that cellulose is a covalent polymer. A useful comparison is with a synthetic polymer such as polythene: both have covalently bonded molecular structures, but their chemical composition, origin and properties differ. One shared bonding category does not make them interchangeable materials.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Cellulose in wood
blocks.text:

Checking the response: Covalent bonding (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Synthetic polymer structures
blocks.text:
Polythene, nylon, polyurethane and melamine-based polymers are examples of synthetic polymer materials. Covalent bonds hold atoms together within their polymer structures. The exact chains, connections and added ingredients differ, so the examples should not be treated as one identical molecular substance. Polythene packaging, nylon fibres and rigid melamine-based products illustrate the range of behaviour possible within this category.

The word synthetic describes manufacture, while polymer describes large molecular structure. A natural polymer such as cellulose also contains covalent bonds, so covalent bonding does not prove that a material is synthetic. Conversely, manufacturing a metal object does not turn its bonding into polymeric covalent bonding. When classifying a product, keep origin, structure, physical form and use separate. A nylon rope is synthetic in origin, polymeric in structure, fibrous in form and used to carry tension. Each description answers a different question, and combining them carefully gives a more useful account than memorising a single label.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Synthetic polymer structures
blocks.text:

Covalent bonding.

Checking the response: Covalent bonding (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

C. They describe different aspects of nylon. Classification can use different criteria.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Classification can use different criteria. Distractor explanations: D: fibres can be synthetic. A: the criteria are compatible. B: nylon has covalent polymer structures.

Why can concrete contain both ionic and covalent bonding?
A. Its constituents are several substances with different structures.
B. Every bond alternates between ionic and covalent each second.
C. Water removes every covalent bond.
D. All concrete particles are metal ions.

topics/12/content-units/CU-6117-12.5.jso.title: 12.5 — Plan an investigation with predictions, suitable apparatus and techniques.

blocks.heading: Planning a fair investigation
blocks.text:
An investigation plan needs a testable question, a justified prediction, an independent variable, a measured dependent variable and controlled conditions. Name suitable apparatus and explain the sequence well enough for another person to follow. State quantities or a justified range rather than saying 'some water'. Define timing and the endpoint, include repeats, and explain how results will support a conclusion.

For comparing insulation, vary the jacket material while keeping vessel, water amount, initial temperature, jacket thickness and surrounding conditions matched. Record temperature at fixed times, compare cooling curves and repeat the trials. Predict less temperature loss for a better insulator. A six-mark plan should contain distinct method, control, measurement and interpretation points, not six rephrasings of 'make it fair'. A marked cross in a clouding experiment has a different role: it sits beneath the flask as a visual endpoint marker. It is not chromatography paper used to separate the mixture.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Planning a fair investigation
blocks.text:
Plan a fair comparison of two insulation materials using cooling water. Include the measurements and conclusion method.

Wrap identical vessels with equal-thickness jackets of the two materials and add equal water volumes at the same starting temperature. Keep lids and surroundings matched. Record temperature at fixed time intervals with correctly positioned thermometers, repeat trials, and compare temperature drops or cooling curves; the smaller loss indicates better insulation under those conditions.

Checking the response: Same vessel and water volume (1). Same starting temperature (1). Material varied with thickness/lids controlled (1). Temperature measured at fixed times (1). Repeats with matched surroundings (1). Compare cooling to draw a conditional conclusion (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Planning a fair investigation
blocks.text:
State the uncontrolled variable in a plan that compares equal fabric jackets but starts one water sample at 80 °C and the other at 60 °C.

Starting water temperature.

Checking the response: Starting water temperature (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Planning a fair investigation

Explain the error in placing marked-cross paper inside a clouding reaction as though it were chromatography paper.

Checking the response: The cross belongs beneath the flask; time until the developing cloudiness hides it when viewed from above. It marks the endpoint rather than separating components (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-12-P01 (d)
blocks.text:
Plan a fair comparison of two insulation materials using equal 100 cm³ water portions starting at 80 °C in identical vessels in a room at 22 °C. Include controls, measurements, repeats, safety and how the results would support a conclusion.

Use identical vessels and 100 cm³ water portions, each starting at 80 °C. Fit equal-thickness jackets of the two materials with the same covered area and identical lids. Place them in the same 22 °C surroundings away from differing draughts. Position thermometer bulbs in the water without touching glass and record temperatures at fixed times, for example every two minutes for ten minutes. Repeat each arrangement and compare mean cooling curves or temperature drops; the smaller drop indicates better insulation under the test conditions. The teacher supplies the hot water, vessels stand on heatproof mats and handling avoids burns. Predict that a more effective jacket gives a smaller temperature fall.

Same vessel and water volume (1). Same starting temperature (1). Vary material while controlling thickness/covered area/lids (1). Record temperature at fixed times with suitable apparatus (1). Repeat and control ambient conditions (1). Compare cooling curves or drops for a conditional conclusion (1). Safety and a sensible prediction are expected supporting plan details; no invented extra marks.

topics/12/content-units/CU-6117-12.4.jso.title: 12.4 — Identify sources of error and suggest procedural improvements.

blocks.heading: Specific errors and improvements
blocks.text:
An improvement should address a named source of error. If gas escapes while a stopper is being fitted, some early product is missed; a suitable closed starting arrangement can reduce this loss. If a temperature probe touches the container, reposition it in the liquid. 'Be more careful' is not a method change unless the action and error are specified.

Random variation and systematic error require different responses. Repeats help assess random scatter, while calibration or correction is needed for a consistent instrument offset. Increasing sample size can reduce some relative uncertainties but may introduce new practical constraints. A proposed improvement must remain feasible and safe. Do not choose a more precise instrument if its range is unsuitable or if a much larger uncontrolled error dominates. Explain the chain: source of error, effect on the measured result, and procedural change. When the direction of bias is not known, say so rather than guessing that every error makes the result too low.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Specific errors and improvements
blocks.text:
Identify a procedural improvement when gas is lost before a bung is fitted at the start of a reaction.

Checking the response: Start the reaction within an already connected collection arrangement, for example by releasing one reactant after closure (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Specific errors and improvements
blocks.text:

Each repeat has the same systematic error; calibration or correction is needed.

Checking the response: Each repeat has the same systematic error; calibration or correction is needed (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Precautions with reasons
blocks.text:
A precaution is useful when its purpose is clear. Reading a meniscus at eye level reduces parallax. Keeping a thermometer bulb off the vessel wall makes it more representative of the liquid temperature. Wearing eye protection reduces injury risk from splashes, but it does not by itself improve numerical accuracy. Distinguish safety precautions from measurement controls, even when both belong in the method.

Evaluate a proposed improvement against the actual task. A lid can reduce evaporation and make cooling comparisons more controlled, but identical lid arrangements must be used for both samples. A stopper must not create a sealed pressure hazard in a gas-producing reaction with no outlet. Controlled heating and a heatproof mat address hot-apparatus risks, while constant starting temperature addresses fairness. The best response is specific and causal: state the action and explain the hazard or error it reduces. A long list of generic laboratory rules does not substitute for the one relevant precaution asked for.

topics/12/content-units/CU-6117-12.3.jso.title: 12.3 — Justify a conclusion by reference to the data.

blocks.heading: Conclusions supported by data
blocks.text:
A conclusion should answer the investigation question using the observations actually obtained. Quote a relevant comparison, trend or calculated value with units. Original cooling results at ten minutes are 50 °C without insulation and 63 °C with insulation, from the same 80 °C starting temperature. The insulated vessel lost less temperature under the stated conditions, supporting better insulation in that test.

Do not claim more than the design establishes. If vessel size or water mass also changed, the result cannot isolate insulation material. If only one trial was made, acknowledge that variation has not been measured. A result consistent with a prediction supports it but does not prove it in every possible setting. 'The graph goes down' is an observation; 'temperature falls as time increases under these conditions' is a more precise trend, and a justified comparison needs the relevant values. Avoid making up a reading outside the measured range. Where differences are small compared with measurement uncertainty, a cautious conclusion may be more appropriate than a definite ranking.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Conclusions supported by data
blocks.text:

The insulated vessel cools less over ten minutes, retaining a temperature 13 °C higher under the matched conditions.

Checking the response: Insulated vessel loses less heat/temperature under conditions (1). Uses 63 versus 50 °C or 13 °C difference (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Conclusions supported by data
blocks.text:
State the supported conclusion if sample A produces 30 cm³ gas in 20 s and B produces 12 cm³ in the same time under matched conditions.

A has the greater average gas-production rate over that interval.

Checking the response: A has the greater average gas-production rate over that interval (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Observation, inference and limitations
blocks.text:
An observation records what is seen or measured; an inference explains what it may mean. 'A white precipitate formed' is an observation. 'The sample may contain chloride' is an inference that requires the reagent and test conditions. A result cannot be interpreted reliably without knowing the procedure. Colour, physical state and behaviour on adding excess reagent may all matter.

Evaluate whether the data distinguish the proposed alternatives. A white precipitate with sodium hydroxide alone is not enough to choose between several cations. Additional observations, such as solubility in excess ammonia, can narrow the possibilities. Similarly, a gas volume difference does not prove a different amount of reactant if temperature, pressure or leakage changed. In this course numerical gas tasks use their stated room-condition relationships; practical comparisons still require matched conditions. A cautious conclusion identifies what is supported and what remains unresolved. Do not replace a missing observation with the expected one. If an outcome conflicts with a prediction, report it and investigate the method or explanation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Observation, inference and limitations
blocks.text:

The precipitate is what is seen; identification is an inference that also needs the reagent and any further distinguishing observations.

Checking the response: White precipitate describes a visible insoluble solid; naming an ion is an inference from the observation (1). A white precipitate alone is not unique: reagent conditions and further test results are needed to distinguish possible ions (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Observation, inference and limitations
blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Plotting and interpreting graphs
blocks.text:
A graph should label both axes with quantities and units, use an even suitable scale and place points accurately. Time usually belongs on the horizontal axis in a cooling experiment. Choose a scale that uses the available grid well while covering the data. The plotted line should represent the relationship: a cooling curve is usually a smooth decreasing curve, whereas a justified linear relationship uses a straight best-fit line. Do not force every noisy point into a zigzag merely to connect them.

For DATA-12, time in minutes is 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and uninsulated temperature in °C is 80, 72, 65, 59, 54, 50. The insulated series is 80, 76, 72, 69, 66, 63. The graph shows slower cooling with insulation under matched conditions. Read between nearby data points only within the supported range, and state a reasonable tolerance. A curve should not swing above or below the trend because of an unsuitable fitting method. Marking separates axes/scales, point accuracy and the line or curve. A correct answer read from a badly labelled graph does not repair the missing axis information.

blocks.text:

blocks.heading: Gradient, intercept and intersection
blocks.text:
Gradient measures change in the vertical quantity divided by change in the horizontal quantity. A temperature–time graph therefore has gradient in °C/min when those are the axis units. For a straight segment from (2 min, 72 °C) to (6 min, 59 °C), the average gradient is (59 − 72)/(6 − 2) = −3.25 °C/min. The negative sign means temperature falls. A cooling-rate magnitude can be reported as 3.25 °C/min if the question asks how quickly temperature decreases.

Use a large appropriate triangle on a best-fit line when finding its gradient; nearby points amplify reading uncertainty. For a curved graph, distinguish an average rate over an interval from the instantaneous rate represented by a tangent. The vertical intercept is the value where the graph crosses the vertical axis, often the initial value when time is zero. An intersection represents equal vertical values at the same horizontal value. Those meanings depend on the axes, so do not state simply 'the answer is where lines meet' without naming the physical quantity. An extrapolated intersection outside the data is less secure than an observed one.

topics/12/content-units/CU-6117-12.2.jso.title: 12.2 — Describe and explain experimental arrangements and techniques.

blocks.heading: Explaining an arrangement
blocks.text:
An apparatus arrangement should make the intended measurement possible and control relevant conditions. To measure gas production, a reaction vessel can be connected through a bung and delivery tube to a freely moving gas syringe. Connections must prevent unintended leakage while allowing gas into the measuring device. A sealed reaction vessel with no expansion or outlet is not an appropriate substitute.

Explain the role of each feature. A thermometer bulb should contact the liquid being measured without touching the hot vessel wall. A condenser's cooling water enters at the lower connection and leaves at the upper connection so the jacket remains filled. A lid in a cooling investigation helps standardise evaporation and heat loss, but must allow the intended thermometer arrangement. General phrases such as 'make it accurate' are weaker than naming the error being reduced. An experimental arrangement also includes timing: define when the reaction starts and when the measurement is taken. For a rate comparison, a delayed bung or timer can lose early gas and bias the measured rate. Link the diagram to the procedure rather than treating it as decorative. In an acid-rate comparison, specify acid identity and concentration: strong/weak describes ionisation, whereas concentrated/dilute describes amount per volume. Changing both at once confounds the comparison.

Checking the response: Close unintended leakage at flask while preserving collection path (1). Connect delivery tube into suitable gas syringe (1).

blocks.heading: Tables and numerical processing
blocks.text:
A results table should identify each quantity and place its unit in the heading. Record raw measurements before calculating derived values. For mass loss, subtract later mass from earlier mass; for burette delivery, subtract initial reading from final reading. The direction follows the physical quantity being requested, not a universal rule to subtract the smaller printed number from the larger without thought.

Original data: a reaction vessel falls from 104.36 g to 103.92 g, so 0.44 g has left the measured system. If gas escape is the intended cause, the result can represent mass of gas lost under suitable controls, but evaporation or splashing could also affect the measurement. A table column headed 'mass lost / g' is different from 'mass / g'. Keep units consistent during processing and show the formula or relationship. A calculator output should be rounded to a precision justified by the input data. Processed data do not replace raw readings; retaining both allows another person to check the subtraction and interpret a possible error.

blocks.heading: Drawing usable apparatus diagrams
blocks.text:
A scientific apparatus diagram shows the functional connections and positions clearly. Simple two-dimensional lines are usually more useful than decorative perspective. Label the vessel, measuring device and relevant liquid or solid. A gas-delivery tube must connect to the gas space or intended reaction arrangement and lead into the collection device without an unexplained break. A label line should end at the component it names.

For filtration, show a funnel containing filter paper above a receiving vessel. The residue remains on the paper and the filtrate passes through. A soluble product is not recovered from the residue merely because the residue is easier to see. For a thermometer in a cooling experiment, show the bulb immersed but clear of the vessel wall and bottom. Diagrams need not reproduce manufacturing details, but they must not imply impossible flow through solid glass. When evaluating a supplied diagram, name the specific missing connection or incorrect position and its consequence. A neat drawing can still be scientifically wrong, while a simple correct schematic can communicate the method well.

blocks.heading: Choosing apparatus for a purpose
blocks.text:
Choose apparatus by the quantity, range and precision required. A volumetric pipette is suitable for transferring one specified volume accurately. A burette delivers a measured variable volume, such as during titration. A measuring cylinder is useful for many less precise volume measurements, while an ordinary beaker is usually unsuitable for a precise titre. A balance measures mass, not volume.

The reason should connect the device to the task. Saying that a pipette is 'better' is incomplete without stating the fixed accurate transfer it provides. The instrument range must also fit the quantity: a device that cannot contain the required amount is unsuitable even if its scale is fine. Select a thermometer with an appropriate range and division size for a cooling investigation. A stopwatch is useful for timed observations but does not measure temperature. For gas measurements, consider whether the gas is soluble or reactive in a collection liquid before choosing displacement over water. The choice belongs to the chemistry and measurement requirements together, not to habit.

blocks.text:
Calculate the average cooling-rate magnitude for the uninsulated water from 2 to 6 min using the data 72 °C at 2 min and 59 °C at 6 min.

Temperature decrease = 72 − 59 = 13 °C; interval = 6 − 2 = 4 min. Average cooling-rate magnitude = 13/4 = 3.25 °C/min. The signed temperature gradient is −3.25 °C/min.

Temperature change divided by elapsed time, 13/4 (1). 3.25 °C/min as magnitude, or −3.25 °C/min clearly identified as signed gradient (1). Exact supplied-data answer is 3.25; accept 3.0–3.5 only when a permitted graph read-off is explicitly used, with follow-through.

topics/12/content-units/CU-6117-12.1.jso.title: 12.1 — Read scales accurately and record appropriate precision.

blocks.heading: Reading scales with appropriate precision
blocks.text:
A measurement needs a quantity, value and unit. Before reading a scale, identify its direction and the value represented by one small interval. A thermometer usually increases upwards, whereas a burette increases downwards because it records volume delivered from its upper zero. Read an aqueous liquid's lower meniscus at eye level to avoid parallax. Record enough precision to reflect the scale and method, without adding unsupported digits.

For a burette, volume delivered is final reading minus initial reading. If the readings are 1.20 and 24.80 cm³, the delivered volume is 23.60 cm³. Adding the readings gives a number without the required physical meaning. A negative result in an ordinary delivery experiment should prompt a check of reading order. Two readings both have measurement uncertainty, so a very small delivered volume may have a relatively large percentage uncertainty. Instrument readings are evidence; changing a recorded reading to match an expected answer is not legitimate. If a mistake is found, retain a clear correction rather than silently manufacturing agreement.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reading scales with appropriate precision
blocks.text:
Describe two corrections if a learner reads the top of a water meniscus from above and records every burette reading to the nearest whole cm³ despite 0.1 cm³ divisions.

Read the lower meniscus at eye level and record precision appropriate to the divisions, typically to 0.05 cm³ by estimation.

Checking the response: Eye-level lower-meniscus reading (1). Precision based on the 0.1 cm³ divisions, not whole cm³ rounding (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Reading scales with appropriate precision
blocks.text:
Explain the error in adding burette readings 1.20 and 24.80 cm³ to obtain a titre of 26.00 cm³.

A titre is the increase in reading, so subtract initial from final: 24.80 − 1.20 = 23.60 cm³. The addition is the error.

Checking the response: A titre is the increase in reading, so subtract initial from final: 24.80 − 1.20 = 23.60 cm³. The addition is the error (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Interpolating between divisions
blocks.text:
Interpolation estimates a value between nearby marked values. First determine the size of an interval from two numbered marks and the number of spaces between them. If 20 and 30 cm³ are separated by ten equal intervals, each interval is 1 cm³. A liquid level halfway between 24 and 25 cm³ is about 24.5 cm³, provided the drawing or instrument supports that estimate.

Count spaces rather than tick marks. Including both end marks in the count can give the wrong interval size. An estimate between divisions is not a licence to report many decimal places. The useful precision depends on the clarity of the scale, the width of the meniscus or pointer and the instrument. If a diagram is only schematic and has no readable scale, do not infer a precise value from its size. The visual panels for this topic have specified divisions so readings can be checked. Compare upward and downward scales explicitly: a lower meniscus position on a burette corresponds to a larger reading, while a higher liquid column on a thermometer corresponds to a higher temperature.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Interpolating between divisions
blocks.text:
Describe how to estimate a reading halfway between the 24 and 25 cm³ marks on a clear scale.

Identify the 1 cm³ interval and estimate its midpoint as 24.5 cm³.

Checking the response: The interval from 24 to 25 cm³ is 1 cm³; halfway is 0.5 cm³ above 24 (1). Estimated reading 24.5 cm³ (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Interpolating between divisions
blocks.text:

Checking the response: 18.1 cm³, commonly recorded as 18.10 cm³ with consistent burette precision (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Repeats and anomalous results
blocks.text:
Repeated measurements help reveal random variation and allow a more reliable estimate of a result. Keep the method and controlled variables the same. Results that agree closely can be averaged where an average is meaningful. A markedly different reading should be investigated; it must not be deleted merely because it is inconvenient or differs from a prediction.

For original practice data, titres 20.10, 20.20 and 20.10 cm³ are close together, while 23.80 cm³ warrants checking and a repeat. If a specific procedural error is documented for the outlier, explain why it is excluded from a final average. Repetition does not automatically remove systematic error: a miscalibrated instrument can give very similar but biased results. Distinguish repeatability from accuracy. Also distinguish a preliminary rough trial from carefully repeated measurements when the method calls for that distinction. Record all relevant results, then justify the processing decision. More decimal places in the mean do not necessarily represent greater experimental precision.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Repeats and anomalous results
blocks.text:
Describe how repeated measurements help assess a practical result and one limitation.

They reveal variation and support a representative mean, but do not remove a systematic calibration error.

Checking the response: Variation/reliability or justified mean (1). Systematic error can remain (1).

topics/12/content-units/CU-6117-12.6.jso.title: 12.6 — Describe gas and ion tests and draw conclusions from results.

blocks.heading: Reagent, observation and inference
blocks.text:
A qualitative test response should name the reagent or procedure, state the observation and give a conclusion limited by that evidence. For hydrogen, a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop; oxygen relights a glowing splint. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Confusing the splint conditions changes the test, so 'a splint' alone is incomplete.

Ion tests often need observations both before and after adding excess reagent. Copper(II) with aqueous ammonia can first form a light-blue precipitate that dissolves in excess to give a deep-blue solution. The final colour belongs to a solution, not a precipitate. Use fresh portions for separate tests and avoid contamination. The complete test tables are taught in Topic 8. This consolidation chapter organises the syllabus practical skills rather than adding a twelfth content topic to the official eleven; the linked practical index points back to all 55 suggested experiences in their teaching contexts.

The white appearance is a precipitate in the limewater, not the gas; insoluble calcium carbonate causes it.

Checking the response: Distinguish gas appearance from liquid suspension (1). Calcium carbonate precipitate identified (1).

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.4.4.jso.title: 2.4.4 — describe the structures of the common allotropes of carbon, graphite and diamond, as giant covalent lattices with high melting points

blocks.heading: Diamond and graphite structures
blocks.text:
Diamond and graphite are giant covalent allotropes of carbon. In diamond, each carbon atom bonds to four others in a three-dimensional network. In graphite, each carbon bonds to three others in layers containing hexagonal rings. Strong covalent bonds extend through each layer, while weaker attractions act between layers. One electron per carbon is delocalised in graphite, enabling electrical conduction. Diamond has no equivalent mobile-electron system and does not conduct.

Both structures withstand high temperatures because breaking their giant covalent frameworks requires considerable energy. Do not explain graphite's high-temperature stability using only its weak interlayer attractions: those weak attractions allow sliding, while the strong bonds within layers maintain the carbon network. A diagram of diamond should not look like separate four-carbon molecules, and a graphite diagram needs more than one layer to show the contrast between strong intralayer bonding and weak interlayer attraction. Different structures explain different properties even though the element is the same. Carbon atom identity does not determine a single fixed set of bulk properties.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Diamond and graphite structures
blocks.text:
Describe which carbon model fits diamond and the model that fits graphite: A has each carbon joined to four neighbours in a 3D network; B has three neighbours in flat sheets. Reference key: diamond has a four-bond 3D network; graphite has three-bond sheets.

A fits diamond and B fits graphite.

Checking the response: Diamond assigned using four-neighbour network (1). Graphite assigned using three-neighbour sheets (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Diamond and graphite structures
blocks.text:
Describe why both diamond and graphite have very high melting or sublimation temperatures.

They contain extensive networks of strong covalent bonds, requiring much energy to break.

Checking the response: Strong covalent networks (1); large energy requirement (1).

blocks.heading: Using carbon structures
blocks.text:
Diamond is very hard because strong covalent bonds connect carbon atoms throughout a three-dimensional network. Moving one part relative to another would require disrupting strong bonds, so diamond is useful in cutting and drilling tools. The useful property is hardness, not simply a high melting point or the fact that it contains carbon. A material can withstand heat yet still allow layers to slide, as graphite demonstrates.

Graphite can act as a lubricant because its layers slide over one another relatively easily. The attractions between layers are weak compared with the covalent bonds within each layer. Sliding does not require breaking every carbon–carbon bond. This distinction lets graphite reduce friction while retaining its layered structure. When choosing a material, connect the requested performance to the relevant structural feature: cutting needs resistance to deformation, while lubrication benefits from easy sliding. Graphite's electrical conductivity is another useful property, but it is not the reason layers can slide. Avoid combining unrelated facts without showing the causal link.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Using carbon structures
blocks.text:
Explain why graphite can be used as a lubricant.

Weak attractions between its layers allow the layers to slide over one another.

Checking the response: Weak attractions between its layers allow the layers to slide over one another (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Using carbon structures
blocks.text:
Suggest which carbon allotrope suits a tool surface that must resist scratching during cutting, and give the structural reason.

Diamond, because strong covalent bonds form a rigid three-dimensional network.

Checking the response: Diamond, because strong covalent bonds form a rigid three-dimensional network (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Silicon dioxide
blocks.text:
Silicon(IV) oxide, or silicon dioxide, has formula SiO2 and a giant covalent structure. Each silicon is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms, while each oxygen links two silicon atoms. The network extends through the solid. Sharing oxygen atoms between silicon centres gives the overall one-silicon-to-two-oxygen ratio; the formula does not describe separate O=Si=O molecules in this solid.

The strong network accounts for hardness and a high melting point. There are no mobile charged particles to carry an electric current in the usual solid, so it does not conduct. Compare the formula with CO2 carefully: similar atom ratios do not guarantee similar structures. Carbon dioxide consists of separate molecules, whereas silicon dioxide forms a continuous network. A diagram should show silicon atoms linked through oxygen atoms, not a direct Si–Si skeleton with unattached oxygens. Count local neighbours and the overall ratio as two separate checks. The network can be represented by a small fragment as long as continuing bonds indicate that it extends beyond the drawing.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Silicon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe why a model can have four oxygen neighbours around each Si yet the overall formula is SiO2, if each oxygen bridges two silicon atoms.

Each of the four oxygen neighbours is shared between two Si centres, so there are two oxygens per silicon overall.

Checking the response: Four bridging neighbours counted with sharing between two Si (1). 4/2 gives the 1:2 overall atom ratio (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Silicon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe why solid silicon dioxide has a high melting point.

Its giant network contains strong covalent bonds, and much energy is needed to disrupt them.

Checking the response: Strong covalent network (1); high energy requirement (1).

blocks.heading: Comparing diamond and silicon dioxide
blocks.text:
Diamond and silicon dioxide are both hard giant covalent solids with high melting points and no mobile charge carriers in their usual structures. Their strong bonds extend in three dimensions, making widespread rearrangement difficult. The similarity in properties follows from this network structure, even though diamond contains only carbon and silicon dioxide contains two elements. One is an elemental allotrope and the other a compound.

State the shared structure before explaining a shared property. High melting point follows from the large energy needed to disrupt strong covalent bonds; hardness follows from the rigid connected arrangement; lack of electrical conduction follows from the absence of mobile charged particles. Do not use “no electrons” as the conductivity explanation: both substances contain electrons, but those electrons are not free to move through the solid as charge carriers. Graphite is a useful contrast because its layers and delocalised electrons give different properties. A comparison should therefore be limited to diamond and silicon dioxide rather than asserted for every covalent substance.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing diamond and silicon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe which sample better fits silicon dioxide: X is hard, has a high melting point and does not conduct when solid; Y is soft and melts at a low temperature. Link the choice to structure.

X better fits the strong continuous covalent network of silicon dioxide.

Checking the response: X chosen using hardness/high melting evidence (1). Strong extended covalent bonds explain that evidence (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing diamond and silicon dioxide
blocks.text:
Describe why diamond and silicon dioxide both fail to conduct electricity in their usual solid forms.

Their electrons are held in covalent bonds and they have no mobile charged particles to carry current.

Checking the response: Bonded rather than mobile electrons (1); absence of mobile charge carriers (1).

blocks.text:
Why does graphite withstand very high temperatures despite its layers sliding readily?
A. The weak interlayer attractions are stronger than covalent bonds.
B. Strong covalent bonds remain within each layer.
C. All carbon atoms form separate molecules.
D. There are no bonds in graphite.

B. Strong covalent bonds remain within each layer. Sliding involves weaker interlayer attractions, while strong intralayer covalent bonds require much energy to break.

Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Sliding involves weaker interlayer attractions, while strong intralayer covalent bonds require much energy to break. Distractor explanations: D: graphite has extensive covalent bonds. C: it is a giant layered structure. A: the relative strengths are reversed.

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.4.5.jso.title: 2.4.5 — describe metallic bonding as a lattice of positive ions in a ‘sea’ of delocalised electrons

blocks.heading: Metallic bonding
blocks.text:
Metallic bonding is electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons. In a simple model of a metal, the positive ions form a regular lattice and the outer electrons are free to move through the structure rather than belonging to one particular atom. The phrase sea of electrons is a model for this shared mobile electron population, not a literal liquid inside the metal.

The whole metal remains electrically neutral: positive ionic charge is balanced by negative electronic charge. Do not draw a metal as a lattice alternating positive and negative metal ions; that would resemble an ionic model with the wrong particles. A useful diagram labels positive metal ions and delocalised electrons separately and shows the electrons throughout the structure. The attraction holds the lattice together, while electron mobility explains conduction. The same model can explain why many metals have high melting points and why layers can move without the structure immediately splitting into separate molecules. Each property needs its own link to the model.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Metallic bonding
blocks.text:
Describe why positive ions in a metal do not simply repel apart, and why the metal can conduct while solid.

Delocalised electrons attract the positive ions and maintain bonding; those electrons can move through the solid and carry charge.

Checking the response: Ion–electron attraction opposes separation of the ions (1). Mobile delocalised electrons carry current through the solid (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Metallic bonding
blocks.text:
Describe why a metal can stay bonded when layers of its ions slide rather than separating into individual atoms.

Delocalised electrons remain among the positive ions; electrostatic attraction is maintained as the arrangement shifts.

Checking the response: Delocalised electrons remain available throughout shifted layers (1). Continuing ion–electron attraction maintains bonding (1).

blocks.heading: Metal properties from structure
blocks.text:
Metals conduct electricity because delocalised electrons move through their structure and carry charge. The positive ions do not migrate through a solid wire to carry the current. Many metals have high melting points because considerable energy is needed to overcome the strong attraction between ions and delocalised electrons, although melting points vary and some metals melt at much lower temperatures than others.

Malleability means the ability to be hammered or pressed into shape; ductility means the ability to be drawn into wire. Layers of metal ions can slide while remaining attracted to the delocalised electrons, allowing deformation without an immediate loss of cohesion. This differs from an ionic crystal, where displacement can bring like charges alongside one another and promote fracture. The mobile-electron model therefore supports both conduction and deformability, but the causal steps differ. When explaining a property, identify the relevant motion: electrons move to carry current, while layers of ions shift during shaping. Avoid saying simply that “particles move” without identifying which ones.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Metal properties from structure
blocks.text:
Describe why a metal can be hammered into a new shape and remain bonded, whereas moving layers of an ionic crystal can cause fracture.

Metallic layers can shift while retaining attraction to delocalised electrons; shifted ionic layers can bring like charges together, causing repulsion and cleavage.

Checking the response: Maintained ion–electron attraction after metal layers shift (1). Like-charge repulsion after ionic layers shift (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Metal properties from structure
blocks.text:
Explain why a solid copper wire conducts electricity.

Its delocalised electrons are mobile and carry charge through the metal.

Checking the response: Its delocalised electrons are mobile and carry charge through the metal (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Drawing the metallic model
blocks.text:
Represent a typical metal by a regular array of positive ions with delocalised electrons between and around them. Use a clear key: large circles with plus signs can represent ions and small dots or e⁻ symbols can represent electrons. The diagram is a simplified section through a three-dimensional solid, not an exact scale image. Include enough repeated ions to show a lattice rather than an isolated molecule.

Charge balance matters conceptually even when the sketch is not counting every real particle. If the drawing explicitly represents singly charged ions and individual electrons, use equal numbers of positive charges and electrons in the complete model. Do not attach each electron permanently to one ion, since that would conceal delocalisation. An arrow can indicate possible electron motion but should not imply that every electron travels in a perfect circle around one atom. A diagram can be interpreted by identifying which particles are mobile and which form the regular framework. Labels prevent the small dots from being mistaken for neutral atoms or neutrons.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Drawing the metallic model
blocks.text:
Sketch the corrected metallic model if the proposed drawing contains neutral atoms with electrons fixed to individual atoms. Show the particles that permit conduction.

Show a regular array of positive metal ions with delocalised electrons between them.

Checking the response: Positive-ion array replaces neutral-atom labels (1). Mobile delocalised electrons replace atom-bound electrons (1).

blocks.heading: Choosing a bonding model
blocks.text:
Covalent bonding involves attraction between nuclei and shared electrons, ionic bonding involves attraction between oppositely charged ions, and metallic bonding involves attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons. These descriptions identify the actual charged particles participating in each attraction. They should not be reduced to “all bonding is attraction” without the distinctions needed to explain structure and properties.

Position in the Periodic Table helps predict common patterns. A metal combined with a non-metal often forms an ionic compound; non-metals together commonly form covalent substances; an elemental metal has metallic bonding. Use these as starting points and check any supplied structural evidence. A compound ion can have covalent bonds inside it and ionic attractions to counter-ions, so one substance can involve more than one kind of interaction at different scales. For example, ammonium chloride contains covalent N–H bonds within NH4⁺ and ionic attractions between NH4⁺ and Cl⁻. The level of description must match the question.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Choosing a bonding model
blocks.text:

Ionic bonding attracts positive and negative ions; metallic bonding attracts positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

Checking the response: Ionic bonding: attraction between positive and negative ions (1). Metallic bonding: attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons (1).

Checking the response: Ionic bonding, following formation of positive metal ions and negative halide ions (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P01 (12)
blocks.text:
Which pairing correctly matches a structure with its bonding model?
A. Copper: alternating positive and negative copper ions.
B. Diamond: separate molecules held by weak intermolecular forces.
C. Sodium chloride: positive ions in a sea of electrons.
D. Chlorine molecule: a shared electron pair between two atoms.

D. Chlorine molecule: a shared electron pair between two atoms. Cl2 contains a single covalent bond.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Cl2 contains a single covalent bond. Distractor explanations: A: copper has positive ions and delocalised electrons. B: diamond is a giant covalent network. C: NaCl contains positive and negative ions.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-18 — Testing metal properties
blocks.text: Compare metal strips or wires using a current-limited low-voltage circuit and teacher-approved bending tests. Record conduction and ease of shaping; consult supplied melting-point data instead of trying to melt the metals. Delocalised electrons explain conduction, while sliding layers retained by metallic attraction explain malleability and ductility. Keep wire dimensions comparable when comparing resistance or bending behaviour. A thicker wire can appear harder to bend for geometrical reasons, so differences in sample size must not be mistaken for differences in bonding. Avoid sharp edges and switch off before changing samples.

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.4.2.jso.title: 2.4.2 — describe how the reaction between a metal and a non-metal results in the transfer of electrons from metal atoms to non-metal atoms so that both achieve full outer shells and form positive ions (cations) and negative ions (anions) respectively

blocks.heading: Electron transfer and ions
blocks.text:
When a suitable metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons can transfer from metal atoms to non-metal atoms. The metal forms positive ions, or cations, after losing electrons. The non-metal forms negative ions, or anions, after gaining electrons. For sodium chloride, a sodium atom with arrangement 2,8,1 loses one electron and a chlorine atom with arrangement 2,8,7 gains it. The ions have arrangements 2,8 and 2,8,8 respectively. Proton numbers remain unchanged.

Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺, so two bromine atoms must each gain one electron to form two Br⁻ ions. The resulting formula is MgBr2. Show transferred electrons with a clear key in a dot-and-cross diagram, complete outer shells, brackets and charges. Do not draw a shared pair between magnesium and bromine as though the product were a covalent molecule. Electron transfer describes how ions form; ionic bonding describes the electrostatic attraction that holds oppositely charged ions together. Those statements answer different questions and should not be treated as interchangeable definitions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Electron transfer and ions
blocks.text:
Describe the ions formed when atom X with arrangement 2,8,1 transfers its outer electron to atom Y with arrangement 2,8,7.

X becomes X⁺ with 2,8; Y becomes Y⁻ with 2,8,8.

Checking the response: X⁺ and its completed remaining shell arrangement (1). Y⁻ and its completed outer shell arrangement (1).

blocks.text:
Describe why losing two electrons gives a magnesium atom a 2+ charge.

Its proton count is unchanged, but it has two fewer electrons, leaving two more positive charges than negative charges.

Checking the response: Unchanged protons with two electrons lost (1); resulting excess positive charge (1).

Explain the mistake in a magnesium-bromide drawing that shows a shared electron pair between Mg and each Br atom.

Magnesium bromide is ionic: Mg transfers one electron to each of two Br atoms, forming Mg²⁺ and two Br⁻ ions, rather than sharing pairs.

Checking the response: Magnesium bromide is ionic: Mg transfers one electron to each of two Br atoms, forming Mg²⁺ and two Br⁻ ions, rather than sharing pairs (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: What an ionic bond is
blocks.text:
An ionic bond is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. A positive ion attracts a negative ion because their charges have opposite signs. The attraction acts through the ionic lattice rather than creating one isolated pair of ions for each formula unit. Sodium chloride is therefore represented by the ratio NaCl, not as a collection of small NaCl molecules. The lattice contains many sodium and chloride ions, with attractions extending in different directions.

Electron transfer produces ions but is not itself the bond. A full explanation separates formation from attraction: sodium loses an electron, chlorine gains an electron, and the resulting oppositely charged ions attract. High melting points of many ionic compounds reflect the substantial energy needed to overcome these strong attractions. In the solid the ions are held in fixed lattice positions, although they vibrate. When molten, ions can move, allowing electrical conduction. The electrons used to describe ion formation should not be mistaken for mobile electrons passing through the molten salt; the moving charge carriers there are ions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — What an ionic bond is
blocks.text:
Explain why an ionic solid resists separating into individual ions.

Separating oppositely charged ions requires overcoming their electrostatic attraction.

Checking the response: Separating oppositely charged ions requires overcoming their electrostatic attraction (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — What an ionic bond is
blocks.text:
Explain why the supplied particles Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ attract each other.

They carry opposite electric charges, so there is electrostatic attraction between them.

Checking the response: They carry opposite electric charges, so there is electrostatic attraction between them (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Naming atoms and ions
blocks.text:
A chlorine atom is neutral, while a chloride ion has charge −1. The name changes to indicate the simple negative ion. Similar examples include oxygen and oxide, sulfur and sulfide, and bromine and bromide. A metal ion usually retains the element name, such as sodium ion or magnesium ion, with its charge shown in the symbol. Where a metal has more than one common ion charge, the name can specify it, as in iron(II) and iron(III).

Names must agree with formulae. Cl identifies a chlorine atom, Cl2 a chlorine molecule, and Cl⁻ a chloride ion. They are different particles despite involving the same element. The formula of sodium chloride contains chloride ions, not chlorine gas trapped between sodium atoms. In written explanations, name the particle that actually exists at that stage. Saying “chlorine gains an electron” can describe an atom becoming an ion, but the resulting particle is chloride. A correct charge without a correct particle name may leave the chemical explanation ambiguous.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Naming atoms and ions
blocks.text:
Distinguish a chlorine atom from a chloride ion in charge and electron count.

A chlorine atom is neutral with seventeen electrons; chloride is −1 with eighteen electrons.

Checking the response: Neutral versus −1 (1); seventeen versus eighteen electrons (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Naming atoms and ions
blocks.text:
Suggest the correct name for the supplied particle O²⁻.

Oxide ion.

Checking the response: Oxide ion (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Predicting simple ion charges
blocks.text:
For main-group elements in familiar ionic compounds, use electron loss or gain to reach a complete outer shell. Group I metals commonly lose one electron and form +1 ions; Group II lose two and form +2 ions; aluminium commonly loses three to form Al³⁺. Group VII atoms gain one electron to form −1 ions, Group VI commonly gain two to form −2 ions, and nitrogen can form N³⁻ in suitable ionic compounds. These are useful common patterns, not a claim that every element reacts ionically in every substance.

Count charge from the change in electrons. An atom with arrangement 2,8,2 loses two outer electrons and becomes 2,8 with charge +2. An atom with arrangement 2,6 gains two and becomes 2,8 with charge −2. Do not change the nuclear proton number to make the charge work. When given a diagram of an ion, add the electrons on all occupied shells and compare with the stated proton number. Equal shell arrangements can belong to different ions: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ both contain ten electrons but have different nuclei and opposite charges.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Predicting simple ion charges
blocks.text:
Predict the ion charges formed when atoms with arrangements 2,8,2 and 2,6 respectively reach complete outer shells by electron transfer.

The first forms 2+ by losing two electrons; the second forms 2− by gaining two.

Checking the response: 2+ for 2,8,2 (1); 2− for 2,6 (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Predicting simple ion charges
blocks.text:
State the charge inferred from an ion diagram showing ten electrons around a nucleus containing thirteen protons.

3+.

Checking the response: 3+ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: The ionic lattice and conduction
blocks.text:
An ionic crystal has a regular arrangement of positive and negative ions. In a simple two-dimensional representation of sodium chloride, alternate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ symbols to show the repeating pattern, while remembering that the real lattice extends in three dimensions. The charges belong to whole ions. Do not join neighbouring symbols with covalent bond lines, and do not draw separate neutral NaCl molecules. The formula states the simplest ratio needed for electrical neutrality.

In solid sodium chloride, ions vibrate around fixed positions and cannot carry charge through the solid. When the compound melts, the ordered lattice breaks down enough for ions to move. Both positive and negative ions can then carry current through the liquid. This differs from a metal, where delocalised electrons carry current. The phrase “electrons move” is therefore not a universal explanation of conductivity. For molten magnesium chloride, name Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ as the mobile charged particles. A substance containing charges can still fail to conduct if those charges are not mobile.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The ionic lattice and conduction
blocks.text:
Describe the correction to a sodium-chloride lattice model that places only Na⁺ nearest neighbours around one central Na⁺.

The nearest neighbours should be oppositely charged Cl⁻ ions in a repeating three-dimensional ionic arrangement.

Checking the response: Opposite-charge nearest neighbours replace like-charge neighbours (1). Repeating lattice rather than isolated molecular pairs (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The ionic lattice and conduction
blocks.text:
Describe why sodium chloride conducts when molten but not when solid.

Its ions are mobile when molten but held in fixed lattice positions in the solid.

Checking the response: Mobile ions in the melt (1); ions fixed in the solid (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The ionic lattice and conduction
blocks.text:
Explain the error in “molten magnesium chloride conducts because its electrons move through the liquid”.

The mobile charge carriers in molten magnesium chloride are Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not delocalised electrons.

Checking the response: The mobile charge carriers in molten magnesium chloride are Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not delocalised electrons (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.text:
Describe the electron transfer when sodium atoms react with chlorine atoms to form sodium chloride.

Each sodium atom loses one electron to form Na⁺. Each chlorine atom gains one electron to form Cl⁻.

Sodium loses one electron and forms Na⁺ (1). Chlorine gains one electron and forms Cl⁻ (1).

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.1.1.jso.title: 2.1.1 — state and describe the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases

blocks.heading: Recognising the three states
blocks.text:
A solid has a fixed shape and volume under ordinary conditions. A liquid has a fixed volume but flows to take the shape of the part of its container that it occupies. A gas has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume: it spreads to fill the available container. These descriptions refer to the material itself. A pile of salt can be poured because separate solid grains move past each other; each grain remains solid. Pourability alone therefore does not establish that a sample is a liquid.

Solids and liquids are difficult to compress because their particles are already close together. A gas is much easier to compress because there is considerable space between its particles. In a sealed syringe, pushing the plunger reduces these spaces rather than shrinking the particles. Gas still has mass even when it is invisible. Classification uses observations such as shape, volume and compressibility together. For example, a transparent sample which spreads throughout a sealed vessel and becomes smaller in volume when compressed is a gas, not an empty space.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Recognising the three states
blocks.text:
State the property of a liquid that distinguishes it from a gas when each is transferred to a larger container.

The liquid retains a fixed volume.

Checking the response: The liquid retains a fixed volume (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Arrangement and movement of particles
blocks.text:
In a typical crystalline solid, particles lie close together in an ordered arrangement. They vibrate about fixed positions, so the whole solid keeps its shape. They are not motionless. In a liquid, particles are also close together but have a less ordered arrangement and move past one another. This mobility explains flow while the small spaces explain why liquids resist compression. In a gas, particles are widely separated and move rapidly and randomly in all directions, repeatedly colliding with each other and the container walls.

A particle picture represents an enormous number of much smaller particles. Circles are symbols: the particles do not become larger circles when the material expands. Draw the same-sized particles before and after a physical change, changing separation, arrangement and motion as appropriate. Use arrows to show motion when requested. A row of touching circles with no enclosing boundary should not be mistaken for the outline of an individual solid grain. The diagram describes the internal arrangement. Explaining a property requires linking that arrangement to what the sample can do, rather than merely naming its state.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Arrangement and movement of particles
blocks.text:
Describe which particle model fits a crystalline solid and why: X has widely separated moving particles; Y has closely packed particles in a repeating arrangement that vibrate at fixed sites.

Y fits because it has a regular close arrangement and fixed mean particle positions.

Checking the response: Select Y from the supplied arrangement (1). Fixed positions/vibration account for a solid rather than gas (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Arrangement and movement of particles
blocks.text:
Describe how particle movement explains why a liquid flows but a solid keeps its shape.

Liquid particles move past one another, whereas solid particles vibrate about fixed positions.

Checking the response: Liquid particles move past one another (1); solid particles remain at fixed positions while vibrating (1).

blocks.heading: Changes of state
blocks.text:
Melting changes a solid to a liquid; freezing reverses this change. Boiling and evaporation both change a liquid to a gas, but boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature for the prevailing pressure, while evaporation occurs at the surface over a range of temperatures. Condensation changes gas to liquid. Sublimation changes solid directly to gas without an intervening liquid stage. The reverse direct change is deposition. A substance retains its chemical identity during these physical changes: water molecules remain water molecules when ice melts.

Heating supplies energy. Before melting, particles vibrate more vigorously as temperature rises. During melting of a pure substance, energy helps overcome attractions holding the particles in fixed positions. The temperature stays approximately constant while solid and liquid coexist under constant conditions. On further heating the liquid, particles move faster. At boiling, energy separates particles much further against their attractions. Cooling removes energy; particles move less vigorously and can become held close together or in fixed positions. Do not describe the particles themselves as melting, and do not say that covalent bonds inside water molecules break when water boils.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changes of state
blocks.text:
Describe the phase-change processes in two records: A loses liquid only at its surface at 25 °C; B forms vapour bubbles throughout at its constant boiling temperature.

A is evaporation; B is boiling.

Checking the response: A is evaporation: liquid leaves its surface below boiling temperature (1). B is boiling: vapour forms throughout the liquid at its boiling temperature (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changes of state
blocks.text:
Describe why the temperature of a pure solid can remain constant while it melts despite continued heating.

The energy supplied overcomes attractions holding particles in fixed positions rather than increasing their average kinetic energy.

Checking the response: Energy overcomes attractions (1); average kinetic energy and hence temperature do not increase during the change (1).

blocks.heading: Diffusion in liquids and gases
blocks.text:
Diffusion is the net spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration because of their random motion. Individual particles travel in many directions, including back towards the concentrated region. The overall movement arises because more particles initially leave the crowded region than enter it. Eventually the distribution becomes more uniform. Particles continue moving after an even distribution is reached; a uniform colour does not mean motion has stopped.

Both liquids and gases can show diffusion. In liquids, moving particles encounter close neighbours frequently, so spreading is generally slower than in gases. A small spot of soluble dye can gradually colour still water without stirring. Stirring speeds mixing by moving bulk liquid and is not itself diffusion. Similarly, a fan or draught transports scented air as a whole, while diffusion results from random molecular motion. When interpreting an experiment, identify what was controlled. An uneven temperature can create convection currents, so a colour spreading through hot and cold water is not automatically evidence for diffusion alone.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Diffusion in liquids and gases
blocks.text:
Explain why a dissolved dye gradually spreads through still water without stirring.

Its particles move randomly, producing net spreading from higher to lower concentration.

Checking the response: Its particles move randomly, producing net spreading from higher to lower concentration (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Diffusion in liquids and gases
blocks.text:
Explain why a dye that has become evenly distributed in a sealed, still water sample does not collect back into its original spot.

The particles continue moving randomly, with no sustained net movement towards the original spot.

Checking the response: The particles continue moving randomly, with no sustained net movement towards the original spot (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Evidence for moving particles
blocks.text:
A coloured solute spreading through still water and a gas spreading through another gas provide visible evidence consistent with movement of particles. The coloured region changes even though no spoon moves it. Take care to distinguish the visible colour from individual molecules: molecules are too small to be seen in this observation. A well-controlled demonstration reduces stirring and temperature differences, which could otherwise move the whole liquid and confuse the interpretation.

Brownian motion gives another kind of evidence. Under suitable magnification, tiny suspended particles, such as smoke particles in air, move irregularly. They receive uneven collisions from much smaller, moving molecules of the surrounding fluid. The observed suspended particles are not air molecules and are not moving because they are alive. Their zigzag paths reflect collisions occurring from changing directions. Brownian motion and diffusion support the particle model in complementary ways: the first reveals irregular movement of a suspended particle, while the second shows net spreading of many particles. Neither observation means that particles in a solid must be completely stationary.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Evidence for moving particles
blocks.text:
Describe which objects are visible and the cause of their movement in this observation: tiny smoke specks jiggle irregularly under a microscope; the surrounding gas molecules are too small to resolve.

The visible objects are smoke particles, moved by uneven impacts from invisible moving gas molecules.

Checking the response: Visible specks distinguished from unresolved gas molecules (1). Uneven molecular impacts explain observed direction changes (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Evidence for moving particles
blocks.text:
Describe the particle explanation for the irregular path of a tiny particle suspended in water.

Moving water molecules collide with it from different directions. Uneven collisions produce changes in its motion.

Checking the response: Collisions by moving water molecules (1); uneven impacts change the direction of motion (1).

blocks.heading: Factors affecting diffusion rate
blocks.text:
Increasing temperature generally increases diffusion rate because particles have greater average kinetic energy and move faster. Compare the same diffusing substance in the same medium while keeping the distance and other relevant conditions constant. A warm sample changing colour sooner may support a temperature effect, but stirring or convection must be considered before attributing the whole difference to diffusion. A controlled comparison changes temperature deliberately and records a clearly defined measure of spreading.

At the same temperature, lighter gas molecules move faster on average than heavier gas molecules. For otherwise comparable gases and conditions, the lighter gas therefore diffuses faster. Molecular mass means the mass associated with a whole molecule, so use H2 rather than a single H atom when comparing hydrogen gas with another gas. Molecular mass and temperature are different variables: a comparison involving both different gases and different temperatures cannot be explained by mass alone. Here a qualitative prediction is sufficient. State the controlled conditions and the direction of the trend before giving the particle explanation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Factors affecting diffusion rate
blocks.text:
Describe both trends in this supplied diffusion table: gas X travels 12 cm in 30 s at 20 °C and 18 cm at 40 °C; at 20 °C lighter gas Y travels 20 cm in 30 s under matched conditions.

X spreads faster at the higher temperature; the lighter Y spreads faster than X at the same temperature.

Checking the response: Temperature comparison uses X at both temperatures (1). Mass comparison uses Y versus X at 20 °C (1).
