blocks.heading: Worked practice — Factors affecting diffusion rate
blocks.text:
Describe why the same gas diffuses more rapidly at a higher temperature.

Its molecules have greater average kinetic energy and move faster, so they spread more rapidly.

Checking the response: Higher temperature increases the molecules’ average kinetic energy (1). Faster molecular motion makes the gas spread more rapidly (1).

blocks.heading: Diffusion in familiar situations
blocks.text:
A perfume contains volatile substances that enter the air. Once in the gas phase, their molecules spread from the region near the source through random motion. Someone farther away can detect the perfume when enough molecules reach their nose. Evaporation supplies molecules to the air; diffusion spreads them through it. The two processes are related but are not the same. Air currents may also contribute substantially to the observed movement in a room, so the example does not prove that all transport is by diffusion.

Tea and soluble coffee contain substances that dissolve in water and spread away from a concentrated region. In an unstirred, nearly uniform-temperature sample, diffusion contributes to this spreading. In a cup of freshly heated water, convection and stirring often make mixing much faster. Explaining an everyday event requires naming the relevant particles and medium. Saying that a smell wants to fill a room gives the particles an intention they do not have. Instead identify random motion and the initial concentration difference. A closed lid reduces escape of vapour; it does not switch off particle motion inside the container.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Diffusion in familiar situations
blocks.text:
Explain how perfume molecules spread through still air after entering it as vapour.

Random motion produces net diffusion from the concentrated region near the perfume into less concentrated air.

Checking the response: Random motion produces net diffusion from the concentrated region near the perfume into less concentrated air (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Diffusion in familiar situations
blocks.text:
Explain why colour gradually spreads beyond a small tea-filled region in unstirred water kept at a uniform temperature.

Dissolved coloured particles move randomly and diffuse from the concentrated region into less concentrated water.

Checking the response: Dissolved coloured particles move randomly and diffuse from the concentrated region into less concentrated water (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P01 (1)
blocks.text:
Which property distinguishes a gas from a liquid?
A. It fills the available container.
B. It has mass.
C. Its particles move.
D. It contains particles.

A. It fills the available container. A gas expands to fill its container; a liquid retains a fixed volume.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: A gas expands to fill its container; a liquid retains a fixed volume. Distractor explanations: B: liquids also have mass. D: both contain particles. C: liquid particles also move.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P01 (2)
blocks.text:
Why can a perfume spread through still air after evaporating?
A. The molecules stop colliding.
B. Air molecules carry it deliberately towards noses.
C. The perfume molecules become larger.
D. Random motion spreads perfume molecules.

D. Random motion spreads perfume molecules. Random molecular motion produces net diffusion from higher to lower concentration.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Random molecular motion produces net diffusion from higher to lower concentration. Distractor explanations: B: particles have no intention. C: spreading changes separation, not molecular size. A: collisions continue.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-05 — Comparing gas diffusion
blocks.text: Use a teacher demonstration in a fume cupboard, or a supplied recording, of ammonia and hydrogen chloride vapours entering opposite ends of a glass tube at the same time. Mark the position of the white ammonium chloride ring and compare distances from the two sources. The ring is nearer the hydrogen chloride source because the lighter ammonia molecules diffuse faster under comparable conditions. Measure from the source positions, not the tube ends if these differ. Timing, temperature and source arrangement must be comparable; draughts and unequal release can affect the result. Learners should not prepare or inhale these irritating gases.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-06 — Everyday spreading in liquids
blocks.text: Compare a small drop of food colouring in two equal volumes of still water at different recorded temperatures. Use identical vessels and add equal drops at the same position without stirring. Record the coloured region after equal intervals. Faster spreading in warm water is consistent with faster particle motion, but convection may also contribute, so do not claim the observation isolates diffusion perfectly. Relate this limitation to tea in hot water and perfume in a draught: bulk fluid movement can accompany molecular diffusion. Use safe warm water rather than boiling water.

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.3.1.jso.title: 2.3.1 — describe the build-up of electrons in ‘shells’ and analyse their structures in terms of:  the relationship between group number of the Periodic Table and number of electrons in the outer shell  the relationship between period number of the Periodic Table and number of shells in atoms

blocks.heading: Groups, periods and electron shells
blocks.text:
For the main-group elements considered here, the group number in the I–VII convention indicates the number of electrons in the outer shell. Sodium, 2,8,1, is in Group I; chlorine, 2,8,7, is in Group VII. The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells in the neutral atom. Both examples are in Period 3 because they have three occupied shells. Group is the vertical column; period is the horizontal row.

The noble gases are treated separately as Group VIII in this syllabus. They have complete outer shells: helium has two electrons in its first and only shell, while neon has 2,8 and argon has 2,8,8. Do not force helium into an eight-electron description. When deducing a position from an electron arrangement, first count occupied shells, then inspect the outer shell. Do this for the neutral atom; the shell arrangement of an ion can resemble that of a different element. For example, Na⁺ has the same electrons as neon but is still an ion of the Period 3 element sodium.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Groups, periods and electron shells
blocks.text:
Describe the group and period of a neutral main-group atom with arrangement 2,8,7, using Groups I–VII.

Group VII from seven outer electrons; period 3 from three occupied shells.

Checking the response: Group VII from supplied outer-shell count (1). Period 3 from occupied-shell count (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Groups, periods and electron shells
blocks.text:
Describe why sodium and lithium have similar chemical behaviour despite being in different periods.

Both have one outer electron, which they can lose in similar reactions; sodium has more occupied shells.

Checking the response: Both sodium and lithium have one outer-shell electron (1). Both can lose that electron in reactions, giving similar chemical behaviour (1).

blocks.heading: Complete outer shells and chemical behaviour
blocks.text:
Noble-gas electron arrangements are associated with very low reactivity under ordinary conditions. Their outer shells are complete, so they do not readily gain, lose or share electrons in common chemical reactions. Helium's complete shell contains two electrons. The complete outer shell in neon and argon contains eight. “Unreactive” describes their behaviour in the ordinary contexts studied here; it should not be rewritten as a claim that no noble gas can form any compound under any circumstances.

Other main-group atoms often form ions or covalent bonds that produce a complete outer shell. Magnesium loses two outer electrons to form Mg²⁺ with arrangement 2,8. Oxygen gains two to form O²⁻ with arrangement 2,8, or shares electrons in covalent compounds. The model explains patterns but should not be anthropomorphised: atoms do not want electrons or make decisions. State the actual electron loss, gain or sharing. A noble-gas electron arrangement also does not change the element's identity; Mg²⁺ remains magnesium because its nucleus still contains twelve protons.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Complete outer shells and chemical behaviour
blocks.text:
Explain why neon is unreactive under ordinary conditions.

Its outer electron shell is complete, so it does not readily gain, lose or share electrons.

Checking the response: Its outer electron shell is complete, so it does not readily gain, lose or share electrons (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

Losing two electrons leaves the complete outer-shell arrangement 2,8.

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.4.3.jso.title: 2.4.3 — describe how non-metal atoms combine with other non-metal atoms by sharing electrons in their outer shells with the result that both atoms achieve full outer shells

blocks.heading: Sharing outer electrons
blocks.text:
Non-metal atoms can form covalent bonds by sharing outer-shell electrons. A single covalent bond contains one shared pair of electrons, normally one contributed by each atom in the simple examples here. The shared pair is counted in the outer shell of both bonded atoms. Hydrogen reaches a complete first shell with two electrons, while carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and chlorine commonly reach eight outer electrons in the molecules considered here.

Sharing differs from complete electron transfer. In H2, neither hydrogen is represented as H⁺ or H⁻: the molecule is neutral and the pair is shared. In water, oxygen shares one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms and retains two non-bonding pairs. A dot-and-cross key records which atom contributed an electron, not two different types of electron. Check both the total number of outer electrons and the count surrounding each atom. A diagram can accidentally give hydrogen four electrons or omit a non-bonding pair while still looking symmetrical, so counting is more reliable than appearance.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sharing outer electrons
blocks.text:
Describe the electron count and bond error in an H2 sketch that places two shared pairs between its two hydrogen atoms.

Hydrogen needs two shell electrons, not four; only one shared pair should join the atoms.

Checking the response: Two-pair sketch overfills each first shell (1). One shared pair corrects the diagram (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Sharing outer electrons
blocks.text:
Describe how sharing one electron pair gives each hydrogen atom in H2 a complete shell.

Each hydrogen contributes one electron and counts both electrons in the shared pair, giving two electrons in its first shell.

Checking the response: One electron contributed by each atom (1); each counts two in a complete first shell (1).

blocks.heading: The attraction in a covalent bond
blocks.text:
A covalent bond is attraction between the nuclei of bonded atoms and their shared electrons. The nuclei are positively charged and the electrons negatively charged, so the attraction is electrostatic. Sharing describes the electron arrangement; the attraction explains why the atoms remain bonded. The nuclei do not attract each other, since they have like charges. A statement that covalent bonding is “two positive nuclei attracting” reverses the electrical explanation.

In a diagram, show the shared electrons between the atoms where both nuclei attract them. A line in a displayed formula represents a shared pair, not a physical rod between atoms. Breaking a covalent bond requires energy because the attractive interaction must be overcome. That is different from separating whole molecules during boiling, where weaker intermolecular attractions can be overcome without breaking the molecular bonds. Always identify whether the process changes the connections inside molecules or the spacing between molecules. This distinction becomes important when explaining why many molecular substances boil at relatively low temperatures despite having strong covalent bonds.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The attraction in a covalent bond
blocks.text:
Explain why shared electrons can hold two positive nuclei together even though the nuclei repel one another.

Each nucleus attracts the shared negative electrons; this attraction binds the atoms despite nucleus–nucleus repulsion.

Checking the response: Each nucleus attracts the shared negative electrons; this attraction binds the atoms despite nucleus–nucleus repulsion (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — The attraction in a covalent bond
blocks.text:
Explain the error in a diagram caption saying that two positive nuclei attract each other to form H2.

The nuclei repel each other; bonding involves each nucleus attracting the shared electron pair.

Checking the response: The nuclei repel each other; bonding involves each nucleus attracting the shared electron pair (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Homonuclear molecules
blocks.text:
A homonuclear molecule contains atoms of the same element. Hydrogen H2, chlorine Cl2, fluorine F2, bromine Br2, iodine I2, oxygen O2 and nitrogen N2 are diatomic examples. Ozone O3 is also homonuclear even though it has three atoms. The prefix concerns sameness of element, not whether there are two atoms or whether every bond is single. Nitrogen remains an element when its atoms occur as N2 molecules.

To classify a formula, count the different element symbols rather than adding all the subscripts. O3 contains only oxygen and is homonuclear; CO2 contains carbon and oxygen and is not. A larger molecule made only of carbon can also be homonuclear. This classification does not say that all these elements have the same properties: O2 and O3 differ structurally and chemically despite containing only oxygen. Detailed ozone structure is not needed here. Keep molecule and atom distinct when counting particles: one O2 molecule contains two oxygen atoms, so three O2 molecules contain six oxygen atoms.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Homonuclear molecules
blocks.text:
State why O3 is a homonuclear molecule.

It contains atoms of only one element, oxygen.

Checking the response: It contains atoms of only one element, oxygen (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Heteronuclear molecules
blocks.text:
A heteronuclear molecule contains atoms of more than one element. Examples include H2O, CH4, NH3, HCl, C2H4, CH3OH and CO2. Water contains hydrogen and oxygen, while methanol contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. A formula with several atoms is not automatically heteronuclear: O3 contains three atoms but only one element. Look for different element symbols, each beginning with a capital letter.

The term molecule still requires an electrically neutral covalently bonded group in this course. An ionic compound such as NaCl contains two elements, but its solid is not described as a collection of heteronuclear NaCl molecules. Instead it is an ionic lattice with a fixed ion ratio. Likewise, sulfate SO4²⁻ contains different elements but is a compound ion because it is charged. These distinctions prevent a formula alone from being used as proof of particle type. Identify the elements present, then use the supplied bonding and charge information to decide whether the particle is a molecule, ion or part of a lattice.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Heteronuclear molecules
blocks.text:
State why CH3OH is a heteronuclear molecule.

It contains atoms of different elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

Checking the response: It contains atoms of different elements: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Hydrogen: one shared pair
blocks.text:
Each hydrogen atom starts with one electron. In H2 the two atoms share their electrons as one pair, forming a single covalent bond. Each hydrogen counts both electrons in the shared region and therefore has a complete first shell. There are no non-bonding electron pairs on either atom. A Lewis dot-and-cross diagram can show H •× H, with the dot from one atom and the cross from the other. The displayed formula H–H represents the same bond with one line.

Count two electrons in the whole diagram, not four. The pair is counted around each atom for shell completion but physically consists of only two electrons. Adding another pair would give a wrong electron total. Hydrogen does not need eight outer electrons; its first shell is complete with two. The molecule is neutral, so brackets with ion charges are inappropriate. A correct drawing shows a shared pair between the atoms rather than two isolated dots outside them. The bond arises from attraction of both nuclei to that shared pair.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen: one shared pair
blocks.text:
Draw an outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for H2, using a dot for one atom’s electron and a cross for the other’s.

H •× H: one shared dot-and-cross pair between two H atoms, with no other electrons.

Checking the response: One electron from each H in a shared pair (1); two H atoms with no extra electrons or ion charges (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen: one shared pair
blocks.text:
Describe the shell completion shown by the representation H •× H.

Both H atoms count the shared pair, so each has two electrons in a complete first shell.

Checking the response: Shared pair counted by both atoms (1); two electrons complete each first shell (1).

blocks.heading: Chlorine: bonding and lone pairs
blocks.text:
Each chlorine atom has seven outer electrons. Two chlorine atoms share one electron each, making one bonding pair in Cl2. Each chlorine then counts eight outer electrons: two in the shared pair and six in three non-bonding pairs. The molecule contains fourteen outer electrons in total. A diagram showing only the shared pair demonstrates the bond but omits twelve outer electrons if a complete outer-electron diagram was requested.

Draw the two Cl symbols, place a dot-and-cross pair between them, and place three lone pairs around each chlorine. Dots and crosses record electron origins; an electron does not become a different physical particle because it is drawn differently. The displayed formula Cl–Cl shows one single bond but does not display the lone pairs. Cl2 must not be confused with two Cl⁻ ions: the molecule is neutral and its atoms share electrons, whereas each chloride ion has gained an electron. This distinction also separates elemental chlorine from chloride present in sodium chloride.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chlorine: bonding and lone pairs
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for Cl2.

Two Cl atoms share one dot-and-cross pair; each Cl has three lone pairs. There are fourteen outer electrons in total.

Checking the response: One shared pair (1); three lone pairs on each Cl with correct total (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Chlorine: bonding and lone pairs
blocks.text:
Describe the error in a Cl2 outer-electron diagram that shows one shared pair but only two lone pairs on each Cl.

Each Cl should have three lone pairs. The proposed diagram leaves each atom short of a complete eight-electron outer shell.

Checking the response: Missing lone pair on each Cl identified (1); correction restores eight electrons around each (1).

blocks.heading: Water: two bonds and two lone pairs
blocks.text:
Oxygen has six outer electrons and each hydrogen has one. In water, oxygen shares one electron with each of two hydrogen atoms, producing two O–H single bonds. Oxygen retains four non-bonding electrons as two lone pairs. The whole molecule has eight outer electrons: four in bonding pairs and four in lone pairs. Each hydrogen counts two electrons and oxygen counts eight.

Place oxygen at the centre of the bonding diagram and connect one hydrogen to each of two shared pairs. Do not add a bond directly between the hydrogen atoms. A Lewis diagram emphasises electrons, whereas a shape diagram shows the bent arrangement of the atoms; a flat electron diagram need not be interpreted as an accurate three-dimensional model. Omitting the two lone pairs leaves the outer-electron diagram incomplete even if the H–O–H connectivity is right. Water molecules remain intact when water boils: the process separates molecules rather than splitting every O–H bond into hydrogen and oxygen atoms.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Water: two bonds and two lone pairs
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for H2O.

O shares one pair with each of two H atoms and has two lone pairs. Each O–H pair contains one electron from O and one from H.

Checking the response: Two correct O–H shared pairs (1); two lone pairs on O and no extra H electrons (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Water: two bonds and two lone pairs
blocks.text:
Describe the correction needed for an H2O electron diagram with two O–H shared pairs but no non-bonding electrons.

Add two lone pairs on oxygen, giving oxygen eight outer electrons while each hydrogen retains two.

Checking the response: Two lone pairs on O (1); correct shell counts retained (1).

blocks.heading: Methane: four single bonds
blocks.text:
Carbon has four outer electrons. In methane, CH4, it shares one with each of four hydrogen atoms. Four shared pairs form four C–H single bonds, so carbon counts eight outer electrons and each hydrogen counts two. There are eight outer electrons altogether and no lone pairs on the carbon atom. In a dot-and-cross drawing, use one symbol type for carbon's four electrons and another for the four electrons supplied by hydrogen.

A displayed formula often places the hydrogens above, below, left and right of carbon for clarity. This layout shows connectivity, not the true shape: methane is tetrahedral, not a flat cross. Do not add C–H bonds between the hydrogen atoms or place four electrons in a single bond. Each line corresponds to one shared pair. An answer can be checked by counting four bonds at carbon and one at each hydrogen. A molecule with only three hydrogen atoms and no charge is not the methane structure specified by CH4.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Methane: four single bonds
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for CH4.

Central C shares one dot-and-cross pair with each of four H atoms, with no lone pairs.

Checking the response: Four C–H shared pairs (1); correct electron origins and no extra electrons/lone pairs (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Methane: four single bonds
blocks.text:
Describe the bonding information and the shape limitation of a flat cross-shaped displayed formula of CH4.

It shows four C–H single bonds; it does not show a flat molecular shape, because methane is tetrahedral.

Checking the response: Four single bonds (1); connectivity diagram distinguished from tetrahedral shape (1).

blocks.heading: Ammonia: three bonds and one lone pair
blocks.text:
Nitrogen has five outer electrons. In ammonia, NH3, it shares one electron with each of three hydrogen atoms, forming three single bonds. The remaining two nitrogen electrons form one lone pair. Nitrogen counts eight outer electrons and each hydrogen counts two. The complete diagram contains eight outer electrons: six in shared pairs and two in the lone pair.

Draw nitrogen centrally with three H atoms bonded to it, then add the lone pair on nitrogen. A fourth N–H bond would change the particle represented and would not be neutral NH3. A complete outer-electron diagram also needs the correct total; three bonds without the lone pair show only six outer electrons. The molecular shape is pyramidal. The lone pair is part of the electron arrangement but is not an extra atom at the top of the pyramid. Distinguish an ammonia molecule from the ammonium ion NH4⁺ when reading formulae: the latter contains four hydrogens and has an overall positive charge.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ammonia: three bonds and one lone pair
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for NH3.

N shares one pair with each of three H atoms and retains one lone pair. Each shared pair contains one N electron and one H electron.

Checking the response: Three N–H shared pairs (1); one N lone pair with no extra electrons (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ammonia: three bonds and one lone pair
blocks.text:
Describe the correction needed for a neutral NH3 diagram with three N–H bonds and two lone pairs on nitrogen.

Remove one lone pair: NH3 has one nitrogen lone pair, giving eight rather than ten electrons around nitrogen.

Checking the response: One lone pair retained (1); corrected eight-electron count (1).

blocks.heading: Hydrogen chloride
blocks.text:
Hydrogen chloride contains one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom joined by a single covalent bond. Hydrogen contributes one electron and chlorine contributes one of its seven outer electrons to the shared pair. Chlorine retains three lone pairs. Hydrogen counts two electrons and chlorine counts eight, with eight outer electrons in the whole molecule. The displayed formula is H–Cl.

The unequal atom types make HCl heteronuclear, but this does not by itself make the molecule an ionic lattice. The dot-and-cross diagram for the molecule shows sharing rather than separate H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Hydrogen chloride ionises when dissolved in water; do not silently replace a molecular drawing task with a description of that aqueous solution. A common drawing error is to give hydrogen three lone pairs by treating both atoms as though each needed eight electrons. Check hydrogen against its two-electron first shell and chlorine against its eight-electron outer shell independently.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen chloride
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for an HCl molecule.

H and Cl share one dot-and-cross pair; Cl has three lone pairs and H has none.

Checking the response: Shared H–Cl pair (1); three Cl lone pairs with no extra H electrons (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Hydrogen chloride
blocks.text:
Describe why a supplied HCl diagram giving hydrogen three lone pairs is incorrect.

Hydrogen needs only the shared pair to complete its two-electron first shell. The three lone pairs belong on chlorine.

Checking the response: Hydrogen’s first shell is complete with the shared pair: no lone pairs on H (1). Place three lone pairs on chlorine, giving chlorine eight outer electrons including the shared pair (1).

blocks.heading: Nitrogen: a triple bond
blocks.text:
Each nitrogen atom has five outer electrons. In N2 the atoms share three pairs, producing a triple covalent bond. Each atom contributes three electrons to the bonding pairs and retains two electrons as one lone pair. Thus each nitrogen counts eight outer electrons, while the whole molecule contains ten. The displayed formula N≡N represents the three shared pairs with three lines.

A single shared pair would not complete the outer shells of two neutral nitrogen atoms with the correct total electron count. Draw three dot-and-cross pairs between the atoms and one lone pair on each atom. Do not interpret three lines as three molecules or three pairs of nitrogen atoms. The formula still contains two atoms. Multiple bonds involve more than one shared pair between the same atoms; they are not ionic charges. Counting each nitrogen's five original electrons provides a second check after counting the completed shells. The triple bond is a feature of the familiar N2 molecule, not a rule for every nitrogen-containing substance.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nitrogen: a triple bond
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron dot-and-cross diagram for N2.

Two N atoms share three dot-and-cross pairs; each N retains one lone pair.

Checking the response: Three shared pairs (1); one lone pair on each N with correct total (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Nitrogen: a triple bond
blocks.text:
Describe the bonding and lone-pair information represented by :N≡N:.

The two N atoms share three pairs in a triple bond, and each N has one lone pair.

Checking the response: Triple bond/three shared pairs (1); one lone pair per N (1).

blocks.heading: Ethene: a carbon–carbon double bond
blocks.text:
Ethene has formula C2H4. Each carbon forms two single bonds to hydrogen and a double bond to the other carbon. The double bond contains two shared pairs; each C–H bond contains one. Each carbon therefore counts four bonding pairs, completing its outer shell, and each hydrogen counts one pair. There are twelve outer electrons in the molecule, all in bonding pairs, with no lone pairs on carbon or hydrogen.

Write the displayed structure as H2C=CH2, expanding all C–H bonds when a fully displayed formula is requested. A single carbon–carbon bond with only four hydrogens would leave the usual neutral carbon shell counts incomplete. Conversely, adding two extra hydrogens changes the formula to ethane, a different molecule. The electron diagram should retain two shared pairs between the carbons without placing an extra hydrogen in that shared region. The carbon–carbon double bond later helps explain ethene's addition reactions, but the task here is to represent electron sharing accurately rather than draw a reaction mechanism.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ethene: a carbon–carbon double bond
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron bonding diagram for C2H4.

Two C atoms share two pairs; each C also shares one pair with each of two H atoms. No lone pairs are present.

Checking the response: C=C represented by two shared pairs (1); four correct C–H pairs and no extra electrons (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Ethene: a carbon–carbon double bond
blocks.text:
Describe the error in a C2H4 diagram with four C–H bonds but only one shared pair between the carbon atoms.

Ethene needs two shared pairs between the carbon atoms. A double bond gives each carbon eight outer electrons.

Checking the response: Second C–C shared pair required (1); complete carbon shell counts (1).

blocks.heading: Methanol: locating the oxygen bonds
blocks.text:
Methanol has formula CH3OH. Carbon is bonded to three hydrogen atoms and to oxygen; oxygen is bonded to carbon and to the fourth hydrogen. All five bonds are single. Oxygen also has two lone pairs, while carbon has none. The total outer-electron count is fourteen: four from carbon, six from oxygen and four from hydrogen. Ten electrons occur in bonding pairs and four in oxygen's lone pairs.

The condensed formula separates CH3 and OH to show how the atoms connect. Placing all four hydrogen atoms on carbon and then adding oxygen would give carbon too many ordinary bonds. Putting oxygen between carbon and the OH hydrogen gives the correct C–O–H sequence. Count bonds around each atom: four at carbon, two at oxygen and one at each hydrogen. A displayed formula records these connections but does not necessarily show the exact spatial geometry. Distinguishing formula, connectivity and electron count prevents a correct total number of atoms from disguising an incorrect molecular structure.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Methanol: locating the oxygen bonds
blocks.text:
Draw a complete outer-electron diagram for CH3OH.

C has three C–H single bonds and one C–O single bond; O also has one O–H bond and two lone pairs.

Checking the response: Three C–H, one C–O and one O–H single bonds, each a shared pair (1). Two lone pairs on oxygen; none on carbon or hydrogen (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Methanol: locating the oxygen bonds
blocks.text:
Describe the correction to a methanol model that puts all four H atoms on C and also joins C to O.

Move one H from C to O: carbon then has four bonds, and oxygen has two bonds plus two lone pairs.

Checking the response: Move one H from C to O (1). Corrected C has four single bonds; O has two single bonds and two lone pairs (1).

blocks.heading: Carbon dioxide: two double bonds
blocks.text:
Carbon dioxide has the structure O=C=O. Carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen, giving two double bonds. Carbon has no lone pairs; each oxygen retains two. There are sixteen outer electrons in total: eight in the four shared pairs and eight in the four oxygen lone pairs. Each of the three atoms counts eight outer electrons when shared pairs are counted around both bonded atoms.

A diagram with two single C–O bonds and the normal neutral atom electron totals does not represent the familiar complete-shell CO2 molecule. Show two pairs on each side of carbon and check the lone pairs on both oxygens. The molecule is linear, so a shape diagram places the three atoms on one straight line. Do not confuse the subscript 2 with a double-bond symbol: the subscript counts oxygen atoms, while the double lines show shared electron pairs. Molecular formula alone does not directly display all bonding. The full electron diagram or displayed formula makes that information explicit.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbon dioxide: two double bonds
blocks.text:
Draw the complete outer-electron diagram for CO2.

O=C=O, with two shared pairs in each C=O bond and two lone pairs on each oxygen; carbon has no lone pairs.

Checking the response: Two shared pairs in each C=O bond (1). Two lone pairs on each oxygen and none on carbon (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Carbon dioxide: two double bonds
blocks.text:
Describe the electron-sharing information in the displayed formula O=C=O.

Carbon shares two pairs with each oxygen, forming two double bonds and completing the outer shells.

Checking the response: Two pairs per C–O connection (1); completed outer shells (1).

blocks.heading: Bohr, Lewis and Couper representations
blocks.text:
Bohr diagrams show electrons in shells around a nucleus. In a bonding diagram, dots and crosses can identify electrons originally supplied by different atoms. Lewis diagrams concentrate on outer electrons, making bonding pairs and lone pairs easier to count without drawing filled inner shells. Couper, or displayed, notation represents a shared pair by a line: one line for a single bond, two for a double bond and three for a triple bond. These representations emphasise different information about the same chemical structure.

For water, the Lewis diagram includes two O–H shared pairs and two oxygen lone pairs, while H–O–H shows the bonds but omits lone pairs. For sodium chloride, draw bracketed ions with charges and complete outer shells; do not use a single covalent line to imply an NaCl molecule. Translate between representations by preserving atom counts, electron totals and charge. A line is not an additional pair on top of the dots: it is an alternative symbol for that pair. Include a dot-and-cross key and label ions clearly so the intended meaning is not left to the reader.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bohr, Lewis and Couper representations
blocks.text:
Draw the corrected displayed formula if a proposed water diagram is H–H–O, given that H forms one bond and O forms two.

H–O–H, with oxygen central and two single O–H bonds.

Checking the response: Move O to the central position (1). Two O–H bonds give each H one bond and O two (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bohr, Lewis and Couper representations
blocks.text:
State the meaning of each line in the supplied displayed formula H–O–H.

One shared pair of electrons forming a single covalent bond.

Checking the response: One shared pair of electrons forming a single covalent bond (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Water: molecular shape
blocks.text:
The molecular shape of water, H2O, is V-shaped (bent). O lies at the vertex with two H atoms on angled arms, not on a straight line. A shape diagram shows the spatial arrangement of atoms, whereas an outer-electron diagram emphasises shared pairs and lone pairs. A correct formula does not by itself guarantee a correct shape drawing. Name the central atom and its neighbours before arranging the bonds, then check the completed diagram against the required shape.

The two O–H bonds and two oxygen lone pairs belong to the electron arrangement; the shape name describes the positions of the three atoms. The lone pairs are not extra atoms. The drawn symbols are not to scale: a large letter does not mean a physically larger atom, and a shortened bond used for perspective does not mean a weaker bond. Use an explicit legend for a three-dimensional drawing. Rotating the whole molecule gives an equivalent drawing as long as the relative positions of the atoms remain correct. Bond angles need not be invented when the task asks only for the shape name. A useful final check is to distinguish the shape from the other three named examples: water is bent, methane tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal and carbon dioxide linear.

blocks.text:
Draw a corrected water model from this comparison. The supplied model places O between two H atoms on a straight line; the reference model has two angled O–H bonds.

O at the vertex of a bent H–O–H arrangement.

Checking the response: O bonded to two labelled H atoms (1). O at the vertex of a bent H–O–H arrangement, not a straight line (1).

V-shaped (bent).

blocks.heading: Methane: molecular shape
blocks.text:
The molecular shape of methane, CH4, is tetrahedral. C is central and the four H atoms point towards the corners of a tetrahedron. A shape diagram shows the spatial arrangement of atoms, whereas an outer-electron diagram emphasises shared pairs and lone pairs. A correct formula does not by itself guarantee a correct shape drawing. Name the central atom and its neighbours before arranging the bonds, then check the completed diagram against the required shape.

A flat cross is a useful connectivity drawing but is not the molecular shape. Use ordinary lines for bonds in the plane and a wedge/dashed bond convention to show bonds pointing towards and away from the viewer. The drawn symbols are not to scale: a large letter does not mean a physically larger atom, and a shortened bond used for perspective does not mean a weaker bond. Use an explicit legend for a three-dimensional drawing. Rotating the whole molecule gives an equivalent drawing as long as the relative positions of the atoms remain correct. Bond angles need not be invented when the task asks only for the shape name. A useful final check is to distinguish the shape from the other three named examples: water is bent, methane tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal and carbon dioxide linear.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Methane: molecular shape
blocks.text:

Central C with four H positions in a tetrahedral arrangement, using wedge/dash or an equivalent clear 3D convention.

blocks.heading: Ammonia: molecular shape
blocks.text:
The molecular shape of ammonia, NH3, is pyramidal. N lies above a triangular arrangement of three H atoms. A shape diagram shows the spatial arrangement of atoms, whereas an outer-electron diagram emphasises shared pairs and lone pairs. A correct formula does not by itself guarantee a correct shape drawing. Name the central atom and its neighbours before arranging the bonds, then check the completed diagram against the required shape.

The nitrogen lone pair is part of the electron arrangement but is not a fourth hydrogen atom. A triangular flat drawing misses the height of the pyramid. A wedge and dashed bond can make the three-dimensional arrangement clear. The drawn symbols are not to scale: a large letter does not mean a physically larger atom, and a shortened bond used for perspective does not mean a weaker bond. Use an explicit legend for a three-dimensional drawing. Rotating the whole molecule gives an equivalent drawing as long as the relative positions of the atoms remain correct. Bond angles need not be invented when the task asks only for the shape name. A useful final check is to distinguish the shape from the other three named examples: water is bent, methane tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal and carbon dioxide linear.

A pyramidal arrangement, with N above the plane of three H atoms.

blocks.heading: Carbon dioxide: molecular shape
blocks.text:
The molecular shape of carbon dioxide, CO2, is linear. The O, C and O atoms lie on one straight line. A shape diagram shows the spatial arrangement of atoms, whereas an outer-electron diagram emphasises shared pairs and lone pairs. A correct formula does not by itself guarantee a correct shape drawing. Name the central atom and its neighbours before arranging the bonds, then check the completed diagram against the required shape.

Each C=O bond contains two shared electron pairs, but a double bond does not bend the molecule. Keep the two oxygen atoms on opposite sides of the central carbon. A V-shaped drawing would describe the wrong shape. The drawn symbols are not to scale: a large letter does not mean a physically larger atom, and a shortened bond used for perspective does not mean a weaker bond. Use an explicit legend for a three-dimensional drawing. Rotating the whole molecule gives an equivalent drawing as long as the relative positions of the atoms remain correct. Bond angles need not be invented when the task asks only for the shape name. A useful final check is to distinguish the shape from the other three named examples: water is bent, methane tetrahedral, ammonia pyramidal and carbon dioxide linear.

Linear O–C–O.

Linear.

blocks.heading: Bonds within molecules and forces between them
blocks.text:
Covalent bonds within a molecule are stronger than the intermolecular attractions between the small molecules studied here. The distinction concerns two different locations: intramolecular means within a molecule, while intermolecular means between molecules. When liquid water boils, molecules move farther apart as intermolecular attractions are overcome, but the O–H covalent bonds remain intact. Steam is still H2O, not a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen created by boiling.

This explains how a substance can have strong covalent bonds yet a relatively low boiling point. The change of state need not break those strong bonds. A diagram should therefore preserve the same bonded groups when changing from closely packed liquid molecules to widely spaced gas molecules. Draw larger gaps rather than breaking every molecule into atoms. Giant covalent substances need a separate explanation because they have a continuous bond network rather than discrete small molecules; their high melting points cannot be explained using only weak forces between molecules. Identify the structure before choosing the appropriate attraction to discuss.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Bonds within molecules and forces between them
blocks.text:
State which attractions are stronger in a small covalent molecular substance: bonds within molecules or forces between molecules.

The covalent bonds within molecules are stronger.

Checking the response: The covalent bonds within molecules are stronger (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Comparing ionic and molecular properties
blocks.text:
Ionic compounds commonly have high melting and boiling points because strong electrostatic attractions hold their lattices together. Small molecular substances commonly have lower melting and boiling points because only intermolecular attractions are overcome during changes of state. They are often more volatile, meaning they vaporise more readily. This comparison does not include giant covalent solids such as diamond as if they were small molecules.

Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because their ions cannot move through the lattice; molten ionic compounds and aqueous solutions of soluble ionic compounds conduct through mobile ions. Small molecular substances usually lack mobile charged particles and do not conduct. Solubility is more varied: many ionic compounds dissolve in water but some do not, and molecular substances may be water-soluble or insoluble depending on their interactions with the solvent. Sugar dissolves without producing ions, whereas hydrogen chloride forms ions in water. Therefore solubility alone does not establish conductivity or bonding type. Use several supplied properties and state any assumptions when identifying an unknown structure.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing ionic and molecular properties
blocks.text:
Compare the melting points of a typical ionic solid and a small molecular solid in terms of the attractions overcome.

The ionic solid usually melts at a higher temperature because its strong ionic attractions require more energy to overcome than the molecular solid’s intermolecular attractions.

Checking the response: The ionic solid usually melts at a higher temperature because its strong ionic attractions require more energy to overcome than the molecular solid’s intermolecular attractions (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Comparing ionic and molecular properties
blocks.text:
Suggest a structure for an unknown sample with a high melting point that does not conduct as a solid but does conduct when molten.

A giant ionic lattice, consistent with ions becoming mobile on melting.

Checking the response: A giant ionic lattice, consistent with ions becoming mobile on melting (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Buckminsterfullerene
blocks.text:
Buckminsterfullerene, C60, is a molecular allotrope of carbon. Each molecule contains sixty carbon atoms joined into a cage-like structure. Because all the atoms are carbon, the molecule is homonuclear. The existence of separate C60 molecules distinguishes it from the continuous giant covalent networks of diamond and graphite. The subscript 60 counts atoms in one molecule; it is not a charge, mass number or number of molecules.

Allotropes differ in structural form, while isotopes differ in neutron number. C60, diamond and graphite can therefore be discussed as carbon allotropes without asserting that their carbon nuclei differ. In solid C60, covalent bonds hold each cage together and intermolecular attractions act between cages. A particle diagram should preserve that distinction: several separate cages represent a molecular solid, whereas joining every cage into one unexplained network would suggest a different structure. Detailed cage geometry is unnecessary for identifying the classification here. State molecular, homonuclear and allotrope only when each describes the specific feature being asked about.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Buckminsterfullerene
blocks.text:
State the structural classification of buckminsterfullerene, C60, as a form of carbon.

A homonuclear molecular allotrope of carbon.

Checking the response: A homonuclear molecular allotrope of carbon (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P01 (8)
blocks.text:
Which attraction is responsible for a covalent bond?
A. Attraction between two positive nuclei.
B. Attraction between two electrons.
C. Nuclei attract the shared electron pair.
D. Attraction between neutral molecules only.

C. Nuclei attract the shared electron pair. Positive nuclei attract the negative shared electrons.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Positive nuclei attract the negative shared electrons. Distractor explanations: A: positive nuclei repel. B: electrons repel. D: intermolecular attraction is distinct from the bond within the molecule.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P01 (9)
blocks.text:
Which electron arrangement correctly describes neutral NH3?
A. Three N–H bonds and two nitrogen lone pairs.
B. Two N–H bonds and no lone pairs.
C. Three N–H bonds and one nitrogen lone pair.
D. Four N–H bonds and no lone pair.

C. Three N–H bonds and one nitrogen lone pair. Three shared pairs plus one lone pair complete nitrogen’s outer shell using the available eight outer electrons.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Three shared pairs plus one lone pair complete nitrogen’s outer shell using the available eight outer electrons. Distractor explanations: D: four hydrogens are not NH3. A: it adds two excess electrons. B: it omits one H and does not complete nitrogen’s shell.

B. V-shaped.

B. V-shaped. The H–O–H arrangement is bent or V-shaped.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P02 (c)
blocks.text:
Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity.

The ions are charged, but they are held in fixed positions in the solid lattice and cannot move through it to carry current.

Ions are the charged particles (1). They cannot move through the solid lattice (1); do not credit “there are no charges”.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P02 (d)
blocks.text:
Explain the bonding and conductivity of sample X from these supplied observations: it melts at a high temperature, does not conduct as a solid, and conducts when molten.

X has an ionic lattice. Strong electrostatic attractions require much energy to overcome, giving a high melting point. When molten, its ions can move and carry current.

Ionic structure inferred (1). Strong attractions linked to high energy/melting point (1). Mobile ions in the melt carry current (1); do not substitute electrons.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P03 (a)
blocks.text:
Draw a circuit for comparing conductivity using a 3 V current-limited DC supply, a switch, an indicator and two graphite electrodes in a sample beaker. Label the components; the electrodes must not touch.

A single series circuit connects supply, switch, indicator and two separated graphite electrodes dipping into the sample. The sample completes the path between electrodes. See the labelled reference circuit in visuals/VIS-6117-2-circuit.svg.

Supply and switch in a complete series path (1). Indicator correctly in the path (1). Two separated electrodes contact the sample and complete the path through it (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P03 (b)
blocks.text:
Describe a method for comparing aqueous sodium chloride with sugar solution using the low-voltage apparatus. Include how the observations are recorded and how contamination between samples is reduced.

Test each solution with the same voltage, electrode spacing and immersion depth. Record the indicator response in a results table for each named sample. Switch off between tests and rinse electrodes with deionised water, removing residual rinse water before the next sample.

Test the named solutions using the apparatus (1). Record the indicator response against each sample in a table (1). Rinse electrodes between samples to avoid contamination (1); switching off is required safe procedure.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P03 (c)
blocks.text:
Explain these supplied observations from an original teaching dataset: a copper strip conducts; solid sodium chloride does not; aqueous sodium chloride conducts; sugar solution does not. Identify the charge carriers where present.

Copper conducts through mobile delocalised electrons. Aqueous sodium chloride conducts through mobile ions, whereas the ions in solid sodium chloride are fixed. Sugar dissolves as neutral molecules, so its solution has no appreciable concentration of mobile ions from the sugar and does not light the indicator in this test.

Mobile electrons in copper (1). Mobile ions in aqueous NaCl, distinguished from fixed solid ions (1). Neutral sugar molecules give no appreciable ionic conduction in this test (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Describe improvements to this method: the electrode gap changes between solutions, immersion depth is not fixed, and the supply is changed from 3 V to 6 V for the second solution. Link each improvement to the comparison.

Fix electrode spacing with a holder so the current path length is comparable. Mark and maintain immersion depth so the electrode contact area is comparable. Keep the supply at 3 V so a changed driving voltage cannot explain the different response.

Fixed spacing linked to comparable current path (1). Fixed depth linked to comparable contact area (1). Same 3 V supply linked to a fair electrical comparison (1).

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-17 — Comparing bonding through properties
blocks.text: Compare supplied data for sodium chloride, sugar and a volatile molecular substance, noting melting behaviour, water solubility and electrical response. Use the supervised low-voltage conductivity method for safe prepared solutions; use data rather than attempting to melt salts or heat volatile liquids. Sodium chloride solution conducts through ions, while sugar can dissolve without forming a conducting ionic solution. Control electrode spacing, depth and voltage. Combine several properties before inferring structure, since dissolving in water does not by itself prove ionic bonding. Label any invented teaching values as synthetic.

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.3.2.jso.title: 2.3.2 — describe the changes that occur in the electron arrangement of elements in Period 3 and relate that to the change from metallic to non-metallic character of the elements across the period, and to the trend in atomic radius

blocks.heading: Changes across Period 3
blocks.text:
Across Period 3 from sodium to argon, proton number rises by one at each element. Electrons are added to the third shell, so the outer-electron count increases from one to eight while the occupied-shell count stays at three. Metallic character decreases across the period: sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals; silicon has intermediate properties; phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine and argon are non-metals. This is a pattern of chemical and physical behaviour, not a claim that all properties vary smoothly.

Atomic radius generally decreases across the period. Nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same main shell, so the stronger attraction draws the electron region closer to the nucleus. An explanation must include both features; merely saying “more protons” leaves out why adding electrons does not introduce a new occupied shell. Use comparable definitions when interpreting radius data. The trend concerns neutral atoms, whereas ions may have lost an entire outer shell or gained electrons. Do not mix atomic and ionic radii in a single unexplained sequence.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changes across Period 3
blocks.text:
Describe both trends in this supplied Period 3 sequence: Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Al 2,8,3 are metals, whereas P 2,8,5; S 2,8,6; Cl 2,8,7 are non-metals.

Outer-electron count rises across the sequence; the listed elements change from metallic to non-metallic.

Checking the response: Increasing outer-electron count from the supplied arrangements (1). Metal-to-non-metal trend from the supplied classifications (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Changes across Period 3
blocks.text:
Describe why atomic radius generally decreases across Period 3.

Nuclear charge increases, while added electrons occupy the same main shell, producing stronger attraction towards the nucleus.

Checking the response: Nuclear charge increases across Period 3 while added electrons enter the same main shell (1). Stronger attraction draws the electrons closer to the nucleus, reducing atomic radius (1).

blocks.heading: Similarities within a group
blocks.text:
Elements within a main group share the same number of outer electrons. Lithium is 2,1, sodium is 2,8,1 and potassium is 2,8,8,1. Each has one outer electron, so each commonly forms a +1 ion and shows related chemical reactions. Their occupied-shell counts differ, placing them in different periods. A shared group predicts a family resemblance rather than identical reaction rates or physical properties.

The same reasoning applies to Group VII: fluorine, chlorine and bromine have seven outer electrons and commonly gain one to form −1 ions. A chlorine atom and a chloride ion are not interchangeable examples: the neutral atom has seven outer electrons, while the ion has a complete outer shell. When comparing group members, describe the neutral atom arrangements first and then relate their common outer-electron count to the reactions. Differences in distance from the nucleus and shielding help explain changes in reactivity down a group. These changes do not remove the underlying similarity in the kinds of ions formed.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Similarities within a group
blocks.text:
Describe one chemical similarity and one period difference predicted for atoms X 2,1 and Y 2,8,1.

Both tend to lose one outer electron and form +1 ions; X is period 2 and Y period 3.

Checking the response: Common +1 ion prediction from one outer electron (1). Periods correctly inferred from occupied shells (1).

blocks.text:
Describe how the outer-electron arrangements of Group VII atoms account for their similar ion formation.

They have seven outer electrons and gain one electron to obtain a complete outer shell, forming −1 ions.

Checking the response: Seven outer electrons (1); gain one to form −1 ions with complete shells (1).

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.4.1.jso.title: 2.4.1 — explain that atoms, molecules and ions are the building blocks of all material (an extension of the particle model) (NOTE: the term “molecule” will be used only for electrically neutral groups of atoms held together by covalent bonds, including macromolecules)

blocks.heading: Atoms, molecules and ions
blocks.text:
An atom is an electrically neutral particle of an element with equal numbers of protons and electrons. An ion is an atom or group of atoms with a net charge after gaining or losing electrons. A molecule is an electrically neutral group of atoms joined by covalent bonds. These distinctions identify different kinds of chemical particle, not different sizes of visible grain. A single salt crystal contains very many ions, while a sample of water contains very many molecules.

Argon gas consists of individual atoms. Oxygen gas contains O2 molecules, each made of two oxygen atoms. Sodium chloride contains Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions arranged in a giant lattice, rather than separate sodium-chloride molecules. A compound ion such as NH4⁺ contains several bonded atoms but has an overall charge, so it is not a neutral molecule. When a question asks for particles, name them precisely. “Atoms” is not an adequate replacement for “ions” when explaining conduction in a salt solution, because the charge and mobility of the particles are the reason conduction occurs.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Atoms, molecules and ions
blocks.text:
Explain why NH4⁺ is described as a compound ion rather than a molecule in this course.

It is a bonded group of atoms with an overall positive charge, whereas a molecule is neutral.

Checking the response: It is a bonded group of atoms with an overall positive charge, whereas a molecule is neutral (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Atoms, molecules and ions
blocks.text:
Explain the classification of a particle containing one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms and no net charge.

It is a water molecule: a neutral group of covalently bonded atoms.

Checking the response: It is a water molecule: a neutral group of covalently bonded atoms (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Elements, compounds and mixtures
blocks.text:
An element contains one kind of atom, identified by proton number. A compound contains atoms of different elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. A mixture contains substances together without requiring chemical combination between them, and its composition can vary. Oxygen gas is an element even though its particles are O2 molecules: both atoms are oxygen. Water is a compound because hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

Air is a mixture containing several gases. Its components retain their identities and can be separated by suitable physical methods. A salt-and-sand mixture can be separated using differences in solubility, followed by filtration and recovery of the salt. By contrast, separating a compound into its elements requires chemical change rather than merely sorting its particles. A diagram can represent these distinctions: one atom type may form an element, identical unlike-atom groups can represent a pure compound, and multiple distinct substances together can represent a mixture. Purity concerns the number of substances, not whether a sample looks clean or transparent.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Elements, compounds and mixtures
blocks.text:
Distinguish a compound from a mixture in terms of composition and how the components are combined.

A compound has elements chemically combined in fixed proportions; a mixture contains substances together in variable proportions without requiring chemical combination between them.

Checking the response: Fixed versus variable composition (1); chemical combination versus physical mixing (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Elements, compounds and mixtures
blocks.text:
Suggest the classification of a sample containing separate nitrogen molecules and oxygen molecules in variable proportions.

A mixture, because two substances are present without fixed chemical combination.

Checking the response: A mixture, because two substances are present without fixed chemical combination (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Neutral groups and compound ions
blocks.text:
Atoms can join to form a neutral molecule or a charged group called a compound ion. Water, H2O, is a neutral molecule, while hydroxide, OH⁻, is a compound ion. Both contain more than one atom, so atom count alone does not decide the classification. The net charge is essential. The atoms within a compound ion remain joined when that ion is represented as a unit in an ionic compound or in solution.

Ammonium sulfate contains NH4⁺ and SO4²⁻ ions. Within each compound ion, atoms are covalently bonded, while electrostatic attractions between the positive and negative ions hold the ionic solid together. This allows more than one bonding description within the same substance without contradiction. Read brackets and charges carefully. The formula NH4⁺ represents a group of one nitrogen and four hydrogen atoms carrying a total +1 charge; it does not mean each atom carries +1. When building a salt formula, balance the total charges of whole ions rather than changing the internal subscripts of a compound ion.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Neutral groups and compound ions
blocks.text:
Explain why atom count alone cannot distinguish H2O from OH⁻ as a molecule or an ion.

Both contain bonded atoms, but H2O is neutral and OH⁻ has a net negative charge.

Checking the response: Both contain bonded atoms, but H2O is neutral and OH⁻ has a net negative charge (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Neutral groups and compound ions
blocks.text:
Explain what the + sign means in the supplied formula NH4⁺.

The whole bonded group has a net charge of +1, not each individual atom.

Checking the response: The whole bonded group has a net charge of +1, not each individual atom (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Molecular and giant lattices
blocks.text:
A crystal lattice is a regular, repeating arrangement of particles. In a molecular crystal, the repeating units are molecules. Iodine crystals contain I2 molecules held near one another by intermolecular attractions; the covalent bonds inside each molecule are distinct from those attractions. In a giant structure, bonding extends throughout a large network rather than stopping at separate small molecules. Examples include sodium chloride, copper and diamond, although their bonding types differ.

The word giant describes the connected structure, not the visible size of one piece. A tiny diamond fragment still has a giant covalent structure. Likewise, a large iodine crystal remains molecular. To classify a lattice, identify both its particles and the attractions holding them together. A diagram showing several separate bonded pairs with gaps between pairs can represent a molecular substance; a continuous network of bonds represents a different organisation. Changes of state depend on which attractions must be overcome. Melting a molecular solid generally overcomes intermolecular attractions without breaking the covalent bonds inside each molecule.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Molecular and giant lattices
blocks.text:
Explain why a large iodine crystal is still described as molecular.

It consists of separate I2 molecules held together by intermolecular attractions; visible size does not make the bonding a giant network.

Checking the response: It consists of separate I2 molecules held together by intermolecular attractions; visible size does not make the bonding a giant network (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Molecular and giant lattices
blocks.text:
Explain the classification of a diagram showing a continuous network of covalently bonded atoms with no separate small molecules.

It represents a giant covalent lattice because the bonding extends through the network.

Checking the response: It represents a giant covalent lattice because the bonding extends through the network (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Three kinds of giant structure
blocks.text:
A giant ionic lattice contains positive and negative ions held together by electrostatic attraction. A giant metallic structure contains positive metal ions attracted to delocalised electrons. A giant covalent lattice contains atoms connected by covalent bonds throughout a network. The common word giant does not mean the three structures have identical particles, charge carriers or properties. Sodium chloride, copper and diamond illustrate the three descriptions respectively.

Use the structure to explain behaviour. Solid sodium chloride contains charged ions but they cannot move through the lattice, so it does not conduct electricity. Copper has mobile delocalised electrons and conducts as a solid. Diamond has strong covalent bonds and no mobile charged particles, so it does not conduct. Graphite is an important contrasting giant covalent structure with mobile electrons. Thus a statement such as “all giant structures conduct” is false, and a statement such as “all covalent substances fail to conduct” is also too broad. Name the actual particles and their mobility before drawing a conclusion.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Three kinds of giant structure
blocks.text:
Explain why “giant structure” does not by itself establish whether a solid conducts electricity.

Giant structures can have different particles; conduction requires mobile charged particles, which are present in metals but absent in solid ionic lattices and diamond.

Checking the response: Giant structures can have different particles; conduction requires mobile charged particles, which are present in metals but absent in solid ionic lattices and diamond (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Three kinds of giant structure
blocks.text:
Explain the bonding classification of a sample described as positive metal ions surrounded by mobile delocalised electrons.

Metallic bonding: electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and delocalised electrons.

Checking the response: Metallic bonding: electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and delocalised electrons (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Alloys
blocks.text:
An alloy is a mixture containing a metal together with other elements. Brass contains copper and zinc; bronze commonly contains copper and tin; steel contains iron with carbon and may contain other elements. These names describe families of mixtures rather than single fixed-ratio compounds. Changing the composition can change properties, so an alloy does not need one universal chemical formula. Distinguish alloying from plating: adding a surface coating is not the same as mixing elements throughout a metal.

In a pure metal, regularly arranged layers of similar-sized atoms can slide relatively easily. Atoms of different sizes in an alloy disrupt the regular arrangement and hinder this movement, often making the alloy harder. This explanation concerns the internal structure rather than a claim that the added atoms glue the layers together. Alloys are selected for combinations of properties such as hardness, corrosion resistance or ease of shaping. A harder alloy is not automatically better for every purpose: an application requiring bending may favour a different balance of properties.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Alloys
blocks.text:
Describe the alloy names supported by these composition records: P contains copper and zinc; Q contains iron and a controlled small percentage of carbon. Reference key: brass is a copper–zinc alloy; steel is an iron–carbon alloy.

P is brass; Q is steel.

Checking the response: P is brass, matching copper and zinc in the reference key (1). Q is steel, matching iron and carbon in the reference key (1).

Different-sized atoms disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for layers to slide.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-2-P01 (7)
blocks.text:
Why can brass have different copper-to-zinc proportions in different products?
A. Brass is a variable-composition mixture.
B. Its atoms change proton numbers during mixing.
C. All alloys contain only one element.
D. Copper and zinc have identical atoms.

A. Brass is a variable-composition mixture. Alloy composition can vary because the components are mixed rather than fixed in one compound formula.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Alloy composition can vary because the components are mixed rather than fixed in one compound formula. Distractor explanations: D: the elements have different proton numbers. C: brass contains two elements. B: alloying does not change nuclear identities.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-07 — Building particle models
blocks.text: Use coloured spheres with a written key to build an elemental molecule, a compound molecule, a mixture of both, and a fragment of a giant covalent network. Compare atom types, bonds and the number of distinct substances. Keep molecule boundaries visible and mark where a giant network continues beyond the model. A mixture should contain separate substances rather than new bonds invented between every component. Different sphere sizes or colours are conventions, not evidence of actual atomic dimensions. Check each model against its formula and explain which features the model simplifies.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-16 — Mixture versus compound
blocks.text: Compare an unheated iron-and-sulfur mixture with a teacher-prepared sample of iron sulfide, using observations or a recording where heating is unsuitable. A magnet can remove iron from the unreacted mixture; the compound has different properties and is not separated into iron and sulfur by the same simple sorting. Use a separate salt solution to show a mixture that can be separated by evaporation or distillation. Observe the prepared sulfide without adding chemical reagents in this activity. The limitation is that one physical test does not establish every detail of composition; connect it with preparation history and formula.

topics/2/content-units/CU-6117-2.1.2.jso.title: 2.1.2 — outline the development of the atomic model from the ancient Greek times, Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr and Chadwick

blocks.heading: How the atomic model developed
blocks.text:
Ancient Greek thinkers proposed that matter might consist of tiny indivisible particles. This was a philosophical idea rather than a model established by experimental measurements. Dalton developed an atomic theory in which elements consisted of atoms and compounds contained atoms combined in fixed proportions. His solid-sphere picture was later revised when evidence showed that atoms contained smaller particles. Thomson's discovery of the electron led to a model with negative electrons embedded in distributed positive charge.

Rutherford's scattering results supported a small, dense, positively charged nucleus, with most of the atom being empty space. Most incident particles passed through the foil with little deflection, while a few changed direction greatly. Bohr introduced electrons occupying particular energy levels, represented here as shells. Chadwick established the neutron, a neutral particle in the nucleus, helping account for nuclear mass without extra positive charge. The sequence shows how evidence changes a model. A useful model explains observations but can be refined when new observations expose its limits; later discoveries do not mean that all earlier measurements were worthless.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — How the atomic model developed
blocks.text:
Outline which later discovery contradicts each model: A contains only a diffuse positive body with embedded electrons; B has a nucleus but assigns all its mass to protons. Supplied evidence: positive charge is concentrated; nuclei also contain neutral massive particles.

Concentrated positive charge contradicts A; neutron evidence contradicts B’s proton-only mass account.

Checking the response: Match concentrated charge evidence to A (1). Match neutral nuclear particles to B (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — How the atomic model developed
blocks.text:
Explain why Rutherford’s observation that a few incident particles were deflected through large angles supported a concentrated positive nucleus.

A small, concentrated region of positive charge could exert the strong repulsion needed for those large deflections.

Checking the response: A small, concentrated region of positive charge could exert the strong repulsion needed for those large deflections (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.

blocks.heading: Proton number and the Periodic Table
blocks.text:
Elements are arranged in increasing proton number in the modern Periodic Table. Proton number identifies an element: all sodium atoms have eleven protons, while all magnesium atoms have twelve. Changing electron number makes an ion of the same element; it does not move that particle to a different element's position. Changing neutron number creates a different isotope. Thus proton number is a more reliable identifier than either the total mass of an atom or the number of electrons in an ion.

For a neutral atom, electron number equals proton number. The first twenty elements therefore build up from hydrogen with one electron to calcium with twenty. Repeating outer-electron arrangements lead to repeating patterns in chemical behaviour. Reading across a period increases proton number by one at each successive element, while reading down a group finds related outer-shell arrangements. A table entry may show a relative atomic mass that is not an integer; that is an average over isotopes and is not the mass number of every atom. Before counting neutrons, use a specified isotope mass number rather than silently rounding an average.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Proton number and the Periodic Table
blocks.text:
State the quantity that determines the order of elements in the modern Periodic Table.

Increasing proton number.

Checking the response: Increasing proton number (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Proton number and the Periodic Table
blocks.text:
Explain why removing an electron from a sodium atom does not turn it into a different element.

The nucleus still contains eleven protons, and proton number determines the element.

Checking the response: The nucleus still contains eleven protons, and proton number determines the element (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
