blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentrated hydrochloric acid
blocks.text:
Describe why the balanced chloride oxidation equation requires two chloride ions for each chlorine molecule.

Cl2 contains two chlorine atoms; each starting Cl⁻ must lose one electron, giving two electrons in total.

Checking the response: Two atoms needed for one Cl2 molecule (1). Two single-electron losses balance the charge (1).
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride
blocks.text:
Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride, or brine, gives hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at an inert anode. Sodium metal is not deposited from this aqueous solution. At the cathode, water can be represented as gaining electrons: 2H2O + 2e⁻ → H2 + 2OH⁻. At the anode, 2Cl⁻ → Cl2 + 2e⁻. Sodium ions remain in solution with hydroxide ions, giving sodium hydroxide solution when the products are appropriately separated.

Compare this with molten sodium chloride, which has no water and gives sodium metal at the cathode. Omitting aqueous or molten changes the meaning of the question. Similarly, the concentrated chloride condition matters for the anode product. In manufacture, separation prevents the products reacting undesirably with one another; technical cell construction is not required here. Keep the essential starting material, conditions and half-equations clear. Chlorine is hazardous, so the learner resource uses diagrams and supplied observations rather than instructions to generate it unsupervised.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride
blocks.text:
Describe why concentrated aqueous NaCl can leave an increasingly alkaline solution during electrolysis with inert electrodes.

Water reduction produces H2 and leaves hydroxide ions at the cathode; sodium ions remain in solution with increasing OH⁻.

Checking the response: Water reduction accounts for hydrogen and OH⁻ production (1). Dissolved sodium with accumulating hydroxide explains alkalinity (1).
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.
blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride
blocks.text:
Describe why concentrated aqueous NaCl gives hydrogen rather than sodium at the cathode.

Water is present and is reduced in preference to sodium ions, producing hydrogen and hydroxide ions.

Checking the response: Water as competing species (1); hydrogen formation rather than sodium deposition (1).

blocks.heading: Predicting products of a molten binary compound
blocks.text:
A binary compound contains two elements. For a molten ionic binary compound with inert electrodes, identify the positive metal ion and negative non-metal ion. The metal ion gains electrons at the cathode, while the anion loses electrons at the anode. Molten magnesium chloride therefore gives magnesium and chlorine. Its half-equations are Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg and 2Cl⁻ → Cl2 + 2e⁻.

Check the element's normal product form. Chlorine and bromine are diatomic, so write Cl2 and Br2 rather than isolated neutral atoms as the final bulk products. Balance electrons and charges separately at each electrode. A supplied compound formula establishes the ion ratio but does not mean both electrodes release the same number of atoms per electron. Keep molten explicit: water-derived hydrogen and oxygen competition belongs to aqueous conditions. If an electrode can react, that additional information must be considered instead of applying the inert-electrode prediction automatically.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Predicting products of a molten binary compound
blocks.text:
Predict the products at inert electrodes during electrolysis of molten MgCl2.

Magnesium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode.

Checking the response: Mg/cathode (1); Cl2/anode (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Predicting products of a molten binary compound
blocks.text:
State the anode product inferred from a molten binary electrolyte containing Ca²⁺ and Br⁻ ions with inert electrodes.

Bromine, Br2.

Checking the response: Bromine, Br2 (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Copper sulfate: active and inert anodes
blocks.text:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate behaves differently with carbon and copper anodes. With an inert carbon anode, oxygen is produced, while Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons and deposit as copper at the cathode. The solution's Cu²⁺ concentration decreases as those ions are removed without being replenished, so its blue colour can fade. State that the solution is aqueous and the anode is carbon before applying this description.

With a copper anode in aqueous copper(II) sulfate, the anode dissolves: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. At the cathode, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu still deposits copper. Ideally, anode dissolution replaces the copper ions removed at the cathode, so their concentration remains approximately steady. The copper anode loses mass while the cathode gains mass. This is the active-electrode case; do not claim that copper-ion concentration stays constant with an inert carbon anode. Compare cells at the same current and time, and measure clean, dry electrodes to distinguish real metal transfer from retained solution.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Copper sulfate: active and inert anodes
blocks.text:
State the anode half-equation when aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using a copper anode.

Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

Checking the response: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Copper sulfate: active and inert anodes
blocks.text:
Explain the error in “Cu²⁺ concentration remains constant” for aqueous CuSO4 electrolysed with an inert carbon anode and a copper-depositing cathode.

The carbon anode does not supply Cu²⁺, so cathode deposition removes copper ions without replacing them; their concentration decreases.

Checking the response: The carbon anode does not supply Cu²⁺, so cathode deposition removes copper ions without replacing them; their concentration decreases (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Electroplating
blocks.text:
Electroplating deposits a thin metal coating on a conducting object by electrolysis. The object is the cathode, where metal ions gain electrons and form metal. The electrolyte must supply ions of the coating metal. For copper plating, aqueous copper(II) sulfate can supply Cu²⁺ and a copper anode can replenish ions as copper deposits on the object. Clean the object first so dirt or grease does not prevent a coherent coating.

The choice of object and solution matters. Some reactive metals can displace copper from a copper-ion solution even without an external current; a zinc object in CuSO4 therefore requires a no-current comparison if the aim is to attribute deposition specifically to electroplating. Keep applied current, time and exposed area controlled when comparing coatings. Rinse and dry objects before comparing mass. A heavier wet object does not establish a thicker metal deposit. The classroom account uses teacher-supervised low-voltage equipment and prepared dilute solutions; product quality and safe handling are separate from simply observing a colour change.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Electroplating
blocks.text:
Describe why a copper-electroplating bath needs dissolved copper ions and why the object must receive electrons.

The ions supply copper atoms; cathodic electron gain converts Cu²⁺ to metal on the object.

Checking the response: Copper ions supply the deposited material (1). Electron gain at the object produces its metal coating (1).

blocks.reviewed_unchanged: Related factual teaching remains correct; worked application revised where it cites the changed example.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Electroplating
blocks.text:
Describe why a metal object is cleaned before electroplating.

Grease and dirt can block contact with the electrolyte, giving an uneven or poorly adhering deposit.

Checking the response: Grease or dirt prevents electrolyte contacting parts of the metal surface (1). Cleaning permits an even deposit that adheres to the metal instead of depositing unevenly or on contamination (1).
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Uses of electroplating
blocks.text:
Electroplating can improve appearance, protect a surface or give a component a useful surface property while retaining a different bulk material underneath. Examples include a decorative metal finish on an object or a corrosion-resistant coating on a suitable component. The coating is not the same as mixing the two metals throughout the object to form an alloy. A plated item has a surface layer over a base material.

Protection depends on the coating and conditions. A damaged coating may expose the base metal, and different metal combinations can behave differently. Therefore “electroplating prevents all corrosion” is too broad. For this objective, name a clear use and connect it with a purpose rather than claiming that every shiny object is electroplated. Some similar-looking finishes are produced by other processes. A product description or manufacturing information provides stronger evidence than appearance alone. The underlying electrochemical principle remains reduction of coating-metal ions at the cathode.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Uses of electroplating
blocks.text:
Name one use of electroplating.

Applying a decorative or protective metal coating to an object.

Checking the response: Applying a decorative or protective metal coating to an object (1). Accept scientifically equivalent wording.
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Manufacturing aluminium
blocks.text:
Aluminium is obtained by electrolysis of pure aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite. Cryolite allows the process to operate below the temperature required to melt pure aluminium oxide alone. The electrolyte must be molten so ions can move. At the cathode, Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al forms aluminium. Oxide ions lose electrons at the anode: 2O²⁻ → O2 + 4e⁻.

The hot oxygen reacts with carbon anodes, producing carbon dioxide in the simplified overall account, so the carbon anodes are consumed and require replacement. This is why carbon cannot be called inert without qualification in this industrial example. Essential knowledge is the purified oxide feed, molten cryolite, electrical energy and electrode reactions; technical cell diagrams and construction details are not required. An aqueous aluminium-ion solution is not an interchangeable feed for obtaining aluminium at the cathode, because water competes and hydrogen is produced instead in the usual aqueous case. Distinguish the element extracted from the solvent material used to help achieve suitable operating conditions.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Manufacturing aluminium
blocks.text:
Suggest the feed and medium needed when a proposed aluminium-extraction process incorrectly uses an aqueous aluminium-ion solution.

Use pure aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, giving mobile ions without the competing aqueous medium.

Checking the response: Pure aluminium oxide feed (1); molten cryolite medium (1).

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Manufacturing aluminium
blocks.text:
Outline the cathode reaction and the reason for choosing mixture Y from these supplied process data. X: pure aluminium oxide, operating temperature above 2000 °C. Y: aluminium oxide dissolved in molten cryolite, operating temperature about 950 °C. Both contain Al³⁺ ions.

Al³⁺ gains three electrons to form Al; molten cryolite allows the oxide-containing electrolyte to operate at a lower temperature than pure alumina alone.

Checking the response: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (1); lower operating-temperature role of cryolite (1).

blocks.heading: Manufacturing chlorine and sodium hydroxide
blocks.text:
Chlorine and sodium hydroxide are manufactured by electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride. Chloride ions lose electrons at the anode to form chlorine: 2Cl⁻ → Cl2 + 2e⁻. At the cathode, water gains electrons: 2H2O + 2e⁻ → H2 + 2OH⁻. Sodium ions remain in solution with hydroxide ions, so the liquid product contains sodium hydroxide. Hydrogen is a useful additional product.

Maintain the distinction between concentrated aqueous brine and molten sodium chloride. The molten salt would produce sodium metal at the cathode and would not supply hydroxide from water. Industrial product separation is necessary to limit unwanted reactions between products, but detailed apparatus design is outside this objective. When explaining the process, organise the answer as starting material, condition, anode reaction, cathode reaction and remaining solution. This keeps chlorine gas, hydrogen gas and sodium hydroxide solution separate rather than assigning the liquid product to a gas-collecting electrode.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Manufacturing chlorine and sodium hydroxide
blocks.text:
Suggest the correction to a proposed chlorine-and-sodium-hydroxide process that uses molten NaCl as its electrolyte.

Use concentrated aqueous NaCl instead; water then supplies the cathode hydrogen/hydroxide process needed for sodium hydroxide solution.

Checking the response: Replace molten NaCl with concentrated aqueous NaCl (1). Water is reduced at the cathode to hydrogen and hydroxide ions, allowing sodium hydroxide solution to remain (1).
blocks.repair_note: October 29 review: stimulus and explicit credit repaired; independent semantic review remains open.

blocks.heading: Worked practice — Manufacturing chlorine and sodium hydroxide
blocks.text:
Outline how these observations support sodium hydroxide formation during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous NaCl: hydrogen forms at the cathode, hydroxide-ion concentration increases, and sodium ions remain dissolved.

Cathode reduction of water produces OH⁻ and H2; sodium ions remain in solution with the hydroxide ions.

Checking the response: Cathode water reduction gives hydroxide (1); remaining sodium ions give NaOH solution (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (1)
blocks.text:
Which description fits an electrode in an electrolytic cell?
A. A liquid that supplies electrons through the solution.
B. A neutral gas produced at either pole.
C. A container that prevents ion movement.
D. A conductor contacting the electrolyte.

D. A conductor contacting the electrolyte. An electrode carries electrons to or from the reaction boundary.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: An electrode carries electrons to or from the reaction boundary. Distractor explanations: A: mobile ions carry solution current. C: ions must move. B: a product is not an electrode.
blocks.repair_note: Independent-review repairs: original MC key permutation, direct credit points, corrected wording and separated learner visual assets; claim references refreshed.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (2)
blocks.text:
Why does molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
A. Its ions can move and carry charge.
B. Its ions disappear on melting.
C. Its sodium atoms move to both electrodes.
D. Its molecules carry free electrons.

A. Its ions can move and carry charge. Melting releases ions from fixed lattice positions.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Melting releases ions from fixed lattice positions. Distractor explanations: B: ions remain. D: the melt is ionic, not molecular. C: the mobile species before discharge are ions.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (3)
blocks.text:
Which process defines the anode in electrolysis?
A. Neutralisation at either electrode.
B. Electron gain at the negative electrode.
C. Condensation at the positive electrode.
D. Electron loss at the positive electrode.

D. Electron loss at the positive electrode. Oxidation, loss of electrons, occurs at the anode.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Oxidation, loss of electrons, occurs at the anode. Distractor explanations: B: describes cathodic reduction. A: acid-base neutralisation is not the definition. C: a physical state change is not the electrode reaction.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (4)
blocks.text:
Which arrangement is suitable for an electrolytic cell?
A. Two touching electrodes connected to AC.
B. Separated immersed electrodes across a DC supply.
C. Two electrodes above the liquid and disconnected.
D. One electrode connected to a battery.

B. Separated immersed electrodes across a DC supply. The external circuit and mobile ions provide a complete path through separated electrodes.

Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The external circuit and mobile ions provide a complete path through separated electrodes. Distractor explanations: A: touching bypasses the electrolyte and AC reverses polarity. C: the path is incomplete. D: a single connection cannot complete the circuit.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (5)
blocks.text:
Which half-equation represents reduction of copper(II) ions?
A. Cu + 2e⁻ → Cu²⁺
B. Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
C. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻
D. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

D. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu Copper ions gain two electrons, balancing charge.

Correct option/key D (1 mark). Reason: Copper ions gain two electrons, balancing charge. Distractor explanations: C: oxidation. B: charge is unbalanced and electrons are on the wrong side. A: charge is unbalanced.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (6)
blocks.text:
Which products form from molten lead(II) bromide with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen.
B. Cathode: lead oxide; anode: hydrogen.
C. Cathode: lead; anode: bromine.
D. Cathode: bromine; anode: lead.

C. Cathode: lead; anode: bromine. Pb²⁺ gains electrons and Br⁻ loses electrons.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Pb²⁺ gains electrons and Br⁻ loses electrons. Distractor explanations: A: the molten binary salt contains no water. D: reverses ion discharge. B: introduces oxygen and hydrogen absent from the specified melt.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P01 (7)
blocks.text:
Why does dilute sulfuric acid give twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by volume during electrolysis with inert electrodes, at equal gas conditions?
A. Sulfuric acid supplies twice as much sulfur.
B. The overall change is 2H2O → 2H2 + O2.
C. Oxygen is twice as soluble as hydrogen in every solution.
D. Hydrogen has twice the relative molecular mass.

B. The overall change is 2H2O → 2H2 + O2. The balanced overall equation gives a 2:1 gas amount ratio.

Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: The balanced overall equation gives a 2:1 gas amount ratio. Distractor explanations: A: sulfur is not the gas product. C: does not establish the stoichiometric ratio. D: hydrogen has lower molecular mass and volume ratio follows amounts.

blocks.text:
Which products form during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous hydrochloric acid with inert electrodes?
A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine.
B. Cathode: sodium; anode: chlorine.
C. Cathode: copper; anode: oxygen.
D. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: sulfur dioxide.

A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: chlorine. Hydrogen ions gain electrons and chloride ions lose electrons under these conditions.

Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: Hydrogen ions gain electrons and chloride ions lose electrons under these conditions. Distractor explanations: B: sodium is absent. D: sulfur is absent. C: copper is absent and concentrated chloride favours chlorine.

A. Cathode: hydrogen; anode: oxygen.
B. Cathode: lithium hydroxide; anode: hydrogen.
C. Cathode: lithium; anode: bromine.
D. Cathode: bromine; anode: lithium.

C. Cathode: lithium; anode: bromine. Apply cation reduction and anion oxidation to the specified water-free melt.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Apply cation reduction and anion oxidation to the specified water-free melt. Distractor explanations: A: no water is present. D: reverses electrode products. B: introduces oxygen and hydrogen.

A. Copper ions gain electrons on the anode.
B. Sulfate becomes metallic sulfur.
C. Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺.
D. Oxygen is the main specified anode product.

C. Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Distractor explanations: D: the expected inert-carbon anode case differs. A: gain occurs at the cathode. B: sulfate is not discharged to metallic sulfur.

A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P02 (a)
blocks.text:
State whether reduction or oxidation occurs at the cathode during electrolysis.

Reduction.

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P02 (b)
blocks.text:
Describe the products at each electrode during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride using inert electrodes.

Hydrogen forms at the negative cathode; chlorine forms at the positive anode.

Hydrogen at cathode (1). Chlorine at anode (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P02 (c)
blocks.text:
Explain the decrease in copper-anode mass during electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes.

With an active copper anode in aqueous CuSO4, copper atoms leave the anode as dissolved Cu²⁺ ions by losing two electrons each: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.

Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺ (1). Loss of two electrons per copper atom (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P02 (d)
blocks.text:
Explain how replacing the copper anode with inert carbon changes the anode product and the blue colour of aqueous copper(II) sulfate during continued electrolysis. The cathode remains copper.

Replacing the active copper anode with inert carbon in aqueous CuSO4 gives oxygen at the carbon anode instead of copper dissolving. Cu²⁺ still gains electrons and deposits at the cathode. These removed ions are no longer replenished by the anode, so the blue colour fades as their concentration decreases.

Oxygen replaces copper dissolution at anode (1). Cu²⁺ continues to deposit as copper at cathode (1). No anode replenishment, so Cu²⁺ concentration and blue colour decrease (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P03 (a)
blocks.text:
Draw a labelled arrangement for teacher-supervised electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 using separated carbon electrodes and a low-voltage DC supply. Include an inverted, initially water-filled tube to collect a small gas sample above the positive electrode. Keep the cell open to the atmosphere.

The DC positive lead connects to a carbon anode and the negative lead to a separate carbon cathode. Both dip into aqueous CuSO4 without touching. An inverted water-filled tube has its submerged open mouth over the anode so bubbles displace water; the connecting lead enters through the open mouth, not through glass. The beaker remains open.

DC supply with positive anode and negative cathode (1). Separated electrodes immersed in named electrolyte (1). Workable gas collection above anode with open submerged mouth and no sealed cell (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P03 (b)
blocks.text:
Describe how to collect a small uncontaminated sample of the gas from the carbon anode in aqueous CuSO4, and test it for oxygen, including the positive observation. The teacher handles the powered apparatus.

Fill and invert a collection tube under water so it starts without an air pocket, position its submerged mouth above the carbon anode, and collect a small gas sample by water displacement. After the teacher disconnects the supply, test the sample with a glowing splint; oxygen relights it.

Collection without an initial air pocket or mixing with the other electrode gas (1). Glowing splint test (1). Splint relights (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P03 (c)
blocks.text:
Deduce the identity of a gas that relights a glowing splint. This observation is from an original synthetic classroom dataset for aqueous CuSO4 electrolysis using carbon electrodes.

Oxygen.

Oxygen (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P03 (d)
blocks.text:
Explain how charge is carried through the aqueous electrolyte and through the external metal leads in this cell.

Mobile positive and negative ions transport charge through the electrolyte. Electrons transport charge through the external metal leads; electrons are transferred at the electrode surfaces.

Mobile ions carry charge in electrolyte (1). Electrons carry charge in external leads (1).

blocks.heading: Activity worked example ITEM-6117-5-P03 (e)
blocks.text:
Plan a teacher-supervised comparison of carbon and copper anodes in aqueous CuSO4. Include a fair comparison, electrode-mass measurements, a gas test and a conclusion method. Both trials have copper cathodes and a low-voltage current-controlled supply.

Compare a carbon anode with a copper anode, using a copper cathode in each fresh CuSO4 sample. Keep solution concentration and volume, immersed electrode area and temperature the same. Set equal measured current for equal time. Clean, rinse and dry electrodes consistently and weigh before and after each run. Collect any anode gas separately and test with a glowing splint after disconnecting. Compare anode mass change and gas observations: a copper anode should lose mass while a carbon anode produces oxygen; both cathodes gain copper. Repeat to check consistency.

Compare carbon and copper anodes explicitly (1). Same CuSO4 concentration and volume (1). Equal measured current and electrolysis time (1). Clean dry electrode masses before and after (1). Collect and test anode gas (1). Compare mass changes and products to conclude effect of anode material (1). Accept equivalent controlled apparatus; do not substitute voltage alone for controlled current. No extra marks beyond six.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-24 — Comparing conductivity
blocks.text: In a teacher-supervised low-voltage, current-limited circuit, compare sodium chloride solution, lemon juice and distilled water with the same clean electrodes and spacing. Record a meter reading, rather than treating a lamp that does not visibly glow as proof of zero current. Rinse electrodes between samples, keep immersed area and temperature comparable, and disconnect between brief readings. Both salt solution and lemon juice contain mobile ions, but their current readings depend on ion concentrations as well as mobility and the cell arrangement. Lemon juice contains a weak acid; weak does not mean dilute, and a concentrated weak-acid solution is not equivalent to a dilute strong-acid solution. Do not prolong a conductivity test into unsupervised gas production. Interpret a measured difference as a difference under the stated conditions, not a universal ranking of all salts and acids.

blocks.heading: Suggested practical SP-6117-25 — Copper coating on zinc
blocks.text: For a teacher demonstration, clean a small zinc object and connect it to the negative terminal of a low-voltage current-limited DC supply. Place it in copper(II) sulfate solution opposite a copper anode connected to the positive terminal. Keep the electrodes apart. Record initial appearance and the coating after a fixed measured current and time. Disconnect before removing the object, then rinse and dry consistently. A positive copper anode can replenish Cu²⁺ while copper deposits at the cathode. Include a second zinc sample in the same solution without a current: zinc can displace copper chemically from Cu²⁺, so a coating alone does not prove electrical deposition. Because zinc can dissolve while copper is deposited, the net object mass change is not automatically the mass of copper plated. Compare the powered and unpowered observations, identify this limitation and keep solution concentration, exposed area and immersion time comparable. This demonstration connects electrolysis with displacement rather than treating the two mechanisms as mutually exclusive.

parts.content_target: Separate and interpret hydrolysis products by chromatography, then plan an extraction/separation method. Plan an investigation with predictions, suitable apparatus and techniques.
parts.credit_requirement: Plan chromatography of hydrolysed food extract: prepare/filter sample (1), pencil baseline above solvent (1), small dried sample/reference spots (1), develop in covered chamber (1), mark solvent front and visualise spots appropriately (1), compare with references for a conclusion (1).
parts.prompt: Plan chromatography to compare the components of a teacher-prepared carbohydrate hydrolysate with glucose and reference sugar B. Include preparation, apparatus, development, observation and a defensible conclusion. No specific locating-agent identity is required.
parts.canonical_answer: Filter a suitable diluted portion of the teacher-prepared hydrolysate if suspended solids remain. Draw a pencil baseline above a shallow solvent reservoir in a covered chamber. Apply small hydrolysate, glucose and B spots in separate lanes, drying between applications. Develop all lanes on the same paper in the same solvent, with the paper upright and solvent initially below the baseline. Remove the paper before the front reaches the top, mark the solvent front immediately, and visualise the spots by a suitable supervised method. Compare positions or Rf values with references: in the original DATA-10 example the two detected sample spots match glucose and B, supporting their possible presence rather than proving unique identities.
marking_guidance: Prepare an appropriate sample, including filtration if needed (1).
Pencil baseline above solvent with suitable chamber/paper arrangement (1).
Small dried sample and reference spots in separate lanes (1).
Develop together in covered chamber under the same solvent conditions (1).
Mark front promptly and visualise spots suitably (1).
Compare reference positions/Rf for a qualified conclusion (1). Accept equivalent sound sequencing; no named locating chemical required.

8.0 cm ±0.1 cm from the baseline (1). Reject uncorrected heights from paper bottom.

parts.content_target: Separate and interpret hydrolysis products by chromatography, then plan an extraction/separation method. Interpret and evaluate observations and experimental data.

parts.prompt: Calculate Rf for the lower sample spot. For this part, the measured baseline-to-spot distance is 2.4 cm and baseline-to-front distance is 8.0 cm.

0.30 without units (1). Accept 0.28–0.32 from permitted visual readings, with correct follow-through.

parts.prompt:
Which anode change occurs during electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 with copper electrodes?
A. Copper ions gain electrons on the anode.
B. Sulfate becomes metallic sulfur.
C. Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺.
D. Oxygen is the main specified anode product.
parts.canonical_answer: C. Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺. Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.
marking_guidance: Correct option/key C (1 mark). Reason: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Distractor explanations: D: the expected inert-carbon anode case differs. A: gain occurs at the cathode. B: sulfate is not discharged to metallic sulfur.

parts.content_target: name the uses of electroplating
parts.credit_requirement: One mark for the uniquely correct option for name the uses of electroplating. Supply the key, its chemical explanation and three distinct misconception-based distractor explanations.
parts.command_word_basis: Four-option multiple choice; no written-response command.
parts.planned_cognitive_demand: Recognise the specified fact, identity or definition among alternatives.
parts.blooms_level_basis: Provisional demand from the named objective and explicit MC task brief; confirm against the authored stem and options.
parts.prompt:
Which is a use of electroplating?
A. Separating sand by filtration.
B. Applying a decorative metal coating.
C. Drying a wet gas.
D. Measuring a boiling point.
parts.canonical_answer: B. Applying a decorative metal coating. Electroplating deposits a metal coating on a conducting object.
marking_guidance: Correct option/key B (1 mark). Reason: Electroplating deposits a metal coating on a conducting object. Distractor explanations: A: physical filtration is different. D: temperature measurement is different. C: gas drying does not deposit metal.

parts.content_target: outline the manufacture of  aluminium from pure aluminium oxide in molten cryolite (cross reference to 9.3)  chlorine and sodium hydroxide from concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (Starting materials, essential conditions and equations for electrode reactions should be given but not technical details or diagrams.) — focus: aluminium from aluminium oxide in molten cryolite
parts.credit_requirement: One mark for the uniquely correct option for outline the manufacture of  aluminium from pure aluminium oxide in molten cryolite (cross reference to 9.3)  chlorine and sodium hydroxide from concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (Starting materials, essential conditions and equations for electrode reactions should be given but not technical details or diagrams.) — focus: aluminium from aluminium oxide in molten cryolite. Supply the key, its chemical explanation and three distinct misconception-based distractor explanations.
parts.command_word_basis: Four-option multiple choice; no written-response command.
parts.planned_cognitive_demand: Recognise a scientifically correct explanation, description or comparison of the stated familiar concept.
parts.blooms_level_basis: Provisional demand from the named objective and explicit MC task brief; confirm against the authored stem and options.
parts.prompt:
Why is molten cryolite used with pure aluminium oxide in aluminium manufacture?
A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature.
B. It replaces electricity with combustion.
C. It supplies all the aluminium.
D. It makes aluminium ions move through solid oxide.
parts.canonical_answer: A. It dissolves oxide at a lower temperature. The conducting molten mixture permits electrolysis at a lower temperature.
marking_guidance: Correct option/key A (1 mark). Reason: The conducting molten mixture permits electrolysis at a lower temperature. Distractor explanations: C: aluminium oxide is the feedstock. D: the electrolyte is molten. B: electrical energy is still required.

parts.content_target: describe the reactions at the electrodes during electrolysis of molten and aqueous electrolytes (the oxidation and reduction reactions) using half equations (cross reference to 6.6)
parts.credit_requirement: State reduction occurs at the cathode (1).
parts.ao_basis: A: recalled fact or explanation of a familiar chemical mechanism.
parts.prompt: State whether reduction or oxidation occurs at the cathode during electrolysis.
parts.canonical_answer: Reduction.
marking_guidance: Reduction (1).

parts.content_target: describe the electrode products, using inert electrodes, in the electrolysis of — focus: concentrated aqueous sodium chloride
parts.credit_requirement: Describe hydrogen formation at the cathode (1) and chlorine at the anode (1) for concentrated aqueous NaCl with inert electrodes.
parts.ao_basis: A: recalled fact or explanation of a familiar chemical mechanism.
parts.prompt: Describe the products at each electrode during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride using inert electrodes.
parts.canonical_answer: Hydrogen forms at the negative cathode; chlorine forms at the positive anode.
marking_guidance: Hydrogen at cathode (1).
Chlorine at anode (1).

parts.content_target: recall the different anode reactions and the products of electrolysis during the electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate, using carbon or copper as the electrodes (cross reference to 9.3)
parts.credit_requirement: For CuSO4 with copper electrodes, explain copper-anode dissolution (1) as Cu atoms lose two electrons to form Cu2+ (1).
parts.ao_basis: A: recalled fact or explanation of a familiar chemical mechanism.
parts.prompt: Explain the decrease in copper-anode mass during electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate with copper electrodes.
parts.canonical_answer: With an active copper anode in aqueous CuSO4, copper atoms leave the anode as dissolved Cu²⁺ ions by losing two electrons each: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻.
marking_guidance: Copper dissolves as Cu²⁺ (1).
Loss of two electrons per copper atom (1).

parts.content_target: recall the different anode reactions and the products of electrolysis during the electrolysis of copper(II) sulfate, using carbon or copper as the electrodes (cross reference to 9.3)
parts.credit_requirement: For replacing the copper anode with inert carbon, explain oxygen replaces dissolving copper as the anode process (1), Cu2+ still deposits at the cathode (1), and Cu2+ is no longer replenished so solution blue colour fades (1).
parts.ao_basis: B: apply chemistry to the supplied new case or interpret its evidence.
parts.prompt: Explain how replacing the copper anode with inert carbon changes the anode product and the blue colour of aqueous copper(II) sulfate during continued electrolysis. The cathode remains copper.
parts.canonical_answer: Replacing the active copper anode with inert carbon in aqueous CuSO4 gives oxygen at the carbon anode instead of copper dissolving. Cu²⁺ still gains electrons and deposits at the cathode. These removed ions are no longer replenished by the anode, so the blue colour fades as their concentration decreases.
marking_guidance: Oxygen replaces copper dissolution at anode (1).
Cu²⁺ continues to deposit as copper at cathode (1).
No anode replenishment, so Cu²⁺ concentration and blue colour decrease (1).

parts.content_target: Predict and test electrode products in an explicitly aqueous or molten electrolyte with stated electrodes. Describe and explain experimental arrangements and techniques.
parts.credit_requirement: Draw DC supply and polarity (1), separated electrodes in electrolyte (1), gas collection at the specified electrode (1).
parts.prompt: Draw a labelled arrangement for teacher-supervised electrolysis of aqueous CuSO4 using separated carbon electrodes and a low-voltage DC supply. Include an inverted, initially water-filled tube to collect a small gas sample above the positive electrode. Keep the cell open to the atmosphere.
parts.canonical_answer: The DC positive lead connects to a carbon anode and the negative lead to a separate carbon cathode. Both dip into aqueous CuSO4 without touching. An inverted water-filled tube has its submerged open mouth over the anode so bubbles displace water; the connecting lead enters through the open mouth, not through glass. The beaker remains open.
marking_guidance: DC supply with positive anode and negative cathode (1).
Separated electrodes immersed in named electrolyte (1).
Workable gas collection above anode with open submerged mouth and no sealed cell (1).

parts.content_target: Predict and test electrode products in an explicitly aqueous or molten electrolyte with stated electrodes. Read scales accurately and record appropriate precision.
parts.credit_requirement: Describe gas collection without contamination (1), the appropriate test reagent/procedure (1), its positive observation (1).
parts.prompt: Describe how to collect a small uncontaminated sample of the gas from the carbon anode in aqueous CuSO4, and test it for oxygen, including the positive observation. The teacher handles the powered apparatus.
parts.canonical_answer: Fill and invert a collection tube under water so it starts without an air pocket, position its submerged mouth above the carbon anode, and collect a small gas sample by water displacement. After the teacher disconnects the supply, test the sample with a glowing splint; oxygen relights it.
marking_guidance: Collection without an initial air pocket or mixing with the other electrode gas (1).
Glowing splint test (1).
Splint relights (1).

parts.content_target: Predict and test electrode products in an explicitly aqueous or molten electrolyte with stated electrodes. Interpret and evaluate observations and experimental data.
parts.credit_requirement: Deduce the collected gas from the supplied observation (1).
parts.prompt: Deduce the identity of a gas that relights a glowing splint. This observation is from an original synthetic classroom dataset for aqueous CuSO4 electrolysis using carbon electrodes.
parts.canonical_answer: Oxygen.
marking_guidance: Oxygen (1).

parts.content_target: Predict and test electrode products in an explicitly aqueous or molten electrolyte with stated electrodes. Interpret and evaluate observations and experimental data.
parts.credit_requirement: Explain charge transport by ions in electrolyte (1) and electrons in external circuit (1).
parts.prompt: Explain how charge is carried through the aqueous electrolyte and through the external metal leads in this cell.
parts.canonical_answer: Mobile positive and negative ions transport charge through the electrolyte. Electrons transport charge through the external metal leads; electrons are transferred at the electrode surfaces.
marking_guidance: Mobile ions carry charge in electrolyte (1).
Electrons carry charge in external leads (1).

parts.content_target: Predict and test electrode products in an explicitly aqueous or molten electrolyte with stated electrodes. Plan an investigation with predictions, suitable apparatus and techniques.
parts.credit_requirement: Plan the electrode comparison: name carbon/copper anodes (1), same CuSO4 concentration and volume (1), same current and time (1), measure clean dry electrode masses before/after (1), collect/test anode gas (1), compare mass changes and products to conclude the effect of electrode material (1).
parts.prompt: Plan a teacher-supervised comparison of carbon and copper anodes in aqueous CuSO4. Include a fair comparison, electrode-mass measurements, a gas test and a conclusion method. Both trials have copper cathodes and a low-voltage current-controlled supply.
parts.canonical_answer: Compare a carbon anode with a copper anode, using a copper cathode in each fresh CuSO4 sample. Keep solution concentration and volume, immersed electrode area and temperature the same. Set equal measured current for equal time. Clean, rinse and dry electrodes consistently and weigh before and after each run. Collect any anode gas separately and test with a glowing splint after disconnecting. Compare anode mass change and gas observations: a copper anode should lose mass while a carbon anode produces oxygen; both cathodes gain copper. Repeat to check consistency.
marking_guidance: Compare carbon and copper anodes explicitly (1).
Same CuSO4 concentration and volume (1).
Equal measured current and electrolysis time (1).
Clean dry electrode masses before and after (1).
Collect and test anode gas (1).
Compare mass changes and products to conclude effect of anode material (1). Accept equivalent controlled apparatus; do not substitute voltage alone for controlled current. No extra marks beyond six.

topics/9/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 63% in this topic (31 objectives against 49 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/11/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 57% in this topic (45 objectives against 79 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/7/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 56% in this topic (35 objectives against 62 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/6/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 58% in this topic (40 objectives against 69 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

visual_requirements.geometry_and_values: Original exothermic profile: reactants80, peak140, products30 in arbitrary energy units; Ea60 and ΔH−50.

visual_requirements.learner_answer_separation: Where a reading/identity is assessed, supply an unkeyed learner panel and a separate labelled answer overlay.

requirements: Original scientifically accurate drawing

visual_requirements.scientific_acceptance_criteria: Curves start at origin; fast never falls below slow; do not extend above limiting-reactant endpoint.
visual_requirements.learner_answer_separation: Where a reading/identity is assessed, supply an unkeyed learner panel and a separate labelled answer overlay.

requirements: Original scientifically accurate drawing

visual_requirements.scientific_acceptance_criteria: At equilibrium rates equal, not necessarily amounts; no leaking vessel or stopped-reaction symbolism.

topics/1/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 51% in this topic (38 objectives against 74 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/10/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 59% in this topic (48 objectives against 81 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/8/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. topics/4/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 39% in this topic (16 objectives against 41 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/3/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 63% in this topic (27 objectives against 43 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/12/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. topics/2/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 53% in this topic (83 objectives against 158 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.

topics/5/work_order.json.ao_mix_note: The syllabus states its AO weights as a share of MARKS, so planned_ao_mix_by_marks is the one that answers "does this resource match the exam". It values each card at the tariff of the question it models, split across the AOs the card declares, and values each performance task at the marks of the paper part it models. The count-based mix below is reported only because it is what a reader expects to see; do not balance against it. AO shares by ITEM COUNT: Every objective needs one recall anchor, so AO1 has a structural floor of about 52% in this topic (17 objectives against 33 slots) and cannot reach the None% target by count however many other cards are added - padding the bank to chase it makes the resource worse. The framework already measures the AO4 share in practice time rather than by count for the same reason. Treat AO1 above target as expected, and AO2/AO3/AO4 below target as the thing worth fixing.
